problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

Einstein thought that the "Galilean principle of relativity", which states that "the laws of mechanics take the same form in every inertial frame", holds not only in mechanics but also in optics and electromagnetism. This is called the "principle of special relativity". If the laws of electromagnetism take the same form in any inertial frame, then the speed $c$ of light, which is an electromagnetic wave, must be the same in any inertial frame. This is called the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light".

Exactly 100 years ago, in 1905, Einstein succeeded in constructing the special theory of relativity using the principle of special relativity and the principle of the constancy of the speed of light.

[I] As shown in Fig. 1, consider adjusting (synchronizing) clocks that are at rest at two points A and B separated by a distance $l$ in the same inertial frame (a coordinate system in which the law of inertia holds).

When the clock placed at point A shows the time $t_{\mathrm{A}}$, light is emitted from A. When this light arrives at point B, a distance $l$ away, the time $t_{\mathrm{B}}$ shown by the clock placed at point B is set to

$$t_{\mathrm{B}}=t_{\mathrm{A}}+\frac{l}{c} .$$

In the same way, the case in which light emitted from point B arrives at point A is treated likewise, and the readings of the two clocks are adjusted to each other.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Q1. Light emitted from B when the clock placed at point B showed the time $t_{\mathrm{B}}$ arrived at point A. At this moment the clock at point A showed the time $t'_{\mathrm{A}}$. Show that the time $t'_{\mathrm{A}}$ coincides with the time $t''_{\mathrm{A}}$ at which light that left A when the clock placed at point A showed $t_{\mathrm{A}}$ is reflected by a mirror at point B and returns to A again.

Here, use the relation

$$2l=ct ,$$

where $t$ is the time taken by light emitted from point A to be reflected by the mirror placed at point B and return to point A.

[II] As shown in Fig. 2a, light is emitted simultaneously from the point O at the centre of a train moving along a straight line with a constant speed $v$, in the direction of motion of the train and in the opposite direction. Each light beam is reflected by a mirror attached to the front end A or the rear end B of the train and returns to point O. Let us consider this using

Principle of the constancy of the speed of light: in each of the inertial frames moving relative to one another with arbitrary speeds, the speed of light is the same, $c$.

Consider an inertial frame S fixed to the ground at rest and an inertial frame S′ moving together with the train with a constant speed $v$. The length of the train moving with speed $v$, measured with a ruler fixed in the inertial frame S, was $2L$. Here, measuring the length of the moving train with a ruler fixed in the inertial frame S means: clocks synchronized by the method considered in [I] are placed at each point of the ruler, the positions of the points passed by the front end A and the rear end B of the train at one and the same time are read on the scale of the ruler, and the distance between A and B is obtained.

Further, an observer at rest at the central point O in the train observes simultaneously the light emitted from point O at time $t=0$ in the direction of motion of the train and in the opposite direction, which has been reflected at the front end A and the rear end B respectively and has returned to point O again. If this time is $t'$, then $2L'=ct'$ represents the length of the train measured with a ruler fixed in the inertial frame S′.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2a [慣性系 S′ = inertial frame S′; 慣性系 S = inertial frame S]

When the times at which the light emitted from the central point O of the train reaches the front end A and the rear end B are observed with the clocks of the inertial frame S, A and B are each moving while the light travels to A and to B, so there is a difference between the time at which the light reaches A and the time at which it reaches B.

Q2. Let $T_{\mathrm{A}}$ be the time taken by the light to reach the front end A and $T_{\mathrm{B}}$ the time taken by the light to reach the rear end B. Find the time difference $\Delta T=T_{\mathrm{A}}-T_{\mathrm{B}}$.

From this it follows that clocks placed in the inertial frames S and S′ run at different rates.

Q3. Let $2L_0$ be the difference between the position of point A in the inertial frame S when the light reached the front end A and the position of point B in the inertial frame S when the light reached the rear end B (Fig. 2b). Find $L_0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-1-fig3.png

Fig. 2b [慣性系 S = inertial frame S]

This also means that when a rod of length $2L_0$ fixed in the inertial frame S, which moves to the left with speed $v$ relative to the inertial frame S′, is observed in the inertial frame S′, the length of the rod is $2L'$.

Q4. Using the fact that the motion of the inertial frame S′ seen from the inertial frame S and the motion of S seen from S′ are equivalent, show that the relation

$$L=L'\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}} \qquad \text{(i)}$$

holds between the lengths $L$ and $L'$.

Equation (i) shows that the length, in the direction of the velocity, of a body moving with speed $v$ contracts by the factor $k=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

Q5. Consider the time taken by the light emitted from point O and reflected at the front end A and the rear end B to return to point O. Let $T$ be this time measured with the clocks of the inertial frame S and $T'$ this time measured with the clocks of the inertial frame S′. Show that the relation

$$T'=T\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}} \qquad \text{(ii)}$$

holds between $T$ and $T'$.

Equation (ii) shows that in a body (coordinate system) moving with speed $v$, time runs slower, by the factor $k=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

[III] As shown in Fig. 3, at the moment when spaceship B, moving uniformly in a straight line with relative speed $0.6c$ ($c$: speed of light in vacuum) with respect to spaceship A, which is moving uniformly in a straight line in gravity-free space, passes just above A, the clocks of A and B were set to 9 a.m. At the moment when the clock of spaceship B shows 10 a.m., the crew of B send a light signal towards spaceship A. As soon as the crew of spaceship A observe this light signal, they reply with a light signal towards spaceship B.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-1-fig4.png

Fig. 3

Q6. What time does the clock of A show when the crew of spaceship A observe the light signal from spaceship B? Also, at what time by the clock of B do the crew of spaceship B observe the reply signal from spaceship A?

[IV] In the inertial frame S, when a charge $q$ moves with velocity $\vec{v}$ (speed $v$) perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ in an electric field $\vec{E}$ (magnitude $E$) and a magnetic field of magnetic flux density $\vec{B}$ (magnitude $B$), a force of magnitude $qE$ in the direction of the electric field and a Lorentz force of magnitude $qvB$ in the direction in which a right-handed screw advances when turned from $\vec{v}$ towards $\vec{B}$ act on $q$. These two forces are collectively called the electromagnetic force.

When this phenomenon is viewed in an inertial frame S′ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ relative to the inertial frame S, the charge $q$ is at rest, so no Lorentz force from the magnetic field acts on $q$. However, if an electromagnetic force acts on the charge $q$ in the inertial frame S′, then an electric field must have arisen that acts on $q$ even though the velocity of $q$ is 0. How does this electric field arise? Let us think about it taking into account the "length contraction" considered in [II].

Below, you may use the following a) and b) if necessary.

a) When a current of strength $I$ flows in a sufficiently long straight wire, a magnetic field is produced in the sense in which a right-handed screw advancing in the direction of the current turns. The magnitude of the magnetic flux density at a point at distance $r$ from the wire is

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} .$$

Here $\mu_0$ is a constant called the permeability of vacuum.

b) When a sufficiently long straight wire carries a charge $\rho\ (>0)$ per unit length, the magnitude of the electric field produced at a point at distance $r$ from the wire, directed away from the wire (towards it when $\rho<0$), is

$$E=\frac{\rho}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} .$$

Here $\varepsilon_0$ is a constant called the permittivity of vacuum.

The $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes are taken as in Fig. 4. With a current of magnitude $I$ flowing in the wire in the negative $x$ direction, the wire, seen in the inertial frame S, was electrically neutral (Fig. 4a). We assume that in the wire, monovalent positive ions with charge $\rho_0\ (>0)$ per unit length are at rest, lined up along the $x$ axis at equal spacing $a$, and free electrons with charge $-\rho_0$ per unit length, lined up at the same equal spacing $a$, move with speed $v$ in the positive $x$ direction. Then $I=\rho_0 v$. Now a positive point charge $q$ is moving through the point P, at distance $r$ from the wire in the positive $y$ direction, parallel to the wire, in the positive $x$ direction with the same speed $v$ as the electrons in the wire.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-1-fig5.png

Fig. 4a: inertial frame S. ⊙: direction from the back to the front (out of the page). [導線 = wire]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-1-fig6.png

Fig. 4b: inertial frame S′ [導線 = wire]

Consider this phenomenon in an inertial frame S′ moving uniformly with speed $v$ in the positive $x$ direction relative to the inertial frame S (Fig. 4b). In the inertial frame S′ the point charge $q$ is at rest, and no Lorentz force from the magnetic field acts on $q$. In this frame the electrons in the wire are at rest, only the positive ions move with speed $v$ in the negative $x$ direction, and a current $I'$ flows in the negative $x$ direction.

Q7. In the inertial frame S′, the spacing $a_-$ of the electrons and the spacing $a_+$ of the positive ions are different, so the wire is charged. Find $a_-$ and $a_+$ in terms of the spacing $a$ in the inertial frame S and $k$ defined in [II]. Also find the charge $\rho$ per unit length of the wire in terms of $\rho_0$ and $k$.

Q8. Find the magnitude $f'$ and the direction of the force acting on the point charge $q$ as seen in the inertial frame S′. In doing so, use the fact that the speed of light in vacuum $c$ is expressed as

$$c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}} .$$

Also, if $f$ is the magnitude of the force acting on the point charge $q$ in the inertial frame S, how many times $f$ is $f'$? Express it using $k$.

Q9. Consider a current $I=1\,\mathrm{A}$ flowing, in the inertial frame S, in a straight wire made of Cu with cross-sectional area $A=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Assuming that each Cu atom gives one free electron, find the speed $v$ of the free electrons in the wire to two significant figures using the physical constants below.

Also, find to one significant figure the magnitude of the change of the electromagnetic force on going from S to S′, $\dfrac{|f'-f|}{f}$. In doing so, use the approximation

"when $|x|$ is sufficiently small compared with 1 ($|x|\ll 1$), $(1+x)^{\alpha}\fallingdotseq 1+\alpha x$ ($\alpha$: real number)".

• Speed of light in vacuum: $c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
• Atomic weight of the Cu atom: 64 (mass of 1 mol $M=64\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}$)
• Mass per unit volume of Cu: $\sigma=8.9\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$
• Avogadro constant (number of atoms in 1 mol): $N_{\mathrm{A}}=6.0\times10^{23}$
• Magnitude of the electron charge: $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

There is a powder that is denser than water and does not dissolve in water. When this powder is put into water, the powder sinks, but in the end it does not all settle at the bottom; instead a concentration distribution forms that is dilute in the upper part and dense in the lower part. As we shall see in [I], this is determined by the balance of the forces acting on the fine particles. Furthermore, Einstein thought that "the final concentration distribution of such fine particles is determined by the magnitude of the flow of fine particles sinking under gravity becoming equal to the magnitude of the flow diffusing from where the concentration is high to where it is low".

In this way, by combining the static view, in which the same phenomenon is seen as a balance of forces, with the dynamic view, in which the magnitudes of two flows become equal, Einstein saw through to the fact that behind a phenomenon that looks quiet at first sight there is complicated motion of molecules, and he proposed a relation.

In [I]–[III] below, taking gravity into account, we find the coefficient, defined in [III], that expresses the action of diffusion of fine particles in water, that is, the diffusion coefficient.

The magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

[I] It is known that fine particles thinly spread in water behave like the gas molecules of an ideal gas. With the gas constant $R$, the equation of state $pV=RT$ holds among the pressure $p$, the volume $V$ and the absolute temperature $T$ for 1 mole of an ideal gas. Similarly, if $p$ is the pressure due only to the fine particles in water (this is called the osmotic pressure), $N$ is the number of fine particles in the volume $V$ and $N_{\mathrm{A}}$ is the Avogadro constant, then the number of moles is $\dfrac{N}{N_{\mathrm{A}}}$, so the equation of state $pV=\dfrac{N}{N_{\mathrm{A}}}RT$ holds. Here $T$ is the water temperature (absolute temperature).

Q1. Let the number of fine particles per unit volume (this is the concentration of the fine particles) be $n=\dfrac{N}{V}$ and the Boltzmann constant be $k=\dfrac{R}{N_{\mathrm{A}}}$. For the fine particles described above, express $p$ in terms of $k$, $n$, $T$.

The concentration of the fine particles and the osmotic pressure vary with height. So we assume that at height $h$ the concentration is $n$ and the osmotic pressure is $p$, and at $h+\Delta h$ the concentration is $n+\Delta n$ and the osmotic pressure is $p+\Delta p$. We also assume that the water temperature has a constant value $T$ independent of height.

Q2. From the expression obtained in Q1, express the difference $\Delta p$ between the osmotic pressures at heights $h$ and $h+\Delta h$ in terms of the concentration difference $\Delta n$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1 [高さ = height; 水 = water]

Now, as in Fig. 1, consider in this water a rectangular box of cross-sectional area $A$ and small height $\Delta h$ (lower face at height $h$, upper face at height $h+\Delta h$), and consider the balance of the forces acting on the fine particles (mass $m$) in the box.

Three forces can be considered to act on the group of fine particles in this box: gravity, the force due to the osmotic pressure from above and the force due to the osmotic pressure from below. Here the density of the fine particles is sufficiently large, so the buoyancy can be neglected.

Since $\Delta h$ is a small height, the concentration $n$ of the fine particles in this box can be regarded as constant, and the number of fine particles in the box is $nA\Delta h$. Thus the gravitational force acting on these fine particles is expressed as $nA\Delta h\cdot mg$. The force due to the osmotic pressure acting on the fine particles in the box from above is $(p+\Delta p)A$, and the force due to the osmotic pressure received from below is $pA$.

Q3. From the balance of the forces acting on the fine particles in the box, express $\Delta p$ in terms of $\Delta h$.

Q4. Using the results of Q2 and Q3, express the concentration gradient $\dfrac{\Delta n}{\Delta h}$ in terms of $g$, $k$, $m$, $n$, $T$.

With such a static view one cannot discuss the motion of the fine particles that actually exists, but in [II] and [III] we consider a mechanism for measuring it.

[II] First, water is put into a sufficiently long vertical container and the fine particles are put into it. Since the container is sufficiently long, the effect of settling at the bottom can be neglected. Then a fine particle of mass $m$ sinks in the water under gravity and receives a resistive force from the water. Stokes' law is known, according to which the resistive force $F$ is proportional to the speed $u$: for the sinking speed $u$, $F=Cau$. Here $C$ is a constant determined by the viscosity of water, and $a$ is the radius of the fine particle. Then, even if an initial velocity is given to a fine particle, its velocity quickly becomes constant. Between the speed $u$ when it has become constant and the gravitational force $mg$ there is the relation $u=Bmg$. We call $B$ the mobility.

Q5. Express the mobility $B$ in terms of $a$ and $C$.

Hence the amount of the downward flow of fine particles at constant velocity produced by gravity and viscous resistance (the number of fine particles passing through a horizontal unit area per unit time) is expressed as $J=nu=nBmg$.

[III] Now let us consider in general the case in which the concentration of the fine particles differs with position $x$.

If the concentration at position $x$ is $n$ and the concentration at $x+\Delta x$ is $n+\Delta n$, the concentration gradient is expressed by $\dfrac{\Delta n}{\Delta x}$. As in Fig. 2, the amount of diffusion flow $J(x)$ at position $x$ (the number of fine particles passing per unit time through unit area from the region on the left of plane $x$ to the region on its right) is proportional to this concentration gradient and flows from where the concentration is large towards where it is small, so it is expressed as

$$J(x)=-D\frac{\Delta n}{\Delta x} \qquad \text{(i)}$$

This $D$ is called the diffusion coefficient.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2 [水 = water; x 軸 = x axis]

It can be considered that the magnitude of the downward flow explained in [II] and the magnitude of the diffusion flow directed from below upwards become equal, and the concentration gradient found in [I] is produced.

Q6. Express the relation between $D$ and $B$ using $k$, $T$.

This is called the Einstein relation.

Q7. Find, to two significant figures, the diffusion coefficient $D$ [$\mathrm{m^2/s}$] of fine particles of radius $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$ in water at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (absolute temperature $293\,\mathrm{K}$).

Here the Boltzmann constant is $k=1.38\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/deg}$ and the proportionality constant determined by the viscosity of water is $C=2.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$ ($20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$).

The diffusion coefficient found here does not depend on whether gravity acts on the fine particles or not.

Next, we put water into a horizontal container, so that the effect of gravity does not appear in the concentration distribution of the fine particles, and observe how the fine particles diffuse in it. In doing so, the gravity acting on the fine particles is neglected. The $x$ axis is taken in the horizontal direction (Fig. 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3 [ここに粉末を挿入する = the powder is inserted here; 水 = water; x 軸 = x axis]

[IV] Let us consider a little further why, as stated in [III], the diffusion flow is proportional to the concentration gradient. In reality the fine particles collide with water molecules and change their direction of motion. Let the mean value of the speed of a fine particle be $\bar{v}$. It can be considered that after a time $t_{\mathrm{m}}$ has passed, the direction becomes random. $l=\bar{v}t_{\mathrm{m}}$ is called the mean free path; over this distance the particle can travel straight.

The number of fine particles jumping from the left region to the right, per unit area of the cross-section at position $x$ and per unit time, can be considered to be proportional to the product of the speed $\bar{v}$ and the concentration $n(x-l/2)$ at position $x-l/2$ (Fig. 4).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4 [水 = water; x 軸 = x axis]

Furthermore, the velocities of the fine particles point in various directions, but if, for simplicity, we assume that they move equally in the positive and negative directions of each of $x$, $y$, $z$, we can consider that $1/6$ of the whole travels in the positive $x$ direction and passes through the cross-section. Then the number of fine particles jumping from the left region to the right, per unit area and per unit time, is expressed as $\dfrac{1}{6}\bar{v}n(x-l/2)$. Similarly, the number of fine particles jumping from the right region to the left is expressed as $\dfrac{1}{6}\bar{v}n(x+l/2)$.

Then the amount of flow $J(x)$ of fine particles at position $x$ can be considered as the difference between the number of fine particles moving from left to right and the number of fine particles moving from right to left.

Q8. Using the fact that, when $l$ is sufficiently small,

$$n(x-l/2)=n(x)-\frac{l}{2}\frac{\Delta n}{\Delta x} ,\qquad n(x+l/2)=n(x)+\frac{l}{2}\frac{\Delta n}{\Delta x} ,$$

express the diffusion coefficient $D$ in terms of $l$, $\bar{v}$.

[V] Let us consider what kind of motion a single fine particle actually performs. During a time $t$, the fine particle changes its direction $N=\dfrac{t}{t_{\mathrm{m}}}$ times. If the $x$ component of the displacement from the $i$-th change of direction of the fine particle to the $(i+1)$-th change is $\Delta x_i$, the position $x$ at the $(N+1)$-th collision is expressed as

$$x=\Delta x_1+\Delta x_2+\cdots+\Delta x_N=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta x_i \qquad \text{(ii)}$$

Since the direction of each displacement is random, the mean value of each displacement $\Delta x_i$ is $\overline{\Delta x_i}=0$. That is, the displacement after a time $t$ is zero on average. So, to learn about the diffusion, let us consider not the mean of the displacement but the mean of the square of the displacement.

From equation (ii), the mean of the square of the displacement is

$$\overline{x^2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{(\Delta x_i)^2}+\sum_{\substack{i,j\\ i\neq j}}\overline{\Delta x_i\Delta x_j} \qquad \text{(iii)}$$

Here, considering that the directions of the displacements are independent and random, $\overline{(\Delta x_1)^2}=\overline{(\Delta x_2)^2}=\cdots=\overline{(\Delta x_N)^2}\neq 0$ and $\overline{\Delta x_i\Delta x_j}=\overline{\Delta x_i}\cdot\overline{\Delta x_j}=0$ ($i\neq j$).

Q9. Using the fact that the number of displacements of the fine particle during a time $t$ can be written as $N=\dfrac{t}{t_{\mathrm{m}}}$, express the root-mean-square displacement $\sqrt{\overline{x^2}}$ of the fine particle in the $x$ direction after a time $t$ in terms of the diffusion coefficient $D$ and the time $t$.

Here, each displacement $\Delta x$ is independent, and if the $x$ component of the velocity of the fine particle is $v_x$, it is expressed as $\Delta x=v_x t_{\mathrm{m}}$. Also, since the gravity acting on the fine particles is neglected, their motions in the $x$, $y$ and $z$ directions are equivalent, and if the $y$ component of the velocity is $v_y$ and the $z$ component is $v_z$, then from $\overline{v_x^2}+\overline{v_y^2}+\overline{v_z^2}=\overline{v^2}$ it follows that $\overline{v_x^2}=\overline{v_y^2}=\overline{v_z^2}=\dfrac{1}{3}\overline{v^2}$. Also use $\bar{v}\fallingdotseq\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}$.

Q10. From the discussion so far, it can be considered that fine particles in water put into a container will, if left alone, eventually spread over the whole container.

Find, to two significant figures, the time $t$ required for a powder of fine particles of radius $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$, inserted at the end of a container of length $10\,\mathrm{cm}$, to spread over a distance of the order of the size of the container.

Also, from this result, state whether it is realistic to observe the powder spreading without stirring. The water temperature is $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

problems.title: Problem 3A
problems.problem:
Problem 3

Answer the following questions A, B and C.

A

As shown in Fig. 1, six resistance wires of equal resistance $r$ are connected to form a regular tetrahedron. When a voltage $V$ is applied between point O and point M, a current $I$ flowed in at point O and a current $I$ flowed out at point M. Answer the following questions. The resistance of a resistance wire is proportional to its length, and the resistances of all the junctions can be neglected. Point M is the midpoint of the resistance wire BC.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Q1. When the voltage $V$ is applied between O and M, let $i$ be the current flowing between O and B. How is $i$ expressed in terms of $I$? Also, how are the currents flowing in each of the sections OC, OA, AB, AC, BM and CM expressed in terms of $I$?

Q2. Express the combined resistance $R$ between O and M in terms of $\gamma$.

problems.title: Problem 3B
problems.problem:
Problem 3

B

The method of obtaining three-dimensional images by making use of the coherence of light is called holography. Here, let us consider the principle of holography: the formation of a hologram (a photographic negative film on which a real image is recorded as an interference pattern) and the reconstruction of the real image.

In general, when the oscillation of a light wave at time $t$ is expressed as

$$y_0=A_0\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi_0) ,$$

$\omega_0 t+\phi_0$ is called the phase. Here $A_0$ is called the amplitude and $\omega_0$ the angular frequency.

As shown in Fig. 2, a point light source O and a flat photographic film F are arranged. A photograph is taken by illuminating F with the spherical light wave (wavelength $\lambda$) emitted from O and with a light wave that interferes with it (a plane wave of wavelength $\lambda$) incident perpendicularly on F. At point C in Fig. 2 the spherical wave from the light source O and the plane light wave are in phase, and both oscillations are expressed as

$$y_1=A\sin\omega t \qquad (1)$$

Here the amplitude $A$ and the angular frequency $\omega$ are constants.

At an arbitrary point P on the photographic film F, the oscillation of the plane wave is given by equation (1), but the oscillation of the spherical wave from the light source O lags in phase behind the oscillation of the plane wave except at point C; so if the phase lag is $\phi$, the spherical wave at point P is

$$y_2=A\sin(\omega t-\phi) .$$

Here the decrease of the amplitude of the spherical wave has been neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-4-fig1.png

Fig. 2 [平面波 = plane wave]

Q1. When the difference in distance (optical path difference) is $\lambda$, the phase difference is $2\pi$. Using this, and letting $d$ be the optical path difference between OC and OP, express the phase lag $\phi$ of the spherical wave at point P in terms of $d$ and $\lambda$.

Q2. When the resultant of the spherical wave from the light source O and the plane light wave is found at point P, its oscillation is expressed as

$$y=B\sin(\omega t-\theta) .$$

Express the amplitude $B$ and the phase $\theta$, each using the necessary letters among $A$ and $\phi$.

Use the sum-to-product formula of trigonometric functions

$$\sin\alpha+\sin\beta=2\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2} .$$

A photographic film that has been exposed is strongly exposed where strong light fell on it; when it is developed, the exposed parts become transparent and the parts on which almost no light fell become opaque. So, when a plane light wave is shone on the developed photographic negative film (hologram), the amplitude of the transmitted light at point P is assumed to be proportional to the square of the amplitude $B$ of the resultant wave found in Q2.

Q3. As shown in Fig. 3, when the hologram H is illuminated by a plane light wave whose oscillation at the surface H is given by equation (1), find the oscillation $y_{\mathrm{t}}$ of the light transmitted through the hologram H at the surface H, in the form of a sum of three kinds of light waves, using $\phi$ and a suitable proportionality constant $K$ as the amplitude. In doing so, use those of the trigonometric formulae below that are needed.

$$\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2} ,\qquad \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}$$

$$\sin A\cos B=\frac{1}{2}\{\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)\}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2005-4-fig2.png

Fig. 3 [平面波 = plane wave]

Q4. Explain what kind of light wave each of the three kinds of light waves found in the previous question Q3 is.

From this result it can be seen that, when the surface H is viewed from the right-hand side of Fig. 3, it looks as if there were a light source at a point at some depth on the left side of the surface H. Thus, when a hologram on which an object placed at the position of the light source O of Fig. 2 has been recorded is illuminated with a plane light wave, the object is seen as an image with depth. This is the principle of holography.

problems.title: Problem 3C
problems.problem:
Problem 3

C

Clouds are collections of minute water droplets floating in the atmosphere. The diameter of these droplets is about $3\sim10\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ ($1\,\mathrm{\mu m}=1\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$). These droplets are minute, but their density is equal to that of water and much larger than the density of the atmosphere. For this reason, it is puzzling that clouds float in the atmosphere.

Why do clouds not fall down? And what has to happen to the droplets in a cloud for them to fall as rain? Answer the following questions.

Q1. Suppose that an air mass containing a lot of water vapour has formed in the atmosphere near the ground. Describe, in about 120 characters, the process by which this air mass becomes a cloud high up in the sky.

Q2. Why do clouds not fall down? Describe it in about 80 characters.

Q3. Considering the relative motion of the water droplets in the cloud and of the atmosphere containing a lot of water vapour, describe, in about 200 characters, the process until rain begins to fall.

problems.title: Problem 1: Expansion of the universe
problems.problem:
Problem 1

Expansion of the universe

The time evolution of the universe is usually discussed using the general theory of relativity, but apart from effects such as that of the cosmological term, similar results can also be obtained using Newtonian mechanics. Here, let us consider the time evolution of the universe using Newton's law of universal gravitation, without taking the general theory of relativity into account.

[I] When light emitted by an atom in a distant galaxy reaches the Earth, it is observed with a wavelength longer than the wavelength of the light emitted by the atom that originally emitted it (the proper wavelength). This is called the redshift. Let the speed of light in vacuum be $c$.

Q1. When an atom emits light of proper wavelength $\lambda_0$ while receding from an observer with speed $\upsilon$, express the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light measured by the observer using $\lambda_0$, $c$ and $\upsilon$. Here $\upsilon$ is sufficiently small compared with $c$ ($\upsilon\ll c$), and assume that the same Doppler-effect formula as for sound also holds for light.

In 1929, the American astronomer Edwin Hubble, as a result of observing the redshift of light coming from distant galaxies, found that most galaxies are receding from the Earth and that their recession speed $\upsilon$ is approximately proportional to the distance $r$ from the observer (the Earth) to the galaxy. This relation is expressed as

$$\upsilon=H_0 r$$

and $H_0$ is called the Hubble constant. This relation expresses that the ratio of the recession speed of a galaxy to its distance is the same constant value $H_0$ for all galaxies. If this proportionality holds at any time $t$, the relation between the recession speed $\upsilon(t)$ of a galaxy and the distance $r(t)$ from the Earth to the galaxy is expressed, using a function of time $H(t)$, as

$$\upsilon(t)=H(t)r(t) \qquad \ldots(1)$$

Here the velocity is expressed as $\upsilon(t)=\dfrac{dr(t)}{dt}$, and $H(t)$ is called the Hubble parameter.

Thus, if the universe has always been expanding in the past as well, then going back in time one can consider that the universe began from a single point. The cosmological theory according to which the universe began at some moment with a great explosion at a single point (the Big Bang) and has continued to expand since then was proposed in 1946 by George Gamow and is called the Big Bang theory. The Big Bang theory is at present considered correct by most researchers. So here, following the Big Bang theory, let us find with Newtonian mechanics the age of the universe, that is, the time $t_0$ from the moment the Big Bang occurred (time $t=0$) to the present.

[II] The universe has no special place anywhere (homogeneous) and no special direction (isotropic). This is called the cosmological principle. Following this cosmological principle, let us consider the expansion of the universe. To picture such a homogeneous and isotropic expansion of the universe, it suffices to imagine a spherical balloon gradually expanding as air is blown into it. The distance between any two points on the surface of the balloon increases uniformly as the balloon expands. This is a two-dimensional image of the expansion of three-dimensional space.

At present (time $t=t_0$), let the distance from the observer O to the point mass P be $r_0$, and let the distance at time $t$ be $r(t)$. Here we introduce, as the scale of the expansion of the universe, the quantity called the scale factor

$$a(t)=\frac{r(t)}{r_0} \qquad \ldots(2)$$

When the Big Bang occurred (time $t=0$), the point mass P and the observer O can be considered to have been at the same point, so $r(0)=0$ and $a(0)=0$. From now on, $r(t)$ is simply written $r$ and $a(t)$ is written $a$.

Q2. Express the Hubble parameter $H(t)$ using the scale factor $a$ and its time rate of change $\dfrac{da}{dt}$.

[III] At time $t=t_0$, let the mass density (mass per unit volume) inside the sphere of radius $r_0$ centred at point O be $\rho_0$, and let the mass density inside the sphere of radius $r$ at time $t$ be $\rho$. Now, if the mass does not change through the expansion, the masses inside these spheres are the same.

When mass is distributed uniformly, to an observer at any point O the mass appears to be distributed spherically symmetrically about point O. If the distance between the point mass P and point O is $r$, the universal gravitational forces exerted on the point mass P by the mass outside the sphere of radius $r$ centred at point O cancel one another, and the resultant force on P is 0. Therefore, the universal gravitational force acting on the point mass P is equal to the force that would act if the mass $M$ inside the sphere of radius $r$ centred at point O were concentrated at point O (Fig. 1). Below, let the universal gravitational constant be $G$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Q3. If the acceleration of the point mass P at time $t$, in the direction away from point O, is $\dfrac{d^2r}{dt^2}$, then $\dfrac{d^2a}{dt^2}=\dfrac{1}{r_0}\dfrac{d^2r}{dt^2}$. Express $\dfrac{1}{a}\dfrac{d^2a}{dt^2}$ using $\rho$ and $G$.

That the present universe is expanding is considered to mean one of two things: (1) the universe will continue to expand forever, or (2) the universe will at some time turn to contraction. According to recent observational results, the universe is presumed to be close to the boundary between (1) and (2). Considered in Newtonian mechanics, this means that the total mechanical energy is close to 0. Below, let us calculate taking the mechanical energy to be 0.

Q4. At time $t$, using the law of conservation of mechanical energy of the point mass P, express $\left(\dfrac{1}{a}\dfrac{da}{dt}\right)^2$ using $\rho$ and $G$. Here the point mass P moves only in the direction away from point O.

Q5. From the conservation of the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$, express $\rho$ using $\rho_0$ and $a$.

From the results of Q4 and Q5 it follows, using the present time $t_0$ and $a(t_0)=1$, that the scale factor $a(t)$ at time $t$ is expressed as

$$a(t)=\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^n \qquad \ldots(3)$$

Q6. Find the exponent $n$ in equation (3). Also, express the time $t_0$ using the present mass density of the universe $\rho_0$ and the universal gravitational constant $G$.

Q7. Express the present age of the universe $t_0$ using the Hubble constant $H_0$ ($=H(t_0)$), and, using the value $H_0=72\,\mathrm{km/(s\cdot Mpc)}$ obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope, find $t_0$ in units of $10^8$ years to 2 significant figures. Also, taking $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$, find $\rho_0$ to 2 significant figures. Here $1\,\mathrm{Mpc}=10^6\,\mathrm{pc}$ (Mpc is read megaparsec and pc parsec), and 1 pc is defined as the distance at which the distance between the Earth and the Sun subtends an angle of 1 second, $1\,\mathrm{pc}=3.09\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$.

problems.title: Problem 2: Emission of electromagnetic waves by charged particles
problems.problem:
Problem 2

Emission of electromagnetic waves by charged particles

When a charged particle moves with acceleration, the electric field lines produced by the charged particle bend, extra electric-field energy is stored there, and that energy spreads out into the surroundings at the speed of light. This is the electromagnetic wave radiated by a charged particle in accelerated motion. Let us consider this with the following model.

[I] According to the special theory of relativity, when the length of an object moving with speed $\upsilon$ is measured along its direction of motion, it is contracted to $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ times its length at rest. Here $\beta=\dfrac{\upsilon}{c}$, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. Lengths in the direction perpendicular to the direction of motion do not change.

Let S$'$ be a coordinate system moving with constant velocity, with speed $\upsilon$ in the $z$-axis direction, relative to the coordinate system S. At time $t=0$ of the S system, the origins O and O$'$ of the S and S$'$ systems and each pair of coordinate axes, that is, the $x$ axis and $x'$ axis, the $y$ axis and $y'$ axis, and the $z$ axis and $z'$ axis, coincide, and the coordinate axes move as shown in Fig. 1, each remaining parallel to its counterpart. In Fig. 1, the $y$ and $y'$ axes are perpendicular to the page.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1

In the coordinate system S$'$, a rod of length $z'$ is placed with one end at the origin O$'$ and the other end A at the point $(0,0,z')$, and is fixed in the S$'$ system. If the coordinate of end A of this rod at time $t$ of the S system is $z$, the length of the rod seen in the S system is $z-\upsilon t$. Since the rod is moving in the $z$-axis direction with speed $\upsilon$, its length in the $z$-axis direction is contracted to $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ times its original length (the length in the S$'$ system) $z'$. Therefore

$$z-\upsilon t=z'\sqrt{1-\beta^2} \qquad \ldots(1)$$

Also, since lengths in the $x$-axis direction, perpendicular to the $z$ axis, do not change,

$$x=x' \qquad \ldots(2)$$

As shown in Fig. 2, a sufficiently large conducting plate whose side face, in the state of rest, is uniformly charged with charge density (charge per unit area) $\sigma_0\,(>0)$ moves with constant velocity, with constant speed $\upsilon$ relative to the S system, along the $z$ axis, keeping its charged surface coincident with the $z$ axis. In general, charge is distributed only on the surface of a conductor; there is no charge inside a conductor, and there is no electric field inside a conductor either. Moreover, even when the conducting plate moves, the total amount of charge on the surface of the conducting plate does not change. Now,

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2 [導体板 = conducting plate]

when we define "the number of electric field lines passing through a unit area perpendicular to the electric field $E$ to be $E$ lines",

"the number $N$ of electric field lines going out of any closed surface is expressed, with $Q$ the total charge in the region enclosed by the closed surface and $\varepsilon_0$ the permittivity of vacuum, as

$$N=\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\text{"}$$

This is called Gauss's law.

Next, using the above considerations, let us examine what kind of electric field a point charge moving with constant velocity produces.

Q1. In the S system, the length of the conducting plate in the $z$-axis direction is contracted and its side area has become smaller. By applying Gauss's law to the region enclosed by the thin solid line shown in Fig. 2, find the electric field $E_x$ pointing in the positive $x$-axis direction at the point $\mathrm{P}(x,0,z)$ ($x>0$). In this case, if the conducting plate is sufficiently long in the $y$-axis and $z$-axis directions, you may assume that in the region $x>0$ a uniform electric field parallel to the $x$ axis is produced. Also, in the S$'$ system, which moves together with the conducting plate, the side area remains unchanged. Find the ratio $\dfrac{E_x}{E'_x}$ of the electric field $E_x$ found above to the electric field $E'_x$ produced at the point $\mathrm{P}(x',0,z')$ in the S$'$ system.

As shown in Fig. 3, there is a sufficiently large conducting plate uniformly charged, in the state of rest, with charge density $\sigma_0\,(>0)$. The charged surface of the conducting plate is perpendicular to the $z$ axis, and the conducting plate moves in the positive $z$-axis direction with speed $\upsilon$ relative to the S system, remaining parallel to the $x$ axis. At time $t=0$ of the S system, the charged surface of the conducting plate passes through the $x$ axis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3 [導体板 = conducting plate]

Q2. At time $t\,(>0)$ of the S system, find the electric field $E_z$ produced in the positive $z$-axis direction at the point $\mathrm{P}(x,0,z)$ ($z>\upsilon t$). Find the ratio $\dfrac{E_z}{E'_z}$ of the electric field $E_z$ found to the electric field $E'_z$ produced at the same time $t$ at the point $\mathrm{P}(x',0,z')$ of the S$'$ system, which moves together with the conducting plate.

The relations between the electric field in the S system and the electric field in the S$'$ system found above hold in general, regardless of whether the electric field is produced by the charge on a conducting plate.

Suppose that a charged particle with point charge $q\,(>0)$ is at rest in vacuum at the origin O of the coordinate system S. Then, around it, as shown in Fig. 4, a radial electric field is produced, spherically symmetric and directed away from $q$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4

Let us consider the ratio $\dfrac{E_z}{E_x}$ of the $z$ component $E_z$ and the $x$ component $E_x$ of the electric field produced in the S system at time $t\,(>0)$ by a point charge $q$ at rest at the origin O$'$ of the S$'$ system, which moves with constant velocity, with constant speed $\upsilon$ in the positive direction along the $z$ axis, relative to the S system.

Q3. Using equations (1) and (2), express the ratio $\dfrac{E_z}{E_x}$ in terms of $z-\upsilon t$ and $x$.

This result shows that the electric field produced around the point charge $q$ is radial, that is, the electric field is directed away from $q$.

From this it follows that the electric field produced at time $t\,(>0)$ by a point charge $q$ moving with constant velocity, with speed $\upsilon$ in the positive $z$-axis direction relative to the S system (the position of $q$ at this time is the point Q), is as shown in Fig. 5.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5

[II] Next, suppose that the point charge $q$, which was at rest at the origin O of the S system, moves with uniform acceleration, with constant acceleration $a$ in the positive $z$-axis direction, during a short time $\Delta t$ from time $t=0$, reaches the speed $\upsilon=a\Delta t$ and the point O$'$ with coordinate $z=\dfrac{1}{2}a(\Delta t)^2$, and thereafter moves with constant velocity in the positive $z$-axis direction with that speed $\upsilon=a\Delta t$. Let us now consider what the electric field looks like at time $t\,(\gg\Delta t)$.

At a time $t\,(<0)$, at a point at distance $r$ from the point charge $q\,(>0)$ at rest at the origin O, an electric field of magnitude

$$E=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$$

directed away from $q$ is produced.

Let the position of the point charge $q$ at time $t$ be Q, and let us draw the electric field lines at that time. The electric field produced by the point charge $q$ propagates from $q$ into the surroundings at the speed of light $c$. Therefore, in the space outside the radius $ct$ from the origin O, the electric field due to the charge as it was while at rest at the origin until time 0 is produced radially and spherically symmetrically about the point O. However, inside the sphere of radius $c(t-\Delta t)$ centred at the point O$'$, the electric field due to the point charge $q$ moving with constant velocity is produced. Therefore, as in Fig. 5, the electric field inside that sphere is represented by radial electric field lines centred at the position Q of the charge at time $t$.

Inside the sphere of radius $c(t-\Delta t)$ centred at the point O$'$, consider the number of electric field lines that go out of the cone obtained by rotating about the $z$ axis the sector with central angle $\theta$ centred at the point Q, passing through the base of the cone. Further, outside the sphere of radius $ct$ centred at the point O, consider the number of electric field lines passing through the base of the cone obtained by rotating about the $z$ axis the sector with central angle $\phi$ centred at the point O.

The angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ are taken so that these numbers of electric field lines are equal. Electric field lines, which are curves connecting the electric field, are not created or annihilated in vacuum and connect continuously. Then the electric field line directed at angle $\theta$ from the $z$ axis inside the sphere of radius $c(t-\Delta t)$ centred at the point Q should connect with the electric field line directed at angle $\phi$ from the $z$ axis outside the sphere of radius $ct$ centred at the point O. In this way, the electric field lines at time $t$ look as shown in Fig. 6.

In the region between the spherical surface of radius $c(t-\Delta t)$ centred at the point O$'$ and the spherical surface of radius $ct$ centred at the point O, a magnetic field is also produced, and the electric and magnetic fields spread into the surroundings at the speed of light $c$. This is the electromagnetic wave radiated by an accelerated charge.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6

Now consider the case where the time $t$ is sufficiently large compared with the time $\Delta t$ ($t\gg\Delta t$) and the speed $\upsilon=a\Delta t$ of the point charge $q$ at time $t$ is sufficiently small compared with the speed of light $c$ ($\upsilon\ll c$). Then, at time $t$, the electric field around $q$ spreads out radially and almost spherically symmetrically about $q$, so we can regard $\theta=\phi$, and since $\overline{\mathrm{OO'}}\ll\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}$, the points O and O$'$ almost coincide.

Consider the electric field line going out from the point charge $q$ in the direction at angle $\theta$ to the $z$ axis. In this case, the electric field line going out from the point charge $q$ in the direction at angle $\theta$ to the $z$ axis inside the sphere of radius $c(t-\Delta t)$ centred at the point O$'$ connects with the electric field line in the direction at angle $\theta$ to the $z$ axis outside the sphere of radius $ct$ centred at the point O.

As shown in Fig. 7, suppose that the electric field emitted at the instant when the uniformly accelerated motion began at the point O at time $t=0$ passes, at time $t$, the point P at distance $ct$ from the point O, and that the electric field emitted at the instant of the transition to uniform motion at the point O$'$ at time $t=\Delta t$ passes, at time $t$, the point P$'$ at distance $c(t-\Delta t)$ from the point O$'$. Here the point O$'$ is drawn coinciding with the point O. If the position of the charged particle at time $t$ is the point Q, then since $t\gg\Delta t$, we have $\dfrac{1}{2}a(\Delta t)^2\ll\upsilon t$ and $\upsilon\Delta t\ll\upsilon t$, so

$$\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}=\frac{1}{2}a(\Delta t)^2+\upsilon(t-\Delta t)\approx\upsilon t=at\Delta t$$

and the length of the segment OQ in the direction parallel to O$\to$P is $at\Delta t\cos\theta$, and its length in the perpendicular direction is $at\Delta t\sin\theta$. Since $\overline{\mathrm{OP}}=r=ct\gg\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}$, we have $c(t-\Delta t)=\overline{\mathrm{O'P'}}\approx\overline{\mathrm{OH}}$, and the length of the electric field line P$'$P in the O$\to$P direction can be regarded as $\overline{\mathrm{HP}}=\Delta r=c\Delta t$. Then $\overline{\mathrm{OH}}=r-\Delta r$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig7.png

Fig. 7

Apply Gauss's law to the sufficiently thin strip-shaped region V$_1$ enclosed by the side faces S$_1$ and S$_2$ shown in Fig. 8. Since the region V$_1$ is sufficiently thin, all the electric field lines passing through V$_1$ can be considered to enter through the side face S$_2$ and leave through the side face S$_1$. Also, if the side faces S$_1$ and S$_2$ are taken sufficiently small, the electric field on each face can be regarded as uniform.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig8.png

Fig. 8

Q4. Express the component $E_1$, in the O$\to$P direction, of the electric field directed from the point P$'$ towards P in terms of $\varepsilon_0$, $q$ and $r$. Here $\Delta r=c\Delta t\ll r$, and the electric field on P$'$P can be regarded as constant.

Q5. Find the component $E_2$, perpendicular to O$\to$P, of the electric field in the direction P$'\to$P, and express it in terms of $\varepsilon_0,\theta,a,c,q,r$.

As seen above, at the instant the charge begins its accelerated motion, the electric field lines bend, and this propagates into the surroundings at the speed of light $c$. Also, the electric field emitted during the accelerated motion (the electric field on P$'$P) stores extra energy compared with the electric field emitted at rest and in uniform motion (the electric field on PR and QP$'$). Moreover, the same amount of energy is stored additionally as a magnetic field, and the sum of these extra energies due to the electric and magnetic fields is radiated into the surroundings at the speed of light $c$ as the energy of the electromagnetic wave. So next, let us find this radiated energy.

As shown in Fig. 9, when a certain charge was stored on a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area $S$ and plate separation $d$ placed in vacuum, a uniform electric field of magnitude $E$ was produced between the plates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2006-2-fig9.png

Fig. 9

Q6. Find the electrostatic energy $U$ stored in this capacitor and express it using $\varepsilon_0,d,E,S$. Also, assuming that all this energy is stored in the electric field produced between the plates, express the energy stored per unit volume between the plates (the energy density) $u$ using the magnitude of the electric field $E$ and $\varepsilon_0$.

In general, in a space where an electric field exists, the energy per unit volume found in Q6 can be considered to be stored.

Q7. In the region of the spherical shell centred at the point O and bounded by the spherical surfaces of radii $r-\Delta r$ and $r$, extra electric-field energy is stored because the electric field lines bend. This extra energy is due to the electric field $E_2$ found in Q5. Find the extra stored energy $\Delta E$ and express it using $\varepsilon_0,\Delta t,a,c,q$. In doing so, use the fact that the volume of the spherical shell bounded by the spherical surfaces of radii $r-\Delta r$ and $r$ is given by $4\pi r^2\Delta r$. Here neglect the change in the magnitude of the electric field between $r-\Delta r$ and $r$, and you may use the fact that the average value of $\sin^2\theta$ over a spherical surface is $\overline{\sin^2\theta}=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Also, find the sum of the extra energies due to the electric and magnetic fields, and show that the energy $P$ of the electromagnetic wave radiated per unit time by a charged particle with charge $q$ moving with acceleration of magnitude $a$ is expressed as

$$P=\frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3} \qquad \ldots(3)$$

Equation (3) shown in the previous question Q7 holds regardless of the sign of the charge of the charged particle, the sign of the acceleration and its direction.

[III] Take the structure of the hydrogen atom to be an electron (charge $-e$, mass $m_e$) moving in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around the atomic nucleus (charge $e$) (the nucleus does not move). Assume that the classical electromagnetism considered above can be applied as it is to the motion of this electron. Then the electron, which moves in a circle under the Coulomb force from the nucleus, has an acceleration, so it radiates electromagnetic waves and loses energy. Consequently the orbital radius of the electron gradually decreases and the atom collapses. The energy of the electromagnetic waves radiated by the electron in this process can also be calculated using equation (3) found in Q7.

In numerical calculations, use the following physical constants.

• Speed of light in vacuum: $c=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
• Permittivity of vacuum: $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$
• Elementary charge: $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$
• Mass of the electron: $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$

Q8. Express the mechanical energy (kinetic energy + potential energy) $E$ of an electron moving in a circle of radius $r$ around a nucleus at rest, acted on only by the Coulomb force, using $\varepsilon_0$, $e$ and $r$.

Q9. Assuming that the mechanical energy of the electron decreases by the energy of the radiated electromagnetic waves, express the rate of decrease of the orbital radius $r$ of the electron, $\dfrac{dr}{dt}$, as a function of $r$ using the physical constants $\varepsilon_0$, $c$, $e$, $m_e$. Here the decrease of the orbital radius during the time in which the electron goes once around is extremely small, so the electron may be regarded as moving in a circle at each instant.

Q10. For a hydrogen atom with electron orbital radius $r_{\mathrm{B}}=5.29\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}$ (the Bohr radius), find, to 2 significant figures, the time $T$ until the orbital radius of the electron becomes 0 and the atom collapses. If necessary, you may use the following integration formula:

$$\int r^n\frac{dr}{dt}\,dt=\int r^n\,dr=\frac{r^{n+1}}{n+1}+C \qquad (n=1,2,3,\ldots,\ C\text{ is a constant of integration})$$

Thus, in classical theory, the electron would always radiate electromagnetic waves, and the atom would collapse. To overcome this difficulty, Niels Bohr introduced the quantum hypothesis and assumed that an electron does not radiate electromagnetic waves while it moves in certain particular orbits. At first the basis of this assumption was vague, but Bohr's theory could explain various experimental results well and led to the later development of quantum mechanics. Today, quantum mechanics is considered indispensable for explaining atomic structure.

[IV] The sky looks blue. This is said to be because, when sunlight is scattered by air molecules that are much smaller than its wavelength, blue light of short wavelength is scattered more easily than red light of long wavelength.

Q11. When visible light of angular frequency $\omega$ (electromagnetic waves with wavelengths of about $3.8\times10^{-7}$ to $7.7\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$) falls on an air molecule, an electron in the molecule receives forces from the oscillating electric field of the electromagnetic wave and from the atomic nucleus, so that its position $x(t)$ oscillates with time $t$ as

$$x(t)=x_0\sin\omega t \qquad (x_0\text{ is a constant independent of }t\text{ and }\omega)$$

From this, explain, using equation (3), why the sky looks blue.

problems.title: Problem 3A: Dimensional analysis and scale transformations
problems.problem:
Problem 3A

Dimensional analysis and scale transformations

[I] Once fundamental units serving as standards, such as those of length and time, are fixed, the units of physical quantities are expressed as combinations of them. What shows in this way which combination of fundamental units the unit of a physical quantity is, is called the dimension. When a relation between physical quantities is expressed by an equation, the dimensions of the two sides must be equal. Using this, one can examine how a certain physical quantity is related to other physical quantities. Such a method is called dimensional analysis.

Denoting the dimension of mass by [M], the dimension of length by [L] and the dimension of time by [T], let us examine physical phenomena using the method of dimensional analysis.

Example. Assuming that the speed of sound $\upsilon_s$ is determined by the air pressure $p$ and the density of air $\rho$, and supposing that

$$\upsilon_s=k\,p^a\rho^b \qquad (k\text{ is a dimensionless constant}) \qquad \ldots(1)$$

the dimensions of $\upsilon_s$, $p$, $\rho$ can be expressed respectively as $[\upsilon_s]=[\mathrm{LT^{-1}}]$, $[p]=[(\mathrm{MLT^{-2}})/\mathrm{L^2}]=[\mathrm{ML^{-1}T^{-2}}]$, $[\rho]=[\mathrm{M/L^3}]=[\mathrm{ML^{-3}}]$. Then the dimensions of the two sides of equation (1) are

$$[\mathrm{LT^{-1}}]=[\mathrm{ML^{-1}T^{-2}}]^a[\mathrm{ML^{-3}}]^b=[\mathrm{M}^{a+b}\mathrm{L}^{-a-3b}\mathrm{T}^{-2a}]$$

From this,

$$0=a+b,\quad 1=-a-3b,\quad -1=-2a$$

and $a=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $b=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ are obtained.

Q1. Consider the lift of an aeroplane. Assume that the wing of the aeroplane is a rectangle of length $W$ and depth $L$. This aeroplane is flying in an atmosphere of density $\rho$ with velocity $\upsilon$ relative to the atmosphere. Since the lift $F$ of the aeroplane is considered to be proportional to the length of the wing, we put

$$\frac{F}{W}=k\rho^a\upsilon^bL^c \qquad (k\text{ is a dimensionless constant})$$

How are $a$, $b$, $c$ determined? Find the numerical values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

Q2. This aeroplane takes off on the ground at a speed of $250\,\mathrm{km}$ per hour and flies at an altitude of $10{,}000\,\mathrm{m}$ at a speed of $900\,\mathrm{km}$ per hour. If the lift acting on this aeroplane at the altitude of $10{,}000\,\mathrm{m}$ is equal to the lift acting on this aeroplane when it takes off on the ground, what is the ratio $\dfrac{\rho_1}{\rho_0}$ of the density $\rho_1$ of the air at the altitude of $10{,}000\,\mathrm{m}$ to the density $\rho_0$ of the air on the ground?

[II] When a physical quantity is expressed by powers of other physical quantities, physical laws can be examined by the technique called scale transformation. Now consider the case in which the scale of length is transformed as $r\to r_1=\alpha r$ and the scale of time as $t\to t_1=\beta t$.

Q3. The velocity $V$ and the acceleration $A$ are transformed as

$$V\to V_1=\alpha^i\beta^jV,\qquad A\to A_1=\alpha^k\beta^lA$$

Find the values of $i$, $j$, $k$, $l$ above.

Q4. A miniature object with lengths $1/100$ of the real ones was made and dropped, and this was filmed on video. To make it look real, it suffices that the acceleration be invariant under the scale transformation of length and time. From this, find by what factor the playback speed of the video should be changed relative to the original.

problems.title: Problem 3B: Hand-cranked generator and miniature bulb
problems.problem:
Problem 3B

Hand-cranked generator and miniature bulb

There are a $12\,\mathrm{V}$–$1.5\,\mathrm{W}$ miniature bulb (a miniature bulb whose power consumption is $1.5\,\mathrm{W}$ when a voltage of $12\,\mathrm{V}$ is applied to it), a hand-cranked generator that has the same structure as a motor and can generate an emf of at most $8\,\mathrm{V}$, and a DC power supply of emf $9\,\mathrm{V}$. When these were connected in series, the handle of the hand-cranked generator began to rotate and the miniature bulb lit up.

After a sufficiently long time, the number of rotations of the handle per unit time became constant and the brightness of the miniature bulb also became constant. This state is called the "initial state". Note that when the handle of the generator rotates, a resistive force acts in the direction that stops the rotation. Answer the following questions.

Q1. In the "initial state", the operations shown in 1) to 3) below were performed on the handle of the hand-cranked generator. How does the brightness of the miniature bulb change as a result of these operations? Also state the reason.

1) The rotating handle of the hand-cranked generator was held down by hand and its rotation was stopped.

2) A force was applied by hand to the handle of the hand-cranked generator, and its number of rotations in the same direction as in the "initial state" was increased by a certain amount.

3) A force was applied to the handle of the hand-cranked generator, and it was rotated at a constant number of rotations in the direction opposite to the direction in which it was originally rotating.

Q2. The $12\,\mathrm{V}$–$1.5\,\mathrm{W}$ miniature bulb was replaced by a $12\,\mathrm{V}$–$5\,\mathrm{W}$ miniature bulb, and the miniature bulb, the hand-cranked generator and the DC power supply of emf $9\,\mathrm{V}$ were connected in series. State how the brightness of the miniature bulb and the number of rotations of the handle of the hand-cranked generator per unit time change compared with the "initial state". Also state the reason briefly.

problems.title: Problem 3C: Bubbles in carbonated drinks
problems.problem:
Problem 3C

Bubbles in carbonated drinks

When a carbonated drink such as soda (サイダー) is uncorked, bubbles can be seen forming near the walls of the container and rising. Observing them carefully, one finds that the bubbles increase their speed as they rise. In contrast, when an air bubble is put into water, it rises at an almost constant velocity. Explain briefly why such a difference occurs.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (100 points)

According to Einstein's special theory of relativity, when the positions of two clocks change relative to each other, like the clock of a person riding a moving train and the clock of a person standing beside the track, the hands of the clocks advance at different rates. Here we derive the basic relations of that theory and consider applying them to car navigation systems. Below we consider experiments in which sound or light is generated on carts moving uniformly with respect to the ground; times and coordinates measured with a clock and a ruler fixed to the ground are denoted $t$, $x$, etc., and those measured with a clock and a ruler fixed on the carts are distinguished by a prime "$'$", as in $t'$, $x'$.

[I]

First, consider sound waves propagating through air as the medium. In [I] and [II], light is assumed to propagate instantaneously.

As in Fig. 1, two carts, kept a fixed distance apart by a rigid thin rod, are moving to the right along the $x$ axis with constant velocity $v$. Each of the two carts carries a speaker, and their separation is $L$. When the left speaker passes point O, it emits a sound pulse from there and, at the same time, the left light bulb is flashed instantaneously to signal this. That instant is taken as $t=0$ of the clock fixed to the ground. Also, the end of the ruler fixed to the ground is placed at O, and that point is taken as $x=0$. When the person on the right cart hears this sound pulse, he flashes the right light bulb instantaneously to signal it and, at the same time, emits a sound pulse from the right speaker. When the person on the left cart hears the sound coming from the right, he again flashes the left light bulb instantaneously. Although the running carts disturb the surrounding air, most of the air in the space through which the sound propagates is at rest with respect to the ground, and therefore the sound waves travel between the two speakers with a constant speed $V$ relative to the ground. Also, in both problems [I] and [II], $v<V$. Suppose that a person standing on the ground observes and records this with a clock and a ruler fixed to the ground.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1:

Q1 Prove that, if $t_1$ is the time at which the person standing on the ground observes the flash of the right light bulb, then

$$t_1=\frac{L}{V-v}.$$

Q2 Express the time $t_2$ at which this person observes the second flash of the left light bulb in terms of $L$, $v$ and $V$.

[II]

Next, as in Fig. 2, a long sealed box was placed on two coupled carts and the same experiment was carried out while the whole was moved to the right with constant speed $v$. Since the air enclosed in the box is at rest relative to the carts, the sound waves propagate inside the box with speed $V$ relative to the carts. Suppose that a person on the carts observes this experiment with a clock and a ruler fixed to the carts. When the sound pulse leaves the left speaker, the clock fixed to the carts reads $t'=0$, and the mark $x'=0$ of the ruler fixed to the carts is at the position of the left speaker.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2:

Q3 Suppose that the clock on the carts read $t'_1$ when the right light bulb flashed. Express $t'_1$ using all or some of $L$, $V$ and $v$.

Q4 Suppose that the hand of the clock on the carts read $t'_2$ when the left light bulb flashed for the second time. Express $t'_2-t'_1$ in the same way as above.

Q5 Take the time at which the sound left the left speaker as $t=0$ on the clock fixed on the ground. Also take the position of the speaker at that time as $x=0$ on the ruler fixed to the ground. Using quantities measured with these clock and ruler, calculate the time $t_1$ at which the right light bulb flashed, and derive that it is equal to $t'_1$.

[III]

The result of Q5 means that the clock fixed to the carts and the clock fixed to the ground always showed the same time. However, Einstein showed, by a thought experiment using light waves instead of sound waves, that strictly speaking this is not correct.

As in Fig. 3 on the next page, a light bulb is placed at one end of a cart moving to the right in vacuum with speed $v$, and a mirror at the other end. The distance between the bulb and the mirror, measured with a ruler placed on the ground, was $L$. When the bulb is flashed briefly, a light pulse travels to the right, is reflected by the mirror and returns to the left end. Since the speed of sound $V$ is a speed relative to the medium at rest, the speed relative to the ground and the speed relative to the carts are different. By contrast, Einstein considered that the speed of light travelling back and forth between the bulb and the mirror must be the same whether it is measured with a clock and ruler fixed to the ground or with a clock and ruler fixed to the carts. Let this speed be $c$. The value of $c$ is $3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Below, the instant at which the bulb flashes is taken as $t=t'=0$, and the position of the bulb at that instant as $x=x'=0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3:

Q6 When the light from the bulb reached the mirror on the right, the clock fixed to the ground read $t_1$. Express $t_1$ in terms of $L$, $v$ and $c$.

Q7 When the light, reflected by the mirror, came back to the bulb, the clock fixed to the ground read $t_2$. Express $t_2$ in terms of $L$, $v$ and $c$.

[IV]

Since the light emitted from the bulb went back and forth on the cart with constant speed $c$, the time $t'_1$ at which the light emitted from the bulb at $t'=0$ arrived at the mirror and the time $t'_2$ at which it came back to the bulb must satisfy the relation $t'_2=2t'_1$. Therefore, if the clock fixed to the cart and the clock fixed to the ground advanced at the same rate, we should have $t_2=2t_1$, but according to the results calculated above this does not hold. This means that the two clocks do not advance at the same rate. Einstein therefore considered that there is a relation

$$t'=at+b(x-vt) \qquad (1)$$

so that the time $t'$ of the clock on the cart depends on the time $t$ of the clock on the ground and on the position $x$. He further considered that for the coordinate $x'$ measured with the ruler on the cart there would be a relation

$$x'=\alpha t+\beta(x-vt) \qquad (2)$$

We shall now determine the $a$, $b$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ appearing here. Note that, as these ideas are developed, the distance between the bulb and the mirror measured with the ruler fixed to the cart is no longer $L$, so that $t'_1=L/c$ does not hold.

First, using in Eq. (2) the fact that the position of the left bulb is always at $x=vt$ and that $x'=0$ regardless of the value of $t$, we obtain $\alpha=0$.

Q8 Next, as above, the bulb is flashed instantaneously at $t=t'=0$. Seen on the cart, the light pulse reaches

$$x'=ct' \qquad (3)$$

at time $t'$. Seen on the ground, the light pulse reaches

$$x=ct \qquad (4)$$

at time $t$. Using these two relations, derive an expression for $\beta$ in Eq. (2) in terms of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $v$.

Q9 From $\dfrac{t'_2}{t'_1}=2$, which holds in the experiment of Fig. 3, and Eq. (1) above, derive an expression for $b$ in terms of $a$, $c$ and $v$.

Q10 Now consider a second cart moving with velocity $(-v)$ as seen from the cart considered so far. Times and coordinates measured with a clock and a ruler fixed to it are denoted $t''$, $x''$. Using $a$, $c$ and $v$, write the relations expressing $t''$ and $x''$ in terms of $t'$ and $x'$.

Q11 However, the second cart is not moving with respect to the ground, so in fact $x=x''$, $t=t''$. Using this, express $a$ using only $c$ and $v$. Also show from this result that

$$t'=\frac{t-(v/c^2)x}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}},\qquad x'=\frac{x-vt}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}} \qquad (5)$$

hold. Below, $v$ is taken to be sufficiently small compared with $c$.

Q12 Using the fact that, when $z$ is a number sufficiently small compared with 1, one may take $(1+z)^p\fallingdotseq 1+pz$, express the right-hand side of the left equation of (5) in an approximate form as the sum of a term not containing $c$ and a term proportional to $(1/c)^2$.

Below, the term proportional to $(1/c)^2$ is called the (special) relativistic correction.

[V]

GPS (Global Positioning System) is a system that tells us our position and the time using information sent on radio waves from artificial satellites, and it has so far been used in car navigation systems and the like. Recently, terminals have also been built into mobile phones, making it possible to know the position of the owner. Here, let us consider one example showing that GPS, which uses artificial satellites orbiting the Earth at high speed, must take the relativistic correction into account.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-1-fig4.png

Fig. 4:

[Labels in the figure: 衛星1 = satellite 1; 衛星2 = satellite 2.]

A car navigation system always communicates with 4 satellites in order to know its position in three-dimensional space, but here we consider the simplified system of Fig. 4. Two artificial satellites are flying to the right with a common velocity $v$ along the same track as the car. Suppose that, when the pulse from satellite 1, which was at $x_1$ at time $t_1$, reached the car navigation system, the pulse from satellite 2, which was at $x_2$ at time $t_2$, also reached the car navigation system at the same time. Furthermore, suppose that the exact values of $t_1$, $x_1$, $t_2$, $x_2$ were also communicated by the respective satellites. However, these coordinates and times are those measured with the ruler and clock on the ground. If the two pulses arrived at time $t$ and the position of the car at that time is $x$, the relations

$$|x-x_1|=c(t-t_1),\qquad |x-x_2|=c(t-t_2) \qquad (6)$$

hold. Solving these equations should give the position $x$ of the car, but to obtain correct information the relativistic correction must also be taken into account. Let us show this. Below, you may restrict yourself to the case $x_1<x<x_2$. Also, in numerical calculations take $v=3.8\times10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ if necessary.

Q13 In GPS, clocks play an important role. Clocks are carried both on the satellites and in the car navigation system. It would then seem acceptable to use the time $t_\mathrm{r}$ measured with the clock of the car navigation system in place of $t$ in one of the two equations (6), and to solve that equation for $x$. To ensure that the value of $x$ obtained in this way does not contain an error of $1\,\mathrm{m}$ or more, the error of the clock of the car navigation system must be at most how many seconds?

Q14 Even electronic clocks have errors of about $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ (millisecond), so one can imagine that making the error of the car navigation clock small, as in the previous question, is very difficult. By contrast, the error of the atomic clocks carried on the satellites is about $1\,\mathrm{ns}$ (nanosecond $=10^{-9}\,\mathrm{s}$). Therefore, solve the two equations (6) and find an expression giving the position $x$ of the car using the information $x_1$, $x_2$, $t_1$, $t_2$ from the satellites and $c$.

Q15 $x_1$, $x_2$ and $t_1$, $t_2$ are quantities measured with the ruler and the clock on the ground, but they are calculated using relativity on the basis of the information sent from each satellite according to its clock and flight plan. Now suppose that the times at which the left and right satellites of Fig. 4 emitted their pulses, and their positions $(t',x')$ at those times, measured with the satellites' clock and ruler, were exactly $(t'_1,0)$ and $(t'_2,L)$, respectively. Express $x$ using $t'_1$, $t'_2$, $L$, $c$ and $v$. Take the relativistic effects into account in the approximate form of Q12.

Q16 Pulses emitted from the satellites at $t'_1=t'_2=0$ arrived at the car navigation system simultaneously. If no relativistic correction were needed, the position of the car navigation system at this time would be $x=\dfrac{L}{2}$. However, the actual position of the car navigation system is not here. For $L=24{,}000\,\mathrm{km}$, by how many m is the position of the car navigation system shifted from the case without the relativistic correction?

The result of Q16 means that, if the relativistic correction were not taken into account when making the software installed in car navigation systems, errors would arise that would be a practical obstacle. Moreover, in actual GPS, the artificial satellites, the car navigation system and the radio waves travelling between them are all affected by the Earth's gravity and by the rotation of the Earth, and so the system is designed to output the correct position by also taking general-relativistic effects into account.

problems.title: Problem 2A
problems.problem:
Problem 2

A (50 points)

The lunar explorer "KAGUYA" was launched on 14 September 2007 under Japan's lunar exploration programme SELENE. After making 2.5 revolutions along an elliptical orbit with the Earth at a focus, "KAGUYA" headed for a lunar orbit. Its first lunar orbit was an elliptical orbit with the Moon at one of its foci. After that, it released sub-satellites on two occasions and settled its own orbit into a circular orbit. The two sub-satellites "OKINA" and "OUNA" each revolve along different elliptical orbits.

First, consider "KAGUYA" revolving along an elliptical orbit with the Earth at a focus.

In order to place the explorer "KAGUYA", launched by a rocket to a certain altitude, into an orbit around the Earth, "KAGUYA" was given a velocity perpendicular to the line segment joining the centre of the Earth and "KAGUYA" (this is called the radius vector). The orbit is determined by the magnitude of this velocity. Letting $M$ be the mass of the Earth, the magnitude $F$ of the universal gravitational force acting between the Earth and "KAGUYA" of mass $m$ is expressed as

$$F=G\frac{Mm}{r^2} \qquad (1)$$

Here, $G$ is the universal gravitational constant and $r$ is the distance from the centre of the Earth to "KAGUYA". The potential energy $U$ of "KAGUYA" for this force, with infinity as the reference, is given by

$$U=-\frac{GMm}{r} \qquad (2)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1:

For describing circular or elliptical motion, it is more convenient to use polar coordinates than $x-y$ coordinates (Cartesian coordinates). We define two-dimensional polar coordinates as follows. As in Fig. 1, the centre of the Earth is taken as the origin O, and the $x$ axis is taken along the major axis of the elliptical orbit of "KAGUYA". Also, the position vector giving the position of "KAGUYA" is $\overrightarrow{r}$ ($|\overrightarrow{r}|=r$), and the angle of $\overrightarrow{r}$ to the $x$ axis is $\phi$ (counterclockwise taken as positive).

In two-dimensional polar coordinates, the coordinate axes are the $r$ coordinate in the radial direction and the $\phi$ coordinate perpendicular to it in the positive direction of $\phi$ (see Fig. 1). The position of "KAGUYA" is then expressed by $(r,\phi)$. As in Fig. 2, if the coordinate components of the velocity of "KAGUYA" moving on the elliptical orbit are $\overrightarrow{v}=(v_r,v_\phi)$, then

$$v_r=\dot{r},\qquad v_\phi=r\dot{\phi}$$

Here the time derivative $\dfrac{dA}{dt}$ of a physical quantity $A$ is written $\dot{A}$. From this, with $|\overrightarrow{v}|=v$,

$$v^2=v_r^2+v_\phi^2=\dot{r}^2+r^2\dot{\phi}^2 \qquad (3)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2:

Therefore, the total mechanical energy $E$ of "KAGUYA", expressed in polar coordinates, is

$$E=\frac{1}{2}mv^2-\frac{GMm}{r}=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{r}^2+\frac{1}{2}mr^2\dot{\phi}^2-\frac{GMm}{r} \qquad (4)$$

Also, in elliptical motion due to universal gravitation, Kepler's three laws of planetary motion hold.
