From Kepler's second law, "the law of constant areal velocity", if the areal velocity is $V_\mathrm{s}$, we can write $V_\mathrm{s}=$ constant. Expressed in polar coordinates, this $V_\mathrm{s}$ is

$$V_\mathrm{s}=\frac{1}{2}rv_\phi=\frac{1}{2}r^2\dot{\phi}=\text{constant} \qquad (5)$$

Here, $\dot{\phi}$ is the angular velocity. Using Eq. (5) to eliminate $\dot{\phi}$ from the total energy equation (4) and rewriting it as an equation with only $r$ and $\dot{r}$ as variables gives

$$E=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{r}^2+\frac{2mV_\mathrm{s}^2}{r^2}-\frac{GMm}{r} \qquad (6)$$

In this way, the total mechanical energy $E$ of "KAGUYA" in elliptical motion has been expressed in terms of $r$ and $\dot{r}$ only.

Solving Eq. (6) for $\dot{r}$ gives

$$\dot{r}^2=\frac{2}{mr^2}\left(Er^2+GMmr-2mV_\mathrm{s}^2\right) \qquad (7)$$

Next, we consider the elliptical orbit in Cartesian coordinates ($x-y$ coordinates).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3:

Using $x-y$ coordinates with the centre of the ellipse as the origin, an ellipse with semi-major axis $a$ and semi-minor axis $b$ is given by

$$\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 \qquad (8)$$

and the geometric relation between the $x-y$ coordinates and the polar coordinates is as in Fig. 3.

In general, for the elliptical orbit of an artificial satellite, the centre of the Earth is at one focus $\mathrm{F_1}$ of the ellipse.

In Eq. (7), motion exists when $\dot{r}^2$ takes a positive value, that is, when $\dot{r}$ is real, so the expression inside the parentheses (  ) on the right-hand side is required to be positive. Since the expression inside (  ) is a quadratic in $r$, the interval of $r$ in which the expression inside (  ) is positive is limited.

Q1 Let $r_1\leqq r\leqq r_2$ be the interval of $r$ in which the expression inside (  ) on the right-hand side of Eq. (7) is positive. Between which points of Fig. 3 are the distances $r_1$ and $r_2$, respectively?

Q2 Derive an expression giving the total mechanical energy $E$ of "KAGUYA" in elliptical motion in terms of the semi-major axis $a$ of the elliptical orbit and $G$, $M$, $m$.

Q3 Express the speed $v_1$ of "KAGUYA" as it passes the perigee (the point closest to the Earth) P in terms of $G$, $M$, $r_1$, $a$.

Q4 Using the constants at the end of the text, find the numerical value of $v_1$ obtained in Q3.

Next, consider "KAGUYA" after it entered an orbit around the Moon. Below, we pay attention only to the Moon and "KAGUYA" and neglect the influence of other celestial bodies. "KAGUYA", which headed from the perigee of its Earth orbit towards a lunar orbit and entered an elliptical lunar orbit, detached the sub-satellite "OKINA" on one elliptical orbit and "OUNA" on the following elliptical orbit, putting each on an elliptical orbit. With the second sub-satellite release, "KAGUYA" itself decelerated and entered a circular orbit around the Moon, and began various measurements such as observation of the lunar surface.

Q5 Letting $R_\mathrm{m}$ be the radius of the Moon and $g_\mathrm{m}$ the gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface, find an expression giving the speed $v_2$ of "KAGUYA" revolving in a circular orbit at altitude $h$ above the lunar surface, in terms of $R_\mathrm{m}$, $g_\mathrm{m}$, $h$.

Q6 Take the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration $g_\mathrm{m}$ on the lunar surface to be $1/6$ of the gravitational acceleration $g$ on the Earth's surface. With $h=100\,\mathrm{km}$, $R_\mathrm{m}=1.74\times10^3\,\mathrm{km}$, find the numerical value of $v_2$ obtained in Q5.

Physical constants

Gravitational acceleration on the Earth's surface: $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

Radius of the Earth: $R=6.38\times10^3\,\mathrm{km}$

(From the SELENE project table)

Mass of "KAGUYA": $m=3.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{kg}$

Altitude above the Earth's surface at the perigee of the Earth-orbiting elliptical orbit of "KAGUYA": $2.8\times10^2\,\mathrm{km}$

Altitude above the Earth's surface at the apogee of the Earth-orbiting elliptical orbit of "KAGUYA": $2.4\times10^5\,\mathrm{km}$

problems.title: Problem 2B
problems.problem:
Problem 2

B (50 points)

The battery invented by Volta in 1800 was to make science develop greatly, because it brought "electric current" to scientists. Twenty years later, Ørsted of the University of Copenhagen discovered that an electric current exerts a force on a magnetic needle, and wrote a short paper in June 1820. This was the beginning of the unification of electricity and magnetism. In September of the same year Ørsted's discovery was reported by Arago at a regular meeting of the French Academy of Sciences, and one week later Ampère announced that between two parallel straight currents there acts an attractive force if they are in the same direction and a repulsive force if they are in opposite directions. Seven weeks later, at the end of October, Biot and Savart clarified and announced the law of the force that a straight current exerts on a magnetic pole.

An outline of the experiment carried out by Biot and Savart is shown in Fig. 1. A current of strength $I$ flows perpendicular to the page in a very long straight wire. AB represents a magnetic needle placed horizontally. The needle is supported at its centre on a pivot and can rotate about it. The mass of the whole needle is $m$ and its length is $2l$. In this problem, "the magnetic needle" always means the same needle. A magnet is placed near this apparatus so as to cancel the influence of the geomagnetic field. They conjectured that "the force acting on a magnetic pole at point P lies in the plane perpendicular to the wire containing point P and points in the tangential direction of a circle centred on the wire. Also, the magnitude of the force is proportional to the strength $I$ of the current and depends on the distance $r$ between the straight current and the magnetic pole." To show clearly that it depends on the distance $r$, we write the magnitude of the force as $F(r)$. When the needle is tilted as in Fig. 1, the distances between the two ends of the needle and the current are $r_\mathrm{A}=\sqrt{r^2+l^2+2rl\sin\theta}$, $r_\mathrm{B}=\sqrt{r^2+l^2-2rl\sin\theta}$, but since $l$ is very small compared with $r$, one may approximate $r_\mathrm{A}=r$, $r_\mathrm{B}=r$. The needle is placed, taking its polarity into account, so that a force $F(r)$ acts at point A and a force $-F(r)$ at point B in the tangential direction of the circle centred on the wire (Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1:

[Label in the figure: 電流 $I$ = current $I$.]

Before the current is switched on, the needle is kept at rest so that it makes a small angle $\theta$ with the direction perpendicular to the wire. If the current is then switched on, the needle will oscillate like a pendulum about point P. Let us find how the period $t$ of this oscillation depends on $m$, $l$, $F(r)$.

Q1 Setting $t=hm^al^b[F(r)]^c$, determine $a$, $b$, $c$ from dimensional considerations and give the expression for $t$. Here $h$ is a dimensionless constant.

(Physical quantities each have fundamental dimensions such as mass [M], length [L], time [T], or combined dimensions such as velocity [LT$^{-1}$] and acceleration [LT$^{-2}$]. From dimensional considerations one can learn what relations hold between physical quantities. For example, consider a pendulum in which a small weight of mass $m$ is suspended by a string of length $l$. The physical quantities involved in this physical system are only $l$, $m$ and the gravitational acceleration $g$, and their dimensions are [L], [M], [LT$^{-2}$]. Since the dimension of the period is [T], the period must be proportional to $\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$. Hence, with $s$ a numerical constant, period $=s\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$ is obtained. This way of thinking is called dimensional analysis.)

Q2 Let $t_2$ be the oscillation period of the needle when the strength of the current is $2I$, and $t_1$ the period when the strength is $I$. Find $\dfrac{t_2}{t_1}$. Assume that the conditions other than the current are the same.

Biot and Savart varied the value of the distance $r$ between the straight current and the magnetic pole, and for each value of $r$ measured the time for 10 periods of the oscillation. Table 1 shows the data they measured.

Table 1: Experimental data of Biot and Savart

$$\begin{array}{c|c} r\ (\mathrm{mm}) & \text{Time for 10 periods, observed value (sec)} \\ \hline 15 & 30.00 \\ 20 & 33.50 \\ 40 & 48.85 \\ 50 & 54.75 \\ 60 & 56.75 \\ 120 & 89.00 \end{array}$$

Q3 Assume $F(r)=ar^n$. Which of the values $n=1,0,-1,-2$ reproduces the data of Table 1 best? Here $a$ is a constant.

From this experiment, it became known "how the force that a straight current $I$ exerts on a magnetic needle at distance $r$ from the straight line depends on $r$", and that "the direction of the force is the tangential direction of a circle centred on the straight current". However, the precision of this experiment is not sufficient. Biot, on the basis of the theory of differential and integral calculus, considered that "the wire consists of elements of small length, and the sum of the small contributions from the elements to the needle is the action of the whole wire on the needle". From physical and mathematical considerations, he assumed one form for the contribution from an infinitesimal element.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2:

[Label in the figure: 電流 $I$ = current $I$.]

As a result, writing $f(r)$ for the magnitude of the force that the part CD in Fig. 2 exerts on a magnetic pole at point P, Biot obtained the following expression for $f(r)$ ($k$ is a constant).

$$f(r)=k\frac{I}{r}\left(-\cos\alpha+\cos\beta\right) \qquad (1)$$

Q4 Based on Eq. (1), express the magnitude $F(r)$ of the force acting on the magnetic needle of Fig. 1 using $k$, $I$, $r$.

Q5 In Fig. 3, the force that the part of the half-line below point M exerts on a magnetic pole at point P is written $G(r)$. Based on Eq. (1), express $G(r)$ using $k$, $I$, $r$, $\theta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3:

[Label in the figure: 電流 $I$ = current $I$.]

To confirm that Eq. (1) is correct, Biot came up with the ingenious method of using a V-shaped current instead of a straight current. He noticed that the force that a V-shaped current exerts on a magnetic pole is equivalent to the force exerted by a straight current with a part missing. A straight current with a part cut off does not exist in reality, but something theoretically equivalent to it is realized by using a V-shaped current.

Q6 Let us write $V(r)$ for the force that the V-shaped current of Fig. 4 exerts on a magnetic pole at point P. Express $V(r)$ using $\alpha$, $i$, $r$ and $k$.

Q7 Express the ratio $\dfrac{t}{t'}$ of the period $t$ when the needle oscillates at point P of Fig. 1 to the period $t'$ when it oscillates at point P of Fig. 4, using the necessary letters among $\alpha$, $i$, $r$, $I$, $k$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4:

[Label in the figure: 電流 $i$ = current $i$.]

Biot varied the strength of the current, the distance between the needle and the current, and the angle of the V-shaped wire in many ways, measured the oscillation periods, and showed that the theory was correct by comparing their ratios with the theoretical values. In the 1820s the existence of charged particles was not yet known, and of course it was not known that an electric current is a flow of charged particles. Since the concept of the magnetic field had not been reached either, for Biot as for the other scientists of the time, the result obtained was a law of the force that a current exerts on a magnetic pole, and not a law of the magnetic field created by a current. Towards the end of the 19th century, the theory of action through a medium (local action) was established: an electric current is a flow of charged particles, a current creates a magnetic field in the surrounding space, and that magnetic field acts on magnetic poles and currents. And so it came to be understood that the Biot–Savart law is in fact the law of the magnetic field created by a current.

problems.title: Problem 3: A mysterious star: the discovery of white dwarfs
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (100 points)

(If necessary for your answers, you may use the values in the table on the last page.)

A mysterious star: the discovery of white dwarfs

The heliocentric theory of Copernicus (1543) was scientifically accepted in the 17th century. However, if the Earth really revolves around the Sun, the Earth changes its position greatly within half a year. Then the direction in which a fixed star is seen should change slightly; this phenomenon is called parallax. Yet even in the 19th century the parallax of fixed stars had not been detected. Bessel observed stars close to the solar system with the aim of measuring this parallax. Specifically, since stars close to the solar system should appear bright, he measured the positions of many bright stars accurately and detected the parallax of a fixed star for the first time. As part of this, he also detected the parallax of Sirius (the brightest star of Canis Major). However, it was found that, besides the parallax, the position of Sirius also wobbles. It was presumed that the cause of the wobbling was an invisible star nearby, i.e. that it was a double star (1844). In 1862 Clark observed Sirius with the most advanced refracting telescope and detected a dark star right next to Sirius. As a result, it was found that the bright one (Sirius A) and the dark one (Sirius B) have about the same surface temperature, but their brightness differs by as much as ten magnitudes. At the same surface temperature, a difference of ten magnitudes in brightness corresponds to the surface areas of the stars differing by a factor of $10^4$. That is, converted to the diameters of the stars, they differ by a factor of 100. On the other hand, from the states of motion of A and B, it was also found that A and B have masses of about the same size. Since A is a star like the Sun and its density is about $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, the density of B is $1\times10^6\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, and it was found to be denser than any substance known at that time. Later it turned out that Sirius B is a white dwarf. Incidentally, the density of pure gold is $19.32\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, and osmium, the densest substance we can touch with our hands, has only $22.57\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The British astronomer Eddington said (1926): "Apart from the point that the result for Sirius is unbelievable, there is physically nothing questionable about it." Now, let us elucidate this unbelievable result.

Motion of particles in the microscopic world: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

The state of a particle such as an electron at a certain time is expressed by the position and the velocity of that particle. In physics, momentum is often used instead of velocity. That is, the state of a particle at a certain time is expressed by the position $\overrightarrow{r}$ and the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$. Here, if for simplicity we consider only one-dimensional motion along the $x$ axis, the state of a particle is expressed by the position $x$ and the momentum $p$. According to quantum mechanics, which deals with the motion of particles of the microscopic world such as electrons, protons and neutrons, the position and the momentum of a particle cannot both be determined precisely at the same time. For example, if the position and momentum of a particle are measured and the position is found to be between $x$ and $x+\delta x$ and the momentum between $p$ and $p+\delta p$, the product of $\delta x$ and $\delta p$ cannot become smaller than a certain value. That is, if the position is determined more precisely (making $\delta x$ smaller), the momentum cannot be determined precisely ($\delta p$ becomes larger), and if the momentum is determined precisely (making $\delta p$ smaller), then the position cannot be determined precisely ($\delta x$ becomes larger). This is a principle of nature derived from Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927), and is not due to technical problems of measurement precision.

A new coordinate system called phase space

Let us consider the concept of "phase space", which represents the state of motion of a particle. Since we are considering the one-dimensional case here, the plane whose horizontal axis represents the position $x$ and whose vertical axis represents the momentum $p$ is the phase space. If the position and momentum of a particle at a certain time are determined, the state of motion of that particle can be represented by a point in phase space. Restating Heisenberg's uncertainty principle mentioned above, one particle in phase space occupies not a point but a certain volume (an area, since it is a plane). Below we restrict ourselves to particles called fermions, such as electrons, protons and neutrons. For fermions, if the width in position is $\delta x$ and the width in momentum is $\delta p$, then, with $h$ the Planck constant, the area $\delta x\,\delta p$ is $h/2$. Moreover, according to the principles of quantum mechanics, the regions in phase space occupied by fermions of the same kind cannot overlap each other. That is, when there are $N$ identical particles, the area they occupy in this phase space is $N\,h/2$. In this way, when many identical particles are considered, they occupy a wide region in phase space. Conversely, a region $\Delta x\Delta p$ in phase space can hold at most $\dfrac{\Delta x\Delta p}{h/2}$ identical particles.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2008-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1: State of phase space at a certain time in the case of one-dimensional motion. In the case of one-dimensional motion, the two-dimensional (planar) coordinate system with $x$ on the horizontal axis and $p$ on the vertical axis is the phase space. The shape of the region occupied by one particle in phase space is indefinite (here, for simplicity, it is shown by figures of 5 kinds), but its volume (here, its area) is constant. The left figure shows a state at low temperature, degenerate. The right figure shows a state at high temperature, not degenerate.

[I]

The degenerate state of electrons

Note that, when we think in terms of momentum instead of velocity, the kinetic energy of a particle of mass $m$ is expressed as $\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$. Now suppose that, in one dimension, $N$ particles (here electrons) are confined in the range $-R\leqq x\leqq R$. Here $N$ is a number much larger than 1, like the Avogadro number. When the temperature is high, the electrons move violently, so the momenta of the electrons are also large, and, as shown on the right of Fig. 1, they are distributed over a wide range in phase space. However, as the temperature decreases, the momenta of the electrons also gradually become smaller. On the other hand, however low the temperature becomes, the area occupied by one electron in phase space is finite, and moreover electrons do not overlap one another in phase space, so the momenta of all the electrons do not become zero; the momentum $p$ completely fills the range from $-p_\mathrm{F}$ to $p_\mathrm{F}$. Here $p_\mathrm{F}$ is called the Fermi momentum. The state in which electrons thus completely fill the region $-p_\mathrm{F}\leqq p\leqq p_\mathrm{F}$ in phase space is called "the electrons are degenerate". This situation is shown on the left of Fig. 1. We now wish to express, for a given $N$, the total kinetic energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ of the degenerate electrons in terms of $R$ and $N$. Let us solve this by following the questions below.

Q1 If the phase space is filled with $N$ electrons, making the magnitudes of the electron momenta as small as possible, the electrons are in the degenerate state. In this case, the electrons completely fill the region $-R\leqq x\leqq R$ on the horizontal axis and $-p_\mathrm{F}\leqq p\leqq p_\mathrm{F}$ on the vertical axis. Show that the maximum momentum $p_\mathrm{F}$ of the electrons is then

$$p_\mathrm{F}=\frac{hN}{8R} \qquad (1)$$

Q2 The kinetic energy does not depend on the position $x$ of an electron and is determined only by the momentum $p$ of the electron. Therefore, regarding $\Delta p$ as sufficiently small, consider the electrons whose momentum in phase space lies between $p$ and $p+\Delta p$ and whose position lies in the region $-R\leqq x\leqq R$; with $m_\mathrm{e}$ the electron mass, they can all be regarded as having the same kinetic energy $\dfrac{p^2}{2m_\mathrm{e}}$. Find the total $\Delta U_\mathrm{d}$ of the kinetic energies of all the electrons contained in this region.

Q3 Next, by summing the kinetic energies over the various momenta $p$, the total kinetic energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ is obtained. That is, $U_\mathrm{d}=\sum\Delta U_\mathrm{d}$. Here, when the sum is turned into an integral, the range of integration is from $-p_\mathrm{F}$ to $p_\mathrm{F}$. Using the above and Eq. (1), find $U_\mathrm{d}$ as a function of $N$ and $R$.

[II]

The degeneracy pressure of electrons

Because of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, electrons become degenerate as the temperature decreases, so however low the temperature is, the total energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ never becomes zero. If, in this situation, the (one-dimensional) volume is compressed by an external force, that is, if $R$ is made smaller, $U_\mathrm{d}$ increases. Since the increase is the work done by the external force, a pressure

$$P=-\frac{dU_\mathrm{d}}{dR} \qquad (2)$$

is acting. This pressure is called the degeneracy pressure of the electrons. Similarly, when a collection of protons is considered, the protons also become degenerate, and a degeneracy pressure arises from this. On the other hand, between different particles such as electrons and protons, the volumes they occupy in phase space can overlap. That is, the degeneracy pressure is a concept that holds only for particles of the same kind, and it is obtained separately for each kind of particle.

Q4 In the case where the temperature is sufficiently low and the electrons and the protons are both degenerate, when a certain volume contains equal numbers of electrons and protons, how many times larger is the degeneracy pressure of the electrons than that of the protons?

[III]

Relativistic or non-relativistic kinetic energy

When the velocity of a particle approaches the speed of light, it is necessary to think in terms of "relativity". By contrast, let us call the case where the velocity of the particle is sufficiently slow compared with the speed of light "non-relativistic".

According to Einstein's relativity, the energy $E$ of a particle is expressed, using the speed of light $c$, the (rest) mass $m$ and the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$, as $E=\sqrt{(mc^2)^2+(pc)^2}$, where $p=|\overrightarrow{p}|$. We shall call the difference between this and the energy $mc^2$ when $\overrightarrow{p}=0$, that is, at rest, the kinetic energy. Written as a formula:

$$\text{kinetic energy}\ =\ E-m\,c^2=\sqrt{(m\,c^2)^2+(p\,c)^2}-m\,c^2$$

In the relativistic case $pc\gg mc^2$ holds, and in the non-relativistic case $pc\ll mc^2$ holds. Also, according to relativity, the velocity of a particle never exceeds the speed of light.

Q5 Show that the kinetic energy of a particle can be approximated as $\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$ in the non-relativistic case and as $pc$ in the relativistic case. If necessary, use the approximation $\sqrt{1+x}\fallingdotseq 1+\dfrac{1}{2}x$ when $|x|\ll1$.

In the non-relativistic case, with $v$ the velocity of the particle, $p=mv$, so the kinetic energy is expressed, as is well known, as $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

[IV]

Degeneracy pressure of electrons in three-dimensional space

Next, on the basis of the one-dimensional example treated in Q1 to Q3, let us consider the three-dimensional case. In this case the phase space is the six-dimensional space formed by the position of the electron $\overrightarrow{r}=(x,\,y,\,z)$ and the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}=(p_x,\,p_y,\,p_z)$. The six-dimensional volume occupied per electron in this phase space is, since the volume with respect to position is $\delta x\,\delta y\,\delta z$ and the volume with respect to momentum is $\delta p_x\,\delta p_y\,\delta p_z$, their product $\delta x\,\delta y\,\delta z\,\delta p_x\,\delta p_y\,\delta p_z$, and this equals $h^3/2$. So, when $N$ electrons are confined in a sphere of radius $R$ and are degenerate, let us express the total kinetic energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ of the electrons in that sphere in terms of $N$ and $R$, following the guided questions below.

On a coefficient to simplify the calculations

In the three-dimensional case, a coefficient $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ appears between the cube of the radius and the volume. Therefore, in the calculations from here on, we introduce the following constant $k$.

$$\begin{array}{rcll} k^3 & \equiv & 2\times\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)^2 & \quad\text{defines } k \\ k & = & 3.274 & \quad\text{is an approximate value} \end{array}$$

Q6 Let us fill the phase space with $N$ electrons, making the magnitudes of the electron momenta as small as possible, so that they are in the degenerate state. In this case they completely fill the region of the inside of a sphere of radius $R$ with respect to the position $\overrightarrow{r}$ (that is, $r\leqq R$) and the inside of a sphere of radius $p_\mathrm{F}$ with respect to the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$ (that is, $p\leqq p_\mathrm{F}$). Here $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$, $p=\sqrt{p_x^2+p_y^2+p_z^2}$. Find the maximum momentum $p_\mathrm{F}$ of the electrons as a function of $N$ and $R$.

Q7 The kinetic energy does not depend on the position $\overrightarrow{r}$ of an electron and is determined only by the magnitude $p$ of the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$ of the electron. Therefore, regarding $\Delta p$ as sufficiently small, consider the electrons whose magnitude of momentum in phase space lies between $p$ and $p+\Delta p$ and whose position lies in the region $r\leqq R$; they can all be regarded as having the same kinetic energy. Note that the volume of this region of phase space can be taken as $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}R^3\,4\,\pi\,p^2\,\Delta p=\dfrac{3}{2}k^3\,R^3\,p^2\,\Delta p$. Referring to Q5, find the total $\Delta U_\mathrm{d}$ of the kinetic energies of all the electrons contained in this region, separately for the non-relativistic case and the relativistic case.

Q8 Next, by summing the kinetic energies over the various magnitudes $p$ of the momentum, the total kinetic energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ is obtained. Here, when the sum is turned into an integral, the range of integration is from 0 to $p_\mathrm{F}$. Using the above and the results of Q6 and Q7, $U_\mathrm{d}$ found as a function of $N$ and $R$ is as follows. For each case, find the exponents $a$, $b$ of $N$ and $R$.

When the kinetic energy is calculated assuming the non-relativistic case:

$$U_\mathrm{d}=\frac{3}{10\,k^2}\,\frac{h^2}{m_\mathrm{e}}\,N^a\,R^b$$

When the kinetic energy is calculated assuming the relativistic case:

$$U_\mathrm{d}=\frac{3}{4\,k}\,h\,c\,N^aR^b$$

[V]

The future of the Sun

The Sun is a typical star in the universe, a sphere of radius $7\times10^8\,\mathrm{m}$, whose central part is in a high-temperature state of as much as $1.4\times10^7\,\mathrm{K}$, where nuclear fusion reactions of hydrogen are taking place. Against gravity, which tries to crush the star, the pressure of the high-temperature gas is sufficiently high, pressure and gravity are balanced, and even now, 5 billion years after its birth, its size and temperature are constant and it shines stably. In the central part of a star at high temperature, hydrogen nuclei (that is, protons) undergo nuclear fusion and are converted into helium nuclei. A large amount of heat energy is released in this process, keeping the star at a high temperature. In the case of the Sun, about 10 billion years after its birth, although following a complicated course, the central part will consist only of helium nuclei, nuclear fusion will stop, energy generation will cease and the temperature will fall. As a result, the pressure will fall and the star will contract because of gravity. Then, how far will it contract? Will it contract without limit? If the contraction stops somewhere, what kind of state will it be in?

The gravitational energy of a star

Now, when a star of uniform density is gradually built up by gathering small masses $\Delta m$, let the mass of the star be $m(r)$ when the radius of the star is $r$, and let us consider the gravitational potential energy of $\Delta m$ (we call this the gravitational energy). With $G$ the universal gravitational constant, when $\Delta m$ is at a distance $x$ ($x\geqq r$) from the centre of the star, the magnitude $F$ of the universal gravitational force acting on $\Delta m$ is as follows.

$$F\ =\ \frac{G\,m(r)\,\Delta m}{x^2}$$

Taking the reference of the gravitational energy at the point at infinity ($x=\infty$), the work $\Delta U_g$ done by an external force against gravity when $\Delta m$ is moved from infinity ($x=\infty$) to the surface of the star ($x=r$) is obtained by integrating $F$ over $x$ as follows.

$$\Delta U_g=\int_\infty^r F\,dx=-\frac{G\,m(r)\,\Delta m}{r}$$

Thus, the gravitational energy of the material $\Delta m$ making up the star is equal to $\Delta U_g$. When the density of the star is uniform, its value is determined by the mass $m(r)$ inside $r$, with $r$ the distance from the centre to $\Delta m$, and is given by the above expression. Let us find, following the questions below, how large the gravitational energy of a star of mass $M$ and radius $R$ (that is, $M=m(R)$) of uniform density is.

Q9 Regarding $\Delta r$ as sufficiently small, if the mass of the material contained in the region of radius from $r$ to $r+\Delta r$ inside the star is $\Delta m$, then its gravitational energy is given by the above expression. Noting that the volume of this region can be taken as $4\,\pi\,r^2\,\Delta r$, find the gravitational energy $\Delta U_g$ of the mass contained in this region using $G$, $M$, $R$, $r$, $\Delta r$.

Q10 Next, by summing over the various radii, the total gravitational energy $U_g$ is obtained. Here, when the sum is turned into an integral, the range of integration is from 0 to $R$. Using the above, find the total gravitational energy $U_g$ of the star using $G$, $M$, $R$.

[VI]

The evolution of stars

Suppose that this star (radius $R$, mass $M$) has uniform density and has converted all its hydrogen into helium by nuclear fusion reactions. Helium consists of neutrons, protons and electrons, in the number ratio $1:1:1$. Neutrons and protons can be regarded as having the same mass, so they are called together nucleons. Electrons are much lighter than nucleons, so the mass of an atom is determined only by the number of nucleons. On the other hand, as seen in Q4, the degeneracy pressure of the electrons is much larger than the degeneracy pressure of the nucleons, so the degeneracy pressure is determined only by the number of electrons. Here, letting $y$ be the ratio of the number of nucleons to the number of electrons, for helium $y=2$. Then, with $m_H$ the nucleon mass, the total number $N$ of electrons contained in the star and the mass $M$ of the star are related by $M=y\,m_H\,N$. Using this relation, the total kinetic energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ due to the degeneracy pressure of the electrons found in Q8 can be expressed using $M$ instead of $N$. When a star of mass $M$ contracts gravitationally, the radius $R$ becomes smaller. The total energy $U$ of the star is the sum of the negative total gravitational energy $U_g$ found in Q10 and the positive total kinetic energy $U_\mathrm{d}$ due to the degeneracy pressure of the electrons found in Q8, so $U=U_g+U_\mathrm{d}$. A contracting star stops contracting and becomes stable where $U$ reaches its minimum value; this stable state is called a white dwarf.

Q11 Assuming that the density inside the white dwarf is uniform and that the behaviour of the electrons is non-relativistic, find its radius and density. In particular, calculate numerically the radius and density if the Sun becomes a white dwarf.

Q12 When a star of mass larger than the Sun contracts to become a white dwarf, its radius becomes smaller and its density higher. As a result, the momenta of the degenerate electrons become larger and enter the relativistic regime. Show that the total energy in the case where all electrons can be regarded as relativistic is proportional to $R^{-1}$. Examine the stability of the star in this case, and explain that, when the mass of the star exceeds a certain value, it does not become a white dwarf but collapses.

Q13 The expression for the kinetic energy of the electrons of a star whose density has become sufficiently high is relativistic. In this case, as examined in the previous question, a star exceeding a certain mass collapses. The limiting mass for the star not to collapse is called, after its discoverer, the Chandrasekhar mass (1930s). Find the Chandrasekhar mass. Also, how many times the solar mass $\mathrm{M_\odot}$ is it?

[VII]

The Chandrasekhar mass

Let us note that, in actual white dwarfs, because $y$ is slightly larger than 2, because the density is not uniform, because not all electrons are relativistic, and so on, the Chandrasekhar mass is slightly smaller than the value calculated here. A star below the Chandrasekhar mass whose density is high and whose expression for the electron momentum is relativistic expands and its density decreases. As a result of the decrease in density, the expression for the electron momentum becomes non-relativistic, and it becomes stable as a white dwarf, as found in Q11. By contrast, in the case of a star above the Chandrasekhar mass, the gravity of the star that has stopped nuclear fusion cannot be supported by the degeneracy pressure of the electrons. Therefore the star contracts further and its density rises. Then the electrons are captured by protons and change into neutrons. In this way, it becomes a neutron star in which all nucleons have become neutrons.

Q14 Applying the discussion so far as it is, consider that, when a star slightly exceeding the Chandrasekhar mass has become a neutron star, all the degenerate neutrons are non-relativistic, and calculate numerically the radius of the neutron star. By contrast, a star slightly lighter than the Chandrasekhar mass becomes a white dwarf. Then, about how many times the radius of the neutron star is the radius of this white dwarf?

Black holes

Thus, when a star like the Sun stops its nuclear fusion reactions and no longer generates heat, it contracts because of gravity. If the mass of the star is about that of the Sun, the electrons become degenerate, their degeneracy pressure stops the contraction, and it becomes a white dwarf. If the mass of the star exceeds the Chandrasekhar mass, the degeneracy pressure of the electrons cannot support gravity, and the electrons are captured by protons and become neutrons. In this way, the neutrons become degenerate, their degeneracy pressure stops the contraction, and it becomes a neutron star. Similarly, if the mass of the star exceeds a certain further value, even the degeneracy pressure of the neutrons can no longer support gravity. In this case, it collapses further and becomes a black hole that swallows everything.

$$\begin{array}{rrcl} \text{Universal gravitational constant} & G & = & 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2} \\ \text{Planck constant} & h & = & 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s} \\ \text{Speed of light} & c & = & 3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s} \\ \text{Electron mass} & m_\mathrm{e} & = & 9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Nucleon (proton, neutron) mass} & m_H & = & 1.67\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}=1830\,m_\mathrm{e} \\ \text{Solar mass} & \mathrm{M_\odot} & = & 1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Solar radius} & \mathrm{R_\odot} & = & 6.96\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (80 points)

There are three forms of heat transfer from a place of high temperature to a place of low temperature: conduction, convection and radiation. Of these, heat transfer by radiation is the flow of energy carried by electromagnetic waves. Since electromagnetic waves propagate even in vacuum, it is also by this flow that solar energy is transmitted to the Earth.

Not only the Sun but every object emits electromagnetic waves from its surface, as long as its temperature is not absolute zero. An object at low temperature emits electromagnetic waves of long wavelength that are invisible to the eye. An object at around $700\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ emits red light. As the temperature rises further, it gradually also begins to emit blue light, and as a result the Sun, whose surface temperature is several thousand degrees, emits white light in which light of the whole visible region is mixed. Such emission of energy determined by the temperature is called thermal radiation.

As a model of the thermal radiation of objects there is what is called black-body radiation or cavity radiation, which contributed to the birth of quantum physics. In this problem, we assume that the radiation emitted by the Sun and by the Earth all has the same properties as black-body radiation.

According to the theory of black-body radiation, the energy radiated per unit time from a portion of area $S$ of an object at temperature (absolute temperature) $T$ is proportional to $S$, so let us write it as $I\times S$. Then $I$ depends only on the temperature $T$ of the object and is proportional to $T^4$. To summarize, the energy radiated per unit time from a portion of area $S$ of the surface of an object at temperature $T$ is

$$IS=\sigma T^4 S .$$

The $\sigma$ on the right-hand side is read "sigma"; $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}$ is called the Stefan–Boltzmann constant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

[Labels in the figure: 地球 = Earth; 太陽光に垂直な半径 $R_\mathrm{E}$ の円盤 = disc of radius $R_\mathrm{E}$ perpendicular to the sunlight.]

[I]

Sunlight, which leaves the Sun radially, is nearly a beam of parallel rays in the vicinity of the Earth, as in Fig. 1. Therefore, letting $R_\mathrm{E}$ be the radius of the Earth (below, the subscript E denotes quantities relating to the Earth), only the light passing through the hatched circle of radius $R_\mathrm{E}$ illuminates the Earth. The energy of sunlight that illuminates, per unit time, a plane of unit area located on the Earth's orbit and perpendicular to the sunlight is nearly constant, apart from small fluctuations, and is therefore called the solar constant. Below, the solar constant is denoted by $J$. As a result of measurements by artificial satellites, the value of $J$ was found to be $1.37\,\mathrm{kW/m^2}$.

Q1. Express the total solar energy illuminating the Earth per unit time using $J$ and $R_\mathrm{E}$. [Hint: Since the altitude of the Sun differs with latitude and time of day, multiplying the solar constant by the surface area of the Earth gives a wrong answer. Answer with reference to Fig. 1.]

Q2. The energy currently consumed by mankind is said to be $1.6\times10^{13}\,\mathrm{J}$ per unit time. Find the ratio of the energy consumed by mankind to the solar energy illuminating the Earth per unit time. Take $R_\mathrm{E}=6400\,\mathrm{km}$, and answer to 1 significant figure.

[II]

Consider a region V in a space through which energy flows by radiation (see Fig. 2). If, per unit time, there is a difference between the energy flowing into this region V from outside and the energy flowing out of it, the energy of the region V increases or decreases. This is because energy is neither created nor destroyed (law of conservation of energy). Conversely, in a state in which the distribution of energy and its flow do not change in time, that is, in a steady state, the amount of energy flowing into the region V per unit time and the amount flowing out of it are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

[Labels in the figure: 流出するエネルギー = outflowing energy; 流入するエネルギー = inflowing energy.]

Q3. Assume that the Sun is a spherical black body of radius $R_\mathrm{S}$ and temperature $T_\mathrm{S}$ (below, the subscript S denotes quantities relating to the Sun). Find the energy $P_\mathrm{S}$ radiated per unit time from the surface of the Sun into space, using $R_\mathrm{S}$ and $T_\mathrm{S}$.

Q4. When the flow of energy is steady, express the energy $P(R)$ flowing outward per unit time through a spherical surface of radius $R$ ($R>R_\mathrm{S}$) concentric with the Sun (see Fig. 3), using $R_\mathrm{S}$ and $T_\mathrm{S}$. Obtain it by comparing the amounts of energy entering and leaving the space between the surface of the Sun and this spherical surface.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

[Label in the figure: 太陽 = Sun.]

Q5. The surface temperature of the Sun is said to be about $6000\,\mathrm{K}$. What value do you estimate for the temperature $T_\mathrm{S}$ of the surface of the Sun from the result of Q4 and the value of the solar constant? Take the mean distance between the Sun and the Earth to be $1.50\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$ and the radius of the Sun to be $6.96\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$. Note that below, whenever a numerical value is asked for, answer to 3 significant figures.

[III]

Of the energy of sunlight reaching the Earth, 30% is reflected by clouds, snow on the ground and so on and escapes into space, 20% is absorbed by the atmosphere, and the rest reaches the Earth's surface (including the sea surface).

Most of the energy reaching the Earth's surface is absorbed by the ground and the sea water and warms them. If that were all, the temperature of the Earth would rise without limit, but at the same time the Earth also emits energy into space by radiation, and the mean temperature of the Earth has been kept constant by the balance between the energy absorbed and the energy emitted per unit time. Let us calculate this temperature, taking various effects into account.

Q6. Assume that the surface temperature of the Earth is uniformly $T_\mathrm{E}$ everywhere and that the Earth is in a constant steady state. If all the energy found in Q1 is absorbed by the Earth and balances the energy radiated by the Earth, what is $T_\mathrm{E}$?

Q7. In reality (as stated above), 30% of the radiant energy from the Sun is reflected and escapes into space. If the rest were all absorbed by the Earth and balanced the radiant energy of the Earth, what would $T_\mathrm{E}$ be?

[IV]

So far we have ignored the temperature changes between day and night, seasonal changes, differences of temperature with latitude, and so on. It is therefore difficult to judge whether the results calculated here are correct. However, it is certain that the temperature obtained in Q7 is considerably lower than the actual mean temperature of the Earth's surface, which is said to be $15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In reality, the surface is warmed by the greenhouse effect due to the atmosphere, clouds and so on, so the temperature of the surface is higher than this.

To consider the greenhouse effect, consider a simple atmospheric model in which around the Earth there is a spherical layer of atmosphere of radius $R_\mathrm{G}$, concentric with the Earth (see Fig. 4; below, the subscript G denotes quantities relating to the atmosphere). This layer absorbs 20% of the radiant energy from the Sun, and absorbs most of the radiant energy from the Earth, which is mainly infrared. Of the energy absorbed by this layer, these two taken together, half is emitted as radiant energy outward into space and half inward, and the latter is absorbed again by the Earth.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-1-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

[Labels in the figure: 地球 = Earth; 大気の層 = layer of atmosphere.]

Q8. Let $P_\mathrm{G}$ be the energy radiated per unit time from the layer of atmosphere towards the Earth. Write an equation, using $R_\mathrm{E}$, $T_\mathrm{E}$, $J$ and $P_\mathrm{G}$, expressing that the energy absorbed by the Earth originating from sunlight and the energy thermally radiated by the Earth are equal.

Q9. Let $a$ $(0\le a\le 1)$ be the fraction of the radiant energy from the Earth to the layer of atmosphere that is absorbed by the layer of atmosphere. Express $T_\mathrm{E}$ as a function of $a$. Since the thickness of the atmosphere is much smaller than the radius of the Earth, take $R_\mathrm{G}=R_\mathrm{E}$.

Q10. The value of $a$ is said to be close to $0.95$. What then is the $T_\mathrm{E}$ calculated with the above model?

In the calculations so far we have ignored the flow of heat into the atmosphere by thermal conduction from the ground and the sea surface, and the flow of heat carried by ocean currents and winds, so we cannot be satisfied with this. In research on climate change due to greenhouse gases, large-scale computer simulations that include all the heat flows in the atmosphere are carried out.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (130 points)

[I]

[Charges and electric fields] A particle carrying electricity is called an electric charge. A space in which a force (other than gravity) acts on a charge at rest is called an electric field. The physical quantity characterizing an electric field is called the electric field vector, which below we denote by $\overrightarrow{E}$. It is defined as the force acting on a charge placed at a point in space divided by the amount of its charge, and it indicates the strength and direction of the electric field at each point. From this definition, a charge of amount $q$ placed at a point where the electric field vector is $\overrightarrow{E}$ is acted on by the force

$$\overrightarrow{F}=q\overrightarrow{E} \qquad (1)$$

Below, for simplicity, the electric field vector is called the electric field.

As a simple example, consider the electric field produced by a charge whose size can be neglected (this is called a point charge). When a point charge $Q$ is in space, the magnitude of the force acting on a point charge $q$ placed at a point P at distance $r$ from it is

$$F=\frac{qQ}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} \qquad (2)$$

and its direction, when $qQ>0$, is the direction from the point charge $Q$ towards $q$ (see Fig. 1(a)). This is called Coulomb's law. Also, $\varepsilon_0$ is a constant called the permittivity of vacuum, and is read "epsilon zero".

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Dividing both sides of equation (2) by $q$, the magnitude of the electric field produced by the charge $Q$ at the point P is expressed as

$$E=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} \qquad (3)$$

Its direction, when $Q>0$, is the direction from the point charge $Q$ towards P (see Fig. 1(b)).

To represent the electric field in space, it is convenient to consider electric field lines. Electric field lines are drawn so that the direction of the tangent at each point on them represents the direction of the electric field vector $\overrightarrow{E}$ at that point, and so that the number of field lines crossing unit area of a surface perpendicular to the field lines is equal to the magnitude $E$ of the electric field. Electric field lines are never created or destroyed in space, except that they originate at positive charges and terminate at negative charges. Also, electric field lines never cross each other.

Q1. The electric field lines leaving a positive charge $Q$ pass through a spherical surface of radius $r$ centred on the charge $Q$, going from the inside to the outside of the sphere. Using the magnitude of the electric field on the spherical surface and the fact that the surface area of a sphere of radius $r$ is $4\pi r^2$, show that the total number of electric field lines leaving the positive charge $Q$ is $\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$.

The above result can be extended to the case in which many point charges are distributed, by superposing the individual point charges and the electric fields they produce. That is, we can say that the total number of electric field lines leaving a charge of amount $Q$ is equal to $\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$ (when $Q$ is negative, $\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$ field lines enter the charge). This is one expression of Gauss's law for the electric field. Here $Q$ may be a point charge, or the charge may be spread out and distributed over some region.

Q2. Charge is uniformly distributed on a straight line with an amount $\lambda$ (read "lambda") per unit length. If the line is infinitely long, the direction of the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ is perpendicular to the line and symmetric about the line taken as an axis. As shown in Fig. 2, consider a cylindrical region of length $L$ centred on the line. If the radius of the cylinder is $r$, what is the total number of electric field lines crossing the side surface of the cylinder? Express it using the magnitude $E$ of the electric field at the surface of the cylinder. Also, what is the charge contained in the cylinder? Express it using $\lambda$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q3. Using the result of Q2 and Gauss's law, "the total number of electric field lines leaving a charge of amount $Q$ is equal to $\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$", find the magnitude $E$ of the electric field at a distance $r$ from the line.

[II]

[Electric currents and magnetic fields] A space in which a force (other than gravity and the force from an electric field) acts on a moving charged particle is called a magnetic field. As the quantity characterizing a magnetic field there is a vector called the magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B}$.

As with electric field lines, there is something called magnetic flux lines that represents the magnetic field. The direction of the tangent at each point on a magnetic flux line represents the direction of the magnetic field at that point. Also, magnetic flux lines are drawn so that the number of flux lines passing through a plane of unit area perpendicular to them equals the magnetic flux density there.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

[Labels in the figure: 電流 = current; 磁場の向き = direction of the magnetic field; 磁束線 = magnetic flux line; 右ネジの進む向き = direction in which the right-handed screw advances; 右ネジの回転の向き = direction of rotation of the right-handed screw.]

Magnetic fields are produced by passing a current through a wire or by using magnets. When a current flows through an infinitely long straight wire, circular magnetic flux lines are formed, centred on the line and perpendicular to it. The direction of the magnetic field is the direction of rotation of a right-handed screw advancing in the direction of the current (see Fig. 3). This is called the right-handed screw rule. If the current is $I$, the magnitude of the magnetic flux density of the magnetic field produced at a place at distance $r$ from it is

$$B=\mu_0\frac{I}{2\pi r}$$

$\mu_0$ is read "mu zero" and is called the permeability of vacuum. Between $\mu_0$, the $\varepsilon_0$ that appeared in equation (3), and the speed of light in vacuum $c$, there is the relation

$$c^2=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0\mu_0} \qquad (4)$$

Now, if a point charge of amount $q$ moves with speed $v$ perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field in a magnetic field whose flux density is uniform in direction and magnitude, this charge receives from the magnetic field a force of magnitude

$$F=qvB \qquad (5)$$

When $q>0$, as shown in Fig. 4(a), if the thumb, index finger and middle finger of the left hand are spread at right angles, and the middle finger is aligned with the direction of the velocity of the charge $q$ and the index finger with the direction of the magnetic flux density, the direction of this force is the direction of the thumb. This force acting on a charge in a magnetic field, together with the force of equation (1) acting in an electric field, is called the Lorentz force.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

[Labels in the figure: 力の向き = direction of the force; 磁場の向き = direction of the magnetic field; 正の点電荷の速度の向き = direction of the velocity of the positive point charge; 電流の向き = direction of the current.]

If charge of amount $\lambda>0$ per unit length is distributed in a wire and moves with a common speed $v$, a current of magnitude

$$I=\lambda v \qquad (6)$$

flows.

Therefore, when a current is passed through a wire placed in a magnetic field, the Lorentz force acts on the charges flowing in it, and as a result the wire experiences a force. When the wire is placed perpendicular to the magnetic field, to find the direction of the force on the wire one may replace the direction of the velocity of the positive charge in Fig. 4(a) by the direction of the current flowing in the wire, as in (b). This rule is called Fleming's left-hand rule.

Q4. A current $I$ flows in a straight wire of length $a$. Show that, when this wire is placed perpendicular to a magnetic flux density of magnitude $B$, the force acting on this wire is $F=BaI$. [Hint: Letting $v$ be the speed of the charges in the wire, first find the amount of charge in the wire.]

Q5. A point charge with positive charge $q$ moves with speed $v$ parallel to a straight current $I$, in the same direction as the current, at distance $r$ from it. What is the force acting on this point charge from the magnetic field produced by $I$? Also, what is its direction?

Q6. As shown in Fig. 5, a uniform magnetic field of flux density of magnitude $B$ is applied perpendicular to the $xy$-plane (from the back of the page towards the front) within the square P'Q'R'S'. A square single-turn coil PQRS of mass $m$ and side length $\ell$, placed in the $xy$-plane, is moving under gravity acting in the positive $x$ direction. QR is parallel to P'S' and is inside the magnetic field, and PS is outside the magnetic field. When a current $I$ flows in the coil from Q towards R, find the force $F$ in the $x$ direction acting on the coil (the sum of the force the current receives from the magnetic field and gravity). Let $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity, and take the sign of the force as positive in the direction of gravity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

[III] and [IV] below are applications of what has been understood so far, and they should be solvable in either order. Solve whichever is easier for you first.

[III]

[Electromagnetic induction and self-induction] Below, we consider the motion of the single-turn coil of Fig. 5. QR and PS are parallel to P'S' (the $y$ direction), and the coil moves in the $xy$-plane with its plane always perpendicular to the magnetic field.

The position coordinate of QR in the $x$ direction is denoted by $x$, and the position of P'S' is $x=0$. Initially the coil was at rest at $x=0$, and it started to move at $t=0$. Below, we consider the subsequent motion of the coil. The current flowing in the coil is zero until $t=0$. Also, below, the electrical resistance of the coil is $0$, and the coil is not deformed by external forces.

The number of magnetic flux lines passing through a single-turn coil placed in a magnetic field is called the magnetic flux through the coil. According to the rule for drawing magnetic flux lines, the magnetic flux $\varPhi_B$ through a coil of area $S$ placed perpendicular to the magnetic field in a magnetic field of uniform flux density $B$ can be calculated as

$$\varPhi_B=BS$$

When a current flows in the coil, magnetic flux lines passing through the coil are produced. Therefore, the current produces a magnetic flux through the coil. The calculation of this magnetic flux $\varPhi_I$ is mathematically complicated, but the result is always proportional to the current flowing in the coil, so it is expressed as

$$\varPhi_I=LI$$

$L$ is a quantity that can be calculated from the shape of the coil alone, and is called the self-inductance of the coil.

When a current flows in a coil placed in a magnetic field, the magnetic flux through this coil is

$$\varPhi=\varPhi_B+\varPhi_I$$

Here the current is taken as positive when the direction in which a right-handed screw, turned in the direction of the current flowing in the coil, advances is the same as the direction of $\overrightarrow{B}$. In the case of Fig. 5, a current flowing in the direction P→Q→R→S is positive. Below we shall also use the sign of the current defined in this way. Then the direction of the current can be expressed by its sign.

When the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a current flows that opposes this change. The electromotive force produced in the coil to drive this current is called the induced electromotive force. When the electrical resistance of the wire is $0$, this current flows so that the magnetic flux $\varPhi_B+\varPhi_I$ through the coil is always constant. In particular, when initially the coil was outside the magnetic field and no current was flowing, so that there was no magnetic flux at all through the coil, the current flows so that, even when magnetic flux is produced, the relation

$$\varPhi_B+\varPhi_I=0 \qquad (7)$$

is maintained.

In the case of Fig. 5, taking into account that the magnetic flux exists only within the area $\ell x$, the relation

$$B\ell x+LI=0 \qquad (8)$$

is derived from (7).

Q7. Using the relation between $I$ and $x$ obtained in equation (8), when the force $F$ found in Q6 is expressed as

$$F=-k(x-x_0)\qquad (k>0) \qquad (9)$$

express $k$ and $x_0$ using $m$, $g$, $\ell$, $B$ and $L$ (not necessarily all of them).

Q8. As long as $x<\ell$ is satisfied, the force expressed by equation (9) acts on the coil, and the coil performs simple harmonic motion with angular frequency $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$. For the case where $x<\ell$ is satisfied, express $x$ as a function of time.

As stated in Q8, if $x<\ell$ is satisfied, the force expressed by equation (9) acts and the coil performs simple harmonic motion; but once $x$ exceeds $\ell$, the whole coil enters the magnetic field, the magnetic flux through the coil becomes constant independent of time ($=B\ell^2$), no induced electromotive force is produced, and the force that the current receives from the magnetic field becomes zero for the coil as a whole. Therefore, once $x$ exceeds $\ell$, the coil falls freely under gravity until QR reaches Q'R'.

Q9. For the coil to perform the simple harmonic motion found in Q8, a certain condition must hold among $m$, $g$, $\ell$, $B$ and $L$. Find this condition.

Q10. When the condition found in Q9 does not hold, QR eventually reaches Q'R'. In what case is the speed of the coil at that time a minimum, and what is this minimum speed $v_m$? Also, for the case in which the speed when QR reached Q'R' was $v_m$, what is the current $I_0$ flowing in the coil at that time?

[IV]

[Electric and magnetic fields and relativity] An electric field is produced around a charged particle. If the charged particle moves with constant velocity, it constitutes a current, so it also produces a magnetic field around it. That is, the electric and magnetic fields produced around a charged particle change with the motion of the charged particle.

Conversely, do the electric and magnetic fields produced by a charged particle look different when seen by an observer at rest relative to the charged particle and by an observer in motion?

To consider this problem, Einstein's special theory of relativity must be used. According to it, a rod whose length was $l$ when at rest relative to an observer appears contracted to a length $\sqrt{1-(v^2/c^2)}\cdot l$ when it moves relative to the observer with a constant speed $v$ along its length (Lorentz contraction).

Q11. Charges move with constant velocity along a straight wire. Let the charge per unit length be $\lambda$ and the speed at which the charges move be $v$. Suppose an observer moving with the charges at speed $v$ looks at this wire. The system of linearly distributed charge of amount $\lambda$ has a length of $1\,\mathrm{m}$ as seen by an observer at rest with the wire, but as seen by an observer moving with the charges, its length is no longer $1\,\mathrm{m}$. This is because, relative to the observer at rest with the wire, those charges were moving with constant speed $v$, and the length of the system in the direction of its velocity must have been Lorentz-contracted. Seen by the observer moving with the charges, that portion is at rest; what is its length?

Q12. From Q11, it can be seen that the amount of charge that was contained in a portion of unit length of the wire at rest is no longer the amount of charge contained in unit length when seen by an observer moving with speed $v$. Seen by the moving observer, what is the amount of charge per unit length?

Q13. A wire at rest carrying a current is electrically neutral. This is because, besides the charges flowing as the current, the wire contains charges of opposite sign fixed in the line, which cancel the charges making up the current. Seen from a frame moving with speed $v$, what does the amount of charge per unit length of the charges fixed in the wire appear to be?

Q14. Seen from the frame moving with speed $v$ together with the charges, this wire appears to be uniformly charged with the sum of the amounts of charge per unit length obtained in Q12 and Q13. Seen by the moving observer, what is the magnitude $E$ of the electric field at a position at distance $r$ from the line?

Q15. The charges fixed in the wire considered in Q13 appear to an observer moving with speed $v$ as a flowing current. What is the magnitude $I$ of this current?

Q16. What is the magnitude $B$ of the magnetic flux density produced by the current of Q15 at a position at distance $r$ from the wire?

Q17. As shown in Fig. 6, suppose that a point charge $q$ was at rest at a position at distance $r$ from the line (this distance does not change when seen by the moving observer). Seen by an observer moving with speed $v$, this point charge appears to move with speed $v$ in the opposite direction. As seen by the moving observer, how is the magnitude $F$ of the Lorentz force acting on this point charge (the sum of the forces due to the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ and the magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B}$) expressed?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

[Label in the figure: 電流 = current.]

The force acting on a point charge $q$ at rest due to an electrically neutral wire at rest carrying a current should be zero. Since the physical phenomenon should not change even if this is viewed by an observer moving with constant velocity together with the current, the point charge should not be accelerated. The results of Q14 and Q16 show that, as seen by an observer moving with the current, an electric field and a magnetic flux density appear that did not exist in the frame at rest relative to the wire, but as a result of both acting on the charge, the physical phenomenon did not change at all. The electric field and magnetic flux density acting on a charge look different depending on the frame from which they are observed; for example, a system in which only an electric field existed becomes, depending on the point of view, a system in which only a magnetic flux density exists. Thus we see that the electric field and the magnetic flux density transform into each other depending on the motion of the observer who looks at them.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (90 points)

[I]

When we hear the word "wave", the first thing that comes to mind is probably waves on water. These waves propagating along the water surface (surface waves) are familiar waves, but they are more complicated than waves on a string or sound waves. Surface waves behave in various ways depending on the conditions; here, let us examine the properties of these surface waves on the basis of some assumptions.

Surface waves are produced by the motion of the medium, water, under gravity. Surface waves are complicated, unlike other waves, because the periodic motion of the medium is two-dimensional. A wave on a string is a transverse wave in which the medium, the string, vibrates perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave. A sound wave propagating in air is a longitudinal wave in which the medium, the air, vibrates parallel to the direction of propagation of the wave. In contrast, in surface waves the motion of the water has both a component parallel and a component perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

Since in surface waves the water surface moves up and down, it is certain that the motion of the water has a component perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave. On the other hand, if you go swimming in the sea and float holding on to a swim ring, you experience being moved towards the shore when floating on the crest of a wave and towards the open sea when floating in the trough of a wave, so it is also certain that there is a motion of the water parallel to the direction of propagation of the wave.

In general, such a motion can be thought of as a motion along an elliptical orbit in a vertical plane, but here let us first assume that the water performs uniform circular motion as in Fig. 1. The wave is assumed to travel to the right with speed $V$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

[Labels in the figure: 波の進行方向 = direction of propagation of the wave; 波がないときの水面 = water surface when there is no wave; 水面 = water surface; 波の速さ $V$ = speed of the wave $V$.]

In Fig. 1(a)–(c), the centre O of the circle shown by the broken line is fixed in space. (a) shows the situation when the trough of the wave has come below O. At this time, the parcel of water that was at the lowest point of the water surface (shown by the black dot) moves clockwise along the circular orbit with time, and eventually comes to the same height as O, as in (b). The surrounding water also rises together with the parcel of water at the black dot. As more time passes, the parcel of water at the black dot reaches the point directly above O, as in (c), and at that time this parcel of water is at the top of the crest of the wave.

Near the surface of surface waves, as shown in Fig. 1(d), the water performs such circular motion everywhere. However, the radius of the circular motion generally becomes smaller as the position of the centre becomes deeper. Such waves occur when the water depth is large compared with the wavelength, and are therefore called deep-water waves.

Suppose that at some moment a wave as shown by the solid line in this figure arrives. Suppose that each of the parcels of water that were at the places on the water surface shown by the black dots then moves, while performing circular motion, to the positions of the white dots. The broken line obtained by joining these white dots is the new water surface of the wave at that time. The water surface of the broken line is the water surface of the solid line translated parallel to the right. Let the radius of the circular orbit be $a$, and let the angle (in radians) through which a parcel of water advances per unit time be $\omega$ (this $\omega$ is called the angular velocity, and its unit is rad/s).

Q1. The period of the wave is the period of the medium performing periodic motion. When the wavelength of the wave is $\lambda$, express the speed $V$ of the wave using $a$, $\omega$ and $\lambda$ (it is not necessary to use all of these quantities).

[II]

In many cases, such as waves on a string and sound waves, the speed of the wave is treated as being determined only by the properties of the medium and as common to all waves of different wavelengths. However, even light, which propagates in vacuum with a common speed regardless of wavelength, changes its speed with wavelength in a medium. The fact that sunlight can be decomposed into a spectrum using a prism is also because the speed of light in glass differs according to its wavelength. The speed of the surface waves that we shall now consider also depends on the wavelength. First, let us derive this relation for deep-water waves.

Let us look at this wave and the circular motion of the water from a coordinate system fixed to the surface wave. This is shown in Fig. 2. In this coordinate system, the water surface is at rest keeping the shape of the wave, but the circular orbits of the water, whose centres were fixed on one horizontal axis as considered so far in Fig. 1, here move to the left with speed $V$. Therefore, the motion of the water in this coordinate system is the superposition of a circular motion of radius $a$ and a translation to the left with speed $V$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

[Labels in the figure: 静止した波のある水面 = water surface with the stationary wave; 円運動の速さ ; $a\omega$ = speed of the circular motion: $a\omega$; 波がないときの水面 = water surface when there is no wave; 水流の速度 = velocity of the water flow; 波の速さ ; $V$ = speed of the wave: $V$.]

The many arrows drawn in Fig. 2 in the directions of the tangents to the circles are the velocity vectors of the circular motion of the parcels of water at the positions of the white dots; since the actual velocity vector of the water is this with a uniform leftward velocity $\overrightarrow{V}$ superposed on it, the velocity vector of the water is tangent to the water surface, as shown by the open arrow attached at $\mathrm{A}_2$. That is, seen in this coordinate system, the water flows along the water surface, meandering up and down.

However, this explanation is valid only when the length of the arrow attached at $\mathrm{A}_5$ at the crest of the wave is shorter than the arrow of $\overrightarrow{V}$. Written as a formula, this condition is $a\omega<V$.

Q2. Let the white dot (small circle) in Fig. 2 be a small parcel of water of mass $\Delta m$. After expressing the speeds of this parcel when it is at the position $\mathrm{A}_1$ and when it is at the position $\mathrm{A}_5$, respectively, using $a$, $\omega$ and $V$, write an equation expressing that the mechanical energies at these two positions are equal, since no external force other than gravity acts on the water. Let $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity.

Q3. Using the result of the previous question, derive the relation between the speed $V$ of the wave and the wavelength.

Q4. Using the result of the previous question, what are the wavelengths expected for a wave of period 5 seconds and a wave of period 10 seconds, respectively? Take the acceleration due to gravity as $g=9.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

A law in physics is a relation between physical quantities. In the case of mechanics, physical quantities have fundamental dimensions such as mass [M], length [L] and time [T], or composite dimensions such as velocity $[\mathrm{LT^{-1}}]$, acceleration $[\mathrm{LT^{-2}}]$ and density $[\mathrm{ML^{-3}}]$, and a quantity $C$ having dimensions of order $p$, $q$ and $r$ in length, time and mass is written $[C]=[\mathrm{L}^p\mathrm{T}^q\mathrm{M}^r]$. Such a relation involving only dimensions is called a dimensional formula or dimensional relation. Using such dimensional relations, it is sometimes possible to derive relations between physical quantities.

Q5. Here, assuming that the speed $V$ of deep-water waves depends only on the density $\rho$ of the moving water, the acceleration due to gravity $g$ that causes the motion, and the wavelength $\lambda$ of the wave produced by the motion, write the dimensional relation as $[V]=[g^p][\lambda^q][\rho^r]$, determine $p$, $q$ and $r$ by rewriting both sides in terms of the fundamental dimensions, and re-derive the result obtained in Q3. If a dimensionless constant appeared in your answer to Q3, compare with that constant set equal to 1.

[III]

So far we have assumed that the water performs circular motion. We have also considered only the motion of the water at the surface. However, under the influence of the bottom, circular motion becomes impossible. For example, if there is a horizontal bottom, near it the water can move only horizontally. Near the water surface, since the surface moves up and down, the vertical motion of the water does not disappear completely, but where the water is shallow we may consider that the water moves approximately only horizontally. Such waves are called shallow-water waves. Now let us consider the properties of shallow-water waves. Real water has a smaller amplitude where it touches the bottom because of friction with the bottom and the viscosity of the water, but here we make the idealization that the viscosity of the water can be neglected. We therefore assume that the water oscillates horizontally in the same way at every depth.

Even for shallow-water waves, we know from the experience of swimming in the sea that the water moves in the direction of propagation of the wave at the crests of the wave and in the direction opposite to the direction of propagation in the troughs. The oscillation at that time is shown in Fig. 3(a). In this figure, the arrows represent velocity vectors. Here too, the wave is assumed to travel to the right with speed $V$.

As in [II], we shall consider the motion of the water in a coordinate system moving with the surface wave. This is shown in Fig. 3(b). Here, the speed of the water at each place is the superposition of what is shown by the arrows in Fig. 3(a) and a translation to the left with speed $V$. Then the water, although its speed differs from place to place, moves to the left; the speed of the water flow at the position A, where the water depth is exactly the mean depth $h$, is $V$, and the speed of the water flow at the position B of the crest of the wave is $(V-v)\ (<V)$ (for the meaning of $v$ see Fig. 3(a)). Below, let the height of the crest and the depth of the trough of the surface wave, measured from the mean water depth, be $a$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

[Labels in the figure: 波がないときの水面 = water surface when there is no wave; 波の速さ $V$ = speed of the wave $V$; 平均の深さ = mean depth.]

Q6. By the law of conservation of mass, the amount of water passing per unit time through any of the vertical cross-sections shown in Fig. 3(b) is equal. Using this condition, express the speed $(V-v)$ of the water at the position B using the speed $V$ at the position A, $a$ and $h$.

Q7. A small parcel of water of mass $\Delta m$ leaves the point A and passes the point B along the surface of the water. Using the fact that the mechanical energies of the parcel of water at these two instants are equal, find an equation giving the relation between the speed $V$ of this wave and the mean water depth $h$. Also, since $(a/h)$ is sufficiently small compared with 1, in the final result neglect $(a/h)^2$ and higher-order terms. If necessary for this, use the fact that, for a number $a$ sufficiently small compared with 1, the approximation $(1+a)^b\simeq 1+ba$ can be made.

Q8. Tsunamis, which are often observed in connection with earthquakes, have wavelengths sufficiently long compared with the water depth and are therefore classified as shallow-water waves. At one time a tsunami with a period of 30 minutes was observed. Find roughly how long the wavelength is then in a sea of depth 4000 metres. In this calculation take the acceleration due to gravity as $g=9.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Q9. When a coastline is viewed from far away, it is observed that the wavefronts of the waves approaching the coast become parallel to the coastline. Make a suitable model of the coastline and of the sea bottom near the coast, and explain the reason for this using the result of Q7.

[IV]

So far we have considered the flow of water near the surface, but when the flow of the water does not change with depth, as in Fig. 3, the same result as before can be derived by considering the energy for the flow near the bottom as well. However, the fact that the pressure of the water differs with the depth below the surface must be used.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2009-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

[Labels in the figure: 波がないときの水面 = water surface when there is no wave; 平均の水深 $h$ = mean water depth $h$.]

As in Fig. 4, consider an imaginary tube AC fixed in the space in which the water is flowing. Here A is below the lowest point of a trough of the surface wave, and C is below the highest point of a crest of the surface wave. The height of the crest and the depth of the trough, measured from the surface of the water at rest when there was no wave, were both $a$. The water entering at A leaves at C, and no water flows in or out through the side of the tube. Such an imaginary tube is called a stream tube.

Suppose that during the time in which water that entered at A reaches B, the water that flowed out of C reaches D. Let the cross-sectional areas of the tube at A and C be $S_\mathrm{A}$ and $S_\mathrm{C}$, respectively, and let the lengths of the tube between A and B and between C and D be $l_\mathrm{AB}$ and $l_\mathrm{CD}$, respectively. Answer the following questions assuming that the density of the water is uniformly $\rho$ everywhere.

Q10. During this time, what is the work done on the water in the tube by the pressure $P_\mathrm{A}$ of the water at the point A? Also, what is the work done by the pressure $P_\mathrm{C}$ at the point C on the water flowing out of the tube?

Q11. If the difference $W$ of the works in the previous question is not 0, it is stored as mechanical energy in the water that was between A and C while this water moves to between B and D. However, since the part between B and C is common, $W$ can be expressed using the energy $E_\mathrm{AB}$ of the water between A and B and the energy $E_\mathrm{CD}$ of the water between C and D. Assuming that the density $\rho$ of the water is constant everywhere, derive the following equation.

$$P_\mathrm{C}+\frac{1}{2}\rho(V-v)^2=P_\mathrm{A}+\frac{1}{2}\rho(V+v)^2$$

Q12. Rewrite $P_\mathrm{A}$ and $P_\mathrm{C}$ using the density of the water $\rho$, the acceleration due to gravity $g$, the mean water depth $h$ and the amplitude of the wave $a$, and re-derive the result of Q7.

We have thus considered two typical behaviours of surface waves: deep-water waves and shallow-water waves. In cases such as ripples, whose wavelength is even shorter, the speed of surface waves differs from the value found for deep-water waves because of the action of the surface tension of the water. The water waves occurring in nature that are most familiar to us contain even more complicated and difficult problems.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (100 points)
