[I] According to Newton's second law of motion, when a force $\overrightarrow{F}$ acts on a body of mass $m$, the body has an acceleration $\overrightarrow{a}=\overrightarrow{F}/m$. Usually this relation is written in the form

$$m\overrightarrow{a}=\overrightarrow{F} \qquad (1)$$

This is the fundamental equation of mechanics and is called the equation of motion. Using this equation, the motion of a body subject to forces can be derived. However, this law does not hold in every coordinate system. A coordinate system in which Newton's laws of motion hold is called an inertial (coordinate) system.

Below, we consider a body that, seen from an inertial system, moves on a circle with constant speed. This motion is called uniform circular motion. The angle through which the body turns per unit time is called the angular velocity; if we denote it by $\omega$ (read "omega"), the angle turned during a time $\varDelta t$ is $\omega\varDelta t$ (see Fig. 1(a)). The unit of angular velocity is $\mathrm{rad/s}$ (radians per second). When $\omega$ is expressed in this unit, the length of the arc $\overset{\frown}{\mathrm{PP'}}$ in Fig. 1(a) is equal to $r\omega\varDelta t$, where $r$ is the radius of the circular motion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Q1. How is the speed $v$ of a body in uniform circular motion with angular velocity $\omega$ on a circle of radius $r$ expressed?

Next, we consider the acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion and the force acting on the body. First, let us find the acceleration of the body in Fig. 1(a).

Q2. A body in uniform circular motion is at point $\mathrm{P}$ at time $t$ and has moved to point $\mathrm{P'}$ at the time $t+\varDelta t$ a short time later. Using the arrows of the velocity vectors at these two times, the arrow representing the change of velocity $\varDelta\overrightarrow{v}$ during $\varDelta t$ can be drawn as in Fig. 1(b). Prove that the magnitude of the acceleration of this body, $a=\dfrac{\varDelta v}{\varDelta t}$, is expressed as

$$a=r\omega^2=\frac{v^2}{r}$$

where $\varDelta v$ is the magnitude of $\varDelta\overrightarrow{v}$. If necessary, use the following approximation, which holds when $b\varDelta t$ is sufficiently small compared with 1, $b$ being an arbitrary constant:

$$\sin(b\varDelta t)\fallingdotseq b\varDelta t$$

As can be seen from the above, the acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion points toward the centre; it is called the centripetal acceleration. Moreover, according to equation (1), a force equal to the product of the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration and the mass acts on the body in the direction of the centre. This force is called the centripetal force. From now on, the acceleration of a body in circular motion and the force acting on the body are taken to be positive when they point toward the centre.

Q3. As in Fig. 2, one end of a spring with spring constant $k$ is fixed at point $\mathrm{O}$, and a small body of mass $m$ is attached to the other end. This body moves uniformly on a circular orbit of radius $r$ centred at point $\mathrm{O}$ with angular velocity $\omega$. Find the extension $l$ of the spring from its natural length.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[Labels in the figure: 円軌道 = circular orbit; 釣り合いの位置 = equilibrium position; 自然長 = natural length.]

[II] As in Fig. 3(a), there is a disc rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ about the origin $\mathrm{O}$ of the inertial system $(x,y)$. Consider the $(x',y')$ coordinate system fixed to this disc. The two coordinate systems share the origin $\mathrm{O}$. When one rides on this disc, the $(x',y')$ coordinate system appears to be at rest.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3

Seen in this $(x',y')$ coordinate system, consider a body of mass $m$ in uniform circular motion with angular velocity $\omega'$ on a circle of radius $r$ centred at the origin (see Fig. 3(b)). This body is connected to the central axis by a spring and receives from the spring an elastic force of magnitude $F$. This elastic force plays the role of the centripetal force.

Q4. Express the centripetal acceleration of this body in the inertial system $(x,y)$ using $\omega$ and $\omega'$, and write the equation of motion in the centripetal (central) direction.

Q5. The equation derived in the previous question is rewritten as

$$ma'=F+F_1+F_2$$

where $a'$ is the centripetal acceleration seen in the $(x',y')$ coordinate system, and $F_1$, $F_2$ are the term proportional to $\omega\omega'$ and the term proportional to $\omega^2$, respectively. Write the expressions for $a'$, $F_1$ and $F_2$.

Q6. Show that when $F_1$ is rewritten using the velocity $v$ of the body seen in the $(x',y')$ coordinate system, it is expressed as

$$F_1=-2mv\omega$$

where the sign of the velocity $v$ is taken positive when the body goes round counterclockwise in the $(x',y')$ coordinate system.

The equation of Q5 above means that in the $(x',y')$ coordinate system fixed to the rotating disc, the equation of motion $ma'=F$, which uses only the elastic force $F$ of the spring acting in the inertial system $(x,y)$, does not hold. A coordinate system in which the equation of motion does not hold is called a non-inertial (coordinate) system. We see that a coordinate system rotating relative to an inertial system, that is, a rotating (coordinate) system, is a non-inertial system.

However, the equation of Q5 means that if $F_1$ and $F_2$ are regarded as special forces that appear in the rotating system, the equation of motion holds even in the non-inertial system. Whereas the real force $F$ is exerted by the spring, there is no other body exerting $F_1$ and $F_2$, and they are forces that do not exist in the inertial system; they are therefore called apparent forces (or inertial forces). In particular, $F_2$, which also acts on a body at rest on the disc, always acts in the direction away from the centre of rotation, as can be seen from its sign, and is called the "centrifugal force". The force $F_1$ proportional to the velocity of the body is called the "Coriolis force".

Here we have considered the special case in which the body moves on a circle centred at $\mathrm{O}$; when a body moves in a general way in a rotating system, the Coriolis force is directed perpendicular to both the direction of the rotation axis and the direction of the velocity: to the right of the direction of the velocity in a counterclockwise rotating system such as the one considered so far, and to the left of the direction of the velocity in a clockwise rotating system.

Q7. The magnitude of the gravity acting on a body of mass $m$ at rest near the Earth's surface is written $mg$, and $g$ is called the gravitational acceleration. Here, gravity means the sum of the universal gravitational attraction between the Earth and the body and the centrifugal force due to the Earth's rotation. By how much is the gravitational acceleration at the equator smaller than at the poles, owing to the centrifugal force due to the rotation? Assume that the Earth is a sphere of radius $6400\,\mathrm{km}$.

[III] We on the Earth rotate together with the Earth's rotation. At a point of latitude $\theta$ in the northern hemisphere, consider the coordinate system with the $z$ axis along the vertical, the $x$ axis eastward in the horizontal plane and the $y$ axis northward. As the Earth rotates, not only does the origin of this coordinate system move, but the directions of the $x, y, z$ axes also change. When the Earth makes one rotation and the origin passes through $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$, $\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{D}$ and returns to the original point $\mathrm{A}$, the direction of the $y$ axis changes from the direction of $\mathrm{AP}$ in Fig. 4(a), through the directions of $\mathrm{BP}$, $\mathrm{CP}$, $\mathrm{DP}$, and returns again to the direction of $\mathrm{AP}$. Now, if the lateral surface of the cone with base $\mathrm{ABCDA}$ and apex $\mathrm{P}$ is cut along $\mathrm{AP}$ and unrolled, it becomes as in Fig. 4(b). $\mathrm{A'}$ in the development corresponds to the position of $\mathrm{A}$ before unrolling. When the Earth has made one rotation, the $y$ axis has turned about the $z$ axis from the direction of $\mathrm{AP}$ to the direction of $\mathrm{A'P}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig4.png

Fig. 4

Q8. When the Earth makes one rotation, that is, when it turns through the angle $2\pi$, the angle of rotation about the $z$ axis of the $y$ direction of the coordinate system fixed at the point of latitude $\theta$ is equal to the angle $\alpha=\angle\mathrm{APA'}$ in Fig. 4(b). From this, show that, if the angular velocity of the Earth's rotation is $\omega$, the angular velocity $\omega'$ about the vertical axis ($z$ axis) of the coordinate system fixed at the point of latitude $\theta$ is given by

$$\omega'=\omega\sin\theta$$

On a body moving horizontally with speed $v$ at a point of latitude $\theta$, the Coriolis force of the rotating system with angular velocity $\omega'$ acts in the horizontal plane perpendicular to the velocity (in the northern hemisphere, to the right of the direction of motion). Since the Coriolis force is small compared with gravity, it may be neglected when dealing with the motion of ordinary bodies, but it plays an important role when dealing with the motion of the atmosphere. According to a more detailed theory, the Coriolis force acting on a horizontally moving body in general also has a vertical component, but this does not matter when dealing with the horizontal motion of the atmosphere.

Suppose that the atmospheric pressure $p$ increases uniformly in the $x$ direction. If only the force produced by the pressure gradient (the pressure gradient force) is considered, the air flows from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side. However, since the Coriolis force always acts to the right of the air flow, the steady air flow arises parallel to the isobars, with the high pressure on the right-hand side. Such an air flow is called the geostrophic wind (see Fig. 5). Here, the effect of the friction that the air receives from the ground is not considered. Below, the density of the air is $\rho$ (read "rho").

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig5.png

Fig. 5

[Labels in the figure: 風速 $v$ = wind speed $v$; 気圧傾度力 = pressure gradient force; コリオリの力 = Coriolis force; 等圧線 $p_1$ = isobar $p_1$; 等圧線 $p_2\,(>p_1)$ = isobar $p_2\,(>p_1)$.]

Q9. Show that the pressure gradient force $f$ acting on the air per unit volume is expressed as

$$f=-\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta x}\fallingdotseq-\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}x}$$

Refer to Fig. 6 below. The minus sign means that the direction of the force is the direction in which the pressure decreases.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig6.png

Fig. 6

[Label in the figure: 面積 $S$ = area $S$.]

Q10. The magnitude of the Coriolis force acting on air moving with wind speed $v$ at latitude $\theta$ is $2\rho\omega v\sin\theta$ per unit volume. From the condition of balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force acting on the air, express the wind speed $v$ of the geostrophic wind at latitude $\theta$ using the magnitude of the pressure gradient $\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}x}\right|$, the density of the air $\rho$ and the angular velocity of the Earth's rotation $\omega$. The density of the air $\rho$ may be treated as constant. You need not consider the region near the equator, where $\sin\theta$ becomes 0.

Q11. At latitude $35^\circ$ north, when the gradient of the atmospheric pressure is $1\,\mathrm{hPa}/100\,\mathrm{km}$, calculate the wind speed of the geostrophic wind. Take the density of the air as $\rho=1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. ($1\,\mathrm{hPa}=100\,\mathrm{Pa}$)

Near the ground surface, the air receives a resistive force due to friction with the ground, so, as shown in Fig. 7, the steady wind direction is deflected toward the side of lower pressure. In this case the three forces, the pressure gradient force, the Coriolis force and the resistive force, are in balance.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig7.png

Fig. 7

[Labels in the figure: 風速 = wind speed; 気圧傾度力 = pressure gradient force; コリオリの力 = Coriolis force; 抵抗力 = resistive force; 等圧線 $p_1$ = isobar $p_1$; 等圧線 $p_2\,(>p_1)$ = isobar $p_2\,(>p_1)$.]

Next, suppose that the atmospheric pressure is axially symmetric about a fixed axis perpendicular to the ground surface and changes monotonically with the distance from the centre, and that the air moves steadily in the horizontal plane along a circle of radius $r$ about the centre with speed $v$. This is a model of a high-pressure system when $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}r}<0$ and of a low-pressure system when $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}r}>0$. Considering the direction of the geostrophic wind, in the case of a high-pressure system the air flows clockwise along the isobars, and in the case of a low-pressure system counterclockwise along the isobars. Such a wind is called the gradient wind.

Q12. Considering that, per unit volume of air, the difference between the pressure gradient force $\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}r}\right|$ and the Coriolis force $2\rho\omega v\sin\theta$ provides the centripetal force $\dfrac{\rho v^2}{r}$ of the circular motion, express the speed of the air flow (wind speed) $v$, for the high-pressure and for the low-pressure case respectively, using $r$ and $\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}r}\right|$ (see Fig. 8). Solving the quadratic equation in $v$ gives two solutions; adopt the one for which $v=0$ when $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}r}=0$. The density of the air $\rho$ may be treated as constant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-1-fig8.png

Fig. 8

[Labels in the figure: (a) 高気圧の場合 = (a) case of a high-pressure system; (b) 低気圧の場合 = (b) case of a low-pressure system; 高 = high; 低 = low; コリオリの力 = Coriolis force; 気圧傾度力 = pressure gradient force; 風向 = wind direction.]

Q13. From this result, explain why it is impossible for a high-pressure system that the pressure gradient toward the centre becomes very large and brings violent strong winds, as happens in a typhoon, which is a kind of developed low-pressure system.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (100 points)

(The numerical values of physical quantities that appear in common in many questions of Problem 2 are collected at the end of Problem 2; refer to them and use them if necessary.)

[I] Mechanics of charged particles

Viewed microscopically, matter consists of atoms, and an atom consists of one nucleus at the centre and the electrons surrounding it. Among these, the electron has remained the leading actor in the study of electrical phenomena ever since its discovery by J.J. Thomson a little over 100 years ago. Here, centring on the electron, let us consider problems related to electrical phenomena.

The charge of the electron is negative, while the charge of the proton in the nucleus is positive; since an atom contains equal numbers of positive and negative charges, electrical neutrality is maintained in matter, which is an assembly of atoms. The amounts of charge carried by the electron and the proton are $-e$ and $+e$, respectively. The $e$ appearing here is called the elementary charge, and

$$e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$$

The $\mathrm{C}$ on the right-hand side is the unit of charge, read "coulomb". In nature, normally, no charge with absolute value smaller than $e$ exists. The mass of the electron $m_{\mathrm{e}}$ is very small compared with the mass of the proton $M_{\mathrm{p}}$, only about $1/1800$ of it.

Between two point charges, a repulsive force acts if their charges have the same sign, and an attractive force if they have opposite signs. This force is called the Coulomb force; if the charges of the two point charges are $Q$, $q$ and the distance between the charges is $r$, its magnitude is given by

$$F=k\frac{Qq}{r^2} \qquad (1)$$

(Coulomb's law). Here $F>0$ represents a repulsive force and $F<0$ an attractive force. $k$ is a proportionality constant, called the Coulomb constant.

For practical electricity used by us, the current $1\,\mathrm{A}$ is defined as an SI base unit. The amount of charge passing through one cross-section of a wire carrying a current of $1\,\mathrm{A}$ in $1\,\mathrm{s}$ is $1\,\mathrm{C}$. In electrostatic phenomena the amount of charge $1\,\mathrm{C}$ is very large: the magnitude $F$ of the force acting between point charges of $1\,\mathrm{C}$ separated by $1\,\mathrm{m}$ is about $9.0\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{N}$, and this force corresponds to the force needed to lift a body of mass 900 thousand tonnes.

Q1. In a hydrogen atom, the proton and the electron attract each other. The distance between the two in a stable hydrogen atom is about $5\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}$. With how large a Coulomb force do the proton and the electron attract each other?

Q2. The magnitude $F_{\mathrm{G}}$ of the universal gravitational force acting between the proton and the electron of a hydrogen atom can be written, with the gravitational constant $G$, as

$$F_{\mathrm{G}}=G\frac{m_{\mathrm{e}}M_{\mathrm{p}}}{r^2} \qquad (2)$$

Find the magnitude of this force and find its ratio to the magnitude of the Coulomb force found in Q1.

Now, suppose that there is a point charge $Q$ at some point; then a Coulomb force from the point charge $Q$ acts on another point charge $q$ around it. Since no such force acts on $q$ if the charge $Q$ is absent, we can consider that a space producing such an electric force is created by the charge $Q$. This space is called the "electric field". The strength $E$ of the electric field at a point is defined so that the force acting on a point charge $q$ placed at that point is expressed as $F=qE$. Setting the magnitude $F$ of the Coulomb force given by equation (1) equal to $qE$, the magnitude $E$ of the electric field at a distance $r$ from the charge $Q$ is

$$E=k\frac{Q}{r^2} \qquad (3)$$

Note that, since the Coulomb force is a vector quantity, the resulting electric field is also a vector quantity. When this electric field is introduced, we consider that the point charge $q$ receives the force of equation (1) from the electric field created by the point charge $Q$.

By the way, when a body moves near the Earth's surface with some speed, in general both the speed and the height change with time, yet there is a law that the mechanical energy, defined as the sum of the kinetic energy, proportional to the square of the speed, and the potential energy, expressed as a function of the height only, is constant. This is called the law of conservation of mechanical energy, and the same law holds also for a charged particle moving in an electric field. However, since the nature of the force acting changes, the form of the potential energy also changes. Let us derive the law of conservation of energy of a charged particle in an electric field.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1

As in Fig. 1, a point charge $Q$ is fixed at the origin of coordinates. Now we perform the hypothetical experiment of holding a particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ at rest at a point $\mathrm{A}$ at distance $r$ from the origin and then releasing it. Fig. 1 is the case of a repulsive force ($qQ>0$). Then the point charge $q$ receives from the electric field a Coulomb force in the direction of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OA}}$. When the point charge $q$ moves through a small distance $\varDelta r$, the work done on it can be written $qE\varDelta r$ using the strength $E$ of the electric field. Therefore, the work $W$ done by the force from the electric field while the point charge $q$ moves from point $\mathrm{A}$ in Fig. 1 to point $\mathrm{B}$ at distance $r'$ from the origin can be expressed and calculated using an integral as follows:

$$W=\int_r^{r'}qE(r)dr\ =\ \int_r^{r'}k\frac{Qq}{r^2}dr\ =\ kQq\left(\frac{1}{r}\ -\ \frac{1}{r'}\right) \qquad (4)$$

Fig. 1 shows the case of a repulsive force ($Qq>0$) with $r'>r$, but the calculation of equation (4) gives the correct result regardless of the signs of the charges $Q$ and $q$, and regardless of which of $r'$ and $r$ is larger.

In general, when work is done on a body, it gains kinetic energy equal to the work $W$ done. Therefore, while the point charge $q$ of Fig. 1 moves from point $\mathrm{A}$ to point $\mathrm{B}$, its kinetic energy also increases by the amount calculated by equation (4).

Q3. Calculate the kinetic energy that a particle released gently at point $\mathrm{A}$ has when it passes point $\mathrm{B}$, and find the speed of the particle at that time. Also, state the condition for $r'>r$ and the condition for $r'<r$.

In deriving equation (4) we have, for simplicity, considered the case in which the charged particle $q$ moves along a straight line through the origin; according to a detailed analysis, when the charged particle $q$, subject to the Coulomb force from the charge $Q$ fixed at the origin, changes from the position at distance $r$ from the origin to the position at $r'$, the work done on the particle by the Coulomb force is given by equation (4) independently of the path in between. This means that the work does not depend on the intermediate path but is determined only by the initial and final positions, and it guarantees that a potential energy can be defined.

Q4. Suppose that initially this particle had speed $v_1$ at the position at distance $r_1$ from the origin, and that, subject to the Coulomb force from the charge $Q$ at the origin, it moved to the position at distance $r_2$ from the origin, where its speed became $v_2$. Find the relation between the speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$. Also, denoting the potential energy by $V(r_1)$ at the initial position and by $V(r_2)$ at the final position, define the potential energy $V(r)$ from the fact that the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particle is conserved. Make the potential energy equal to 0 at the position at distance $r_0$ from the origin.

A force for which, as in the case of this Coulomb force, a potential energy can be defined and the law of conservation of mechanical energy holds is called a conservative force. Not all forces are conservative forces. The universal gravitational force expressed by equation (2) is also a conservative force; this is because, like the Coulomb force, it acts along the straight line joining the two particles and is a function of the distance between them only. The frictional force and the like are examples of forces that are not conservative.

$V(r)$ introduced in Q4 divided by $q$, that is, the potential energy per unit charge, is called the electric potential at the position at distance $r$ from the origin. When many charges create an electric field, the sum of the electric potentials due to the individual charges is the electric potential created by the set of charges.

The difference of the electric potentials of two places is called the voltage between these two points, and its unit is $\mathrm{V}$ (volt). The kinetic energy gained by an electron when it is accelerated through a voltage of $1\,\mathrm{V}$ is called 1 electronvolt and written $1\,\mathrm{eV}$. $1\,\mathrm{eV}\ =\ 1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

[II] Motion of electrons in a metal (1)

Among substances, which are assemblies of atoms, those that conduct electricity easily are called conductors. Metals are typical conductors. A metal is filled with so-called free electrons, which are not bound to atoms. When a voltage is applied across the two ends of a metal wire, an electric field arises in the wire, and it produces a flow of free electrons. This is the electric current. Let us examine the relation between this current and the voltage.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[Labels in the figure: 電流 $I$ = current $I$; 電圧 $V$ = voltage $V$.]

As in Fig. 2, consider the case in which a voltage $V$ is applied across the two ends of a wire of cross-sectional area $S$ and length $L$ and a current of magnitude $I$ flows. The number per unit volume of free electrons that flow as the current is denoted $n$ and called the number density. Its product with the charge $(-e)$ of one electron, $(-en)$, represents the charge per unit volume, that is, the charge density of the electrons. Let us consider that these free electrons all move with the same velocity $v_{\mathrm{D}}$ (called the drift velocity). Note that, for a flow of negatively charged particles, the direction of the drift velocity is opposite to the direction of the current $I$.

The charged particles that passed at some moment through the cross-section $\mathrm{A}$ shown hatched in Fig. 2 reach, after a time $\varDelta t$, the cross-section $\mathrm{B}$ at a distance $v_{\mathrm{D}}\varDelta t$. Therefore, the charged particles that passed through the cross-section $\mathrm{A}$ during this $\varDelta t$ are between $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$. Multiplying the volume $Sv_{\mathrm{D}}\varDelta t$ of the cylinder $\mathrm{AB}$ by the charge density $(-en)$ and dividing by $\varDelta t$, we obtain the charge $(-e)nv_{\mathrm{D}}S$ passing through the cross-section $\mathrm{A}$ from left to right per unit time. The strength of the current $I$ flowing from right to left in the wire is obtained by reversing this sign:

$$I=env_{\mathrm{D}}S \qquad (5)$$

In the metal there are also positive ions, left behind after emitting these electrons, in a number that neutralizes the negative charge of the electrons, but these are taken to be immobile.

For a wire of length $L$ and cross-sectional area $S$, the magnitude $R$ of the resistance of the wire is given by

$$R=\frac{\rho L}{S} \qquad (6)$$

Here $\rho$ (read "rho") is the electrical resistivity, which differs with the material of the wire and changes with temperature. The unit of electrical resistivity is $\Omega\mathrm{m}$ ($\Omega$ is the unit of electrical resistance, the ohm). When the temperature rises, the thermal vibrations of the atoms and ions that make up the wire become intense and restrict the motion of the free electrons, so the electrical resistivity increases. Its temperature dependence near room temperature is expressed as

$$\rho=\rho_0\,(1+at) \qquad (7)$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the resistivity at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $t$ is the Celsius temperature, and $a$ is the temperature coefficient of the resistivity, with unit $1/^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In the case of an incandescent light bulb, when the voltage is raised the current flowing in the tungsten filament increases, heat is generated and the filament becomes hot, so the resistance increases together with the current.

Q5. At room temperature $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$, a voltage of $1\,\mathrm{V}$ was applied to a copper wire of cross-sectional area $0.173\,\mathrm{mm^2}$ and length $10\,\mathrm{m}$, and a current was passed. Calculate the drift velocity $v_{\mathrm{D}}$ of the electrons in this case. The resistivity of copper at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $\rho_0=1.55\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\mathrm{m}$ and its temperature coefficient is $a=4.3\times10^{-3}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$. [Note also the relation $T\,[\mathrm{K}]=273+t\,[^\circ\mathrm{C}]$ between absolute temperature and Celsius temperature. The number density of free electrons in copper is given on page 14.]

Next, let us consider the electrical resistivity $\rho$ from the standpoint of the mechanics of the metal electrons. When a voltage $V$ is applied across the two ends of a wire of length $L$, a uniform electric field of magnitude $E=\dfrac{V}{L}$ arises in the conductor. A free electron of charge $(-e)$ moving in this wire receives from the electric field a force of magnitude $eE\ \left(=\dfrac{eV}{L}\right)$ in the direction opposite to the field and is accelerated. On the other hand, on an electron that has been accelerated and acquired the drift velocity, a resistive force opposite to the drift velocity acts, due to the thermal vibrations of the ions, impurity ions present in small amounts, and so on. Through the balance of these two forces, the electrons move with a constant drift velocity $v_{\mathrm{D}}$ in the direction opposite to the electric field. The magnitude of the resistive force acting in this case is expressed, with a proportionality coefficient $\gamma$ (called the resistance coefficient), as $\gamma mv_{\mathrm{D}}$. This way of thinking about electrical conduction in metals was proposed by Drude more than 100 years ago.

Q6. From the condition of balance between the force on an electron in the wire due to the electric field and the resistive force described above, express the drift velocity $v_{\mathrm{D}}$ of the electrons using the mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, the charge $e$, the resistance coefficient $\gamma$ and the electric field $E$.

Q7. From the above, express the electrical resistivity $\rho$ of the conductor using $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, $e$, $n$, $\gamma$.

So far we have considered that all the electrons move with a common velocity $v_{\mathrm{D}}$, but in reality all the electrons move around in the metal with various velocities. However, when there is no electric field, electrons moving in any direction exist in equal proportions, and the vector sum of the electron velocities is 0, so no net flow arises. When an electric field is applied, however, the number of electrons with velocities opposite to the electric field increases slightly, and the average value of the electron velocities remains as a nonzero value. This average value of the velocity is the drift velocity.

Owing to quantum effects, this motion of the electrons does not vanish even at $T=0\,\mathrm{K}$. In a typical metal, the average kinetic energy of these free electrons is of the order of several $\mathrm{eV}$. On the other hand, if the free electrons are treated by classical theory, their average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature, and its value even at room temperature ($300\,\mathrm{K}$) is of the order of $10^{-2}\,\mathrm{eV}$, about 2 orders of magnitude smaller than the value for the free electrons of a typical metal. Thus the behaviour of the free electrons of a metal, which obey quantum theory, is completely different from the case in which they are assumed to obey classical theory.

Q8. The average kinetic energy of the free electrons of copper is $4.2\,\mathrm{eV}$. Find the speed of an electron having this average kinetic energy. Also, find the ratio of the drift velocity $v_{\mathrm{D}}$ found in Q5 to this electron speed.

[III] Motion of electrons in a metal (2)

When charges $\pm Q$ are distributed uniformly on two sufficiently wide parallel plates of equal area $S$ placed a distance $d$ apart in vacuum, a uniform electric field $E$ perpendicular to the planes is produced between the two planes. Its magnitude, when the separation $d$ is sufficiently small, is independent of $d$:

$$E=\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 S} \qquad (8)$$

Here $\varepsilon_0$ is a constant expressed, using the proportionality constant $k$ that appeared in Coulomb's law, as $\varepsilon_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi k}$, and is called the permittivity of vacuum.

Now suppose that, for some reason, the group of free electrons in a metal undergoes all at once a small equal displacement in the $x$-direction relative to the group of positive ions of the host. Then, as in Fig. 3, a negatively charged layer consisting only of electrons forms at the right end of the metal, and a positively charged layer consisting only of positive ions lacking electrons forms at the left end.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[Labels in the figure: 電場 = electric field; 正電荷 = positive charge; 負電荷 = negative charge.]

Q9. Denoting the displacement of the electrons by $x$, the cross-sectional area perpendicular to it by $S$, and the number density of free electrons in the metal by $n$, show that the charge produced at the right end is $Q=-enxS$.

The positive ions are fixed in space, and only the free electrons move. In this case, as shown in Fig. 3, charges $\pm Q$ face each other like flat plates at the two ends. Therefore, in this state a uniform electric field $E=-\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 S}$ is produced in the metal. Its direction is the direction shown in Fig. 3; each electron of the group of free electrons receives the force $F=-eE$ due to this electric field, is accelerated from right to left, and tends to return to the original equilibrium position before the displacement. However, since the electrons have inertia, they overshoot the equilibrium position, and this time a negatively charged layer consisting only of free electrons forms at the left end and a positively charged layer lacking electrons forms at the right end. In this state the signs of the plate-like charges on the left and right are reversed and the direction of the internal electric field is also reversed, so this time the group of electrons is accelerated in the opposite direction (from left to right) and returns again to the initial displacement. In this way the group of free electrons oscillates about the equilibrium position. This oscillation is called the plasma oscillation, and its angular frequency is called the plasma angular frequency. In various oscillation phenomena both the frequency $f$ and the angular frequency $\omega$ are used; between them there is the relation $\omega=2\pi f$.

Q10. Show that the equation of motion of an electron performing plasma oscillation in a metal is

$$m_{\mathrm{e}}\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0}x$$

Using the displacement $x$ of the electron, the acceleration of the electron is expressed as $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$.

Q11. The solution of the equation of motion found in Q10 is written $x=A\sin\omega_{\mathrm{P}}t+B\cos\omega_{\mathrm{P}}t$ ($A$, $B$ are constants). This $\omega_{\mathrm{P}}$ is the plasma angular frequency. Express $\omega_{\mathrm{P}}$ using $e$, $n$, $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, $\varepsilon_0$. You may use the relations

$$\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\sin(ax)=-a^2\sin(ax),\qquad \frac{d^2}{dx^2}\cos(ax)\ =\ -a^2\cos(ax)$$

Q12. What is the plasma angular frequency of the free electrons of copper?

Usually, since the plasma oscillation is a sufficiently fast oscillation of the electron group, the motion of the heavy ions and the effect of scattering by the ions described in [II] may be neglected. However, if left alone, the oscillation of the electron group eventually stops owing to the electrical resistance, and the system returns to a spatially uniform equilibrium state.

Up to here we have considered only the electric field produced by the displacement of the free electrons inside the metal; here we consider what happens when an oscillating electric field reaches the metal surface from outside. When a static electric field is applied to a metal, electrostatic induction occurs so that no static electric field can exist inside the metal, and the electric field cannot penetrate from the metal surface into the interior. Likewise, an oscillating electric field of sufficiently low frequency cannot enter the interior of the metal either. On the other hand, when an oscillating electric field of very high frequency is applied, the free electrons, because of their inertia, cannot follow the oscillating field and remain almost at rest. Therefore such an oscillating electric field passes through the interior of the metal almost unaffected by the free electrons.

According to a detailed calculation, an electromagnetic wave with angular frequency smaller than the plasma angular frequency is reflected at the surface of the metal, and an electromagnetic wave with angular frequency larger than the plasma angular frequency enters the metal.

Q13. The plasma angular frequency of a typical metal is larger than $10^{16}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Find the wavelength in vacuum of an electromagnetic wave of angular frequency $10^{16}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

Q14. Why do metals have lustre? Answer with the wavelength range of visible light in mind.

Reference data

1. Elementary charge: $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$

2. Masses of the electron and the proton: $m_{\mathrm{e}}=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\quad M_{\mathrm{p}}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$

3. Coulomb constant: $k=9.0\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{Nm^2/C^2}$

Permittivity of vacuum: $\varepsilon_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi k}=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2/Nm^2}$

4. $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$

5. Number density of free electrons in copper: $n=8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$

6. Wavelength range of visible light: $\lambda=3.8\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}\sim7.8\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$

7. Speed of light in vacuum: $c_0=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$

8. Gravitational constant: $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{Nm^2/kg^2}$

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (100 points)

It is known that light is an electromagnetic wave that propagates through the coupled oscillations of an electric field and a magnetic field. An electromagnetic wave travelling in free space is a transverse wave in which the electric field and the magnetic field oscillate in mutually perpendicular directions and which travels through space perpendicular to both. The speed at which the crests and troughs (wavefronts) of the oscillations of the electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave move is constant in vacuum, independent of the frequency or wavelength (that is, the colour of the light), and its value is about $3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

In isotropic substances such as water and air, electromagnetic waves propagate in the same way as in vacuum, but the velocity at which the wavefronts of light move in a substance (the velocity of light) $c$ depends on the frequency and differs from substance to substance. The reciprocal of the ratio of the speed of light $c$ in a substance to the speed of light in vacuum $c_0$ is the refractive index $n=\dfrac{c_0}{c}$, an important physical quantity that determines the propagation of light. In ordinary media the refractive index is positive. However, by making full use of recent nanotechnology, it is possible to make transparent media with a negative refractive index ($n<0$). Such artificial optical materials are called metamaterials, and the propagation of light in them behaves peculiarly compared with the case of media with a positive refractive index. In a metamaterial, the direction in which the wavefronts of light move is opposite to the direction in which the energy of the light is transmitted. This means that, if the direction in which the energy of the light propagates is taken as positive, the velocity $c$ at which the wavefronts move is negative, and the wave number $k$, defined using the frequency $f$ and the velocity of light as $k=\dfrac{f}{c}=\dfrac{nf}{c_0}$, is negative.

In this problem, let us consider the law of refraction of light in media with a positive refractive index and the way light propagates in a metamaterial, and also consider the relation between the Doppler effect and astronomical observation.

[I] Snell's law

As in Fig. 1, consider the case in which light is incident obliquely on the boundary from water into air.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[Labels in the figure: 媒質2（空気） = medium 2 (air); 媒質1（水） = medium 1 (water).]

The $y$ axis is chosen perpendicular to the boundary between the water and the air, and the $x$ axis along the boundary. When light is incident from the direction at angle $\theta$ to the $y$ axis as in Fig. 1, the wave number vector $\overrightarrow{k}$ is defined by $(k_x, k_y)$, with the wave number in the $x$ direction $k_x=k\sin\theta$ and the wave number in the $y$ direction $k_y=k\cos\theta$. The direction of the wave number vector $\overrightarrow{k}$ is perpendicular to the wavefront, and it points in the direction in which the wavefront advances. In general, it is known that when light passes through the boundary between two media 1 and 2, the $x$ component of the wave number vector (the component along the boundary) is continuous at the boundary and has the same value above and below it.

Below, $\mathrm{rad}$ is used as the unit of angle $\left(\text{where } 1\,\mathrm{rad}=\dfrac{360^\circ}{2\pi}\right)$.

Q1. Using the above property of light, show that, with the refractive index of water $n$ and the refractive index of air $n'$, the relation between the angle of incidence $\theta$ and the angle of refraction $\theta'$ of light going out of water into air and $n$ and $n'$ is $n\sin\theta=n'\sin\theta'$ (Snell's law).

Q2. Taking the refractive index of water as $n=1.33$ and the refractive index of air as $n'=1.00$, find the angle of refraction $\theta'$ when the angle of incidence $\theta$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\,\mathrm{rad}$.

Q3. The angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction becomes $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\,\mathrm{rad}$ is called the critical angle. Light with an angle of incidence larger than this is entirely reflected at the boundary (total reflection). Find the critical angle for light going out of water into air, and state the condition on the angle of incidence for the light to be entirely reflected at the surface of the water.

When light is incident obliquely from a medium with a positive refractive index onto a medium with a negative refractive index (a metamaterial), the wavefronts must be continuous above and below the boundary, so the $x$ component of the wave number vector is equal above and below, and the angle of refraction is negative. Therefore the wavefronts are as shown in Fig. 2, and the direction in which the wavefronts of light advance in the metamaterial is opposite to the direction of propagation of the light (the direction of flow of the energy of the light). From these facts, answer the following questions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[Labels in the figure: 媒質2 ($n$<0) = medium 2 ($n$<0); 媒質1 ($n$>0) = medium 1 ($n$>0); 境界面 = boundary; 波面 = wavefront; 波面の進行方向 = direction of advance of the wavefronts.]

Q4. When light is incident from air ($n=1.00$) into a metamaterial of refractive index $n'=-1.00$ from the directions ①, ②, ③ of Fig. 3, find the angle of refraction of each ray, and draw the direction of propagation of the refracted light in the figure on the answer sheet.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[Labels in the figure: メタマテリアル（屈折率 n'=−1.00） = metamaterial (refractive index n'=−1.00); 空気（屈折率 n=1.00） = air (refractive index n=1.00); 境界面 = boundary.]

[II] Flat-plate lens

It is known that a flat plate of metamaterial acts as a lens. First, let us consider how light incident on a metamaterial of refractive index $n$ passes through it.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4

[Labels in the figure: 空気 = air; メタマテリアル = metamaterial.]

Q5. For a metamaterial of refractive index $-1$ ($n=-1.00$), how do the rays incident from an object $\mathrm{A}$ placed in air as in Fig. 4, as shown by the broken lines, proceed after entering the metamaterial? Draw them with broken lines in the figure on the answer sheet. Find the distance $b$ between the image point in the metamaterial (the position of the image on the horizontal axis) and the left surface of the metamaterial.

Next, let us consider the case of a flat plate of metamaterial of thickness $d$ and refractive index $n<0$.

Q6. Express the positions $b$ and $l$ of the image points in the centre and on the right of Fig. 5 using $a$, $d$, $n$. Assume that the metamaterial is sufficiently thick and satisfies $d>a|n|$. Show with broken lines in the figure on the answer sheet how the light proceeds after entering the metamaterial. Assume that all rays are paraxial rays whose angles with the optical axis are sufficiently small.
(Note: $|n|$ is the absolute value of $n$; for paraxial rays, approximately $\sin\theta\fallingdotseq\tan\theta$.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig5.png

Fig. 5

[Labels in the figure: 空気 = air; メタマテリアル = metamaterial; 光軸 = optical axis.]

The results of Q5 and Q6 show that a metamaterial acts as a lens even though it is a flat plate.

[III] Doppler effect

Let us consider the Doppler effect of light.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6

[Labels in the figure: 観測者 I = observer I; 観測者 II = observer II; 光源 = light source; 光源の速度 $V$ = velocity of the light source $V$.]

As in Fig. 6, there is a light source moving horizontally with speed $V$. While emitting light, the light source went from point $\mathrm{A}$ to point $\mathrm{B}$ during $\varDelta t$. Suppose that observers I and II observed this light. The distance from the light source to the observers is assumed to be sufficiently large compared with the distance $V\varDelta t$ between $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$.

Let $f_0'$ be the frequency of the light observed by observer I, who is in the direction transverse to the direction of motion of the light source (the direction of angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\,\mathrm{rad}$). The frequency $f$ of the wave observed by observer II, who is in the direction at angle $\theta$ to the direction of motion of the light source, is obtained on the basis of the following idea. The speed $V$ of the light source is smaller than the speed of light $c_0$.

When the wavefronts $\mathrm{a_0}$ and $\mathrm{a}$ of the wave emitted by the light source from position $\mathrm{A}$ have reached the respective observers, the wavefronts $\mathrm{b_0}$ and $\mathrm{b}$ of the wave emitted by the light source from $\mathrm{B}$ have come to a little short of the observers. The spacing between the wavefronts $\mathrm{a_0}$ and $\mathrm{b_0}$ in the vertical direction is $c_0\varDelta t$. On the other hand, the spacing between the two wavefronts $\mathrm{a}$, $\mathrm{b}$ in the direction of angle $\theta$ is $(c_0\ -\ V\cos\theta)\varDelta t$. Between $\mathrm{a_0}$ and $\mathrm{b_0}$, and between $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$, there are $f_0'\varDelta t$ waves, counting a wave of one wavelength as one.

Q7. Show that, relative to the frequency $f_0'$ of the light in the transverse direction, the frequency $f$ observed in the direction of angle $\theta$ is $f=\dfrac{f_0'}{1\ -\ \dfrac{V}{c_0}\cos\theta}$.

Q8. When both the light source and the observers in Fig. 6 are in a medium of refractive index $n$, find the frequency of the light in the direction of angle $\theta$. Also, for the cases in which the refractive index $n$ is positive and negative, show the increase or decrease of the frequency when the light source approaches the observer ($\theta=0$) and when it recedes ($\theta=\pi$).

[IV] Relativistic effects and astronomical observation

As in Fig. 7, suppose that the light emitted from a light source $\mathrm{S}$ moving in the $y$ direction with speed $V$ is observed by an observer $\mathrm{P}$ moving in the $y$ direction together with the light source and by an observer $\mathrm{O}$ at rest at the origin of coordinates. Let us derive, by the following procedure, that between the frequency $f_0$ of the light seen by observer $\mathrm{P}$ and the frequency $f_0'$ seen by observer $\mathrm{O}$ in the transverse direction ($\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$), in vacuum, there is the relation $f_0'=f_0\sqrt{1\ -\ \left(\dfrac{V}{c_0}\right)^2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig7.png

Fig. 7

[Labels in the figure: 光源 = light source; 光源と平行移動する観測者 = observer moving parallel to the light source; 静止した観測者 = observer at rest.]

According to Einstein's special theory of relativity, it is known that the speed of light in vacuum $c_0$ is constant regardless of the speed at which the observer moves. As a consequence, the rate at which time advances differs between observers moving with different speeds. To examine this, consider the case in which an observer $\mathrm{P}$, at a point moving in the $y$ direction with the same speed $V$ as the light source $\mathrm{S}$ and separated from it by $a$ in the $x$ direction, and an observer $\mathrm{O}$ at rest at the origin observe the light from the light source $\mathrm{S}$. Suppose that $\mathrm{O}$ observed that the light emitted from the light source $\mathrm{S}$ reached observer $\mathrm{P}$ after a time $t$. During this time $t$, observer $\mathrm{P}$ has moved as far as point $\mathrm{P'}$, so the light observed by $\mathrm{O}$ propagates during this time a distance $b=\sqrt{a^2\ +\ (Vt)^2}$. On the other hand, the time $t'$ for the light to reach $\mathrm{P}$ is $t'=\dfrac{a}{c_0}$.

Q9. From the above, express $\dfrac{t}{t'}$ using $c_0$ and $V$.

This result means that the rate at which clocks advance differs from observer to observer, that is, that time is "relative". This relation can be generalized as it is to the case of a body moving with relative velocity $V$, and phenomena in the body appear slow to an observer in relative motion.

Q10. Using the result of Q9, show that between the frequency $f_0'$ observed by the observer at rest at $\mathrm{O}$ in the transverse direction and the frequency $f_0$ observed by $\mathrm{P}$, who moves together with the light source, there is the relation

$$\frac{f_0'}{f_0}=\sqrt{1\ -\ \left(\frac{V}{c_0}\right)^2}$$

(this is called the transverse Doppler effect due to relativistic effects).

Summarizing the above results, when a light source of frequency $f_0$ moves with speed $V$, the frequency $f$ observed by an observer $\mathrm{O}$ in the direction at angle $\theta$ to its direction of motion is, by the Doppler effect including the relativistic effect,

$$\frac{f}{f_0}=\frac{\sqrt{1\ -\ \left(\dfrac{V}{c_0}\right)^2}}{1\ -\ \dfrac{V}{c_0}\cos\theta}$$

Next, let us consider a method of measuring distances in the universe using the Doppler effect. It is known from the Doppler effect of starlight that the universe is expanding and that the more distant a celestial body is, the faster it is receding from the Earth. In Fig. 8, the celestial body $\mathrm{S}$ is assumed to be receding straight away from the observer $\mathrm{O}$ (the Earth) in the direction $\theta=\pi$. Let us express the distance to a celestial body as $D\times$ 1 million light years. It is known as an observational fact that between the speed $V$ at which a celestial body recedes from the Earth and $D$ there is the relation $V=HD$ (Hubble's law). Here $H=21.6\,\mathrm{km/s}$ is called the Hubble constant. This law was discovered from the fact that, when light emitted from extremely distant galaxies is observed, its wavelength is longer than that of light emitted on the Earth.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2010-3-fig8.png

Fig. 8

[Labels in the figure: S: 天体 = S: celestial body; O: 地球 = O: Earth.]

Q11. When the wavelength of light emitted from a distant nebula is $1.01$ times longer than the wavelength when emitted on the Earth $\mathrm{O}$, find from the Doppler-effect formula and Hubble's law how many light years the distance to the nebula is. Assume that the receding speed is sufficiently small compared with the speed of light, so that the relativistic effect $\left(\dfrac{V}{c_0}\right)^2$ can be neglected.

Q12. Considering Hubble's law and the relativistic Doppler effect together, we see that the frequency, observed on the Earth, of light from a distant light source decreases with the distance to that light source. Assuming that the place where a light source for which this frequency becomes 0 is located is the edge of the universe, find the distance to the edge of the universe.

problems.title: Problem 1A
problems.problem:
Problem 1A (65 points)

Consider a rocket in outer space where there is no gravity, which burns the fuel it carries and ejects it, moving by the reaction. The rocket is initially at rest and its mass is $m_0$. Let $v$ be the speed of the rocket, flying in a straight line, when its mass has become $m$. Also, let $u$ be the relative speed of the fuel ejected backwards, as seen from the rocket.

[I]

Suppose that the speed $u$ of the fuel can be controlled together with the speed $v$ of the rocket as $u=v+u_0$. Here $u_0$ is the speed of the fuel ejection when the rocket is at rest. Then all the ejected fuel moves through space with a constant speed $u_0$, in the direction opposite to the direction of motion of the rocket. In this case the motion of the rocket can be analysed easily. Answer the following questions.

Q1. Find the relation between the speed $v$ and the mass $m$ of the rocket.

Q2. Suppose the rocket is made to move with a constant acceleration $a$. If $t$ is the time since the rocket started moving, the speed of the rocket is $v=at$. Find the mass $m$ of the rocket at time $t$.

Q3. Find the energy $E$ obtained by burning the fuel during the time $t$ after the rocket started moving with constant acceleration. Assume that all this energy became kinetic energy of the moving bodies (the ejected fuel and the rocket).

Q4. When the mass of the rocket has become $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of its initial value, how many times $u_0$ is the speed of the rocket?

Q5. Let $E_{\mathrm{r}}$ be the kinetic energy of the rocket when its mass has become $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of its initial value $\left( E_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \right)$. Find the ratio $\dfrac{E_{\mathrm{r}}}{E}$ of $E_{\mathrm{r}}$ to the energy $E$ obtained from the fuel during this time.

[II]

Let us consider the general motion of a rocket. Suppose that at a certain instant $t$ the mass of the rocket is $m$ and its speed is $v$ (Fig. 1). Suppose that during a short time $\Delta t$ the mass of the rocket becomes $m+\Delta m$ and the speed of the rocket becomes $v+\Delta v$. Note that here, since small changes are taken positive for increases, the mass of the fuel ejected with relative speed $u$ as seen from the rocket is expressed as $-\Delta m$ (Fig. 2). Answer the following.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Time $t$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Time $t+\Delta t$

When $v-u<0$ the ejected fuel moves in the direction opposite to the rocket.

Q6. From the law of conservation of momentum before and after the short time $\Delta t$, find the relation between $\Delta v$ and $\Delta m$. Since $\Delta v$ and $\Delta m$ are small quantities, the product of small quantities $\Delta m\Delta v$ (a second-order small quantity) may be neglected compared with $m\Delta v$ or $u\Delta m$ (first-order small quantities).

Q7. Find the energy $\Delta E$ used during the short time $\Delta t$. Assume that all this energy becomes kinetic energy of the moving bodies (the ejected fuel and the rocket). Terms containing two or more of the small quantities $\Delta m$, $\Delta v$ (second-order small quantities $m(\Delta v)^2$, $v\Delta m\Delta v$, and the third-order small quantity $\Delta m(\Delta v)^2$) may be neglected compared with terms containing one small quantity (first-order small quantities $mv\Delta v$, $v^2\Delta m$). Express the result using only $\Delta m\ (<0)$ and $u$.

[III]

In an ordinary rocket, which obtains its thrust by burning chemical fuel, the speed $u$ of the ejected fuel as seen from the rocket is a constant $u_0$ independent of the speed of the rocket ($u=u_0$). In this case, using the results of the previous questions, answer the following.

Q8. Find the relation between the speed $v$ and the mass $m$ of the rocket. If necessary, refer to the following hint.

[Hint]

Suppose $y$ is a function of $x$. When $x$ changes by a small amount $\Delta x$, suppose the change $\Delta y$ of $y$ is related by $\Delta y=cy\Delta x$. Here $c$ is a constant. Then the relation between $y$ and $x$ is expressed as $y=y_0\,\mathrm{e}^{cx}$, where $y_0$ is an arbitrary constant.

Q9. Suppose the rocket is made to move with a constant acceleration $a$. Find the mass $m$ of the rocket when a time $t$ has passed since the rocket started moving.

Q10. Find the energy $E$ obtained by burning the fuel during the time $t$ after the rocket started moving with constant acceleration. Assume that all this energy became kinetic energy of the moving bodies (the ejected fuel and the rocket).

Q11. When the mass of the rocket has become $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of its initial value, how many times $u_0$ is the speed of the rocket? Find it numerically, using the approximation $\log_{\mathrm{e}}2=0.693$.

Q12. Let $E_{\mathrm{r}}$ be the kinetic energy of the rocket when its mass has become $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of its initial value $\left( E_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \right)$. Find the ratio $\dfrac{E_{\mathrm{r}}}{E}$ of $E_{\mathrm{r}}$ to the energy $E$ obtained from the fuel during this time. Express the result numerically.

problems.title: Problem 1B
problems.problem:
Problem 1B (35 points)

[I]

Thermodynamics deals with the macroscopic physical quantities of macroscopic systems (systems in which the number of particles such as atoms and molecules is very large). It is based on two fundamental laws, the first law of thermodynamics and the second law of thermodynamics. Let us begin with the first law, which is the law of conservation of energy.

First law of thermodynamics: The increase $\Delta U$ of the internal energy of a system is given by the sum of the heat $Q$ added from outside and the work $W$ done on it from outside.

$$\Delta U=W+Q \qquad (1)$$

The internal energy in the first law is the sum of the kinetic energies of the constituent particles and the potential energy due to the interactions between the constituent particles.

Below, we consider an ideal gas, in which there are no interactions between the particles. In an equilibrium state of $n$ moles of an ideal gas, the following equation of state holds between its volume $V$, pressure $P$ and absolute temperature $T$:

$$PV=nRT \qquad (2)$$

Here $R$ is called the gas constant and is given by

$$R=8.31\,\mathrm{J/(K\cdot mol)} \qquad (3)$$

By the equation of state (2), an equilibrium state of the gas is determined if any two of $(P, V, T)$ are fixed. To represent changes of state of a gas, the pressure $P$ and the volume $V$ are often chosen and a $P$-$V$ diagram is used.

According to the kinetic theory of molecules, the pressure $P$ is given by the sum of the impulsive forces per unit area that the wall receives from collisions between the molecules and the wall, and in the case of an ideal gas of monatomic molecules it can be expressed as $P=\dfrac{2E}{3V}$ using the kinetic energy $E$ of the centre-of-mass motion of the molecules. In the case of an ideal gas of monatomic molecules, the internal energy $U$ is equal to $E$. From this, using equation (2), it is given by

$$U=\frac{3}{2}nRT \qquad (4)$$

In the case of diatomic molecules, they can have rotational and vibrational energy, but in the temperature range $100$–$1000\,\mathrm{K}$ the vibrational energy can be neglected and one may consider that only the rotational energy is added to the internal energy, so that

$$U=\frac{5}{2}nRT \qquad (5)$$

The internal energy of an ideal gas does not depend on the volume because there are no interactions between the molecules. Even for real gases, since the distances between the molecules are sufficiently large, regarding them as ideal gases is a good approximation over a wide range.

Q1. The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 mole of a gas by $1\,\mathrm{K}$ at constant volume is called the molar heat capacity at constant volume. What is the value of the molar heat capacity at constant volume $C_V$ of air? Air consists of $\mathrm{O_2}$ ($20.93\%$) and $\mathrm{N_2}$ ($78.10\%$), so it can be regarded as a gas of diatomic molecules.

Q2. As in Fig. 1, a gas is confined in a cylindrical container with a smoothly moving piston. The piston is pushed with a force $F$ and moves a distance $\Delta x$, and the volume decreases by $|\Delta V|$ (volume change $\Delta V<0$). Taking the pressure of the gas to be $P$, show that the work $W$ done on the gas in this process is

$$W=-P\Delta V \qquad (6)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[ヒーター = heater]

Q3. On the $P$-$V$ diagram of Fig. 2 for $n$ moles of an ideal gas, ア→イ is an isobaric process, ア→ウ is an isochoric process and ウ→イ is an isothermal process. By comparing the isobaric process and the isochoric process, find the molar heat capacity at constant pressure $C_P$ of air.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[ア, イ, ウ are the labels of the three states (Japanese letters, kept as printed).]

Q4. In the isothermal process ウ→イ, let $W$ be the work done on the gas from outside and $Q$ the heat absorbed by the gas. Write the relation between them and the signs (positive or negative) of these quantities.

[II]

Thermal phenomena cannot be explained by the first law alone. It is the second law that states the direction of changes of state. The second law has various formulations. Here we give the formulation called Thomson's principle.

Thomson's principle: A process that takes heat from a heat source of uniform temperature and only does an equal amount of work, leaving no other change whatsoever, cannot be realised.

As can also be seen from Joule's paddle-wheel experiment on the mechanical equivalent of heat, all work can be converted into heat, so this principle shows the irreversibility of natural phenomena involving the conduction of heat.

Let us examine such irreversibility with a simple hypothetical example. Initially, as in Fig. 3(a) below, a partition is placed at the centre of a cylindrical adiabatic container of volume $2V$; $n$ moles of an ideal gas are placed in part A, of volume $V$, while part B is kept as a vacuum. Next, a hole in the partition is opened so that the gas can move from A into the evacuated B; eventually, as in Fig. 3(b), the gas reaches equilibrium with the same density. In this process there is neither exchange of heat nor exchange of work with the outside, the internal energy of the gas does not change, and therefore the temperature does not change either.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3(a) (left) and Fig. 3(b) (right)

Q5. The probability of returning from the particle distribution of Fig. 3(b) to the distribution of Fig. 3(a) is infinitely close to $0$. If the molecules can move freely back and forth through the hole, the probability that an individual gas molecule is in A or in B at a given instant is $\dfrac{1}{2}$. Taking Avogadro's number to be $N_{\mathrm{A}}$, find the probability that all the gas molecules of the $n$ moles are in A.

The second law can be discussed quantitatively by introducing a quantity called entropy. Entropy can be called an index of the disorder or uncertainty of a system, and in irreversible phenomena in nature it changes in the direction of becoming disordered and uncertain. In the example above, one can say that the volume in which the particles were confined increased, the uncertainty of their positions increased, and the system became more disordered.

To return from Fig. 3(b) to Fig. 3(a), it is necessary to enclose the gas in a container like that of Fig. 1 and compress it by pushing the piston while keeping the temperature constant.

If $Q$ is the heat that flowed reversibly into a system and $T$ is the temperature at that time, the change $\Delta S$ of the entropy $S$ of the system is related to $Q$ and $T$ as follows:

$$Q=T\Delta S \qquad (7)$$

Also, for a reversible process, substituting equations (6) and (7) into the first law (1), we obtain

$$\Delta U=-P\Delta V+T\Delta S \qquad (8)$$

The entropy $S$, like the internal energy $U$, is a quantity of state determined by the equilibrium state, and the change of entropy between two equilibrium states can be calculated by assuming a suitable reversible process between them.

Q6. Find the amount of heat released to the outside when $n$ moles of an ideal gas are compressed from volume $2V$ to $V$ while keeping the temperature constant. If necessary for this calculation, you may use the following integral formula:

$$\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}=\log x_2-\log x_1=\log\left(\frac{x_2}{x_1}\right)$$

Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm (the logarithm to the base $\mathrm{e}=2.7182\cdots$).

Q7. The process of Q6 is a reversible process, and equation (8) holds. From this, find the difference in entropy between the states of Fig. 3(a) and Fig. 3(b), and calculate the increase $\Delta S$ of the entropy in the process from Fig. 3(a) to Fig. 3(b).

For a general process,

$$Q\leqq T\Delta S \qquad (9)$$

holds; this is called the Clausius inequality. Here $=$ corresponds to a reversible process and $<$ to an irreversible process. Equation (9) is the law of increase of entropy for irreversible processes and expresses the second law of thermodynamics.

In this way, thermodynamics clarifies the relations between the thermal properties of macroscopic quantities on the basis of two fundamental laws. However, the properties specific to a substance, such as the heat capacity and the equation of state, and the temperature dependence of other thermodynamic and electromagnetic macroscopic quantities specific to a substance, are treated as given by experiment. The theory that calculates these substance-specific macroscopic quantities from the microscopic mechanical system is statistical mechanics.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (100 points)

If needed for numerical calculations, you may use the table of numerical values at the end of this problem.

For the development of quantum mechanics, the following three phenomena due to the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter were important research topics.

1) The photoelectric effect

2) The Compton effect

3) The creation of electron–positron pairs

[I]

When discussing these phenomena it is necessary to use the theory of relativity. According to it, the energy of a moving particle, when the magnitude of its momentum is $p$, is expressed as

$$E=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2p^2} \qquad (1)$$

$m$ is the mass of this particle, and $c=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is the speed of light in vacuum. $E$ in equation (1) has the non-zero value $E=mc^2$ even when $p=0$. This energy is called the rest energy.

Since the increase of energy is equal to the amount of work done from outside, when this particle moves with velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ while being acted on by an external force $\overrightarrow{F}$, the relation

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}=(\text{power of the external force }\overrightarrow{F})=\overrightarrow{v}\cdot\overrightarrow{F} \qquad (2)$$

holds. Here the product that appears on the far right-hand side is what is called the inner product of the vectors $\overrightarrow{v}$ and $\overrightarrow{F}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Below, the magnitude (also called the absolute value) of a vector $\overrightarrow{A}$ is written $|\overrightarrow{A}|$ or simply $A$. Now suppose there are two vectors $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$, and let the angle between them be $\theta$ (see Fig. 1). Then $\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}$ defined by

$$\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}=|\overrightarrow{A}|\,|\overrightarrow{B}|\cos\theta \qquad (3)$$

is called the inner product of the vectors $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$. According to equation (3),

$$\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{A}=|\overrightarrow{A}|^2$$

so the magnitude of a vector is obtained by calculating the square root of its inner product with itself. Note that the second law of motion relating force and momentum,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{p}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\overrightarrow{F} \qquad (4)$$

also holds in relativity.

Q1. Consider a particle of mass $m$ moving in one dimension with velocity $v$ in the $x$-axis direction. From the fact that the second law of motion holds for this particle, show that the momentum $p$ is expressed as

$$p=\frac{m}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}\,v \qquad (5)$$

When $(v/c)^2$ on the right-hand side of this equation is sufficiently small compared with 1 and can be neglected (this is called the non-relativistic limit), equation (5) becomes the defining equation of momentum in Newtonian mechanics, $p=mv$.

Q2. Show that, in the non-relativistic limit, the right-hand side of equation (1) becomes the sum of the rest energy and $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

Hint: If necessary, use the fact that when $\alpha$ is sufficiently small compared with 1, one can approximate $(1+\alpha)^{1/2}\approx1+\dfrac{1}{2}\alpha$.

Q3. How many eV (electronvolts) is the rest energy of an electron? [For the conversion between the energy units eV and J, see the end of the problem text.]

Note that for a general particle moving in three dimensions, the relation

$$\overrightarrow{p}=\frac{m}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}\,\overrightarrow{v} \qquad (6)$$

obtained by making equation (5) three-dimensional holds between the velocity vector and the momentum vector. Equations (5) and (6) become meaningless when the speed $v$ of the particle becomes greater than $c$, because the expression under the square root becomes negative. Therefore the speed of any particle is taken to be smaller than the speed of light.

[II]

The "photoelectric effect" of 1) at the beginning is the phenomenon in which, when light is shone on a solid, electrons that were bound in the solid absorb the energy of the light, are released from the solid and fly out. Einstein introduced the light-quantum hypothesis in 1905 and established the theory of the photoelectric effect, and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921.

According to the quantum mechanics of electromagnetic waves, which began with the light-quantum hypothesis, an electromagnetic wave shone on matter is a stream of a collection of particles called photons. A photon has no mass but has energy, and the energy $E$ of one photon has the value

$$E=h\nu$$

where $\nu$ is the frequency of the electromagnetic wave. $h$ is called Planck's constant, and its value is written at the end of the problem text.

To release an electron bound to an atom in matter by the photoelectric effect, it is necessary to give energy from the photon to the electron. Also, one electron can exchange energy and momentum with only one photon at a time.

Q4. The minimum value of the photon energy needed to release an electron from a solid is called the work function of that solid. In order to produce the photoelectric effect in a solid whose work function is $2.0\,\mathrm{eV}$, below what value must the wavelength of the electromagnetic wave shone on it be made? Answer to 1 significant figure.

Electromagnetic waves of this wavelength belong to visible light. Converting the information carried by light into electric signals in a digital camera, and converting the energy of sunlight into electric energy in a solar cell, are also kinds of photoelectric effect.

Q5. A photon has no mass but has momentum, and the relation between its energy and momentum is given by equation (1) with $m=0$. Derive that the magnitude of the momentum of a photon of an electromagnetic wave of wavelength $\lambda$ propagating in vacuum is

$$p=\frac{h}{\lambda} \qquad (7)$$

[III]

When the energy of the photon becomes large, the electron can be released from the solid without the photon giving it all of its energy, and a photon with an energy smaller than the initial energy flies away (Fig. 2). This is scattering of the electromagnetic wave due to an inelastic collision of the photon with the solid; it is called Compton scattering because Compton used it to prove that equation (7), one of the basic relations of quantum mechanics, holds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[入射電磁波 = incident electromagnetic wave; 散乱電磁波 = scattered electromagnetic wave; 電子の初期位置 = initial position of the electron; 解放された電子 = released electron]

Q6. Express the energy $E$ of the electron after it has been released from the matter using the mass of the electron $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, the speed of light $c$, Planck's constant $h$, the wavelength $\lambda$ of the incident electromagnetic wave and the wavelength $\lambda'$ of the electromagnetic wave after scattering. Here, since the work function is sufficiently small compared with $E$ and can be neglected, take the energy of the electron before the scattering to be equal to its rest energy.

Q7. The direction of the momentum vector $\overrightarrow{p}$ of a photon is the direction of propagation of the electromagnetic wave. If the vector of magnitude 1 parallel to this direction is denoted by $\overrightarrow{n}$, the momentum vector $\overrightarrow{p}$, whose magnitude is given by equation (7), is expressed as

$$\overrightarrow{p}=\frac{h}{\lambda}\,\overrightarrow{n} \qquad (8)$$

Express the fact that the total momentum of the photon and the electron is conserved before and after the scattering of Fig. 2, using the momentum $\overrightarrow{P}$ of the emitted electron, $\lambda$, $\lambda'$, $\overrightarrow{n}$, $\overrightarrow{n}'$ for the electromagnetic waves before and after the scattering, and Planck's constant $h$.

Q8. Using the above, derive the following equation:

$$\lambda'-\lambda=\frac{h}{m_{\mathrm{e}}c}(1-\cos\theta) \qquad (9)$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between $\overrightarrow{n}$ and $\overrightarrow{n}'$. Note that since $\overrightarrow{n}$ and $\overrightarrow{n}'$ have magnitude 1, $\overrightarrow{n}\cdot\overrightarrow{n}=\overrightarrow{n}'\cdot\overrightarrow{n}'=1$.

Q9. To confirm by experiment that equation (9) holds, an incident electromagnetic wave suitable for the measurement must be prepared. What is the wavelength $\lambda$ of the incident electromagnetic wave for which $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{2}\lambda'$ and $\theta=60^\circ$? Answer to 1 significant figure. Also, find the energy of the electron released in this case, in units of eV.

Electromagnetic waves of the wavelength found here belong to X-rays. Compton contributed to the construction of the quantum theory of electromagnetic waves using X-rays. Also, the factor $\dfrac{h}{m_{\mathrm{e}}c}$ on the right-hand side of equation (9), which has the dimension of length, is called the Compton wavelength.

[IV]

Furthermore, when electromagnetic waves of short wavelength are used, a phenomenon called pair creation may occur, in which one photon is annihilated and at the same time one pair of a particle and an antiparticle is created. An example of a particle and an antiparticle is the pair of an electron and a positron. A positron is a particle whose mass is equal to that of the electron and whose charge is of opposite sign; if the charge of the electron is $-e$ and its mass is $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, the charge and mass of the positron are $e$ and $m_{\mathrm{e}}$ respectively. Therefore the same relation (1) as for the electron holds between the momentum $p$ and the energy $E$ of the positron.

First, suppose that the pair creation is the reaction shown in Fig. 3(a). In the reaction of this figure, the energy that the photon had before the reaction is shared equally between the electron and the positron after the reaction. Also, the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}_\gamma$ that the photon had is converted into the sum of the momenta $\overrightarrow{p}_+$, $\overrightarrow{p}_-$ of the positron and the electron. Between these momenta the relation $|\overrightarrow{p}_+|=|\overrightarrow{p}_-|$ holds, and since the directions of $\overrightarrow{p}_+$ and $\overrightarrow{p}_-$ are symmetric with respect to the direction of $\overrightarrow{p}_\gamma$, $\overrightarrow{p}_++\overrightarrow{p}_-$ has the same direction as $\overrightarrow{p}_\gamma$. Also, let the angle between $\overrightarrow{p}_+$ and $\overrightarrow{p}_-$ be $\theta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[光子 = photon; 電子 = electron; 陽電子 = positron; 原子核 = atomic nucleus]

Q10. Find, in units of eV, the energy of the photon needed to create, in the reaction of Fig. 3(a), a pair consisting of a positron with $|\overrightarrow{p}_+|=0$ and an electron with $|\overrightarrow{p}_-|=0$.

In experiments on electron–positron pair creation it is necessary to use electromagnetic waves of at least the energy found here.

As in the previous question, if the momenta of the created electron and positron were $0$ although the photon initially had momentum, the law of conservation of momentum would not be satisfied.

Q11. Show that even if a photon of higher energy is used, in the reaction of Fig. 3(a) one has $|\overrightarrow{p}_++\overrightarrow{p}_-|<|\overrightarrow{p}_\gamma|$, so that momentum is not conserved.

Hint: The calculation is easier if you compare $|\overrightarrow{p}_++\overrightarrow{p}_-|^2$ and $|\overrightarrow{p}_\gamma|^2$.

Therefore, for pair creation to occur, the existence of another particle that receives the difference between the momentum the photon had and the momentum of the electron–positron pair is necessary. For this reason, when pair-creation experiments are performed, $\gamma$-rays are shone on matter so that the momentum of the photon is also given to atomic nuclei in that matter. Fig. 3(b) shows this situation. Below, let the mass of the atomic nucleus that received momentum from the photon be $M$ and its momentum be $\overrightarrow{q}$. Also, for the energy of the atomic nucleus, use the expression in the non-relativistic limit.

Q12. Express the photon energy $h\nu$ needed to create an electron–positron pair with $|\overrightarrow{p}_+|=|\overrightarrow{p}_-|=0$ in the reaction of Fig. 3(b) using $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, $M$, $c$ or some of these symbols. Also, find the speed of the atomic nucleus after the reaction, and confirm that it was appropriate to use the non-relativistic-limit expression for the energy of the atomic nucleus.

(Reference)

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Speed of light} & c=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s} \\ \text{Mass of the electron} & m_{\mathrm{e}}=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Mass of the proton} & m_{\mathrm{p}}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Planck's constant} & h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s} \\ \text{Energy conversion} & 1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (100 points)

If necessary, use the differentiation and integration formulas and the physical constants at the end of the problem.
