The magnetosphere outside the Earth's ionosphere and the rarefied gas spread out between the planets of the solar system are in many cases a plasma (ionized gas) ionized into electrons and positive ions. These plasmas move under the strong influence of magnetic and electric fields. Here, let us consider the motion of charged particles in magnetic and electric fields, which is the basis of the motion of plasmas.

[I]

Consider the motion of a charged particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ in a uniform electric field $\overrightarrow{E}=(E,\,0,\,0)$ pointing in the $x$ direction and a uniform magnetic field of magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B}=(0,\,0,\,B)$ pointing in the $z$ direction. If the position of the charged particle is written $(x,\,y,\,z)$ and its velocity $(V_x,\,V_y,\,V_z)$, it is known that one can write

$$\begin{aligned} m\frac{\mathrm{d}V_x}{\mathrm{d}t}&=q(E+BV_y) \\ m\frac{\mathrm{d}V_y}{\mathrm{d}t}&=-qBV_x \\ m\frac{\mathrm{d}V_z}{\mathrm{d}t}&=0 \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$

Such equations are called equations of motion; the left-hand sides are the acceleration multiplied by the mass, and the right-hand sides are the forces exerted on the charged particle by the electromagnetic field. Note that $E$ and $B$ appearing here are both taken to be constant in time as well. Also, since the third equation easily shows that the motion in the $z$ direction is uniform, in [I] only the motion in the plane perpendicular to the $z$ axis is examined in detail.

First, let the electric field be $E=0$. Then from the equations of motion (1),

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}V_x}{\mathrm{d}t}=qBV_y, \qquad m\frac{\mathrm{d}V_y}{\mathrm{d}t}=-qBV_x \qquad (2)$$

are derived.

Q1. From equation (2), derive

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}^2V_x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=-{\omega_{\mathrm{c}}}^2V_x, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}^2V_y}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=-{\omega_{\mathrm{c}}}^2V_y \qquad (3)$$

where

$$\omega_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{qB}{m} \qquad (4)$$

Q2. Equation (3) shows that the charged particle oscillates harmonically in both the $x$ direction and the $y$ direction with angular frequency $|\omega_{\mathrm{c}}|$. $|\omega_{\mathrm{c}}|$ is called the cyclotron angular frequency. Taking $V_x=0$, $V_y=V_\perp>0$ at $t=0$, show that $V_x$, $V_y$ at time $t$ are

$$V_x(t)=V_\perp\sin(\omega_{\mathrm{c}}t), \qquad V_y(t)=V_\perp\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{c}}t)$$

Q3. Also, find the position $x(t)$, $y(t)$ at time $t$ of a particle that was at $x=-\dfrac{V_\perp}{\omega_{\mathrm{c}}}$, $y=0$ at $t=0$, and show that the charged particle performs circular motion of radius

$$r_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{V_\perp}{|\omega_{\mathrm{c}}|} \qquad (5)$$

This circular motion is called cyclotron motion, and $r_{\mathrm{c}}$ is called the cyclotron radius. Note that, using the position coordinates $(x,\,y)$ of the charged particle, its velocity vector can be written

$$V_x(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}, \qquad V_y(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

Q4. The magnitude of the geomagnetic field differs from place to place, but near Tokyo it is about $3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ (tesla). Find the cyclotron angular frequency of an electron in Tokyo.

Q5. Find the cyclotron radius $r_{\mathrm{c}}$ in Tokyo of an electron with speed $3.2\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (the speed of an electron accelerated by a voltage of about 3000 volts). Find the ratio of this cyclotron radius to the radius of the Earth, $6.4\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$.

The Earth's magnetic field, viewed on the scale of the Earth's radius, varies from place to place. However, if the cyclotron radius is much smaller than the radius of the Earth, as here, the charged particle can be regarded as moving in a circle in a uniform magnetic field.

Next, consider the case in which $E$ in equation (1) is not $0$.

Q6. Show that, if one puts $U_x=V_x$, $U_y=V_y+\dfrac{E}{B}$ in this case, the equations of motion (1) can be rewritten as

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}U_x}{\mathrm{d}t}=qBU_y, \qquad m\frac{\mathrm{d}U_y}{\mathrm{d}t}=-qBU_x$$

Q7. With the initial conditions $U_x(0)=0$, $U_y(0)=V_\perp>0$, express $V_x(t)$, $V_y(t)$ using $V_\perp$, $\omega_{\mathrm{c}}$, $E$, $B$, $t$.

Q8. From this result, find the position $x(t)$, $y(t)$ at time $t$ of a particle that was at $x=-\dfrac{V_\perp}{\omega_{\mathrm{c}}}$, $y=0$ at $t=0$, and sketch the outline of the trajectory $(x(t),\,y(t))$ for each of the cases $q>0$ and $q<0$.

Q9. In the example above the electric field was in the $x$ direction. What happens to the trajectory when the electric field points in the $y$ direction? Sketch the outline of the trajectory for each of the cases $q>0$ and $q<0$.

The above results show that the motion, in the plane perpendicular to the magnetic field, of a charged particle in uniform magnetic and electric fields perpendicular to each other is a superposition of cyclotron motion and uniform linear motion in the direction perpendicular to the electric and magnetic fields. This uniform linear motion can be regarded as the motion of the centre of rotation of the circular motion, and is called the $E\times B$ drift.

Q10. When an electric field perpendicular to the magnetic field is applied to a plasma (a gas in which electrons and positive ions are electrically neutralized) in a magnetic field, explain what motion the plasma performs as a whole.

[II]

Next, as shown in Fig. 1, consider the motion of a charged particle that winds around curved magnetic field lines. Take the $z$ axis in the direction in which the centre of rotation of the cyclotron motion of the charged particle advances. The distribution of the magnetic field lines is symmetric about the $z$ axis. When the magnetic field lines are curved in this way, the value of the magnetic flux density is not uniform in the $z$-axis direction. In this case the charged particle in it performs accelerated motion in the $z$ direction. When the particle moves in the $z$ direction, if the change of the magnetic flux density during one period of the cyclotron motion is sufficiently small compared with the value of $B$ at that point, the motion in it can be approximated as the superposition of cyclotron motion in the $x$-$y$ plane and motion of its centre of rotation in the $z$-axis direction.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

However, the angular frequency of the cyclotron motion changes as

$$\omega_{\mathrm{c}}(z)=\frac{qB_z(z)}{m} \qquad (6)$$

using the magnetic flux density $B_z(z)$ at the centre of the circle.

On the other hand, $V_z$, which was constant in [I], depends on $z$. So let us consider the accelerated motion of the charged particle in the $z$ direction. For this we use the relation (equation (5) of Q3) that holds between the cyclotron radius $r_{\mathrm{c}}$, the speed of the circular motion $V_\perp>0$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{c}}$, and the following two laws.

(1) Here, since the change of the magnetic field is sufficiently slow, the force from the magnetic field acting on the charged particle can be regarded as always pointing towards the centre of rotation. Therefore, for the circular motion, the law of constant areal velocity

$$r_{\mathrm{c}}V_\perp=C_1 \quad (\text{constant}) \qquad (7)$$

is assumed to hold.

(2) Since the force due to the magnetic field is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, the kinetic energy is constant, and

$$\frac{1}{2}m\left({V_z}^2+{V_\perp}^2\right)=C_2 \quad (\text{constant}) \qquad (8)$$

holds.

Q11. Express $C_1$ and $C_2$, which appeared in equations (7) and (8), using $V_\perp(0)$, $V_z(0)$, $B_z(0)$, $q$, $m$.

Q12. Show that when the centre of the circular motion moves in the $z$ direction and $B_z$ changes, $\dfrac{1}{2}mV_\perp(z)^2$ changes in proportion to $B_z(z)$.

Q13. Now, introducing the function of $z$

$$U(z)=\frac{mV_\perp(0)^2B_z(z)}{2B_z(0)}$$

show that for the motion of the particle in the $z$ direction the relation

$$\frac{1}{2}mV_z(z)^2+U(z)=C_2 \qquad (9)$$

holds.

If $U(z)$ is regarded as a potential energy as a function of $z$, equation (9) can be considered as the law of conservation of mechanical energy for the one-dimensional motion of the charged particle in the $z$ direction. This shows that when the magnetic flux density changes, a force acts on the charged particle in the direction of the magnetic field lines.

Below, the magnetic flux density $B_z(z)$ is taken to be a function symmetric about $z=0$ that has its minimum value at $z=0$ and increases with $|z|$. The magnetic field represented in Fig. 1 is an example of such a magnetic field.

Q14. As in Fig. 2, there are plates at $z=\pm L$ in the magnetic field, and a charged particle that hits a plate is absorbed and disappears. When the ratio of the maximum value $B_z(L)$ to the minimum value $B_z(0)$ of the magnetic flux density is

$$M=\frac{B_z(L)}{B_z(0)}$$

express, using $M$, the condition on $V_\perp(0)$ and $V_z(0)$ for the charged particle to move back and forth without hitting the plates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2011-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[吸収板 = absorbing plate]

Now consider the space having $V_x$, $V_y$, $V_z$ as its three coordinates (velocity space). The result of the previous question shows that the point representing the velocity of the charged particle at $z=0$ does not lie in a conical region whose axis is the $V_z$ direction. This cone is called the loss cone, and it is characteristic of plasmas confined in the Earth's magnetosphere and the like. The confinement of charged particles in the region outside the loss cone in velocity space around the point where the magnetic flux density is minimum, as in Fig. 2, is called the "magnetic mirror effect".

Q15. Sketch the shape of the loss cone in velocity space, and, when the apex angle of the loss cone is $2\theta$, express $\sin\theta$ using the ratio $M$ of the maximum and minimum values of the magnetic flux density.

It is known that the group of charged particles confined by the magnetic mirror effect of the Earth's magnetic field (the magnetospheric plasma) is sometimes shaken by the wind of plasma blowing out of the Sun, and charged particles leak out of the magnetic mirror (the magnetosphere) and plunge into the ionosphere at places near the South and North Poles where the magnetic field lines of the magnetosphere come down to the Earth's surface. As a result, aurorae occur.

(Reference)

In the following formulas $a$ is a constant.

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\sin(ax)}{\mathrm{d}x}=a\cos(ax), \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}\cos(ax)}{\mathrm{d}x}=-a\sin(ax)$$

$$\int\sin(ax)\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac{1}{a}\cos(ax)+C, \qquad \int\cos(ax)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\sin(ax)+C$$

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Mass of the electron} & m_{\mathrm{e}}=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Elementary charge} & e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Problem 1A
problems.problem:
Problem 1A (50 points)

Small oscillations around a stable point (equilibrium point) are seen in many phenomena around us, and from information about the oscillations one can study the properties of the oscillating system. Here, let us consider the vibration of a diatomic molecule from the standpoint of classical mechanics.

Consider a molecule formed by the bonding of atom A of mass $m_1$ and atom B of mass $m_2$. The two atoms exert forces on each other; let $\overrightarrow{F}$ be the force that atom A exerts on atom B. For simplicity, assume that no external forces act other than the forces that the two atoms exert on each other.

Consider the case in which these two atoms move on the $x$ axis. Introducing the acceleration $a_1$ of atom A and the acceleration $a_2$ of atom B, the equations of motion of the atoms are

$$m_1a_1=-F \quad \text{and} \quad m_2a_2=F \qquad (1)$$

Here we have used the law of action and reaction. The directions of the forces in Fig. 1 are for the case of attraction.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Let $x_1$ be the position coordinate of atom A and $x_2$ the position coordinate of atom B; in general $F$ is a function of $x_2-x_1$. Therefore the simultaneous equations (1) cannot be solved separately as they stand, but by introducing the centre-of-mass coordinate and the relative coordinate they can be transformed into two mutually independent equations of motion.

First,

$$x_{\mathrm{G}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2} \qquad (2)$$

defined in this way, $x_{\mathrm{G}}$ represents the centre-of-mass coordinate of the two atoms. Also,

$$x=x_2-x_1 \qquad (3)$$

defined in this way, $x$ represents the position of atom B relative to atom A; below we simply call it the relative coordinate. We call the time evolutions of these coordinates the centre-of-mass motion and the relative motion, respectively.

The acceleration of a particle can be calculated using the second derivative of its coordinate with respect to time. For example, the acceleration of atom A is

$$a_1=\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x_1}{\mathrm{d}t^2} \qquad (4)$$

The acceleration $a_{\mathrm{G}}$ of the centre-of-mass motion and the acceleration $a$ of the relative motion can be calculated in the same way from the centre-of-mass coordinate $x_{\mathrm{G}}$ and the relative coordinate $x$.

Q1. (a) The centre of mass of the two atoms moves with constant velocity or is at rest. State the reason.

(b) Derive the equation of the relative motion

$$ma=F \qquad (5)$$

where $m$ is the quantity defined by

$$m=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2} \qquad (6)$$

and is called the reduced mass.

The velocity of the centre of mass is determined once the initial conditions are given. From now on, we consider the case in which the centre of mass is at rest at $x_{\mathrm{G}}=0$.

Q2. As the simplest model of molecular vibration, let us regard the two atoms as point masses of mass $m_1$ and mass $m_2$, and suppose that the two point masses are connected by a spring of spring constant $k$ and natural length $R$. At $t=0$ the spring is stretched by $r$ from its natural length and released gently. The relative motion is simple harmonic motion and is in general expressed as

$$x-R=C_1\cos\omega t+C_2\sin\omega t \qquad (7)$$

where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are constants. Find the angular frequency $\omega$ from the equation of motion, and determine $C_1$ and $C_2$ so that the initial conditions are satisfied.

If the centre of mass of the two point masses then remains at rest, what are the initial displacements $r_1$ and $r_2$ of the respective point masses?

In general, when a force $F(x)$ is expressed by a function $U(x)$ of the coordinate as

$$F(x)=-\frac{\mathrm{d}U(x)}{\mathrm{d}x} \qquad (8)$$

$U(x)$ is called the potential of the force $F(x)$. When $x$ is the relative coordinate and the potential of $F(x)$ is $U(x)$,

$$\frac{1}{2}m\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+U(x)=E \qquad (9)$$

holds. Here $E$ is a constant determined by the initial conditions. Equation (9) is the law of conservation of energy of the relative motion, and $E$ represents the mechanical energy. Below, we call $U(x)$ the potential energy of the relative motion. The first term on the left-hand side of equation (9) is the kinetic energy of the relative motion.

Q3. For the force of Q2, derive the potential energy of the relative motion as a function of the relative coordinate $x$. Take the minimum value of the potential energy to be $0$.

The Morse function

$$U(x)=D\left\{\mathrm{e}^{-2\alpha(x-R)}-2\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha(x-R)}\right\} \qquad (10)$$

which is often used as a more realistic model of the potential energy of the relative motion of a diatomic molecule, is shown in Fig. 2. Here $\alpha$ is a positive constant. At $x=R$, $U(R)$ takes its minimum value $-D$. $R$ represents the equilibrium interatomic distance.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2

Q4. When the mechanical energy $E$ of the relative motion is written as $E=-D+\varepsilon$ (where $\varepsilon\geqq 0$), the bond of the molecule breaks if $\varepsilon$ exceeds a certain limit. Give the range of $\varepsilon$ for which the bond of the molecule does not break.

Q5. When $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small, the relative motion of the molecule is a small oscillation in the neighbourhood of the equilibrium point $x=R$.

(a) When $\alpha|x-R|\ll 1$, derive an approximate expression for $U(x)$ up to the term in $\alpha^2(x-R)^2$, and find the interatomic force constant $k$ (the coefficient corresponding to the spring constant in the case of a spring). If necessary, use the fact that when $|z|$ is sufficiently small compared with 1, one can approximate

$$\mathrm{e}^z\fallingdotseq 1+z+\frac{1}{2}z^2 \qquad (11)$$

(b) The small oscillation of the relative motion is simple harmonic motion. Express its angular frequency $\omega$ in terms of the reduced mass $m$ and $\alpha$, $D$.

(c) Express the amplitude $r$ of the simple harmonic motion in terms of $\varepsilon$, $\alpha$, $D$.

Consider a carbon atom (C) as atom A and an oxygen atom (O) as atom B. The masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ of the atoms are then $12.00\,\mathrm{u}$ and $15.99\,\mathrm{u}$ respectively, where $1\,\mathrm{u}=1.660\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ (u is called the unified atomic mass unit). For the CO molecule it is known from observations that $\omega=4.088\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $D=1.780\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J}$, $R=1.128\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$.

Q6. From the observed values one can learn the constant $\alpha$ of the Morse function and the interatomic force constant $k$. Find the values of $\alpha$ and $k$ for the CO molecule.

Q7. When electromagnetic waves with an angular frequency close to the angular frequency of the small oscillation are shone on a collection of CO molecules, the CO molecules start to vibrate by resonance. Find the wavelength in vacuum of the electromagnetic waves that cause such resonance. To which of X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared and radio waves do electromagnetic waves of this wavelength belong? Take the speed of light in vacuum to be $c=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

problems.title: Problem 1B
problems.problem:
Problem 1B (50 points)

The behaviour of magnets is a physical phenomenon with a long history, and it has played an important role in the study of electromagnetism. Bodies that show the properties of magnets are called ferromagnets.

The behaviour of any magnet can be explained by regarding it as "magnetic charges of opposite sign and equal magnitude existing apart from each other". In this case, the place where the positive magnetic charge is located is the N pole, and the place where the negative magnetic charge is located is the S pole. Magnetic charge corresponds to electric charge, but the magnetic charge of an N pole or an S pole alone has never been found; they always exist in pairs. Introducing magnetic charge, magnetism can be treated in the same way as electricity.

[I]

First, let us study the forces acting between magnets. For simplicity, consider bar magnets of negligible thickness. Let the magnetic charge on the N-pole side of a bar magnet be $q\ (>0)$ and that on the S-pole side be $-q$. A pair of magnetic charges of opposite sign existing at some distance from each other is called a magnetic dipole.

When two magnetic charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ are a distance $r$ apart, a force

$$F=\frac{1}{4\pi\mu_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} \qquad (1)$$

acts on each of these magnetic charges along the straight line joining them; it is repulsive if $F$ is positive and attractive if it is negative (Coulomb's law for magnetic charges). Here $\mu_0$ is the magnetic constant (permeability of vacuum).

A bar magnet in which magnetic charges $\pm q$ form a pair a distance $2d$ apart can be represented by a vector $\overrightarrow{m}$. This vector points from the magnetic charge $-q$ to the magnetic charge $q$ and has magnitude $m=2qd$. $\overrightarrow{m}$ is called the magnetic dipole moment.

Now consider two magnets, each with magnetic dipole moment of the same magnitude $m$, in each of which magnetic charges $\pm q$ form a pair a distance $2d$ apart.

Q1. The two magnets are placed with their centres farther apart than $2d$, at a distance $R\ (>2d)$. In the following cases, find the magnitude of the force acting between the two magnets and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.

(a) Both magnets are perpendicular to the straight line joining the centres of the magnets, and the magnetic dipole moments are parallel and in the same direction (Fig. 1(a)).

(b) Both magnets are perpendicular to the straight line joining the centres of the magnets, and the magnetic dipole moments are parallel and in opposite directions (Fig. 1(b)).

(c) Both magnets lie on the straight line joining the centres of the magnets, and the magnetic dipole moments are in the same direction (Fig. 1(c)).

(d) Both magnets lie on the straight line joining the centres of the magnets, and the magnetic dipole moments are in opposite directions (Fig. 1(d)).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Let us consider approximating the magnitude of the force acting between the magnets in Q1 when $R\gg d$. According to a mathematical formula, for $|\varDelta|<1$ the following expansion is possible for any $p$:

$$(1+\varDelta)^p=1+p\,\varDelta+\frac{1}{2}p\,(p-1)\,\varDelta^2+\cdots \qquad (2)$$

Using this, when $R\gg d$ the magnitude of the force can be expanded as

$$\frac{q^2}{4\pi\mu_0R^2}\left\{c_1\left(\frac{d}{R}\right)^2+c_2\left(\frac{d}{R}\right)^4+c_3\left(\frac{d}{R}\right)^6+\cdots\right\} \qquad (3)$$

Here $c_1\ (\neq 0)$, $c_2$, $c_3, \cdots$ are constants. Since $R\gg d$, the second and subsequent terms inside $\{\ \}$ are sufficiently small compared with the first term; the first term is the leading term, and the magnitude of the force can be approximated using the leading term.

Q2. In Q1 (a)–(d), when $R\gg d$, find the leading term of the magnitude of the force (the term proportional to $\dfrac{1}{R^2}\left(\dfrac{d}{R}\right)^2$) and approximate the magnitude of the force by a simple expression.

In general, when forces that are parallel to each other, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction act at the two ends of a rod-shaped body as in Fig. 2, no acceleration arises at the centre of mass and the rod starts to rotate. Such a pair of forces is called a couple, and the product $N=Fl$ of the magnitude $F$ of the forces and the distance $l$ between the lines of action of the two forces is called the moment of the couple. The moment of a couple is taken as positive when it causes a left-handed (anticlockwise) rotation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[In the figure: 回転の向き = direction of rotation.]

Q3. A bar magnet is placed at the origin with its magnetic dipole moment pointing in the positive $z$ direction. Another bar magnet is placed on the $x$ axis at a distance $R\ (\gg d)$ from the origin, with its magnetic dipole moment pointing in the positive $x$ direction. In each bar magnet, magnetic charges $\pm q$ form a pair a distance $2d$ apart (Fig. 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3

(a) For the magnitude $f$ of the resultant of the forces acting on the right-hand bar magnet in Fig. 3, and the moment $N$ of the forces about the rotation axis passing through the midpoint of the bar magnet and parallel to the $y$ axis, find the leading terms as in Q2 (the terms proportional to $\dfrac{1}{R^2}\left(\dfrac{d}{R}\right)^2$ and $\dfrac{1}{R}\left(\dfrac{d}{R}\right)^2$ respectively), and approximate them by simple expressions. Take the moment as positive when it is anticlockwise looking in the positive $y$ direction.

(b) Suppose a couple parallel to the $z$ axis acts on the two ends of this magnet. Find the magnitude $f_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the forces of the couple that gives the same moment as in (a).

[II]

A magnetic charge $q\ (>0)$ placed in a magnetic field $\overrightarrow{H}$ experiences a force of magnitude $F=qH$ in the direction of $\overrightarrow{H}$. Let us consider how a bar magnet placed in a magnetic field behaves. For simplicity, we treat the bar magnet with a model in which point masses of mass $M$ carrying magnetic charges $\pm q$ are fixed at the two ends of a light rod of length $2d$.

Q4. There is a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $H$ in the positive $z$ direction. In it, a bar magnet is held at an angle $\theta$ to the $z$ axis (Fig. 4). Find the magnitude $N$ of the moment of the couple acting on this magnet.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4

Q5. In a uniform magnetic field $H$ in the positive $z$ direction, a bar magnet that was initially pointing in the $z$ direction is slowly rotated by an angle $\theta$. Work is required to perform this rotation. This work increases the potential energy of the two point masses. Thinking in the same way as for point masses acted on by uniform gravity, find the required work from the increase in potential energy.

Q6. The bar magnet is rotated by an angle $\theta$ from the direction of the magnetic field and released gently. The bar magnet starts a rotational oscillation. Assuming that the angle $\theta$ is sufficiently small, find the period $T$ of the oscillation. You may use the approximation $\sin\theta\fallingdotseq\theta$ when $|\theta|\ll 1$.

Now, in a uniform magnetic field the resultant of the forces acting on a magnetic dipole such as a bar magnet is $0$. However, if the magnetic field is not uniform and the magnetic field at the position of $+q$ differs from the magnetic field at the position of $-q$, the resultant of the forces acting on the magnetic dipole is not $0$.

Q7. The magnetic dipole moment of a bar magnet points in the positive $z$ direction. The strength $H$ of the magnetic field in the $z$ direction varies with $z$, and its rate of change $\dfrac{\varDelta H}{\varDelta z}$ is constant within the region considered. Find the direction and the magnitude $f$ of the resultant force acting on the bar magnet in this case. Express $f$ using the magnitude $m\ (=2dq)$ of the magnetic dipole moment. Assume $\dfrac{\varDelta H}{\varDelta z}>0$.

[III]

A ferromagnetic magnet, however finely it is divided, remains in each piece a small magnetic dipole. Eventually this leads to the microscopic world of atoms and molecules. In this microscopic world, what produces ferromagnetism is the electron, and the electron itself is a small magnet.

That the electron is a small magnet was shown by the ingenious experiment of Stern and Gerlach in 1922. They showed that when silver vapour, as an atomic beam, is passed between the poles of an electromagnet of a characteristic shape, it splits into two lines.

In the experiment of Stern and Gerlach, an electromagnet of depth (length) $L$ was used whose N pole and S pole have a cross-section as in Fig. 5(a), producing a magnetic field that is non-uniform in the vertical direction near the centre, and a thin beam of silver atoms was passed through its centre. As a result, the silver atoms deposited on a screen behind it in a pattern split into two, upper and lower, at the centre (Fig. 5(b)).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5

[In the figure: z 軸, y 軸, x 軸 = $z$ axis, $y$ axis, $x$ axis; 銀原子ビーム = silver atom beam; スクリーン = screen.]

Q8. Take the coordinate axes as in Fig. 5, with the $z$ axis in the direction from the N pole towards the S pole, and let the beam of silver atoms be incident along the $x$ axis. Let the mass of a silver atom be $A$. The incident beam of silver atoms is a collection of silver atoms having magnetic dipole moments $\pm m$ in the positive and negative directions with respect to the $z$ axis. When the initial speed of the silver atoms is $v$, find the separation $l$ after they have passed through the length $L$. Assume that $\dfrac{\varDelta H}{\varDelta z}$ is constant along the path of the beam.

Apart from its single outermost electron, a silver atom has closed shells, and the electrons of closed shells have no magnetic properties. Therefore, the splitting of the silver atom beam into two is thought to be due to the single outermost electron. This experiment showed that the electron not only carries electric charge but is also a small magnet, and moreover that its magnetic dipole moment can point only in two directions: the direction of the magnetic field or the direction opposite to it.

In general, the orbital motion of an electron produces a magnetic dipole moment, but it is known that the orbital motion of the outermost electron of the silver atom makes no such contribution, so the observed magnetic dipole moment originates from the electron itself (its spin).

This experiment, by showing that the electron, an elementary particle, has a magnetic dipole moment, provided an important foothold not only for the magnetic properties of the electron but also for the development of quantum mechanics.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (100 points)

Since the Great East Japan Earthquake in March last year, the energy situation in our country has been severe. For the time being, it seems that we will often have to rely on thermal power generation. In thermal power generation, fossil fuels such as natural gas and oil are burned, and the heat (thermal energy) is converted into work (mechanical energy) to generate electricity. It is desirable to raise the thermal efficiency in this process. On the other hand, when electric power is used in daily life for heating and cooling, refrigeration, hot-water supply and so on, it is important to raise the efficiency with which the work (electrical energy) for transferring heat is used. This problem of energy conversion between heat and work is a problem of thermodynamics.

[I]

In general, a device that converts heat into work is called a heat engine. As shown in Fig. 1, a heat engine receives heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$ from a high-temperature heat reservoir, does work $W$ on the outside, and releases heat $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$ to a low-temperature heat reservoir. The heat engine repeats this periodically. The efficiency of the heat engine, that is, the thermal efficiency, is then defined by

$$e=\frac{W}{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[In the figure: 高温熱源 = high-temperature heat reservoir; 熱機関 = heat engine; 低温熱源 = low-temperature heat reservoir.]

As an example of a heat engine, consider a cylinder as in Fig. 2 in which a gas is enclosed by a smoothly moving piston. The left wall conducts heat, and the temperature of the gas in the cylinder can be controlled by bringing this wall into contact with a heat reservoir at constant temperature. The side walls of the cylinder and the piston are made of a heat-insulating material that does not conduct heat. A substance used in a heat engine, like this gas, is called the working substance. The state of the gas in the cylinder is specified by the pressure $P$, the volume $V$ and the absolute temperature $T$ (hereafter simply called the temperature; note that $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}=273\,\mathrm{K}$). The energy that this gas possesses is called the internal energy.

The internal energy $U$ of the gas is a physical quantity determined once the state of the gas is specified, and, like $P$, $V$, $T$, it is called a state quantity (state function). Whatever path the state of the gas follows in changing, if it returns to the initial state, the values of the state quantities return to their initial values. When a system undergoes a change of state, "the change $\varDelta U$ in internal energy is equal to the sum of the heat absorbed by the system during the change of state and the work done on it from outside". This is called the first law of thermodynamics. Heat is one form of energy, and this law is nothing other than the law of conservation of energy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[In the figure: 熱源 = heat reservoir; 気体 = gas; 断熱材 = heat-insulating material.]

Now consider changing the state of the gas in the cylinder of Fig. 2 quasi-statically (extremely slowly, maintaining equilibrium), as shown in Fig. 3. That is:

A → B: The left wall of the cylinder is brought into contact with the high-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$), and the gas is expanded while its temperature is kept at $T_{\mathrm{H}}$ (isothermal expansion). During this, the gas absorbs a positive quantity of heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$ from the high-temperature reservoir.

B → C: The cylinder is separated from the heat reservoir, and the gas is expanded adiabatically, lowering its temperature to $T_{\mathrm{L}}$.

C → D: The left wall of the cylinder is brought into contact with the low-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{L}}$), and the gas is compressed while its temperature is kept at $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ (isothermal compression). During this, the gas releases a positive quantity of heat $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$ to the low-temperature reservoir.

D → A: The cylinder is separated from the heat reservoir, and the gas is compressed adiabatically, raising its temperature to $T_{\mathrm{H}}$.

Of these four processes, in the first two expansion processes the gas does work on the outside, and in the last two compression processes work is done on it from outside. The net work $W$ done on the outside is represented by the area of the figure ABCD in Fig. 3.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[In the figure: AB 等温膨張 = AB isothermal expansion; BC 断熱膨張 = BC adiabatic expansion; CD 等温圧縮 = CD isothermal compression; DA 断熱圧縮 = DA adiabatic compression.]

In general, the periodic motion of a heat engine or the periodic change of the working substance is called a cycle. In particular, the cycle considered here was first studied by Carnot and is therefore called the Carnot cycle. A heat engine that uses the Carnot cycle is called a Carnot heat engine. By the first law of thermodynamics, between the heat and work going in and out while the state of the gas goes through one cycle and the change $\varDelta U$ in internal energy during that time, there is the relation

$$\varDelta U=Q_{\mathrm{H}}-W-Q_{\mathrm{L}} \qquad (1)$$

Q1. Taking into account that the internal energy is a state quantity, find the relation that holds between $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $W$ of equation (1). Using this, express the efficiency $e_{\mathrm{c}}\left(=\dfrac{W}{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}\right)$ of the Carnot heat engine in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$.

The quasi-static changes described above are reversible processes, in which the reverse change can also occur. On the other hand, when a hot body and a cold body are brought into contact, the two bodies eventually reach the same temperature, but heat never flows in the reverse direction to return the bodies to their original temperatures. Such a flow of heat between two bodies with a temperature difference is an irreversible process, in which the reverse change does not occur.

We experience many similar things. The irreversibility of thermal phenomena was studied by Clausius and Thomson (later Lord Kelvin), and as the second law of thermodynamics it is stated as the following two mutually equivalent principles.

Clausius's principle
"A process whose only result is to transfer heat from a colder body (low-temperature reservoir) to a hotter body (high-temperature reservoir), leaving no other change in the surroundings, is impossible."

Thomson's principle
"A process that merely takes heat from a single heat reservoir and does positive work on the outside, bringing about no other change, is impossible."

To describe irreversibility quantitatively, Clausius introduced the entropy $S$, defined as follows, and showed that $S$ is a state quantity. When a quantity of heat $Q$ is absorbed by a system at temperature $T$, the change $\varDelta S$ in the entropy of this system is given by

$$\varDelta S=\frac{Q}{T} \qquad (2)$$

Also, the entropy of a system consisting of several parts at different temperatures is the sum of the entropies of the parts.

In a closed system (a system with no flow in or out of energy, such as heat or work, and no flow in or out of matter), the entropy increases or remains unchanged; it never decreases. This is called the law of increase of entropy. If the adiabatic expansion and adiabatic compression processes are carried out reversibly, as in the Carnot cycle, the entropy does not change, but if they are irreversible, the entropy increases. A detailed argument shows that the law of increase of entropy is another expression of the second law of thermodynamics.

Q2. Two bodies with temperatures $T_{\mathrm{H}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ ($T_{\mathrm{H}}>T_{\mathrm{L}}$) were brought into contact for a short time, and a small quantity of heat $Q$ moved. Express the change $\varDelta S$ in the entropy of the whole made up of the two bodies together in terms of $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$, $Q$, and confirm that the entropy increases in this irreversible process. Assume that the heat capacities of the two bodies are sufficiently large that the temperatures of both bodies do not change during this transfer of heat.

Let us now return to the Carnot cycle. All processes of the Carnot cycle are reversible processes. In the isothermal expansion process AB of Fig. 3, this gas receives the quantity of heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$ from the high-temperature reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$), so according to the definition (2) of entropy above, the entropy of this gas increases by $\varDelta S_{\mathrm{AB}}=\dfrac{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}}}$.

Q3. After calculating the changes $\varDelta S_{\mathrm{BC}}$, $\varDelta S_{\mathrm{CD}}$, $\varDelta S_{\mathrm{DA}}$ of the entropy of the gas in the processes BC, CD, DA, express the total change $\varDelta S$ of the entropy of this gas from the start until one cycle is completed and the gas returns to the initial state A, in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$. Taking into account that the entropy $S$ is a state quantity, what relation holds between $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$?

Q4. Using the result of the previous question, express the efficiency $e_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the Carnot heat engine using only the temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$ of the high-temperature reservoir and the temperature $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ of the low-temperature reservoir.

A cycle in which each process of the change of state is reversible, like the Carnot cycle above, is called a reversible cycle. In a real heat engine, irreversibility is always present in each process, and extra entropy is generated in the working substance. Suppose that the changes of state A → B, B → C, C → D, D → A in Fig. 3 include irreversible processes, and let $S_{\mathrm{i}}\ (>0)$ be the total entropy generated in the working substance during one cycle as a result of irreversibility.

All entropies appearing below are, as so far, entropies in the gas that is the working substance.

Q5. Express the total change $\varDelta S$ of the entropy while this heat engine performs one cycle in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{i}}$. Again taking into account that the entropy $S$ is a state quantity, show that the efficiency $e=\dfrac{W}{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}$ of this heat engine is smaller than the efficiency $e_{\mathrm{c}}$ of a Carnot heat engine using heat reservoirs at the same temperatures.

In general, it is known that the efficiency of a heat engine using a reversible cycle is the theoretical upper limit of the thermal efficiency.

Let us now consider the thermal efficiency of recent thermal power generation. In particular, in power generation using liquefied natural gas (LNG) as fuel, the thermal efficiency has improved remarkably in recent years, and the thermal efficiency of power generation is approaching about 60%. This high efficiency has been achieved by combined cycle power generation, which combines a gas turbine and a steam turbine. In this kind of generation, the gas turbine is driven by the high-temperature gas produced by the combustion of fuel, generating electricity. Since the exhaust gas of the gas turbine is still sufficiently hot, this hot gas is reused as a high-temperature heat reservoir to generate electricity with a steam turbine.

Q6. For simplicity, idealize combined cycle power generation: treat the gas turbine and the steam turbine as two reversible Carnot heat engines, and assume that all the heat discharged to the low-temperature reservoir of the gas turbine is used by the steam turbine. Let the temperature of the high-temperature reservoir of the gas turbine be $T_{\mathrm{gH}}$, the temperature of its low-temperature reservoir be $T_{\mathrm{gL}}$, and its thermal efficiency be $e_{\mathrm{g}}$. Also, let the temperature of the high-temperature reservoir of the steam turbine be $T_{\mathrm{sH}}$, the temperature of its low-temperature reservoir be $T_{\mathrm{sL}}$, and its thermal efficiency be $e_{\mathrm{s}}$.

(a) Express the thermal efficiency $e_{\mathrm{cc}}$, when the whole combined cycle is regarded as a single reversible cycle, in terms of $e_{\mathrm{g}}$ and $e_{\mathrm{s}}$.

(b) Express $e_{\mathrm{cc}}$ in terms of $T_{\mathrm{gH}}$, $T_{\mathrm{gL}}$, $T_{\mathrm{sH}}$, $T_{\mathrm{sL}}$.

(c) Let the combustion temperature of the gas turbine be $1500\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the temperature of the exhaust gas after power generation be $600\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Also, let the temperature of the high-temperature reservoir for the steam turbine be $600\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the temperature of its low-temperature reservoir be $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. How many times the thermal efficiency when only the gas turbine is used is the thermal efficiency of the combined cycle?

[II]

In the previous section we found the thermal efficiency of the Carnot cycle, which constitutes an ideal heat engine, and, as a realistic heat engine, considered the thermal efficiency of a cycle in which irreversible processes are present. Next, let us consider a device that does work on the gas in a cylinder from outside and pumps heat from a low-temperature reservoir to a high-temperature reservoir (a heat pump) (Fig. 4). As an example, let us take a heat pump using the reverse Carnot cycle. The reverse Carnot cycle is a cycle in which work $W(>0)$ is done from outside on the gas in the cylinder of Fig. 2, heat $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$ is absorbed from the low-temperature reservoir ($T_{\mathrm{L}}$), and heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$ is released to the high-temperature reservoir ($T_{\mathrm{H}}$). In the Carnot cycle, the processes of change of state of the gas proceeded clockwise in Fig. 3, but in the reverse Carnot cycle they proceed anticlockwise. The gas starts from state D and returns to the initial state D through the following four quasi-static processes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4

[In the figure: 高温熱源 = high-temperature heat reservoir; ヒートポンプ = heat pump; 低温熱源 = low-temperature heat reservoir.]

D → C: The left wall of the cylinder is brought into contact with the low-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{L}}$), and the gas is expanded while its temperature is kept at $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ (isothermal expansion). During this, the gas absorbs a positive quantity of heat $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$.

C → B: The cylinder is separated from the heat reservoir, and the gas is compressed adiabatically, raising its temperature to $T_{\mathrm{H}}$.

B → A: The left wall of the cylinder is brought into contact with the high-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$), and the gas is compressed while its temperature is kept at $T_{\mathrm{H}}$ (isothermal compression). During this, the gas releases a positive quantity of heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$.

A → D: The cylinder is separated from the heat reservoir, and the gas is expanded adiabatically, lowering its temperature to $T_{\mathrm{L}}$.

In the case of the reverse cycle, work is done on the gas in the cylinder from outside in the compression processes C → B, B → A, and the gas does work on the outside in the expansion processes D → C, A → D. The difference is the net work $W$ done on the gas from outside, and it is represented by the area of the figure ABCD in Fig. 3.

Since the reverse Carnot cycle consists of quasi-static processes, it is a reversible cycle, just like the Carnot cycle.

Q7. Express the change $\varDelta U$ in the internal energy of the gas during one cycle of the reverse Carnot cycle in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $W$. Taking into account that the internal energy is a state quantity, find the relation between these three quantities.

Q8. Express the total change $\varDelta S$ of the entropy in the processes during one cycle of the reverse Carnot cycle in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$. Next, taking into account that the entropy is a state quantity, find the relation between $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$.

Q9. The heat pump is used as a cooling device (air conditioner), with the room as the low-temperature reservoir and the outdoors as the high-temperature reservoir. The cooling efficiency of a general cooling device is defined as $\varepsilon=\dfrac{Q_{\mathrm{L}}}{W}$, and in particular the efficiency of a reversible heat pump using the reverse Carnot cycle is denoted $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}$. Express $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}$ only in terms of the temperatures $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$.

So far we have assumed that all processes are reversible processes. In reality, entropy due to irreversibility is always generated in each process of the cycle.

Q10. Let $S_{\mathrm{i}}\ (>0)$ be the entropy generated in the working substance during one cycle as a result of irreversibility. Express the total change $\varDelta S$ of the entropy over all the processes during one cycle of the reverse Carnot cycle in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{i}}$. Taking into account that the entropy is a state quantity, find the relation that holds between $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{i}}$. Show that in this case the efficiency $\varepsilon$ of a general cooling device including irreversible processes is smaller than the cooling efficiency $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}$ of a heat pump using the reverse Carnot cycle with heat reservoirs at the same temperatures.

Just as a heat engine using a reversible cycle is ideal with regard to thermal efficiency, a heat pump using a reversible cycle such as the reverse Carnot cycle is, as far as cooling efficiency is concerned, an ideal cooling device.

Q11. When the outdoors is a high-temperature reservoir at temperature $30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the room is a low-temperature reservoir at temperature $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, calculate the theoretical upper limit $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}$ of the cooling efficiency. What does $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}$ become when the room temperature is set higher, changing it to $27\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$? Also, in each case, what is the minimum electric power, in W, required to extract $1000\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat per second from the room?

Q12. The above argument holds in exactly the same way for cooling by a refrigerator, if the inside of the refrigerator is taken as the low-temperature reservoir and the room in which the refrigerator is placed as the high-temperature reservoir. Assuming all processes are reversible, find the cooling efficiency $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rc}}$ of this ideal refrigerator when the temperature inside the refrigerator is $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the room temperature is $27\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. What is the minimum electric power, in W, required to remove $1000\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat per second from inside the refrigerator, the low-temperature reservoir?

Reference: For heating and hot-water supply, an argument similar to the one for cooling and refrigeration is possible. For example, for heating, one may take the room as the high-temperature reservoir and the outdoors as the low-temperature reservoir, and consider the heating efficiency of a reversible heat pump using the reverse Carnot cycle (the efficiency $Q_{\mathrm{H}}/W$ with which heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$ is pumped from outdoors into the room by doing work $W$ on the gas) in the same way as for cooling. In practice, the efficiency of a heat pump is called the energy consumption efficiency (Coefficient of Performance: abbreviated COP, also called the coefficient of performance (成績係数)), and it is an important indicator of the performance of the air conditioners we use every day at home. According to recent data, the energy consumption efficiency is about $6\sim7$ even in the best cases, considerably lower than the efficiency of a reversible heat pump. To use energy effectively, in addition to effectively reusing waste heat and the like, efforts on the technical side are needed to bring the thermal efficiency of heat engines and the efficiency of heat pumps closer to their theoretical upper limits (that is, to reduce the losses due to irreversibility).

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (100 points)

[I]

About 80 years ago, Hubble discovered that distant galaxies are receding from us with speeds proportional to their distances from the Earth. This is called Hubble's law, and the speed at which a galaxy recedes is called the recession velocity. It was the result of discovering that the wavelengths of visible light from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer (redder) wavelengths (this is called redshift), interpreting the reason for the lengthening of the wavelength as the Doppler effect of light, and connecting it to the speed at which the galaxies recede. It was the discovery of the expansion of the universe. Between the distance $D$ to a galaxy and the recession velocity $v$, provided $v$ is sufficiently small compared with the speed of light $c$, there is the proportional relation

$$v=H_0\,D \qquad (1)$$

and the proportionality constant $H_0$ is called the Hubble constant (see Table 1 for its value). As a unit of the distance ($D$) to celestial bodies, the light-year (the distance light travels in one year) is sometimes used (for example, $\dfrac{c}{H_0}$ is about 14 billion light-years).

Table 1. Physical constants

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline c & \text{(speed of light)} & 3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s} \\ \hline H_0 & \text{(Hubble constant)} & 1/(14\ \text{billion years}) \\ \hline G & \text{(gravitational constant)} & 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m^2/kg^2} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Q1. At high temperatures, atoms emit light of wavelengths characteristic of the atom. For example, the light emitted by hydrogen atoms in the laboratory includes characteristic light with wavelengths $\lambda_\alpha=656.28\,\mathrm{nm}$, $\lambda_\beta=486.13\,\mathrm{nm}$, $\lambda_\gamma=434.05\,\mathrm{nm}$, and so on. For the various characteristic lines of light that left a certain galaxy and reached the Earth, the ratios of the wavelengths were the same as the laboratory values on Earth, and every wavelength was $2.0\,\%$ longer than the laboratory value on Earth. Regarding this as the Doppler effect of light, by analogy with the Doppler effect of sound and using equation (1), answer how many light-years the distance to this galaxy is estimated to be. Since the recession velocity is very large, the motion of the Earth and the Sun compared with it may be ignored.

Let us confirm that Hubble's law (1) holds regardless of the choice of the observer's position.

Q2. With the Earth E as origin, let the position vector of galaxy A be $\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{EA}}(t)$; then equation (1) is expressed as $\overrightarrow{v}_{\mathrm{EA}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{EA}}(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=H_0\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{EA}}(t)$. Let the position vector of another galaxy C be $\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{EC}}(t)$; if an observer were in galaxy C, the position vector $\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{CA}}(t)$ of galaxy A seen from there would be expressed as $\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{CA}}(t)=\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{EA}}(t)-\overrightarrow{D}_{\mathrm{EC}}(t)$ (Fig. 1). Show that the relation between the velocity of galaxy A and the distance to the galaxy as seen by the observer in galaxy C also satisfies Hubble's law (1) in the same form.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Now let us look at Hubble's law (1) in a little more detail. Imagine a spherical surface like a globe made of a balloon (Fig. 2). When the balloon is inflated, the distance $D_{\mathrm{AB}}(t)$ between any two points A and B on the spherical surface at time $t$ increases with the expansion of the balloon. $D_{\mathrm{AB}}(t)$ can be expressed as $D_{\mathrm{AB}}(t)=a(t)\,r_{\mathrm{AB}}$ using a coefficient $a(t)$ that depends only on time and a distance $r_{\mathrm{AB}}$ that does not depend on time (a value that does not depend on the expansion, expressed for example by the difference in latitude).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Expansion of a balloon sphere
That A and B move away from each other is interpreted as the expansion of the universe. The size of the ants does not change, but the distance $D_{\mathrm{AB}}$ between them increases. On the other hand, $r_{\mathrm{AB}}$, like the difference in latitude, does not change merely through the expansion.

In the same way, if the universe expands uniformly, the distance $D_{\mathrm{AB}}(t)$ between any two points A, B at time $t$ is expressed, using a time-independent distance $r_{\mathrm{AB}}$ and a function $a(t)$ of time only, as

$$D_{\mathrm{AB}}(t)=a(t)\,r_{\mathrm{AB}} \qquad (2)$$

$r_{\mathrm{AB}}$, which does not change even when the universe expands, is called the comoving distance. The actual distance $D_{\mathrm{AB}}(t)$ at time $t$ is called the proper distance. $a(t)$ is called the scale factor of the universe. Below, the present time is denoted $t_0$. The present value $a(t_0)$ of the scale factor is sometimes abbreviated as $a_0$.

(The actual space of the universe is three-dimensional, but above, for ease of understanding, the universe was likened to the two-dimensional space of the surface of a balloon sphere. Because of this the size of the universe became finite, but it is not known whether the actual universe is finite or infinite. However, if we consider a very small region, the curvature of space can be ignored, just as a spherical surface can be approximated by a plane. It has been confirmed by observation that in the actual universe the curvature can be almost ignored up to large regions.)

[II]

Let us consider the energy density of the universe, which is deeply related to the expansion of the universe.

A body of mass $m$ at rest has, using the speed of light $c$, an energy $E$ given by Einstein's relation

$$E=mc^2 \qquad (3)$$

Therefore the energy density $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter (the subscript m means matter) is expressed, using the mass density $\mu$, as

$$\rho_{\mathrm{m}}=\mu c^2 \qquad (4)$$

Here, by matter we mean atoms and molecules and also particles unknown to us that may exist; including these as well, we consider that the masses and numbers of particles do not change even when the universe expands. Then the mass density $\mu$, and therefore the energy density $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter, decreases with the expansion of the universe, in inverse proportion to the expanding volume. Since the volume is proportional to the cube of the proper distance, it increases in proportion to the cube of the scale factor. Hence $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, with $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(t_0)$ its value at the present time $t_0$, will change as

$$\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(t)=\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(t_0)\left(\frac{a_0}{a(t)}\right)^3 \qquad (5)$$

Another important energy density is the "energy density of the vacuum". Recent research has found that the vacuum actually has an energy density, and that, as an effect of it, the rate of expansion of the universe is increasing; for this discovery, S. Perlmutter and two others received the Nobel Prize in 2011.

The properties of the vacuum do not change even when the universe expands, and the energy density of the vacuum is considered to be constant, unchanged by the expansion of the universe. Writing the energy density of the vacuum as $\rho_{\mathrm{v}}$ (the subscript v means vacuum), this is expressed as

$$\rho_{\mathrm{v}}(t)=\rho_{\mathrm{v}}(t_0)=(\text{constant}) \qquad (6)$$

Below, we use this property (6) for the energy density of the vacuum.

The total energy density $\rho$ of the universe is the sum of $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(t)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{v}}(t)$.

It is known that the scale factor $a(t)$ of the universe, together with its rate of change in time $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t}$, is related to the energy density $\rho$ of the universe by the following equation:

$$\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2=\frac{8\pi G}{3c^2}\,\rho a^2+K \qquad (7)$$

Here $G$ is the gravitational constant (see Table 1), and $K$ is another constant that will be discussed later.

In the case where the universe has no vacuum energy density ($\rho=\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$), equation (7) can be understood as follows, using equation (4) and classical Newtonian laws.

In general, a gravitational force acts between two bodies, and its magnitude obeys the law of universal gravitation: "the force is proportional to the product of the masses $m_1$, $m_2$ of the two bodies and inversely proportional to the square of the distance $D_{12}$ between the bodies".

Now, suppose an observer is at the origin O (Fig. 3) and assume that, with the expansion of the universe, the surrounding matter recedes uniformly from the point O; consider the motion of an arbitrary body A that moves away from O with the expansion of the universe. Let the mass of A be $m$ and the distance OA be $D$. Here $D$ increases with the expansion of the universe and, from equation (2), is expressed using a constant $r$ as

$$D(t)=a(t)\,r \qquad (8)$$

The gravitational forces exerted on body A by the matter outside A pull A from all directions and cancel each other, so they exert no force on A. On the other hand, the gravitational force exerted on A by the matter inside A, within radius $D$, pulls A with the same magnitude as if the total mass $M$ of the matter within radius $D$ were concentrated at the centre O. Therefore, by the law of universal gravitation, the gravitational force on A is expressed as

$$f=-\frac{GmM}{D^2}$$

The proportionality constant $G$ is the gravitational constant. The sign of the force is taken as positive when the force is in the direction of increasing the distance $D$ (repulsive), and negative represents attraction. The speed at which body A recedes is $v=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}D}{\mathrm{d}t}$, and its acceleration is $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3

From Newton's law of motion, "the product of the mass and the acceleration of a body is equal to the force acting on the body", the motion of body A obeys

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\frac{GmM}{D^2} \qquad (9)$$

Noting that in the above equation the mass $M$ is constant in time despite the expansion,

$$\frac{1}{2}v^2-\frac{GM}{D}=C\ (\text{constant}) \qquad (10)$$

is derived.

Q3. Derive equation (10).
Hint: Try differentiating the left-hand side of equation (10) with respect to time. Note that $v=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}D}{\mathrm{d}t}$.

Now, using the mass density $\mu$ of the universe, $M=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\mu D^3$, and from equation (4) this is expressed as

$$M=\frac{4\pi}{3c^2}\,\rho_{\mathrm{m}}D^3 \qquad (11)$$

Q4. For the case $\rho=\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, derive equation (7) from equations (8), (10) and (11).

In the argument above, we were able to derive equation (7) in the case where the energy density $\rho$ is only the energy of matter. In fact, it is known from the general theory of relativity that equation (7) also holds in the general case in which the energy density $\rho$ includes the energy density of the vacuum. Below, we assume equation (7) in general.

Now, equation (10) means that if $C>0$, body A, even after going infinitely far away $\left(D\to\infty,\ \dfrac{GM}{D}\to 0\right)$, retains a finite speed $v=\sqrt{2C}$ and the universe expands, whereas if $C<0$, the body cannot go infinitely far away $\left(\dfrac{GM}{D}\to 0\right)$, and the universe will at some point stop expanding and turn towards contraction. From recent observations of the universe, it is known that the universe is close to $C=0$, the boundary between continuing to expand and stopping in the future, and that therefore the constant $K$ is almost zero. Below, let us assume $K=0$. Then equation (7) becomes $\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2=\dfrac{8\pi G}{3c^2}\,\rho a^2$, and, introducing

$$H=\frac{1}{a}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (12)$$

it can be written as

$$H=\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G\rho}{3c^2}} \qquad (13)$$

Also, differentiating equation (8) with respect to time gives

$$v=\frac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t}\,r=\left(\frac{1}{a}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)(ar)=HD \qquad (14)$$

Considering this equation in the neighbourhood of the Earth and comparing equations (1) and (14), we see that the present value $H(t_0)$ of $H(t)$ is $H_0$, and that, using in equation (13) the present energy density of the universe $\rho_0$ and the present value $H_0$ of $H$, the following relation holds:

$$H_0=\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G\rho_0}{3c^2}} \qquad (15)$$

Q5. Using equation (15) and the values in Table 1, find the present energy density $\rho_0$ of the universe. Also find how many hydrogen atoms per $1\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of volume this value corresponds to in terms of rest energy (3) (two significant figures are enough). Take Avogadro's constant to be $N_{\mathrm{A}}=6.022\times10^{23}/\mathrm{mol}$.

[III]

Suppose a photon leaves a star at time $t$, travels towards the Earth, and reaches an observer on the ground at the present time $t_0$. Let us consider the effect of the expansion of the universe in this case. When light moves a comoving distance $\varDelta r$ during a small time $\varDelta t$, the distance actually travelled by the light (the proper distance) is, using the speed of light $c$,

$$\varDelta D=a(t)\,\varDelta r=c\,\varDelta t \qquad \therefore\ \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{c}{a(t)} \qquad (16)$$

The comoving distance $r$ to the star is $r=\displaystyle\int_0^r \mathrm{d}r=\int_t^{t_0}\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t$, and using (16) here gives $r=\displaystyle\int_t^{t_0}\frac{c}{a(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t$, so the present proper distance $D$ to the star is expressed, using the present scale factor $a_0=a(t_0)$, as

$$D=a_0r=c\int_t^{t_0}\frac{a_0}{a(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t \qquad (17)$$

Here we define the quantity $z$, called the redshift parameter, by

$$\frac{a(t_0)}{a(t)}=1+z \qquad (18)$$

$z$ is a function of time $t$, and at the present time $t_0$, $z=0$. Using the relation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\dfrac{a_0}{a^2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}a}{\mathrm{d}t}=-H\dfrac{a_0}{a}$ (see equation (12)) obtained by differentiating equation (18) with respect to time,

$$\int_0^z\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{H}=\int_{t_0}^{t}\frac{1}{H}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_t^{t_0}\frac{a_0}{a}\,\mathrm{d}t \qquad (19)$$

so, comparing with equation (17), we see that it can be expressed as

$$D=c\int_0^z\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{H} \qquad (20)$$

Next, let us consider two photons emitted from a distant star towards the Earth. Suppose photon 1, emitted from the star at time $t_1$, arrives at the Earth at time $t_0$, while photon 2, emitted from the star at time $t_1+\varDelta t_1$, arrives at the Earth at time $t_0+\varDelta t_0$ (Fig. 4). Owing to the expansion of the universe, $\varDelta t_1$ and $\varDelta t_0$ are not equal. Let us now find the relation between $\varDelta t_1$ and $\varDelta t_0$. (i) Since the comoving distance between the star under consideration and the Earth is constant in time, the comoving distances travelled by the two photons are equal. Also, (ii) the two photons are both flying towards the Earth during the time $t_1+\varDelta t_1\leqq t\leqq t_0$. During this time, the proper distance travelled in a time $\delta t$ is $c\,\delta t$ for both, and the ratio $a(t)$ of the proper distance travelled to the comoving distance travelled is also common to both and equal, so the comoving distances travelled by the two photons in $\delta t$ are equal. Therefore the comoving distances travelled by the two photons between $t_1+\varDelta t_1$ and $t_0$ are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4

[In the figure: 光子 1 = photon 1; 光子 2 = photon 2.]

Q6. Taking (i) and (ii) into account, consider the comoving distance travelled by photon 1 in the first $\varDelta t_1$ and the comoving distance travelled by photon 2 in the last $\varDelta t_0$, and derive the following relation:

$$\frac{\varDelta t_1}{a(t_1)}=\frac{\varDelta t_0}{a(t_0)} \qquad (21)$$

According to equation (21), when the time interval between two events occurring at the star is $\varDelta t_1$, on the ground that time interval is observed stretched to $\varDelta t_0=\varDelta t_1\,(1+z)$.

As a result, when the period of light (the reciprocal of the frequency) on leaving the star is $\varDelta t_1$, by comparing with light emitted one period later, we see that the period when it reaches the ground is stretched to $\varDelta t_0=\varDelta t_1\,(1+z)$. Therefore, when the wavelength of the light on leaving the star was $\lambda_1=c\varDelta t_1$, the wavelength $\lambda=c\varDelta t_0$ observed on the ground is stretched to

$$\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_1}=\frac{a_0}{a}=1+z \qquad (22)$$

This is the general reason for the "redshift", in which the wavelength of visible light is shifted towards the red. When light with a known wavelength $\lambda_1$ characteristic of an element is emitted at a star and is observed on the ground as light of wavelength $\lambda$, $z$ can be observed from (22).

Now, some stars end their lives with a great explosion and are called supernovae. Supernovae of a particular type (called type Ia) have remarkable characteristics: if observed from equal distances, their brightness at maximum is almost the same for all of them, and the time variation of the brightness also follows almost the same course. Therefore supernovae of this kind serve as a standard of brightness independent of place and time.

In astronomy, the brightness of a star when it is hypothetically placed at a distance of $D_{32.6}\equiv 32.6$ light-years is called its absolute luminosity. Here, let the absolute luminosity of a type Ia supernova at its maximum brightness be $L_{32.6}$.

Now, the brightness $L$ of a star is expressed as the energy of the light from the star passing per unit time through unit area perpendicular to its direction of propagation. Therefore $L$ (i) not only decreases depending on a power of the proper distance $D$ from the star, but also (ii) is proportional to the number of photons the star emits per unit time. The number emitted per unit time is inversely proportional to the mean time interval $\varDelta t$ between emissions, but the time interval seen by an observer on the ground is, from equation (21), stretched by a factor $(1+z)$ compared with the time interval observed near the star. Because of this, to an observer on the ground the number of photons emitted per unit time appears reduced to $\dfrac{1}{1+z}$. Furthermore, $L$ is (iii) proportional to the mean energy of one photon, and it is known that the energy of one photon is proportional to the frequency of the light (the reciprocal of the period) and inversely proportional to the wavelength. Therefore the mean energy of one photon seen by an observer on the ground is reduced compared with the mean energy seen near the star, because the wavelength changes as in equation (22).

Q7. Assuming that a type Ia supernova emits light equally in all directions, and taking (i), (ii), (iii) above into account, derive that the brightness $L$ of a type Ia supernova at proper distance $D$ is inversely proportional to $(1+z)^2D^2$.

Thus, since the apparent brightness $L$ of a type Ia supernova is inversely proportional to $(1+z)^2D^2$,

$$\frac{L}{L_{32.6}}=\frac{{D_{32.6}}^2}{(1+z)^2D^2} \qquad (D_{32.6}=32.6\ \text{light-years}) \qquad (23)$$

To express the apparent brightness $L$, the quantity called the "distance modulus" (距離指標)

$$m_{\mathrm{D}}=-\frac{5}{2}\log_{10}\frac{L}{L_{32.6}}=5\log_{10}\frac{(1+z)\,D}{D_{32.6}} \qquad (24)$$

is used. The observation diagram in Fig. 5 shows $z$ and $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ for many observed supernovae.

Now, when $z\ll 1$, $H=H_0$. Therefore, from equation (20) we obtain the following equation:

$$D=\frac{cz}{H_0}, \qquad (z\ll 1) \qquad (25)$$

Q8. Find the distance modulus $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ of a supernova in the case of a sufficiently small redshift $z=0.01$, using equations (24), (25) and the value of the Hubble constant in Table 1, and enter the result with a ○ mark on the observation diagram on the last page of the answer sheets.

Of the present energy density $\rho_0$ of the universe, let the "energy density of matter" be $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(t_0)=x\rho_0$ and the remaining "energy density of the vacuum" be $\rho_{\mathrm{v}}(t_0)=(1-x)\,\rho_0$ ($0\leqq x\leqq 1$). The energy density of the vacuum is constant in time, from equation (6):

$$\rho_{\mathrm{v}}(t)=(1-x)\,\rho_0 \qquad (26)$$

On the other hand, the energy density of matter, because of the expansion of the universe, is from equations (5), (18)

$$\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(t)=(1+z)^3\,x\rho_0 \qquad (27)$$

Therefore the total energy density is $\rho(t)=\{(1+z)^3x+(1-x)\}\,\rho_0$. Using this and the relation $H=H_0\sqrt{\dfrac{\rho}{\rho_0}}$ obtained from equations (13), (15), we obtain $H=H_0\sqrt{x(1+z)^3+(1-x)}$, so equation (20) becomes

$$D=\frac{c}{H_0}\int_0^z\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\sqrt{x(1+z)^3+(1-x)}} \qquad (28)$$

Therefore, if the present fraction $x$ of the energy density of matter $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ is given, the distance modulus $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ of a type Ia supernova with redshift parameter $z$ can be found from (24), (28), and it can be compared with observations.

Q9. In the case where the energy density of the universe is entirely the energy density of the vacuum ($x=0$), find the distance modulus $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ at $z=1$ and at $z=1.4$, and enter the results with ● marks on the observation diagram on the last page of the answer sheets.

Q10. In the case where the energy density of the universe is entirely the energy density of matter ($x=1$), find the distance modulus $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ at $z=1$ and at $z=1.4$, and enter the results with ◎ marks on the observation diagram on the last page of the answer sheets.

[Editorial note: the observation diagram on the last answer sheet is the same graph as Fig. 5.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2012-4-fig5.png

Fig. 5. Observed values of the redshift parameter and the distance modulus of supernovae

[In the figure: $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ (距離指数) = $m_{\mathrm{D}}$ (distance modulus); $z$ (赤方偏移パラメータ) = $z$ (redshift parameter).]

From the comparison of the above results with the observation diagram in Fig. 5, it will be understood that the universe clearly contains vacuum energy density (often called the density of dark energy). A detailed analysis gives $x=0.27$. Because the vacuum energy density is large, the increase of the scale factor $a(t)$ of the universe (the expansion of the universe) satisfies $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2a}{\mathrm{d}t^2}>0$ and is accelerating.

problems.title: Problem 1A
problems.problem:
Problem 1A (55 points)

A coordinate system in which Newton's laws of motion hold is called an inertial coordinate system (inertial frame). Problems in mechanics are usually treated in an inertial frame, but it is sometimes convenient to use a coordinate system that moves with an acceleration relative to an inertial frame (a non-inertial frame). In a non-inertial frame Newton's laws of motion do not hold as they are, but if one takes into account "apparent forces" called inertial forces, problems can be treated using Newton's laws of motion.

Consider a bob hanging by a string from the ceiling inside a vehicle moving horizontally with a constant acceleration $\overrightarrow{a}$. Seen from the ground (an inertial frame), the bob moves with a constant acceleration, so a force $m\overrightarrow{a}$, equal to the product of the acceleration and the mass, must act on the bob. For this reason the string is tilted from the vertical, with a tilt such that the horizontal component of the tension of the string equals $m\overrightarrow{a}$ (see Fig. 1(a)). On the other hand, seen from inside the vehicle (a non-inertial frame), the bob is at rest, so the forces acting on the bob must balance. To explain the observed tilt of the string, a force $-m\overrightarrow{a}$ is necessary (see Fig. 1(b)). This $-m\overrightarrow{a}$ is the inertial force in an accelerated coordinate system that moves with constant acceleration $\overrightarrow{a}$ relative to an inertial frame.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2013-1-fig1.png

[Labels in the figure: 慣性力 = inertial force; (a) 慣性系 = inertial frame; (b) 加速度座標系 = accelerated coordinate system.]

Fig. 1.

Next, consider the case in which, in an inertial frame, a point mass suspended by a string revolves about a vertical axis on a circle of radius $r$ with a constant angular velocity $\omega$. For the point mass to perform uniform circular motion of radius $r$, a centripetal force of magnitude $mr\omega^2$ is necessary. For this reason the string is tilted from the vertical, making a tilt angle such that the horizontal component of the tension of the string equals $mr\omega^2$ (see Fig. 2(a)). On the other hand, when this is seen from a rotating coordinate system rotating with the same angular velocity, the point mass is at rest, so the sum of the forces acting on the point mass (the resultant force) must be $0$ (see Fig. 2(b)). For this, a force balancing the centripetal force must act outward. This force is the inertial force in the rotating coordinate system and is called the centrifugal force.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2013-1-fig2.png

[Labels in the figure: 向心力 = centripetal force; 遠心力 = centrifugal force; (a) 慣性系 = inertial frame; (b) 回転座標系 = rotating coordinate system.]

Fig. 2.

A car of mass $M$ and wheelbase (distance between the axles) $l_1+l_2$ is travelling with speed $v$ on a horizontal straight road. The centre of gravity G of the car is located a distance $l_1$ behind the front axle, at height $h$ above the road surface (see Fig. 3). This car braked suddenly and stopped. Let the magnitude of the acceleration from the start of the deceleration until it stops be $a$ (constant). In a real car a spring mechanism called the suspension is placed between the wheels and the body, but below the suspension is not considered. Therefore the position of the centre of gravity is assumed not to change. Let the coefficient of static friction between the road surface and the tyres be $\mu$, and the gravitational acceleration be $g$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2013-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Q1. Considering the balance of forces and the balance of moments of forces in the coordinate system moving together with the car, find the normal forces $R_1, R_2$ received by the front wheels (sum of left and right) and the rear wheels (sum of left and right) (see Fig. 3).

Q2. Find the upper limit $a_1$ of the magnitude of the acceleration for which no slipping occurs during the deceleration. Also, what relation is necessary between the friction forces $F_1$, $F_2$ of the front and rear wheels and the respective normal forces $R_1$, $R_2$ in order to realize this upper limit?

Q3. Let the mass be $M=1540\,\mathrm{kg}$, the wheelbase $l_1+l_2=2.8\,\mathrm{m}$, $l_1=1.2\,\mathrm{m}$, the height of the centre of gravity $h=56\,\mathrm{cm}$, the coefficient of static friction $\mu=1.0$, and $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. When the braking distance is $L=40\,\mathrm{m}$, calculate $a_1$ and the speed $v_1$ before braking that gives $a_1$.

Next, the car is travelling with constant speed $v$ along a horizontal circular-arc curve. The radius of the circular arc described by the centre of gravity of the car is $r$. The road surface is tilted from the horizontal by an angle $\theta$ as in Fig. 4. Let the height of the centre of gravity of the car be $h$ and the distance between the left and right wheels be $s$, and answer the following. Let the coefficient of static friction between the road surface and the tyres be $\mu$, and the gravitational acceleration be $g$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2013-1-fig4.png

[Label in the figure: 中心の方向 = direction of the centre.]

Fig. 4.

Q4. Find the normal forces $R_1, R_2$ acting on the left wheels (sum of front and rear) and the right wheels (sum of front and rear), and the sum $F_1+F_2$ of the friction forces acting parallel to the road surface.

Q5. Find the upper limit of the speed $v$ for which no sideslip occurs. Here $\tan\theta<\dfrac{1}{\mu}$, and the car is assumed not to roll over.

Q6. Find the upper limit of the speed for which the car does not roll over. Here $\tan\theta<\dfrac{2h}{s}$, and no sideslip is assumed to occur.

Q7. Let $s=1.54\,\mathrm{m}$, $h=0.56\,\mathrm{m}$, $\mu=1.0$. When the road surface has no tilt ($\theta=0$), if the speed is too high, does the car sideslip before rolling over, or does it roll over before sideslipping?

problems.title: Problem 1B
problems.problem:
Problem 1B (55 points)

[I]

If we consider a small plane inside a body, the two parts separated by the plane exert forces on each other. Such a force acting per unit area is called stress. Pressure is a kind of stress; it is a force by which the two parts push each other perpendicular to the plane. The molecules that make up a body are bound to the surrounding molecules and receive forces from the molecules they are bound to; of these forces, the force per unit area received from the molecules on the opposite side of the plane is the stress.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2013-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Near the surface (interface) of a body, the bonds between molecules are different from those in the interior of the body (Fig. 1(a)).
