Gamma-ray cameras have been developed for taking images of gamma-ray sources, for the observation of astronomical phenomena that emit gamma rays, the detection of radioactive substances such as cobalt, and so on. A gamma-ray camera is a measuring instrument for finding out from which direction gamma rays come. For this purpose, quantum effects of electromagnetic waves called the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering are used.

Photoelectric effect

When electromagnetic waves are shone on the surface of a metal, electrons that were bound inside the metal are sometimes "knocked out" of the solid (Fig. 1(a)). This phenomenon is called the photoelectric effect (when it is distinguished from the internal photoelectric effect described later, it is called the external photoelectric effect), and the electrons that have flown out of the metal are called photoelectrons. To explain the photoelectric effect, Einstein introduced the light quantum hypothesis. According to it, an electromagnetic wave is a collection of particles called photons, and if the energy of a photon making up an electromagnetic wave of frequency $\nu$ is $E_\gamma$, the following relation holds between these two quantities.

$$E_\gamma=h\nu \qquad (4)$$

The $h$ appearing here is called the Planck constant, and its value is

$$h=6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$$

When one such photon is absorbed by an electron of the metal, a certain amount $W$ of $E_\gamma$, or a larger energy, is used to take the electron confined in the metal out of the metal, and the remaining energy becomes the kinetic energy of the electron. Thus, between the maximum value $E_\mathrm{M}$ of the kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and the frequency $\nu$ of the electromagnetic wave there is the relation

$$E_\mathrm{M}=h\nu-W \qquad (5)$$

$W$ is a constant determined by the surface of the metal and is called the work function. The kinetic energy of an electron flying around in vacuum is given by equation (3), and since its value is positive, the photoelectric effect does not occur if an electromagnetic wave with $h\nu<W$ is shone on a metal surface with work function $W$.

Q1. When visible light is shone on a metal surface with $W=5.7\,\mathrm{eV}$, does the photoelectric effect occur or not? The eV (electronvolt) appearing here is a unit of energy often used in atomic physics, and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

Q2. A photon has no mass. Therefore, if the magnitude of the momentum of a photon of energy $E_\gamma$ is $p_\gamma$, the relation between these two quantities is given, by setting $m=0$ in equation (1), as

$$E_\gamma=cp_\gamma$$

Find the relation between the magnitude of the momentum of a photon of an electromagnetic wave of wavelength $\lambda$ and the wavelength.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2014-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[In the figure: 束縛電子 = bound electron; γ線 = γ-ray; 原子 = atom; 光電子 = photoelectron; 反跳電子 = recoil electron.]

Internal photoelectric effect

Among semiconductors, those called intrinsic semiconductors have a very small electrical conductivity compared with metals (a very large resistivity). However, it is known that when electromagnetic waves are shone on them, current flows more easily. In this case, photons of the electromagnetic wave "knock out" electrons bound in atoms to the outside of the atoms, and the knocked-out electrons move freely in the semiconductor. When the range of the motion of these electrons is limited to the inside of the semiconductor, this phenomenon is called the internal photoelectric effect. Electrons moving about inside a semiconductor are called conduction electrons, but the conduction electrons produced by the internal photoelectric effect are also called photoelectrons, and their kinetic energy is given by equation (3) with $m$ the mass of the electron.

In the case of the internal photoelectric effect, between the maximum value $E_\mathrm{M}$ of the kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and the frequency $\nu$ of the electromagnetic wave there is the relation, very similar to equation (5),

$$E_\mathrm{M}=h\nu-E_\mathrm{g} \qquad (6)$$

$E_\mathrm{g}$ is called the energy gap; it is a quantity specific to each semiconductor, and even if photons of energy smaller than this are shone on the semiconductor, the internal photoelectric effect does not occur.

In the following consideration of the gamma-ray camera, "photoelectric effect" refers to the internal photoelectric effect.

Q3. When an electromagnetic wave of frequency $\nu$ is incident on an intrinsic semiconductor with energy gap $E_\mathrm{g}$, what is the maximum value $p_\mathrm{M}$ of the momentum of a photoelectron produced by one photon?

Compton scattering

Photons are not only absorbed by matter and annihilated, but may also collide with charged particles and be scattered. The phenomenon in which, through this collision, an electron that was bound to an atom of the solid flies out of the atom, as in Fig. 1(b), is Compton scattering, and the electron knocked out by the photon is called the recoil electron. The relation between the kinetic energy and the momentum of the recoil electron is also given by equation (3). The recoil electrons considered here are conduction electrons moving about in the semiconductor.

If a photon of energy $E_\gamma$ collides with a bound electron of energy $E_\mathrm{e}$ (not including the rest energy), a recoil electron of kinetic energy $E'_\mathrm{e}$ is produced and the energy of the photon becomes $E'_\gamma$, then

$$E_\gamma+E_\mathrm{e}=E'_\gamma+E'_\mathrm{e}$$

holds; but when the incident photon is a gamma ray, $|E_\mathrm{e}|$ is sufficiently small compared with the photon energies $E_\gamma$, $E'_\gamma$ and the energy $E'_\mathrm{e}$ of the recoil electron, so below we set $E_\mathrm{e}=0$. Then the law of conservation of energy is expressed as

$$E_\gamma=E'_\gamma+E'_\mathrm{e} \qquad (7)$$

Also, since the average value $p_\mathrm{e}$ of the magnitude of the momentum of the bound electron is sufficiently small compared with the momenta of the gamma ray and the recoil electron, below we set $p_\mathrm{e}=0$. Then, between the momenta before and after the Compton scattering, the law of conservation of momentum

$$\vec{p}_\gamma=\vec{p}\,'_\gamma+\vec{p}\,'_\mathrm{e}$$

holds, where $\vec{p}_\gamma$, $\vec{p}\,'_\mathrm{e}$ and $\vec{p}\,'_\gamma$ are respectively the momenta of the photon before scattering, and of the recoil electron and of the photon after scattering. Note that the direction of the momentum vector of a photon is the direction in which the electromagnetic wave travels.

Q4. As in Fig. 1(b), let $\theta$ be the angle between the directions of travel of the incident gamma ray and the scattered gamma ray. Express the energy $E'_\gamma$ of the photon after scattering and the kinetic energy $E'_\mathrm{e}$ of the recoil electron each in terms of $E_\gamma$ and $\theta$.

"Multiplication" of conduction electrons

In the case of gamma rays, since the photon energy is very large, both the photoelectrons and the recoil electrons due to Compton scattering have very large energies. These electrons of large energy knock out other electrons bound to atoms one after another, as shown in Fig. 2(a), and the energy of the initial recoil electron is distributed among many electrons. The vacancy from which an electron has been knocked out is called a hole, and it moves through the semiconductor like a particle with positive charge. Finally, as in Fig. 2(b), many conduction electrons and holes are produced in the semiconductor and come to move freely. Therefore, as shown in Fig. 2(b), if a voltage is applied to the semiconductor, a current flows.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2014-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[In the figure: 束縛電子 = bound electron; 原子 = atom; 電子 = electron.]

Fig. 2(b) is a model of a semiconductor sensor that detects this induced current. By detecting this current, one can find the energy of a photon absorbed by the internal photoelectric effect or the kinetic energy of a recoil electron produced by Compton scattering.

Q5. Suppose that the energy needed to create one electron–hole pair in a semiconductor sensor is $0.72\,\mathrm{eV}$. When a photon of energy $122\,\mathrm{keV}$ ($1\,\mathrm{keV}=10^3\,\mathrm{eV}$) is absorbed in this sensor and all its energy is used to create electron–hole pairs, what is the quantity of electric charge induced by the photon that flowed? Take the elementary charge as $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

In this problem we assume that the energy of the photon is uniquely determined from the value of the induced current, but in reality it is difficult to obtain this theoretically. Therefore, in practice, this relation is determined by measuring the size of the current induced when photons of known energy are incident. This is called the calibration of the detector.

In Fig. 3, each of the grey quadrilaterals represents a semiconductor sensor, insulated from one another. A photon that hits sensor A of the first layer is Compton-scattered, and the energy of the recoil electron ($E'_\mathrm{e}$ of Q4) is measured by the current induced in sensor A. Also, the energy of the photon after being scattered at A is $E'_\gamma$ of Q4; if this photon causes the photoelectric effect in sensor B of the second layer and is absorbed, its energy is measured by the current induced in sensor B. By substituting the measured values of these two energies into the formula derived in the next question, Q6, the scattering angle $\theta$ at the location of sensor A can be calculated.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2014-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[In the figure: 光子 = photon; 第1層 = 1st layer; 第2層 = 2nd layer.]

Q6. Using the law of conservation of energy (7), derive a formula for obtaining the value of $\cos\theta$ from the measured values of $E'_\mathrm{e}$ and $E'_\gamma$ of Q4.

Q7. Suppose that, as in Fig. 3, the location A where the Compton scattering occurred and the location B where the photoelectric effect occurred have been detected, and that $\cos\theta$ of Q6 has been determined. From which direction can the gamma ray be considered to have come? Show the predicted result on the answer sheet using a drawing of a cone, and also write a brief explanation. When drawing the figure, if necessary, assume that $\theta$ is about $30^\circ$ (there is no need to draw it accurately using a protractor or the like).

Q8. Suppose that gamma rays emitted from a single point are always scattered with a fixed scattering angle $\theta$; then, with reference to the consideration of Q7, the direction of the gamma-ray source can be identified by three observations. In Fig. 4, the locations $\mathrm{A_1}$, $\mathrm{A_2}$, $\mathrm{A_3}$ where three Compton scatterings occurred are superposed on a single point A, and the locations where the gamma rays scattered then were detected are $\mathrm{B_1}$, $\mathrm{B_2}$, $\mathrm{B_3}$. In this measurement, it was found that the four points $\mathrm{B_1}$, $\mathrm{B_2}$, $\mathrm{B_3}$ and A are at the positions of the vertices of a regular tetrahedron, and that the scattering angle $\theta$ estimated by calculation satisfies

$$\sin\theta=\frac{\mathrm{B_1O}}{\mathrm{AB_1}}$$

From the above conditions, infer the direction from which the gamma rays came. Explain the method using the figure on the answer sheet.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2014-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4

[In the figure: または = or.]

In general, by detecting many Compton scattering events and looking at the distribution of the overlaps of the circles that are the edges of the bases of the many predicted cones, the directional distribution of gamma-ray sources can be observed. Since gamma-ray sources can thus be observed with a gamma-ray camera, gamma-ray cameras are used for measuring the positions of radioactive elements that emit gamma rays, for measuring gamma rays from high-energy particle accelerators, for observing astronomical objects that emit gamma rays, and so on.

problems.title: Problem 3B: Binding energy of atomic nuclei (liquid-drop model)
problems.problem:
Problem 3B (50 points)

The mass of the atoms making up matter is concentrated in a very narrow region at the centre of the atom, and this part is called the atomic nucleus. The atomic nucleus is made up of two kinds of particles of nearly equal mass, protons and neutrons (see Fig. 1), and protons and neutrons are collectively called nucleons. Since the mass of an atomic nucleus is almost determined by the number of nucleons, that is, the total number of protons and neutrons, the number of nucleons in the nucleus is called the "mass number". Below, the mass number is denoted by $A$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2014-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[In the figure, from left to right: 陽子 = proton; 中性子 = neutron; ヘリウム原子核 = helium nucleus; ウランの原子核 = uranium nucleus.]

On the other hand, since the kind of atom is determined by the number of orbital electrons, which equals the number of protons in the nucleus, the number of protons is called the "atomic number". Below, the atomic number is denoted by $Z$.

Regarding the atomic nucleus as a sphere and letting its radius be $R$, there is the relation

$$R=kA^{1/3} \qquad (1)$$

$k=1.2\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$. Since the volume is proportional to $R^3$, according to this equation the volume and the mass number are proportional. That is, we see that the density of atomic nuclei is constant regardless of their size.

However, the mass $M$ of an atomic nucleus, when measured precisely, is smaller than the sum of the masses of the individual nucleons. This difference is called the "mass defect". Denoting the mass defect by $\varDelta m$,

$$\varDelta m=Zm_\mathrm{p}+(A-Z)m_\mathrm{n}-M \qquad (2)$$

Here, $m_\mathrm{p}$ is the mass of one proton and $m_\mathrm{n}$ is the mass of one neutron.

According to the theory of relativity, mass and energy are equivalent; with mass $m$ and energy $E$, for a particle at rest there is the relation $E=mc^2$ (see equation (2) of Problem 3A). $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. Therefore, the fact that the mass of a nucleus in the bound state is smaller than in the state where the nucleons are separate means that its energy is smaller. The energy difference $\varDelta E$ is expressed as $\varDelta E=\varDelta m\,c^2$. $\varDelta E$ is called the "binding energy" of the nucleus. Forces act between protons and neutrons, and work is needed to pull nucleons away from the nucleus; the binding energy can be regarded as the work needed for that.

Now let us consider the binding energy per nucleon, $\varDelta E/A$. This is the average amount of work needed to pull one nucleon away from the nucleus, and it can be regarded as an index of the stability of the nucleus.

Assume that the binding energy is expressed in the form

$$\varDelta E=k_1\cdot f+k_2\cdot g \qquad (3)$$

$f$, $g$ are functions determined by the mass number, and the coefficients $k_1$, $k_2$ are constants independent of $A$, $Z$.

The first term on the right-hand side of equation (3) is the term related to the "nuclear force" that directly binds nucleons to each other. Since the nuclear force has a short range, neighbouring nucleons are bound to each other. The binding is not like the bonding of atoms in a solid; the picture is rather that of liquid molecules in a droplet moving while bound to each other by intermolecular forces.

The work needed to pull one nucleon away is the work to tear off the bonds between that nucleon and the adjacent nucleons, so the presence of nucleons not in contact with it does not matter. Then the total binding energy is proportional to the number of nucleons, so $f=A$. If there were only this term, the binding energy per nucleon would be $\varDelta E/A=k_1$ ($k_1>0$), constant regardless of the size of the nucleus. However, nucleons on the surface of the nucleus have fewer nucleons in contact with them, so they are easier to pull off. The second term of equation (3) takes this correction into account. $k_2<0$.

Q1. Let the function $g$ in the second term of equation (3) be expressed as $g=A^n$. Considering that $g$ is proportional to the surface area of the nucleus, find the value of $n$.

Q2. When the value of the binding energy is expressed in the unit MeV (mega-electronvolt, $1\,\mathrm{MeV}=10^6\,\mathrm{eV}=1.602\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$), the coefficients of equation (3) are $k_1=15.67\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $k_2=-17.23\,\mathrm{MeV}$. For the mass numbers $A=20$, $60$, $90$, $145$, $235$, calculate the energy per nucleon $\varDelta E/A$ from equation (3), and draw a graph joining the points with a smooth curve. You may use the numerical values of Table 1 if necessary.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline A & 20 & 60 & 90 & 145 & 235 \\ \hline A^{1/3} & 2.7144 & 3.9149 & 4.4814 & 5.2536 & 6.1710 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Table 1

So far we have considered only the nuclear force, but a repulsive Coulomb force acts between protons. Therefore, even for the same number of nucleons, the binding becomes weaker the larger the number of protons, so the binding energy becomes smaller. So we add a further correction term to equation (3) and assume

$$\varDelta E=k_1\cdot f+k_2\cdot g+k_3\cdot h \qquad (4)$$

$k_3\cdot h<0$.

Q3. Let us assume that $h$ is a function of the mass number $A$ and the atomic number $Z$, $h=Z^2A^m$. Considering that the potential energy due to the Coulomb force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the average value of the distances between all the nucleons, $h$ can be regarded as approximately proportional to the square of the atomic number $Z$ and to the $-1$ power of the radius of the nucleus. From this, find the value of $m$.

If the balance between the number of protons and the number of neutrons is not good, the nucleus is unstable, and beta decay in which a neutron changes into a proton and emits an electron and an antielectron-neutrino ($\beta^-$ decay), or beta decay in which a proton changes into a neutron and emits a positron and an electron neutrino ($\beta^+$ decay), occurs. Up to an atomic number of about 20, nuclei in which the numbers of protons and neutrons are almost equal are often stable. Taking this into account, we add a further correction term to equation (4) and take

$$\varDelta E=k_1\cdot f+k_2\cdot g+k_3\cdot h+k_4\cdot i \qquad (5)$$

$k_4\cdot i<0$.

It is known that the function $i$ of the fourth term is expressed as $i=(A-2Z)^2A^{-1}$. This term is derived from quantum-mechanical considerations and so on, but the explanation is omitted here. Since the mass number $A$ is the sum of the number of protons $Z$ and the number of neutrons $N$, this term becomes 0 when the two are equal. However, as nuclei become larger, an increase in the number of protons decreases the binding energy because of the third term of equation (5), so a relatively larger number of neutrons gives a larger binding energy and is more stable.

Q4. Nuclei with equal mass numbers but different numbers of protons and neutrons are called isobars. $\varDelta E$ of equation (5), regarded as a function of $Z$, is a quadratic expression and has an extremum. The isobar with the atomic number $Z$ that maximizes $\varDelta E$ is the most stable. The coefficients of equation (5) are $k_3=-0.714\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $k_4=-23.29\,\mathrm{MeV}$. For example, considering the isobars with $A=101$ and expressing equation (5) as a function of $Z$ gives

$$\varDelta E=-1143+93.16Z-1.076Z^2 \quad (\mathrm{MeV}) \qquad (6)$$

Among the isobars with $A=101$, find the most stable atomic number.

Q5. A nucleus whose atomic number is one less than the atomic number found in Q4 is unstable, so it beta-decays and becomes the nucleus with the most stable atomic number found in Q4. How many MeV of energy is released at this time? The energy released includes the rest energy of the electron emitted in the $\beta$ decay.

Q6. Let us calculate the energy per nucleon $\varDelta E/A$ for several cases using equation (5). Table 2 gives, for the mass numbers $A=20$, $60$, $90$, $145$, $235$, the atomic numbers that are most stable by calculation and the element symbols. For the nuclei with the $A$, $Z$ given in Table 2, calculate the energy per nucleon $\varDelta E/A$ and draw a graph joining the points with a smooth curve. It is a good idea to calculate while filling in the table, using the values of $A^{1/3}$ in Table 2 and the values of $\dfrac{k_4\cdot i}{A}=-23.29\Big(1-\dfrac{2Z}{A}\Big)^2$ (in MeV).

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline A & 20 & 60 & 90 & 145 & 235 \\ \hline Z & 9 & 27 & 39 & 60 & 91 \\ \hline \text{Element symbol} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{Co} & \mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{Nd} & \mathrm{Pa} \\ \hline A^{1/3} & 2.7144 & 3.9149 & 4.4814 & 5.2536 & 6.1710 \\ \hline \text{Answer to Q2}\ (1) & & & & & \\ \hline \dfrac{k_3\cdot h}{A}\ \ (2) & & & & & \\ \hline \dfrac{k_4\cdot i}{A}\ \ (3) & -0.233 & -0.233 & -0.414 & -0.692 & -1.185 \\ \hline \dfrac{\varDelta E}{A}\ \ (1)+(2)+(3) & & & & & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Table 2

Q7. Nuclear fission is the phenomenon in which a large nucleus splits into smaller nuclei. Suppose that a nucleus of mass number 235 ($Z=91$) splits into two nuclei, which, after repeated beta decays, finally become the most stable nuclei with mass numbers $A=90$ and $A=145$. Explain that energy is released in this process, and find the value of the energy released (MeV).

problems.title: Problem 1A: Oscillations from energy considerations
problems.problem:
Problem 1A (50 points)

On a smooth horizontal straight line, a body of mass $m$ is attached to the other end of a light spring (spring constant $k$) whose one end is fixed (see Fig. 1). Take the horizontal straight line as the $x$ axis, and let the equilibrium point be $x=0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Let $v\left(=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)$ be the velocity of the body when it is displaced by $x$ from the equilibrium point O. The kinetic energy of the body is

$$K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \qquad (1)$$

The potential energy due to the restoring force of the spring is expressed as

$$U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2 \qquad (2)$$

where the potential energy is taken to be $U=0$ at $x=0$. If there is no mechanism of energy dissipation such as friction or air resistance, the mechanical energy $K+U$ is constant:

$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2=\text{constant} \qquad (3)$$

Differentiating both sides of this equation with respect to time $t$ gives

$$mv\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}+kx\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=0 \qquad (4)$$

Rearranging, $mv\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=-kx\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}$, and using here the relation $v=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}$, we obtain the following equation:

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=-kx \qquad (5)$$

This is the equation of motion of simple harmonic motion, and the angular frequency is

$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \qquad (6)$$

In general, when the kinetic energy and the potential energy are given by equations (1) and (2) respectively, the motion is simple harmonic motion, and its angular frequency is given by equation (6).

[I] On a smooth horizontal plane, three point masses of mass $m$ are connected by three light springs of natural length $l$ and spring constant $k$ in the shape of an equilateral triangle, as in Fig. 2. Let us find, based on the above energy considerations, the frequency of oscillation when the three point masses oscillate keeping the shape of an equilateral triangle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2

Q1. When each spring is stretched by $x$, how many times $v=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}$ is the speed of each point mass?

Q2. Find the total potential energy $U$ of the three springs and the total kinetic energy $K$ of the three point masses. Express the results using $x$, $v$, $m$, $k$. The potential energy is taken to be $U=0$ when none of the springs is stretched or compressed.

Q3. Find the angular frequency $\omega_1$ of the oscillation.

[II] On a smooth horizontal plane, three particles A, B, C carrying equal charges $q$ are connected by light inextensible insulating strings of length $l$ and placed on a straight line. The end particles A and C have mass $m$, and the middle particle B has mass $2m$. Suppose particle B performs small oscillations perpendicular to the initial straight line. The system as a whole does not move in any one direction, and the position of the centre of mass is assumed to be unchanged. Let the electric constant (permittivity of vacuum) be $\epsilon_0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3

Q4. Find the total electrostatic energy (potential energy) $U$ when particle B is at a distance $y$ from the straight line joining particles A and C, as in Fig. 3. The electrostatic energy is taken to be $U=0$ when $y=0$. Assuming that $|y|$ is sufficiently small compared with $l$, find it up to the second-order term in $\dfrac{y}{l}$.

[Reference]

(1) The electrostatic energy when two point charges $q_1$, $q_2$ are separated by a distance $d$ is given by

$$\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{d}$$

(2) For $|x|\ll 1$ the following approximation holds, where $\alpha$ is a constant:

$$(1+x)^{\alpha}\fallingdotseq 1+\alpha x$$

Q5. Find the relation between the distance $y_{\mathrm{B}}$ from the centre of mass, which is a fixed point in space, to particle B, and $y$.

Q6. Let the velocity of particle B be $v_{\mathrm{B}}\left(=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)$. Find the total kinetic energy $K$. Also express the electrostatic energy (potential energy) $U$ using $y_{\mathrm{B}}$. The motion of particles A and C in the $x$ direction may be neglected.

Q7. Find the angular frequency $\omega_2$ of the small oscillations.

problems.title: Problem 1B: Altitude dependence of air temperature
problems.problem:
Problem 1B (50 points)

When you climb a high mountain, you can experience that the temperature drops at the same time as the atmospheric pressure falls. The ultimate aim of this problem is to examine the dependence of the air temperature on altitude.

In this problem, air is treated as an ideal gas consisting of a single kind of diatomic molecule with molar mass $M=2.9\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg/mol}$. When solving the problem, if necessary, take the gas constant $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}$ and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. In Problem 1B, quantities with $\Delta$ appearing in equations are small quantities.

[I] First, assuming that the air temperature does not change up to high altitudes, consider the change of the atmospheric pressure with altitude.

Q1. As in Fig. 1, take the coordinate $h$ vertically upward from the ground, and let the atmospheric pressures at heights $h$ and $h+\Delta h$ be $p$ and $p+\Delta p$, respectively. Letting the density of air be $\rho$, derive the relation between $\Delta p$ and $\Delta h$ from the condition of equilibrium of the forces acting on the layer of air between heights $h$ and $h+\Delta h$. Since $\Delta h$ is sufficiently small, approximate $\rho$ as constant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-2-fig1.png

[地表 = ground]

Fig. 1

Q2. Using the equation of state of an ideal gas at temperature $T$, derive the following equation from the relation obtained in the previous question:

$$\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta h}=-\frac{Mg}{RT}\,p \qquad (1)$$

Since the right-hand side of equation (1) has a negative value, this explains that the atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.

[II] From near the ground up to a height of about 10 000 metres, the average air temperature falls by about $0.6\,\mathrm{K}$ for every $100\,\mathrm{m}$ of rise. A possible cause of this is that the atmosphere is constantly moving in the vertical direction.

Suppose that, for some reason, a parcel of $n\,\mathrm{mol}$ of air rises. Since the pressure of the surrounding air decreases as considered in [I], this parcel of air expands so that its pressure becomes equal to that of the surroundings. This expansion is adiabatic because the thermal conductivity of air is small, and the temperature of the air parcel falls as it rises. Let us investigate how the air temperature changes with height, considering the properties of adiabatic expansion and compression.

Q3. The pressure of the air parcel is $p$, its temperature is $T$ and its volume is $V$. Suppose that the surrounding pressure changes to $p+\Delta p$, the volume of the air parcel to $V+\Delta V$, and the temperature of the air to $T+\Delta T$. Express $\dfrac{\Delta T}{T}$ using $\dfrac{\Delta p}{p}$ and $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}$. Since both $\Delta p$ and $\Delta V$ are small quantities, if their product appears, neglect it.

Q4. Find the relation between $\dfrac{\Delta T}{T}$ and $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}$ in adiabatic expansion using the first law of thermodynamics, and confirm that the temperature of the air falls in adiabatic expansion. Below, if necessary, denote the molar heat capacity at constant volume by $C_{\mathrm{v}}$ and the molar heat capacity at constant pressure by $C_{\mathrm{p}}$.

Q5. Combining the results of Q3 and Q4, derive that in an adiabatic process

$$\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta p}=\frac{R}{C_{\mathrm{p}}}\cdot\frac{T}{p} \qquad (2)$$

holds.

Q6. Derive that when an air parcel rises adiabatically by a distance $\Delta h$, the air temperature falls as

$$\Delta T=-\frac{Mg}{C_{\mathrm{p}}}\,\Delta h \qquad (3)$$

Q7. Taking the ground as $h=0$ and the temperature there as $T_0$, derive an expression for the air temperature at height $h$. Also, by how many degrees does the air temperature fall when rising by 100 metres? (Give the answer to 2 significant figures.) Take the molar heat capacity at constant volume of air to be $C_{\mathrm{v}}=2.5R$.

[III] When we considered the cooling of air by adiabatic expansion in [II], we ignored the fact that air usually contains water vapour, which can release heat when it condenses. In [III], we consider the effect of the water vapour in the air on adiabatic expansion. For this purpose, we call air containing no water vapour at all dry air, and ordinary air containing water vapour moist air, or simply air. Suppose that moist air at temperature $T$, containing dry air and water vapour, is confined in a container of volume $V$. The pressure of the dry air remaining after removing the water vapour from the container is called the partial pressure of the dry air, and the pressure of the water vapour remaining after removing the dry air is called the partial pressure of the water vapour.

When the pressure of $n\,\mathrm{mol}$ of moist air is $p$ and the partial pressure of water vapour (vapour pressure) is $p_{\mathrm{w}}$, the amount of substance $n_{\mathrm{w}}$ of water vapour contained in it is $\dfrac{p_{\mathrm{w}}}{p}n$.

When the proportion of water vapour in the air increases, the vapour pressure also increases, but the vapour pressure $p_{\mathrm{w}}$ of air in thermal equilibrium has an upper limit determined by the temperature. This upper limit is called the saturated vapour pressure, and we denote it by $p_{\mathrm{s}}(T)$ (s = saturation). $p_{\mathrm{s}}(T)$ is a monotonically increasing function of the temperature $T$.

Suppose there is air at a certain temperature $T$ in which the partial pressure of water vapour is smaller than the saturated vapour pressure at that time, so that $p_{\mathrm{w}}<p_{\mathrm{s}}(T)$. When this air is cooled, $p_{\mathrm{s}}(T)$ begins to decrease as the temperature $T$ falls, and eventually $p_{\mathrm{w}}=p_{\mathrm{s}}(T)$. If the air is in thermal equilibrium and the temperature is lowered further, the excess water molecules begin to condense to form water droplets, and the water vapour in the air begins to decrease. At this time, heat of condensation is released from the water vapour. Since the heat of condensation $Q$ is proportional to the amount of substance $-\Delta n_{\mathrm{w}}$ of the water vapour that condenses, below we write

$$Q=-L\Delta n_{\mathrm{w}}$$

$L$ has the meaning of the heat of condensation per $1\,\mathrm{mol}$. The heat of condensation has the same effect as heat added from outside.

Q8. There is $n\,\mathrm{mol}$ of moist air with pressure $p$ and temperature $T$. When this air was expanded adiabatically, the temperature and pressure of the air changed by $\Delta T$ and $\Delta p$, respectively, and at the same time an amount of substance $-\Delta n_{\mathrm{w}}$ of water vapour condensed, releasing heat of condensation. Express the relation between $\Delta T$, $\Delta p$ and $\Delta n_{\mathrm{w}}$ at this time as an equation. Since the amount of substance $n_{\mathrm{w}}$ of water vapour is small, the heat capacity of the air may be taken to be equal to that of dry air.

Q9. When the changes in the temperature and pressure of the air in the previous question occurred while keeping the water vapour saturated, so that the relation $p_{\mathrm{w}}=p_{\mathrm{s}}(T)$ was maintained, express $\Delta n_{\mathrm{w}}$ using $\Delta p$ and $\Delta T$. Terms of second order in small quantities may be neglected. Also, since the amount of substance of water vapour is small, the number of moles $n$ may be regarded as unchanged.

[Hint] When there is a function $y(x)$ of $x$, for $\Delta x$ one can approximate

$$\Delta y=y(x+\Delta x)-y(x)\fallingdotseq\frac{\mathrm{d}y(x)}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\Delta x$$

From this result and the equation derived in Q8, we obtain

$$\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta p}=\frac{RT}{p\,C_{\mathrm{p}}}\cdot\frac{1+\dfrac{L}{RT}\cdot\dfrac{p_{\mathrm{s}}}{p}}{1+\dfrac{L}{C_{\mathrm{p}}T}\cdot\dfrac{p_{\mathrm{s}}}{p}\cdot\dfrac{T}{p_{\mathrm{s}}}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{d}T}} \qquad (4)$$

In this equation, the effect of the condensation of water vapour is contained in $L$. If $L=0$, the value of the second factor on the right-hand side is 1, but because of $L$ this factor deviates from 1. From the size of the deviation, one can judge whether the effect of the condensation of water vapour is important.

Q10. $L\fallingdotseq4\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{J/mol}$. To confirm that the effect of the condensation of water cannot be neglected in the adiabatic expansion of air, find the value of the second factor on the right-hand side of equation (4), assuming the following. Treat the air as a diatomic ideal gas even when it contains water vapour; the temperature is $17\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the atmospheric pressure is $1013\,\mathrm{hPa}$, the vapour pressure is $19.2\,\mathrm{hPa}$ (the saturated vapour pressure at $17\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), and $\dfrac{T}{p_{\mathrm{s}}}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{d}T}\fallingdotseq2\times10$.

Solving this problem, one finds that although air in an updraft expands adiabatically and its temperature falls, the drop in temperature is reduced to about half that of dry air by the heat of condensation released as the water vapour contained in it condenses when the temperature falls.

When moist air ascends a mountainside, it expands adiabatically and the water vapour condenses, so that the air becomes dry air. When the dry air descends the mountainside it is compressed adiabatically, so it is thought that its temperature rises by the same amount as the temperature drop in the adiabatic expansion of dry air considered in [II] of this problem. One cause of the foehn phenomenon is thought to be that, in air crossing a mountain, the temperature rise of the descending current is larger than the temperature drop of the ascending current.

problems.title: Problem 2: Physics of blood circulation
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (100 points)

Blood vessels run throughout the inside of the human body, and the blood flowing through them delivers oxygen and nutrients to the cells that make up the body. Together with the heart, the blood vessels form a closed fluid system called the circulatory system. Blood circulation tends to be regarded as a subject of study only for medicine, but since the laws of physics hold there, it is also a subject of study for physics.

[I] Blood is first pressurized in the part of the heart called the left ventricle and is sent into a single thick artery called the aorta, with an inner diameter of $1.6$ - $3.2\,\mathrm{cm}$. Arteries going to the upper limbs, lower limbs, abdomen, head and so on branch off from the aorta. Eventually the blood passes through arterioles with an inner diameter of about $1\,\mathrm{mm}$ and finally seeps out into the capillaries. After that, it passes through the venous system and finally returns from the vena cava to the part of the heart called the right atrium.

In general, when a fluid such as water flows through a pipe, the volume of fluid passing through a cross-section per unit time is called the flow rate. When a fluid flows with flow speed $v$ through a pipe of cross-sectional area $S$ as in Fig. 1, the fluid that has passed cross-section AB has arrived at CD after a time $\Delta t$, and the volume between AB and CD is $vS\Delta t$; therefore the volume of fluid passing cross-section AB per unit time, that is, the flow rate $J$, can be calculated by $J=vS$. In the case of blood flow, the way of flowing changes with time due to the beating (periodic motion) of the heart, so this relation must be written as $J(t)=v(t)S$. Even in that case, it is often sufficient to consider, rather than the detailed time variation, the mean flow rate $\overline{J}$ or the mean flow speed $\overline{v}$ averaged over a time sufficiently longer than the period of the heartbeat. Between these mean values the relation $\overline{J}=\overline{v}S$ holds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig1.png

[断面積 = cross-sectional area]

Fig. 1

The flow rates of mass, momentum, energy, etc. carried by a fluid can be calculated in the same way. For example, if the energy contained in a unit volume of fluid is $\rho_{\mathrm{E}}$, the energy possessed by the fluid between the two cross-sections AB and CD in Fig. 2 is $\rho_{\mathrm{E}}vS\Delta t$, so the energy passing cross-section AB per unit time can be calculated as $J_{\mathrm{E}}=\rho_{\mathrm{E}}J$.

Fig. 2 on the next page shows an apparatus for producing such a flow by connecting the bottoms of two water tanks with a pipe. When the heights of the water surfaces in the tanks are changed so that the pressures on the two sides of the pipe differ, water flows in the pipe from the side of higher pressure to the side of lower pressure. In general, the flow rate $J$ in the pipe is proportional to the pressure difference $\Delta p$ between the two ends and can be expressed in the form

$$J=\frac{\Delta p}{R} \qquad (1)$$

Here $R$ is called the flow resistance. The flow resistance arises because, owing to the viscosity of the fluid, forces act that tend to hinder the flow. However, when a thin, free-flowing fluid of small viscosity flows through a thick pipe, the flow resistance can sometimes be neglected. Such a fluid is generally called a perfect fluid.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig2.png

[流れ = flow]

Fig. 2

Blood flowing through the aorta may also be regarded approximately as a perfect fluid, but as the blood vessels branch and become thinner, the flow resistance can no longer be neglected.

If necessary, use the following data of basic physical quantities concerning the heart and blood, and express numerical answers in the MKS system of units.

= Basic physical data of the circulatory system =

(1) Volume of blood sent from the left ventricle into the aorta per minute (called the cardiac output): 5 litres/min

(2) Pressure* of the blood when it is sent out of the left ventricle (called the maximum blood pressure or systolic blood pressure): $159\,\mathrm{hPa}$ (In medicine blood pressure is expressed in units of mmHg, but in this problem hPa is used as the unit of pressure. $1\,\mathrm{mmHg}=1.333\,\mathrm{hPa}$.)

(3) Number of cycles of the periodic motion of the heart per minute (called the heart rate): 60

(4) Density of blood: $1.06\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$

* The pressure of liquids such as water or blood in tubes or containers considered in Problem 2 is in all cases the pressure with which the liquid pushes the tube or container from the inside, minus the outside atmospheric pressure.

Q1. Find the values of the mean flow rate $\overline{J}$ and the mean flow speed $\overline{v}$ of the blood flowing through the aorta. Take the diameter of the aorta to be $3.0\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Below, for simplicity, the blood flow is assumed not to change in time with the heartbeat, and the flow rate at the entrance of the aorta and the flow speed there keep the mean values found here; the flow rate is denoted by $J_0$ and the flow speed by $v_0$.

Q2. The network of blood vessels between the aorta and the vena cava is complex, but here we consider that the ends of these two vessels are connected, as in Fig. 3, by a total of $5\times10^{9}$ parallel capillaries with a mean diameter of $8\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. Assuming that the blood considered in Q1 flows through the aorta and the vena cava, find the value of the ratio $v'/v_0$ of the mean flow speed $v'$ of the blood in the capillaries to $v_0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig3.png

[毛細血管 = capillaries; 大静脈 = vena cava; 大動脈 = aorta]

Fig. 3

Q3. Fig. 4(a) shows the part of the aorta directly connected to the outlet of the heart; because of its arched shape it is called the aortic arch. Thin branches come out of it, but if they are ignored, the blood pushed out of the heart passes vigorously through a U-shaped tube as in Fig. 4(b). Express the mean momentum $J_P$ of the blood flowing from the heart into the arch per unit time, using the symbols of quantities that have appeared so far and the density $\rho$ of blood.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig4.png

[大動脈弓部 = aortic arch; 左心室より = from the left ventricle; 腹部及び下肢 = (to the) abdomen and lower limbs]

Fig. 4

Q4. Assume that the direction of the blood flow changes by $180^{\circ}$ in the aortic arch. Find the value of the magnitude of the force exerted by this blood on the curved part of the blood vessel.

[II] Now, as a model of the circulatory system consisting of the heart and blood vessels, let us consider a piping system, as in Fig. 5 on the next page, that circulates water using two pumps. The route going back and forth between the heart and the lungs is omitted from this model.

Water is pushed out by pump 1 at a constant pressure $p_1$. Since valve 1 at the outlet of pump 2 opens only to the right, the water passes from valve 2 through the pipe A → B → C → D and is sucked into pump 2, whose pressure is fixed at $p_2$. If the flow resistance in the pipe were 0, the pipe between A and D would be like a U-tube that lets water through freely, so the water could go once around this circuit even with $p_1=p_2$; but in general water has flow resistance due to viscosity, so it does not circulate unless $p_1>p_2$. Below, the flow resistance is 0 between A and B and between C and D because the pipes there are relatively thick, while between B and C the flow resistance is large because it is a network of thin pipes.

Eventually the volume of water in pump 1 reaches a certain minimum value. At that moment, the force pushing the piston of pump 1 suddenly becomes small, and the pressure in pump 1 drops from $p_1$ to a value slightly lower than $p_2$. At the same time, valve 1 opens to the right and valve 2 closes. Then water returns from pump 2 to pump 1. When the water in pump 2 is used up, the force on the piston of pump 1 becomes large again, and when the pressure of the water in pump 1 has become $p_1$, the system returns to the initial state.

This is the model of the motion of the heart during one cycle. In the case of the heart, this period is called the cardiac cycle; the left ventricle plays the role of pump 1, and the right atrium plays the role of pump 2. In that case, the blood pressure corresponding to $p_1$ is the maximum blood pressure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig5.png

[弁1 = valve 1; 弁2 = valve 2; ポンプ1（左心室）= pump 1 (left ventricle); ポンプ2（右心房）= pump 2 (right atrium)]

Fig. 5

Q5. While pump 1 pushes out water at pressure $p_1$, the water flows at the same constant speed from the outlet A of pump 1 to B and from C to the inlet D of pump 2. What are the pressures of the water at points B and C, which are a distance $h$ vertically below these outlet and inlet? Let the density of water be $\rho$ and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration be $g$.

From this consideration, one can infer that the measured value of blood pressure changes with the difference in height between the place where it is measured and the heart.

In the case of the heart, the pressure of the blood corresponding to the pressure of the water in pump 1 is called the left ventricular pressure, and the quantity corresponding to the volume of the space filled with water in pump 1 of Fig. 5 is called the left ventricular volume. The left ventricular pressure is produced in the pump of Fig. 5 by the force with which the piston pushes the water, but in the actual heart it is produced by the tension and contraction of the heart muscle.

The quadrilateral ABCD shown in Fig. 6 is a schematic representation of the relation between this left ventricular volume and its internal pressure during one cardiac cycle. Referring to the pump model of the heart, answer the following questions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig6.png

[左心室内圧 = left ventricular pressure; 左心室容積 = left ventricular volume]

Fig. 6

Q6. Which part of the rectangle ABCD is the process in which the left ventricle contracts and sends blood out into the aorta? Answer including the direction of the passage of time.

Q7. Express the power of the heart using the cardiac period $T$ and those symbols in Fig. 6 that are needed.

When $\Delta p$ in equation (1) is the pressure difference of the blood between the outlet of the left ventricle and the inlet of the right atrium, and $J$ is the mean flow rate of the blood flowing into the aorta, we call $R$ the flow resistance of the whole body.

Q8. Express the flow resistance of the whole body using the letters in Fig. 6 and $T$.

[III] The narrowing of a blood vessel due to foreign matter adhering to the vessel wall is called stenosis (kyōsaku), and the resulting increase in flow resistance is a cause of serious circulatory diseases. When this happens, an effective treatment is to attach an artificial blood vessel with small flow resistance (a bypass) in parallel with the blood vessel in which the stenosis has occurred.

It is known that the flow resistance of a cylindrical tube of radius $a$ is inversely proportional to $a^4$ (the Hagen-Poiseuille law). Here, as a model of blood vessels, we consider water flowing through the three kinds of tubes in Fig. 7(a), (b), (c), made by connecting pipes whose flow resistance follows this law. In all three, water is pushed through by the pressure difference $\Delta p$ applied between the left and right ends.

Q9. Fig. 7(a) is a tube made by connecting three pipes each of flow resistance $R_0$. Derive that the flow resistance for water flowing through the connected tube is $3R_0$.

Q10. The radius of the middle pipe has become $1/2$ due to stenosis, and its flow resistance has become $R_1$ (Fig. 7(b)). What are the value of the ratio $R_1/R_0$ and the value of the ratio $J_{\mathrm{b}}/J_{\mathrm{a}}$ of the flow rate $J_{\mathrm{b}}$ of water through this tube to the flow rate $J_{\mathrm{a}}$ in case (a)?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig7.png

[付着物 = deposit; 狭窄部分 = stenosed part; バイパス = bypass]

Fig. 7

Q11. Consider attaching a bypass pipe in order to restore the total flow rate (Fig. 7(c)). How many times the radius of the original pipe must the radius of the bypass be for the flow rate to be equal to that of Fig. 7(a)? Answer to 2 decimal places.

[IV] Blood vessels and the heart are made of membranes that have elasticity: like a rubber band, they stretch when pulled and return to their original length when the force is released. So let us use the mechanics of elastic bodies to consider what forces the blood pressure exerts on the blood vessels and the heart.

Suppose an elastic membrane is stretched between rigid plates, as in Fig. 8(a), and pulled to the left and right by applying forces of magnitude $F$ to the plates. The plates then pull the membrane on both sides with forces of magnitude $F$. The part of the membrane to the right of an arbitrary straight line AB perpendicular to the direction of the force pulls the part of the membrane to the left to the right with a force of magnitude $F$, and as the reaction, the part of the membrane to the left of the line AB pulls the right part to the left with a force of magnitude $F$. The arrows with white circles in Fig. 8 schematically represent the points of application and the directions of the former forces, and the arrows with black circles represent their reactions. When forces are applied to the plates from outside, new forces thus arise by which the parts of the membrane pull on each other. The forces arising in this way are called the internal stresses of the elastic membrane.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig8.png

[筋繊維 = muscle fibres]

Fig. 8

The membrane surrounding the heart has the form of a membrane made of muscle fibres arranged side by side, as in Fig. 8(b); a force tending to contract arises in these fibres, and the left and right parts on either side of the straight line CD may pull on each other. In that case, to keep the membrane spread as at first, forces of magnitude $F$ must be continuously applied from outside to the left and right.

In both cases, the force arising in the membrane is characterized by introducing the tensile stress $\alpha$ by the quantity

$$\alpha=\frac{F}{l}$$

obtained by dividing the magnitude $F$ of the force with which the left and right parts of the membrane pull on each other by the length $l$ of the boundary line AB or CD. In the case of the membrane surrounding the heart, the tensile stress is also produced by the tension of the muscle fibres.

Thus, although the causes of the internal stress differ between the heart and a rubber balloon, they can be discussed with common mechanics, so for a while let us consider the case in which air is put into a spherical rubber balloon of radius $r$, as in Fig. 9(a) on the next page, so that the pressure inside is higher than outside by $\Delta p$. From the balance between the force with which this $\Delta p$ tends to push the balloon outward and the force with which the internal stress arising in the rubber balloon tends to restore it, the relation between $\Delta p$ and the tensile stress $\alpha$ is obtained. Answer the following questions.

Q12. When the rubber balloon is imaginarily divided into two by a horizontal great circle as in Fig. 9(a), express the magnitude $F$ of the force with which the upper and lower hemispherical surfaces pull on each other, using the tensile stress $\alpha$ acting in this elastic membrane.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-3-fig9.png

[面A = surface A; 面B = surface B]

Fig. 9

Q13. Express the magnitude of the force with which the upper half of the balloon is pushed up by the high air pressure of the air inside the balloon, using the pressure difference $\Delta p$ between inside and outside.

[Hint] Replace the upper hemisphere of Fig. 9(a) by a stepped surface as in Fig. 9(b). This surface is a superposition of thin cylindrical surfaces, each having a horizontal plane such as surface A as its base and a vertical side surface such as surface B. Consider the magnitude and direction of the sum of the forces acting on this stepped hemisphere when the pressure inside the sphere is higher than outside by $\Delta p$.

From the balance of the forces of the previous two questions, one finds that the relation

$$\Delta p=\frac{2\alpha}{r}$$

holds between the pressure difference $\Delta p$ between inside and outside and the tensile stress $\alpha$ acting on the rubber balloon. This is called Laplace's law.

Now, using this, let us consider the tension that must arise in the heart muscle in order to maintain, in the heart of a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy, whose left ventricle is enlarged and who shows symptoms of heart failure, the same maximum blood pressure of $159\,\mathrm{hPa}$ as in a normal heart. Assuming that the left ventricle has the structure of a balloon surrounded by a spherical heart-muscle membrane, answer the following questions.

Q14. (a) Find the rate of increase of the tensile stress when the radius of the sphere has expanded by $20\%$ from $r$.

(b) The number of muscle fibres is the same in the diseased heart and in the normal heart. What is the rate of increase, per muscle fibre, of the force that the diseased heart must exert in order to maintain normal blood pressure?

The dilated cardiomyopathy considered here is a heart disease in which the heart muscle becomes thinner and stretched more than usual, and the pumping function of the heart is markedly reduced. One of its treatments is partial left ventriculectomy (the Batista operation): as its name says, it is a cardiac surgery in which about one third of the left ventricle of the enlarged heart is excised and the shape of the heart is restored. The name "Batista operation" comes from the Brazilian physician Randas Batista, who devised it. He recalled the physical law (Laplace's law) that, as considered in the problem above, the larger the bulge of the left ventricle, the larger the tension the heart muscle must generate, and he devised this operation thinking that if the heart enlarged by cardiomyopathy were made smaller, the burden on the muscle fibres would become smaller.

This is a clear example of how the laws of physics can be applied in medicine and the biosciences.

problems.title: Problem 3: Propagation of the electromagnetic signal along a ribbon line
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (100 points)

[I] When a battery and a light bulb are connected by wires and the switch is turned on, the bulb lights up. When the wires become long, how much time does it take from turning on the switch until the bulb lights up? Let us consider this with a simple model.

Q1. When a voltage is applied to a wire, electrons move in the wire.

(a) Express the number of electrons passing through a cross-section of the wire per unit time, using the number density of electrons $n$, the speed $v$ with which the electrons move along the wire, and the cross-sectional area $S$ of the wire.

(b) For copper, $n=8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$. When a current of $1\,\mathrm{A}$ flows in a copper wire of cross-sectional area $1\,\mathrm{mm^2}$, what is the speed $v$ with which the electrons move? The charge of the electron is $-1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

If the turning on of the switch travelled along the wire with the speed $v$ found in Q1(b), then for a wire of length $\ell$ it would seem to take a time $\dfrac{\ell}{v}$ from turning on the switch until the bulb lights up. The value of $v$ is surprisingly small, and it is not realistic that the time until the bulb lights up is that long.

[II] Consider two ribbon-shaped metal plates kept at a constant separation $d$ as in the figure (below, a ribbon-shaped metal plate is simply called a ribbon). The width $w$ of the ribbons is sufficiently large compared with the separation $d$, and the length $\ell$ of the ribbons is sufficiently large compared with $w$. Below, we take coordinates with the origin O at the centre of one end cross-section of the ribbons, $x$ in the length direction, $y$ in the width direction, and $z$ in the direction perpendicular to the ribbons. The electric constant (permittivity of vacuum) is denoted by $\epsilon_0$ and the magnetic constant (permeability of vacuum) by $\mu_0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

Q2. (a) For the parallel-plate capacitor consisting of the two ribbons, find the capacitance per unit length in the length direction ($x$ direction).

(b) When the voltage between the ribbons is $V$, express the energy stored per unit length in the $x$ direction using $V$.

(c) The electric field has energy; if the energy per unit volume when the magnitude of the electric field is $E$ (the energy density of the electric field) is

$$\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$$

explain that the energy of the electric field between the ribbons per unit length is equal to the energy found in (b).

As in Fig. 2, a battery of emf $\mathcal{E}$ is connected to one end ($x=0$) of the ribbons and a resistor $R$ is attached to the other end, so that a current flows out and back. The resistance of the ribbons can be neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2

Q3. Express the work done by the battery per unit time in this case in terms of $\mathcal{E}$ and $R$.

When a current $I$ flows out and back along the two ribbons, a magnetic field arises between the ribbons. This magnetic field can be found by regarding the current as a collection of straight currents in the $x$ direction and adding up the magnetic fields of the straight currents. The current is assumed to be uniform within the ribbons.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig3.png

[y 方向の一様な磁場 = uniform magnetic field in the y direction]

Fig. 3

Q4. Explain that the magnetic field at the point $\left(\dfrac{\ell}{2},\,0,\,0\right)$ at the middle between the two ribbons is in the positive direction of the $y$ axis.

When the magnetic fields of the straight currents are actually added up, the magnitude $B$ of the magnetic flux density at the point $\left(\dfrac{\ell}{2},\,0,\,0\right)$ is $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{w}$. Moreover, since $d\ll w\ll\ell$, it may be considered that in the space between the two ribbons (except for narrow regions at the edges) the same uniform magnetic field in the $y$ direction arises, and that the magnetic field outside the ribbons is 0.

Q5. (a) As in Fig. 3, the circuit battery → upper ribbon → resistor → lower ribbon → battery can be regarded as a coil of one turn. The magnetic flux through this coil is proportional to the length $\ell$ in the $x$ direction. Find the (self-)inductance of this coil per unit length (in the $x$ direction).

(b) When a current $I$ flows out and back, express the energy stored per unit length in the $x$ direction using $I$.

(c) The magnetic field has energy; if the energy per unit volume when the magnetic flux density is $B$ (the energy density of the magnetic field) is

$$\frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2$$

explain that the energy of the magnetic field between the ribbons per unit length is equal to the energy found in (b).

Combining Q2(c) and Q5(c), the energy per unit volume of an electromagnetic field with electric field $E$ and magnetic flux density $B$ (the energy density of the electromagnetic field) is given by

$$\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2$$

Now, the "Poynting vector" $\overrightarrow{P}$ at a point where the electric field vector is $\overrightarrow{E}$ and the magnetic flux density vector is $\overrightarrow{B}$ is defined by

$$\overrightarrow{P}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\overrightarrow{E}\times\overrightarrow{B}$$

$\overrightarrow{E}\times\overrightarrow{B}$ is called the vector product of the two vectors $\overrightarrow{E}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$, and when the electric field and the magnetic flux density are perpendicular it can be represented as in Fig. 4. The direction of $\overrightarrow{P}$ is the direction in which a right-handed screw advances when turned from $\overrightarrow{E}$ to $\overrightarrow{B}$, and its magnitude is $\dfrac{EB}{\mu_0}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig4.png

[電場の向き = direction of the electric field; 磁場の向き = direction of the magnetic field; 電磁場のエネルギーが伝わる向き = direction in which the energy of the electromagnetic field is transmitted]

Fig. 4

The Poynting vector $\overrightarrow{P}$ is said to represent the energy of the electromagnetic field passing per unit time through a unit cross-sectional area perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{P}$. Let us check this for the case of Fig. 2.

Q6. For the case of Fig. 2, find the following.

(a) The direction of the Poynting vector on a cross-section perpendicular to the $x$ axis for $0<x<\ell$.

(b) The ratio of the magnitude of the Poynting vector to the work done by the battery per unit time found in Q3.

[III] It has been found that, with the battery connected as in Fig. 2, the energy flowing out of the battery keeps flowing between the two ribbons in the direction of the $x$ axis and is converted into heat at the resistor. Then, with what speed is this energy transmitted between the ribbons? For example, if initially (for time $t<0$) the switch near the battery in Fig. 3 is kept open and the switch is turned on at $t=0$, with what speed do the electric and magnetic fields coming from the battery travel between the ribbons?

In this case, both the electric field and the magnetic field between the facing ribbons, which are initially 0 everywhere, gradually change to non-zero values starting from the places near the switch, so all these quantities are functions of the position $x$, and the form of the functions should change with time $t$. Let us consider finding this form. There are two basic equations for this.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig5.png

Fig. 5

The first equation expresses the law of conservation of charge. To explain the meaning of this law, the ribbons are imaginarily divided, as in Fig. 5(a), into small capacitors of capacitance $\Delta C$, each consisting of a pair of ribbons of length $\Delta x$ facing each other at separation $d$, numbered $n=0,1,2,3,\cdots$ from the end of the ribbons. Let the charges on the two plates of the $n$-th small capacitor be $\pm Q_n$, and denote by $I_n$, as in Fig. 5(a), the current flowing between the $n$-th capacitor and the $(n+1)$-th capacitor. Then the law of conservation of charge in this case states that the increase per unit time of the charge on a plate is equal to the sum of the currents flowing in from the neighbouring electrodes.

The other equation expresses the law of electromagnetic induction. The law of electromagnetic induction is often learned as the relation between the magnetic flux through a coil and the emf generated in the coil, but the emf can also be considered for an imaginary closed path in space. To explain this, the space between the ribbons is divided into lengths $\Delta x$ as in Fig. 5(b). Each of the spaces formed by the division is the same as a rectangular parallelepiped with the quadrilateral ABCD as its base and length $w$, and the magnetic flux passing through the $n$-th parallelepiped from the front to the back of the page is denoted by $\Phi_n$. This magnetic flux is proportional to the current $I_n$ flowing from A to B (and the current of the same strength flowing from C to D). This proportionality coefficient (inductance) is $\Delta L$. When this $\Phi_n$ increases, an emf arises that circulates around the parallelepiped with base ABCD in the direction opposing the increase, so that the potential of A becomes higher than that of B and the potential of C becomes higher than that of D. As a result, the law of electromagnetic induction in this case states that the increase of $\Phi_n$ per unit time is equal to the difference between the voltage $V_n$ between A and D and the voltage $V_{n+1}$ between B and C.

Below, the length of AB in Fig. 5(b) is equal to the length $\Delta x$ of the side, parallel to the $x$ axis, of the small capacitors in Fig. 5(a). Also, A in Fig. 5(b) is made to coincide with the centre of the plate charged with $Q_n$ in Fig. 5(a), and its position $n\Delta x$ is used instead of the $x$ coordinate.

The following questions can also be considered using an "equivalent circuit". First, since the ribbons are a collection of small capacitors, consider a parallel combination of many capacitors of capacitance $\Delta C$. Next, the inductance $\Delta L$, which represents that a magnetic flux density arises between the ribbons due to the currents flowing in the upper and lower parts of a small portion, is incorporated as series connections of coils of $\dfrac{\Delta L}{2}$, divided into upper and lower parts. In this way, one can consider an electric circuit as in Fig. 6, which has properties mathematically equivalent to the physical properties of the ribbons. You may solve the following questions using it.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig6.png

Fig. 6

Q7. Explain that from the law of conservation of charge and the law of electromagnetic induction described above,

$$I_{n-1}(t)-I_n(t)=\Delta C\,\frac{\mathrm{d}V_n(t)}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (n\geqq1) \qquad (1)$$

$$V_n(t)-V_{n+1}(t)=\Delta L\,\frac{\mathrm{d}I_n(t)}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (2)$$

are derived.

Q8. Eliminate $I_n(t)$ from the simultaneous equations (1), (2) and derive the following equation for $V_n(t)$:

$$[V_{n+1}(t)-V_n(t)]-[V_n(t)-V_{n-1}(t)]=\Delta C\Delta L\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}V_n(t) \qquad (3)$$

Q9. Explain that, using the results of Q2(a) and Q5(a) and the following relation involving $\epsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$ ($c$ is the speed of light)

$$\epsilon_0\mu_0=\frac{1}{c^2}$$

one obtains

$$\frac{\Delta x}{\sqrt{\Delta C\Delta L}}=c$$

Here, when finding the expression for $\Delta L$, the magnetic flux density $B_n$ making up $\Phi_n$ may be taken as $B_n=\dfrac{\mu_0I_n}{w}$, in the same way as the expression used in Q5(a).

Q10. Explain that, if an arbitrary function $f(p)$ of $p=ct-n\Delta x$ is considered as a candidate for the solution $V_n(t)$ of equation (3), then $f(p)$ approximately satisfies equation (3) to the accuracy of $(\Delta x)^2$. Note that, since $\Delta x$ is small, on the left-hand side of equation (3) one can use the expansion in the small quantity $a$

$$f(A+a)=f(A)+a\frac{\mathrm{d}f(A)}{\mathrm{d}A}+\frac{1}{2}a^2\frac{\mathrm{d}^2f(A)}{\mathrm{d}A^2}+\cdots$$

Similarly, it can be shown that an arbitrary function $g(q)$ of $q=ct+n\Delta x$ also approximately satisfies equation (3) (and an equation of the same form as equation (3) also holds for $I_n(t)$). Therefore, the solution of the simultaneous equations (1), (2) is approximately expressed, using arbitrary functions $f$, $g$, as

$$V_n(t)=f(ct-n\Delta x)+g(ct+n\Delta x) \qquad (4)$$

In Fig. 5(a), 5(b) (or Fig. 6), suppose that for time $t<0$, $V_n$, $I_n$ are all 0. When at time $t=0$ the battery of emf $\mathcal{E}$ is connected to the end at $x=0$, the voltage of the $n=0$ small capacitor changes from 0 to $\mathcal{E}$. While the change of voltage is being transmitted in the positive direction of the $x$ axis, the solution of the simultaneous equations (1), (2) is given by

$$V_n(t)=f(p)=f(ct-n\Delta x) \qquad (4')$$

Q11. (a) Integrating equation (2) with respect to $t$ and using $I_n=0$ at $t=0$, the following equation is obtained:

$$I_n(t)=\frac{1}{\Delta L}\int_0^t \mathrm{d}t\,[V_n(t)-V_{n+1}(t)]$$

Treating $\Delta x$ as a small quantity, find from this the current $I_n(t)$ for $t>0$.

(b) Explain that, after the voltage and current have changed,

$$\frac{V_n(t)}{I_n(t)}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0}{\epsilon_0}}\,\frac{d}{w}$$

Now, although the ribbons are actually connected continuously, we considered them divided into small capacitors as in Fig. 5(a) for convenience in using the law of conservation of charge and the law of electromagnetic induction. Because of this, the discontinuous quantity $n\Delta x$ has entered equation $(4')$. So, as the voltage at continuously distributed points on the original ribbons, we may use, instead of equation $(4')$, the expression

$$V(x,t)=f(ct-x) \qquad (5)$$

The concrete form of $f$ is not determined mathematically and must be determined by physical consideration of the signal applied at $x=0$. First, note that since the switch in Fig. 2 was turned on at $t=0$, if the position of the switch is taken as $x=0$, $V(0,t)$ changes as in Fig. 7.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2015-4-fig7.png

Fig. 7

Q12. Suppose that $V(x,t)=f(ct-x)$. When $V(0,t)$ changes for $t>0$ as in Fig. 7, represent $V(x,t)$ at some time $t>0$ as a graph as a function of $x$, and using it, explain that the region where $V(x,t)=\mathcal{E}$ advances in the direction of the $x$ axis with speed $c$.

Q13. (a) Explain that, after the change of voltage and current has been transmitted, the energy density of the electric field and the energy density of the magnetic field are equal.

(b) Find the Poynting vector after the change of voltage and current has been transmitted, and explain that the magnitude of the Poynting vector is equal to the product of the energy density of the electromagnetic field found in (a) and the speed $c$.

To summarize, although this was a consideration of a simplified model, we have found that the signal that the switch has been turned on (the change of voltage or current at $x=0$) is transmitted not with the drift speed of the electrons in the wire such as that found in Q1(b), but with the speed of light $c$, and that the energy of the electromagnetic field is transmitted as the Poynting vector with the same speed $c$. Therefore, the dependence on the length of the wire of the time until the bulb lights up is $\dfrac{\ell}{c}$. Furthermore, in Fig. 2, when the resistance $R$ at the terminating (right) end is set equal to the ratio of voltage to current given in Q11(b), that ratio is not disturbed, so the energy of the electromagnetic wave that has travelled in the $x$ direction is completely absorbed by the resistor $R$ and no reflection occurs. This is called matching, and it is used in actual high-frequency circuits (for example, in connecting television antenna cables and oscilloscope signal cables).

[Reference]

Speed of light in vacuum: $c=2.99792458\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Magnetic constant: $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{H/m}\fallingdotseq1.257\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{H/m}$ (or $\mathrm{N/A^2}$)

Electric constant: $\epsilon_0=\dfrac{1}{\mu_0c^2}\fallingdotseq8.854\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$

problems.title: Problem 1A
problems.problem:
Problem 1A (30 points)

Let us consider whether, when crossing a pedestrian crossing without an umbrella, it is better to run or to walk in order to get as little wet as possible.

As in Fig. 1, a person crosses a pedestrian crossing of length $D$ from A to B with speed $v$ (the $z$ axis is the vertical axis). Consider the case in which the wind blows horizontally from the front or from behind with wind speed $w$ ($w>0$ is a head wind blowing straight from the front, $w<0$ is a tail wind blowing straight from behind). Let the constant falling speed of the raindrops be $u$, and the number of raindrops per unit volume (number density) be $n$. The motion of the raindrops is assumed not to be disturbed by the person.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1. (a) As in the figure, suppose that one of the raindrops passes through the point P on a hypothetical horizontal stationary surface of area $S$, falls in the vertical direction with constant speed $u$, is carried by the wind in the horizontal direction with speed $w$, and reaches the point Q after a time $t$. Explain that the number of raindrops that have passed through the horizontal surface of area $S$ during this time is $nSut$. Here $S$ is an area large enough that $nSut$ is sufficiently large compared with 1.

(b) Explain that, if the surface of area $S$ is a stationary vertical surface perpendicular to the wind direction, the number of raindrops passing through this vertical surface during the time $t$ is $nS|w|t$.

Q2. From now on, approximate the person by a cylinder of height $H$, equal to the person's height, and radius $R$. Find the number of raindrops that hit the side surface of the cylinder while crossing the pedestrian crossing.
[Hint] When the person moves with velocity $v$, the relative velocity of the person and the wind is $v+w$.

Q3. When there is no wind ($w=0$), when there is a head wind ($w>0$) and when there is a tail wind ($w<0$), with what speed should one move in order to cross the pedestrian crossing with the side surface of the body (cylinder) getting as little wet as possible?

Q4. Taking into account also the raindrops that hit the head (the top face of the cylinder), find the total number of raindrops that fall on the whole body (the whole cylinder) while crossing the pedestrian crossing.

Q5. Let $y$ be the number of raindrops falling on the whole body divided by $2nHRD$, and let $x$ be the ratio of the speed of motion to the falling speed of the raindrops, $\dfrac{u}{v}$. Taking $\dfrac{R}{H}=0.1$, draw graphs with $y$ on the vertical axis and $x$ on the horizontal axis for the case of a head wind with $\dfrac{w}{u}=0.4$ and the case of a tail wind with $\dfrac{w}{u}=-0.4$.

Q6. With what speed should one move in order to cross the pedestrian crossing with the whole body getting as little wet as possible? Answer separately for the case of no wind or a head wind ($w\geqq 0$) and the case of a tail wind ($w<0$).

problems.title: Problem 1B
problems.problem:
Problem 1B (40 points)

[I] The motion of a rigid body can be represented as the combination of the motion of the centre of mass of the rigid body (called translational motion) and a rotational motion about a rotation axis fixed in the rigid body. Let us consider the equation of motion for the rotational motion of a rigid body with a simple example.

First, consider the equation of motion of a point-like object P of mass $m$ in a plane, performing a circular motion with changing rotational speed while keeping a constant distance $r$ from a fixed point O. Suppose that, besides the centripetal force, a force of magnitude $F$ acts on the object P in the direction tangent to the circular orbit. If the angular velocity of the circular motion is $\omega$, the velocity $v$ of the circular motion is expressed as $v=r\omega$. Since the acceleration $\overrightarrow{a}$ can be written using the velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ as $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}}{\mathrm{d}t}$, the magnitude of the acceleration in the direction tangent to the orbit can be written as $a=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=r\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}$. $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}$ represents the rate of change of the angular velocity with time and is called the angular acceleration. Hence, the equation of motion of the object P in the tangential direction can be written as

$$mr\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=F \qquad (1)$$

Here, multiplying both sides of this equation by $r$, we get

$$mr^2\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=rF \qquad (2)$$

The right-hand side $rF$ of equation (2) is called the moment of force about the rotation axis O, and below it is denoted by $N$. The sign of $N$ is positive when it increases the angular velocity and negative when it decreases it. Since the relation between this moment of force $N$, the angular acceleration $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}$ and $mr^2$ on the left-hand side corresponds to the relation between the force $F$, the acceleration $a$ and the mass $m$ in the case of translational motion, $mr^2$ represents the inertia in rotational motion, just as the mass $m$ does in translational motion. The inertia in rotational motion represents "how hard it is to change the angular velocity" and is called the moment of inertia. With the moment of inertia $I=mr^2$ and the moment of force $N=rF$, the equation of rotational motion of the object P can be expressed as

$$I\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=N \qquad (3)$$

Next, regard the rigid body as a collection of $n$ points having mass, and let the mass of each point be $m_i$ and its distance from the rotation axis O be $r_i$ ($i=1,\,2,\,\cdots n$). The equation of rotational motion of the whole rigid body is obtained by taking the sum of the equations of rotational motion of all $n$ points. Since the angular velocity $\omega$ is the same for all points, if $N$ is the total moment about the point O of the forces acting on the rigid body from outside, the equation of rotational motion of the rigid body is

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i{r_i}^2\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=N \qquad (4)$$

Besides the forces acting from outside (external forces), forces also act between the points that make up the rigid body (internal forces), but since the internal forces acting inside the rigid body cancel each other by the law of action and reaction when the sum over the whole body is taken, they do not affect $N$ in equation (4). From equation (4), the moment of inertia $I$ of the rigid body can be expressed as

$$I=\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i{r_i}^2 \qquad (5)$$

Using these equations (4) and (5), let us consider the following motion.

[II] Let us consider the motion often seen in the hoop (a ring-shaped apparatus) event of rhythmic gymnastics, in which a hoop slid along a horizontal floor stops once and then comes back towards the gymnast (see Fig. 1). The hoop is assumed to move in a vertical plane.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Let the mass of a uniform thin hoop be $M$, its radius $R$, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the hoop and the floor $\mu$. At time 0, this hoop is set sliding to the right while rotating counterclockwise. While it slides on the floor, kinetic friction acts on the hoop, so the speed of the contact point of the hoop relative to the floor gradually decreases and eventually becomes 0, and the hoop comes to roll without slipping. Since the effect of the friction force when the hoop rolls without slipping (rolling friction) is small, from then on the hoop advances rolling at an almost constant speed.

Initially, the velocity of the centre of mass of the hoop is $v_0$ and the angular velocity of rotation is $\omega_0$; the angular velocity of rotation at time $t$ is denoted by $\omega$ and the velocity of the centre of mass by $v$ (see Fig. 2). The angular velocity is taken positive counterclockwise, and the velocity of the centre of mass is taken positive to the right. If necessary, denote the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration by $g$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.
