Q1. Using the fact that the acceleration of the centre of mass of the hoop can be expressed as $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$, write the equation of motion of the centre of mass of the hoop while it slides on the floor.

Q2. If the hoop is divided into $n$ small parts, all these small parts are at distance $R$ from the rotation axis of the hoop, so the moment of inertia of one small part about the central axis can be expressed as $\dfrac{M}{n}R^2$. By summing this over the $n$ small parts, find the moment of inertia $I$ of the whole hoop about its central axis. Also, write the equation of rotational motion of the hoop while it slides on the floor.

Q3. Since the acceleration $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$ is obtained from the equation of motion of the centre of mass in Q1, find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. Similarly, from the equation of rotational motion in Q2, find an expression for the angular velocity $\omega$ at time $t$. Here, the time $t$ is a time before the hoop comes to roll without slipping.

Q4. While the hoop slides, express the velocity $u$ (positive to the right) of the contact point P of the hoop relative to the floor using $\omega$ and $v$.

For the hoop to reverse the direction of motion of its centre of mass and come back, as in a rhythmic gymnastics performance, the velocity of the centre of mass of the hoop must become 0 before the angular velocity of rotation becomes 0.

Q5. Suppose that, while advancing and sliding on the floor, the velocity $v$ of the centre of mass of the hoop becomes 0. Find the time $t_1$ at which this happens and the distance $l$ travelled by the centre of mass up to then.

Q6. Find the time $t_2$ at which the hoop comes to roll without slipping and the velocity $v_2$ of the centre of mass at time $t_2$. Also, what relation must hold between the initial angular velocity $\omega_0$ and the velocity $v_0$ of the centre of mass for the hoop that has moved to the right to start moving to the left?

Q7. With the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu=\dfrac{1}{4.9}$ and the gravitational acceleration $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, a hoop of radius $R=0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ and mass $M=0.30\,\mathrm{kg}$ was slid to the right while rotating; it moved to the right until $1.0\,\mathrm{s}$ later, and then moved to the left. The hoop came to roll without slipping $1.5\,\mathrm{s}$ after the start. Find the values of the initial angular velocity $\omega_0$ of the hoop and the velocity $v_0$ of the centre of mass.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (80 points)

Snow crystals show various beautiful forms with six-fold symmetry (Figs. 1, 2) and fascinate people. Also, the cube in Fig. 3 is a crystal of familiar table salt.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig1.jpg

Fig. 1. Snow crystal$^{*1}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig2.jpg

Fig. 2. Phase diagram of snow crystals$^{*2}$

[Labels in the figure: 結晶サイズ = crystal size (vertical axis); 過飽和度 → = supersaturation → (horizontal axis).]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig3.jpg

Fig. 3. NaCl crystal$^{*3}$

Beyond that, the growth processes and shapes of crystals fascinate even physicists. A crystal is a reflection, in a visible state, of interactions at the atomic and molecular level, and it is physically very interesting. Here we consider the size and shape of crystals using simple models.

$^{*1}$ From the website of the Phase Transition Dynamics group, Institute of Low Temperature Science, Hokkaido University (北海道大学低温研究所相転移ダイナミクス分野の HP より)
$^{*2}$ E. Yokoyama and T. Kuroda, Phys. Rev. A41 (1990) 2038
$^{*3}$ J. C. Heyraud and J. J. Metois, J. Cryst. Growth 84 (1987) 503

Crystal growth of a face that is flat at the molecular (atomic) level (a facet face) begins with the formation, on the flat two-dimensional face, of a stable nucleus that becomes the seed of growth (see Fig. 4).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig4.jpg

Fig. 4. Growth of a facet face by a two-dimensional nucleus

Once a nucleus has formed, new molecules attach to the edges of the nucleus as in Fig. 5, and it grows so as to cover the facet face below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig5.jpg

Fig. 5. Molecular process of the growth of a facet face

Consider a two-dimensional nucleus growing on a large facet face; to keep things simple, we ignore the influence of the underlying facet face and treat it as a completely two-dimensional system.

[I] Let us consider a single crystal sealed in a container. To make the problem simple, the molecules (atoms) are assumed to take only one of two states, crystal or gas. In this case, if a crystal is put into an evacuated container, the crystal vaporizes, and when its vapour pressure reaches the saturated vapour pressure, it reaches an equilibrium state in which the size of the crystal does not change. Here we consider the size of a crystal in the equilibrium state.

If solid carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_2}$) (dry ice) is left in air at room temperature, it all sublimes. However, if it is sealed in a container, part of it sublimes and gaseous carbon dioxide (carbonic acid gas) fills the container, but if the temperature is sufficiently low the rest remains in the solid phase, and if the temperature is kept constant, it reaches an equilibrium state that does not change any further (a thermal equilibrium state). How the solid phase and the gas phase coexist in the thermal equilibrium state is determined by the temperature. In this problem, using a simple model, we consider the physical properties of the crystal and vapour of molecules confined in a container, while quantifying the energy of the molecules in the solid and the gas and the randomness of the molecular arrangement.

Caution: The pressure resistance of PET bottles for carbonated drinks is estimated to be about 6 atmospheres, but there have been quite a few accidents in which a PET bottle burst because dry ice was sealed in it. Never do this.

Now, suppose that $N$ molecules of a single substance are confined in a container; these molecules are divided into crystal and vapour. The molecules in the crystal are called crystal molecules and the molecules in the vapour gas molecules. If the number of crystal molecules is denoted by $N_{\mathrm{c}}$, the number of gas molecules is $N-N_{\mathrm{c}}$. Here $N$ and $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ are sufficiently large compared with 1 (written $N\gg 1$, $N_{\mathrm{c}}\gg 1$).

To simplify the calculation, as in Fig. 6, the inside of the container is divided into many small cubes, and each cube is called a cell. Since the size of a cell is very small, of the order of the size of a molecule, the total number of cells $V$ is a large number of the order of Avogadro's number. Also, each cell can contain at most one molecule.

The crystal consists of $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ mutually adjacent cells, and each of these cells contains one molecule. The size of the crystal is sufficiently small compared with the container, and it is at rest near the centre of the container.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

[Labels in the figure: 気体分子 = gas molecules; 結晶分子 = crystal molecules; 容器 = container.]

The remaining space, excluding the crystal, consists of $V-N_{\mathrm{c}}$ cells, and $N-N_{\mathrm{c}}$ gas molecules are scattered among these cells. Since $V$ may be considered much larger than $N$ ($V\gg N$), most of these cells are empty.

In real matter the molecules move around, but in this model a molecule is at rest within one cell. Therefore, both the gas molecules and the crystal molecules are considered to have no kinetic energy. Also, the gas molecules have no potential energy either, but each crystal molecule, being bound to the surrounding molecules, has a potential energy $-\mu$ ($\mu>0$).

Answer the following questions about this model.

Q1. Explain that, according to this model, the internal energy $U$ of this collection of molecules can be written as

$$U=-\mu N_{\mathrm{c}} \qquad (1)$$

The size of the crystal can change by sublimation and condensation. A phase equilibrium state is one in which, nevertheless, $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ keeps a constant value. The number of molecules $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ of a crystal in phase equilibrium with the vapour in a sealed container of constant volume and temperature is determined, with $T$ the absolute temperature, so as to minimize $F(N_{\mathrm{c}})$ defined by the following equation:

$$F(N_{\mathrm{c}})=U(N_{\mathrm{c}})-TS(N_{\mathrm{c}}) \qquad (2)$$

The functional form of the internal energy $U$ appearing here is the one given in Q1. $S(N_{\mathrm{c}})$ is called the entropy; in the present case it is defined, through the number of ways $W(N_{\mathrm{c}})$ of distributing the $N$ molecules among the cells in the container while satisfying the macroscopic condition "there is a crystal with $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ molecules in the container", by

$$S(N_{\mathrm{c}})=k_B\log W(N_{\mathrm{c}}) \qquad (3)$$

Here $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant. Also, $\log x$ denotes the natural logarithm.

So we consider the number of ways of distributing the molecules among the many cells. In the crystal there is only one way of distributing $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ molecules among $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ cells, so it suffices to consider the ways of distributing the gas molecules among the remaining cells.

Q2. Considering the entropy as described above, derive

$$S(N_{\mathrm{c}})=k_{\mathrm{B}}\log\frac{(V-N_{\mathrm{c}})!}{(V-N)!\,(N-N_{\mathrm{c}})!} \qquad (4)$$

For a large integer $N$, the following approximation can be used (this formula is called Stirling's formula):

$$\log N!\fallingdotseq N\log N-N$$

Using this on the right-hand side of equation (4), the following expression for the entropy is obtained:

$$S(N_{\mathrm{c}})=k_{\mathrm{B}}[(V-N_{\mathrm{c}})\log(V-N_{\mathrm{c}})-(N-N_{\mathrm{c}})\log(N-N_{\mathrm{c}})-(V-N)\log(V-N)] \qquad (5)$$

The thermal equilibrium state is realized where $F(N_{\mathrm{c}})$ is minimum.

Q3. In order to consider the thermal equilibrium state at temperature $T$, we write

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}F(N_{\mathrm{c}})}{\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{c}}}=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\Bigl(-\frac{\mu}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}+f(N_{\mathrm{c}})\Bigr)$$

Taking $\dfrac{N_{\mathrm{c}}}{N}$ on the horizontal axis, sketch the general shape of $f(N_{\mathrm{c}})$.

Q4. The condition for $F(N_{\mathrm{c}})$ to have an extremum, with the number of crystal molecules $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ as the variable, is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}F(N_{\mathrm{c}})}{\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{c}}}=0$$

Explain how the value ${N_{\mathrm{c}}}^*$ of $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ satisfying this condition is given from the graph of Q3. Also, using the graph, explain that the point $N_{\mathrm{c}}={N_{\mathrm{c}}}^*$ gives the minimum value of $F(N_{\mathrm{c}})$.

Q5. Sketch the general shape of the graph of the number of crystal molecules ${N_{\mathrm{c}}}^*$ as a function of $\dfrac{\mu}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}$ (take $\dfrac{{N_{\mathrm{c}}}^*}{N}$ on the horizontal axis and $\dfrac{\mu}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}$ on the vertical axis). Also, explain how the number of crystal molecules ${N_{\mathrm{c}}}^*$ changes when $\dfrac{\mu}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}$ changes.

Q6. Find the temperature $T_0$ at which all the molecules sublime and ${N_{\mathrm{c}}}^*=0$, and confirm that $k_{\mathrm{B}}T_0$ is considerably smaller than the heat of sublimation (heat of evaporation) per molecule, $\mu$.

[II] A crystal in an equilibrium state keeps a definite shape. That shape is determined by the surface tension and is strongly affected by the anisotropy (direction dependence) of the surface tension. From here on, we consider the anisotropy of the surface tension of a crystal and the shape of the crystal. The temperature is taken to be $0\,\mathrm{K}$, and the entropy of the gas molecules is not considered. Also, we consider a two-dimensional crystal. Therefore the surface of the crystal is in general a curve.

Before considering the shape of the crystal, we consider the surface tension in this model. The surface tension is defined as the energy per unit length needed to cut the bonds between molecules along an infinitely long straight line.

Q7. As in Fig. 7, there is a two-dimensional crystal with molecules arranged on the lattice points of a square lattice. The spacing between neighbouring molecules is $a$. When each crystal molecule bonds only with the crystal molecules on the nearest-neighbour lattice points, and the energy decreases by $\varepsilon$ for one bond, find the surface tension in the direction parallel to the lattice axis ($\theta=0$, Fig. 7(a)) and the surface tension in the diagonal direction ($\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, Fig. 7(b)). The number of molecules is sufficiently large.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig7.png

Fig. 7.

[Labels in the figure: 結合エネルギー $\varepsilon$ = bond energy $\varepsilon$; $\theta=0$ の界面 = interface at $\theta=0$; $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ の界面 = interface at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$; 結晶分子 = crystal molecules.]

Q8. Show that the surface tension $\gamma$ of an interface in the direction $\tan\theta=\dfrac{M}{N}$ ($M$, $N$ natural numbers) is

$$\gamma(\theta)=\frac{\varepsilon}{a}(\cos\theta+\sin\theta) \qquad \Bigl(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)$$

$\gamma(\theta)$ reflects the symmetry of the crystal lattice. In the case of Q7 and Q8, the lattice is symmetric with respect to the $x$, $y$ axes and the straight line $y=x$, so for general $\theta$ we have $\gamma(\theta)=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{a}(|\cos\theta|+|\sin\theta|)$.

The shape of a crystal is determined so as to minimize the energy due to the surface tension under a given volume (in the present case, area). Also, the shape of the crystal determined in this way reflects the symmetry of the lattice through $\gamma(\theta)$. For example, the shape of the crystal when $\gamma$ does not depend on $\theta$ is a circle.

Q9. (a) In the case of Q7 and Q8, the shape of the crystal is symmetric with respect to the $x$, $y$ axes and the straight line $y=x$. Therefore, when considering the shape of the crystal, it suffices to consider the part of the crystal with vertex angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ as in Fig. 8.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig8.png

Fig. 8.

In particular, here we consider a polygonal crystal and assume that the surface of this part is a line segment as in Fig. 9. Let the length of the line segment be $l$ and the angle between the line segment and the $x$ axis be $\theta$ $\Bigl(0<\theta\leqq\dfrac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)$; find the area $S$ of the grey part of the crystal in Fig. 9.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-3-fig9.png

Fig. 9.

(b) The energy $E$ due to the surface tension is $E=\gamma(\theta)\,l=\dfrac{\varepsilon l}{a}(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)$. Explain that, under the condition of constant $S$, $E$ is minimum when

$$\frac{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}{\sin\theta}$$

is minimum.

(c) Keeping $S$ constant, find the $\theta$ that minimizes $E$.

(d) What shape does the whole crystal have?

In Q9 the surface was assumed to be a line segment, but the same result as in (d) is obtained even if it is assumed to be a curve.

Q10. For the question of what shape the crystal of Q7 takes, in Q9 we considered it using $\gamma(\theta)$. If there is another way of thinking about the same question, explain it.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (80 points)

When there is a point charge of charge $q$ at the origin, the electric field produced at a point P at position $\overrightarrow{r}$ and the electric potential with infinity as the reference are expressed, with $\varepsilon_0$ the electric constant (permittivity of vacuum), as

$$\overrightarrow{E}(\mathrm{P})=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{r^3}\,,\qquad V(\mathrm{P})=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{1}{r} \qquad (1)$$

When there are many charges $q_1,\,q_2,\,q_3,\,\cdots,\,q_N$, and the electric fields that the individual charges produce at the point P are $\overrightarrow{E}_1(\mathrm{P}),\,\overrightarrow{E}_2(\mathrm{P}),\,\overrightarrow{E}_3(\mathrm{P}),\,\cdots,\,\overrightarrow{E}_N(\mathrm{P})$ and the potentials are $V_1(\mathrm{P}),\,V_2(\mathrm{P}),\,V_3(\mathrm{P}),\,\cdots,\,V_N(\mathrm{P})$, the electric field and the potential at the point P are

$$\overrightarrow{E}(\mathrm{P})=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{E}_k(\mathrm{P})\,,\qquad V(P)=\sum_{k=1}^{N}V_k(\mathrm{P}) \qquad (2)$$

This is called the principle of superposition. This principle is also contained in the basic law (1). Indeed, according to (1), when there is a charge $2q$ at the origin, the electric field at the position $\overrightarrow{r}$ is the superposition of two electric fields produced by a charge $q$.

[I] The experimental fact to be explained

There is a capacitor consisting of two conducting plates (below called the electrode plates). Let the area of the electrode plates be $A$ and the separation between the facing surfaces of the electrode plates be $d$. When this was connected to a battery of electromotive force $V_0$ as in Fig. 1(a), charges $\pm Q$ flowed from the battery into the conducting plates, and the charges that flowed in were distributed on the facing surfaces of the conductors as in Fig. 1(a).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

[Label in the figure: 誘電体 = dielectric.]

The ratio of $Q$ and $V_0$ in this case,

$$C=\frac{Q}{V_0} \qquad (3)$$

is called the capacitance of this capacitor. $C$ is proportional to the area $A$ of the electrode plates and inversely proportional to the distance $d$ between the electrode plates. The proportionality constant in this case is $\varepsilon_0$. Below, $Q>0$ always.

Let $\pm Q'$ be the charge that flows from the battery into the electrode plates when the gap between the electrode plates of this capacitor is filled with a dielectric (insulator) as in Fig. 1(b) and it is connected to the same battery. The $z$ coordinate of Fig. 1(b) is explained just before Q2. In general, $Q'$ ($>0$) is larger than $Q$. Since the potential difference applied between the electrode plates is the same in Fig. 1(a) and (b), this experimental fact means that the capacitance of a capacitor increases when a dielectric is inserted. In this problem we consider the reason for this.

Below, it is assumed that a uniform electric field is produced between the electrode plates of Fig. 1(a). The electric field produced inside the dielectric of Fig. 1(b) is explained after Q1.

Q1. When the dielectric of the capacitor of Fig. 1(b) was changed and the measurement of $Q'$ was repeated while applying the same voltage to the same electrode plates, it was found that the value of the ratio

$$\bar{\varepsilon}=\frac{Q'}{Q} \qquad (4)$$

is a constant determined by the kind of dielectric. Express the capacitance $C'$ of the capacitor of Fig. 1(b) by an expression containing the area $A$ of the electrode plates, the distance $d$ between the electrode plates, and $\bar{\varepsilon}$.

The $\bar{\varepsilon}$ appearing here is a dimensionless quantity called the relative permittivity of that dielectric. Also, $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\bar{\varepsilon}$ is called the permittivity of the dielectric, and its unit is $\mathrm{F/m}$, the same as that of the electric constant.

The electric field in the dielectric of Fig. 1(b) is the superposition of that produced by the charges on the electrode plates and that produced by the charges of the molecules in the dielectric. The former produces a uniform electric field as in Fig. 1(a). The latter is very complicated because of the microscopic structure of the distribution of dielectric molecules, and therefore there is also no means of directly observing the electric field in the dielectric that is their sum.

So, when considering the results of experiments using a macroscopically uniform material to which a uniform electric field is applied from outside, we consider that a hypothetical uniform electric field is produced in the material as well. Such a hypothetical electric field ignores the microscopic structure of the material and is therefore called the macroscopic electric field; in this problem it is denoted by $\overrightarrow{E}$. Then, when the $z$ axis is chosen upward with one point on the lower electrode plate as the origin, the potential inside the dielectric is a function of $z$ only.

Q2. In which direction is the macroscopic electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ produced inside the dielectric of Fig. 1(b)? How is its magnitude expressed using $V_0$, $d$, $A$, $Q$ (it is not necessary to use all four of these letters)? Also, when the potential on a plane $z=$ constant is denoted by $V(z)$, write the relation between it and the $z$ component $E_z$ of the macroscopic electric field. In this Q2, $V(0)=0$.

[II] The microscopic electric field produced by one dielectric molecule

A dielectric is a collection of many molecules. Each molecule consists of positive and negative charges $\pm q$ ($q>0$); if no electric field is applied from outside, the distributions of these charges overlap, and each molecule may be regarded as an electrically neutral sphere as in Fig. 2(a). When an electric field is applied to the dielectric as in Fig. 1(b), forces in mutually opposite directions act on the positive and negative charges. The charges are displaced to the position where this force and the attraction between the positive and negative charges balance, and reach a stable state (see Fig. 2(b)). Such a separation of charge into positive and negative within a molecule is called electric polarization, or simply polarization.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

In general, a pair of a positive charge and a negative charge is called an electric dipole. The vector $\overrightarrow{p}$ defined, using the relative position vector $\overrightarrow{l}$ of the centre of the positive charge distribution as seen from the centre of the negative charge distribution (see Fig. 2(c)), by

$$\overrightarrow{p}=q\overrightarrow{l} \qquad (5)$$

is called the electric dipole moment, and it represents the magnitude and direction of the polarization of the molecule.

Many electric dipoles are produced inside the dielectric, but first we consider the electric field produced by a single electric dipole.

Q3. There is an electric dipole consisting of a charge $q$ ($>0$) at the point $\mathrm{A}\Bigl(0,\,0,\,z=\dfrac{l}{2}\Bigr)$ and a charge $-q$ at the point $\mathrm{B}\Bigl(0,\,0,\,z=-\dfrac{l}{2}\Bigr)$ (see Fig. 3). Find the potential $V(\mathrm{C})$ produced by this dipole moment at a point $\mathrm{C}(x,\,y,\,z)$ whose distance from the origin O is sufficiently large compared with $l$, according to the following steps.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

(a) First, with $r_+$ the distance between A and C and $r_-$ the distance between B and C, express the potential $V(\mathrm{C})$ at the point C using $r_+$ and $r_-$.

(b) Let the distance from the origin to the point C be $r$ and $\angle\mathrm{COA}=\theta$. Show that, since $r$ is sufficiently larger than $l$ ($r\gg l$), by neglecting terms containing $\dfrac{l^2}{r^2}$,

$$V(\mathrm{C})=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{p}{r^2}\cos\theta \qquad (6)$$

Here $p=ql$ is the magnitude of the dipole moment of Fig. 3. If necessary, use the fact that, for a number $a$ whose absolute value is sufficiently small compared with 1, one can approximate $\sqrt{1+a}\fallingdotseq 1+\dfrac{a}{2}$.

To show that $V(\mathrm{C})$ is a function of $(r,\,\theta)$ as in equation (6), we write it as $V(r,\theta)$. Then, as in Fig. 4, denoting the component of the electric field pointing from the coordinate origin O towards C by $E_r$, and the component in the direction perpendicular to it in which $\theta$ increases by $E_\theta$, these components of the electric field can be calculated using the following equations:

$$E_r(r,\theta)=-\lim_{\mathit{\Delta} r\to 0}\frac{V(r+\mathit{\Delta} r,\theta)-V(r,\theta)}{\mathit{\Delta} r}=-\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}V(r,\theta)}{\mathrm{d}r}\right)_{\theta} \qquad (7\mathrm{a})$$

$$E_\theta(r,\theta)=-\lim_{\mathit{\Delta}\theta\to 0}\frac{V(r,\theta+\mathit{\Delta}\theta)-V(r,\theta)}{r\mathit{\Delta}\theta}=-\frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}V(r,\theta)}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\right)_{r} \qquad (7\mathrm{b})$$

As can be seen from the middle expression, the meaning of the rightmost side of (7a) is to regard $\theta$ in the function $V(r,\theta)$ as if it were a constant and to differentiate with respect to $r$ only. When calculating (7b), one regards $r$ in $V(r,\theta)$ as a constant and differentiates with respect to $\theta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

Q4. (a) Find expressions for the two components $E_r(r,\theta)$ and $E_\theta(r,\theta)$ of the electric field at the point C of Fig. 4.

(b) On the answer sheet, one point each in the directions $\theta=0,\,\pi$ and two points in the direction $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ are given. Sketch the electric lines of force passing through each of these four points.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig9.png

[Editorial note: the diagram printed for Q4(b) on the answer sheet (page 11 of the answer booklet).]

[III] The electric field produced by one electric dipole layer

Next, consider a layer of dipoles in which the molecules in the dielectric are arranged regularly. The polarization occurs perpendicular to this layer (see Fig. 5), and the $z$ axis is chosen in that direction. Below, this layer of dipole moments is called a dipole layer. Choosing an $x$ axis and a $y$ axis with an arbitrary point O in the plane of the dipole layer as the origin, let us find the potential produced by the collection of dipole moments of one layer at a point A on the $z$ axis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

The distance between the point A and the dipole layer is sufficiently large compared with the spacing between neighbouring dipoles. Seen from such a distance, the dipoles may be regarded as distributed continuously. Denoting the sum of the dipole moments within unit area by $\overrightarrow{P}_{\mathrm{S}}$, answer the following questions.

Q5. Let the coordinates of the point A be $(0,0,z)$. Explain that the potential there is expressed as

$$V(\mathrm{A})=\frac{P_{\mathrm{S}}z}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^\infty\frac{2\pi R\,\mathrm{d}R}{(z^2+R^2)^{3/2}} \qquad (8)$$

Here $P_{\mathrm{S}}$ is the magnitude of the vector $\overrightarrow{P}_{\mathrm{S}}$, and $R$ is the distance from the origin O in the $x$-$y$ plane. Also, if necessary, you may use the figure on the answer sheet in your explanation, adding to it.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig10.png

[Editorial note: the figure printed for Q5 on the answer sheet (page 12 of the answer booklet).]

Q6. The integral of the previous question can be calculated with the substitution $t=R^2$. Derive that, as a result of this calculation, the potential in the regions on both sides of the dipole layer does not depend on $(x,y)$ and is

$$V(\mathrm{A})=V(z)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{P_{\mathrm{S}}}{2\varepsilon_0} & z>0\\[2ex] -\dfrac{P_{\mathrm{S}}}{2\varepsilon_0} & z<0\end{cases} \qquad (9)$$

The graph of equation (9) is as shown by the solid line in Fig. 6. The potential on both sides of the dipole layer became a discontinuous function of $z$ in this way because the dipole moments, which are distributed with gaps between them, were treated as if they were distributed continuously. As stated above, this is allowed when $|z|$ is sufficiently large compared with the spacing of the dipole moments. Near the dipole layer, the effect of the complicated structure of the electric field produced by the nearby dipole moments appears. Since in general the potential is a continuous function of position, $V(\mathrm{A})$ is also a continuous function of $z$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

One example of this is shown by the broken line in Fig. 6; this part can change depending on the $(x,y)$ coordinates of the point A. However, the $z$ dependence of $V(\mathrm{A})$ deviates from the solid line only in the range $-\delta<z<\delta$, where $\delta$ is a microscopic length sufficiently larger than the spacing of the dipole moments, and the potential at places farther than that from the dipole layer is given by equation (9).

[IV] The electric field produced by stacked electric dipole layers

Suppose that the dielectric of Fig. 1(b) is a plate formed by stacking $N$ electric dipole layers in the $z$ direction (see Fig. 7). If the spacing between neighbouring layers is $a$, the thickness $d$ of the crystal in the $z$-axis direction is $Na$, and the centres of the dipoles are distributed on the planes $z=\dfrac{a}{2},\,\dfrac{3a}{2},\,\dfrac{5a}{2},\,\cdots,\,\Bigl(N-\dfrac{1}{2}\Bigr)a$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig7.png

Fig. 7.

Q7. (a) First, suppose that each dipole layer produces, above and below it, a potential distribution like that shown by the solid line in Fig. 6. Then, denoting by $V(z)$ the potential produced by the $N$ dipole layers on the plane $z=$ constant, explain why $V(z)$ is constant in the region $\Bigl(n-\dfrac{1}{2}\Bigr)a<z<\Bigl(n+\dfrac{1}{2}\Bigr)a$ (where $n=0,\,1,\,2,\,\cdots,\,N$), and derive the expression for $V(z)$ there.

(b) Also, find the change in $V(z)$ when $n$ increases by 1, and derive that the potential difference between $z=0$ and $z=d$ is $\dfrac{NP_{\mathrm{S}}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

Therefore, if a graph is made with $z$ on the horizontal axis and $V(z)$ found in Q7 on the vertical axis, a staircase-like graph with step width $a$ and step height $\dfrac{P_{\mathrm{S}}}{\varepsilon_0}$ is obtained.

Such a staircase structure arises because the potential distribution produced by one layer of dipoles was assumed to have a step structure like the solid line in Fig. 6; in reality the corners of the steps are rounded off as in the broken line in Fig. 6, so the graph of the potential distribution obtained by superposing them also has a structure like a smooth slope without corners. Also, near $z\fallingdotseq\delta+d$ and $z\fallingdotseq-\delta$ outside the dielectric, the slope of the graph of $V(z)$ ends, and the potential on both sides is the one found in Q7. This potential distribution is called the macroscopic potential distribution, and the electric field calculated from it is the macroscopic electric field produced by the polarization of the dielectric of Fig. 1(b); below it is denoted by $\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{P}}$.

Q8. Noting that, since $\delta$ is a microscopic quantity, it may be ignored when considering the macroscopic potential distribution and electric field, find the average gradient of the slope of the potential, and derive the expression

$$\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{P}}=-\frac{\overrightarrow{P}}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad (10)$$

for the macroscopic electric field $\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{P}}$ produced by the polarization. Here $\overrightarrow{P}$ is the sum of the dipole moments $\overrightarrow{p}$ per unit volume of the crystal.

The electric field expressed by equation (10) is sometimes called the depolarizing field, in the sense that it points in the direction opposite to the polarization.

[V] The electric field inside the dielectric

So far we have considered the electric field produced by a collection of dipole moments formed by upward polarization. Here we consider the properties of the macroscopic electric field produced inside the dielectric of Fig. 1(b).

The macroscopic electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ in the dielectric of Fig. 1(b) is the superposition of two kinds of electric field, the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{P}}$ produced by the dipoles and the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{Q}}$ produced by the charges on the electrode plates, and

$$\overrightarrow{E}=\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{Q}}+\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{P}} \qquad (11)$$

holds.

In this problem, it is assumed that between the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ and the dipole moment $\overrightarrow{p}$ of a dielectric molecule produced by it there is the relation

$$\overrightarrow{p}=\alpha\overrightarrow{E} \qquad (12)$$

The $\alpha$ appearing here is a constant with a positive value and is called the polarizability of the molecule. Then, denoting the number of dielectric molecules per unit volume by $n$, the relation

$$\overrightarrow{P}=n\alpha\overrightarrow{E}=\chi_{\mathrm{P}}\overrightarrow{E} \qquad (13)$$

holds. Here we have introduced the quantity called the electric susceptibility by $\chi_{\mathrm{P}}=n\alpha$ ($\chi$ is the Greek letter chi). Substituting this into the right-hand side of equation (10) to eliminate $\overrightarrow{P}$, rewriting the right-hand side of equation (11) using the result, and rearranging, we obtain

$$\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{Q}}=\overrightarrow{E}-\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{P}}=\Bigl(1+\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{P}}}{\varepsilon_0}\Bigr)\overrightarrow{E} \qquad (14)$$

Q9. A capacitor with vacuum between its electrode plates as in Fig. 1(a) was charged by a power supply of electromotive force $V_0$, then the power supply was disconnected, and a dielectric with electric susceptibility $\chi_{\mathrm{P}}$ was inserted between the electrode plates. What is the potential difference between the two electrodes then?

Here, multiplying each side of equation (14) by $\varepsilon_0$ and rewriting equation (14) using the vector quantity defined by

$$\overrightarrow{D}=\varepsilon_0\overrightarrow{E}_{\mathrm{Q}} \qquad (15)$$

we obtain

$$\overrightarrow{D}=\varepsilon_0\overrightarrow{E}+\overrightarrow{P}=(\varepsilon_0+\chi_{\mathrm{P}})\,\overrightarrow{E} \qquad (16)$$

$\overrightarrow{D}$ is called the electric flux density.

Q10. Show that, in the case of Fig. 1(b), the magnitude $D$ of $\overrightarrow{D}$ is equal to the charge density of the upper electrode plate $\Bigl($the charge per unit area $\dfrac{Q'}{A}\Bigr)$.

The $\varepsilon_0+\chi_{\mathrm{P}}$ appearing in equation (16) is the permittivity $\varepsilon$ of the dielectric that appeared just after Q1. Since the polarizability of a molecule is positive, the electric susceptibility $\chi_{\mathrm{P}}$ is also positive. Therefore the permittivity $\varepsilon$ is always larger than $\varepsilon_0$. From this and equation (4), it follows that the capacitance of a capacitor increases when a dielectric is inserted.

[VI] Observation of the electric flux density

The electric field $E$ and the electric flux density $D$ in the dielectric discussed above were in a proportional relation. However, in materials called ferroelectrics, such as barium titanate, the relation between $D$ and $E$ is not linear, and moreover it changes along different relations when $E$ is increased and when it is decreased. Fig. 8 shows the principle diagram of a measurement method for observing such a complicated relation between $D$ and $E$ with an oscilloscope.

First, the dielectric to be measured is cut into a plate of thickness $d$ and sandwiched in close contact between two parallel metal plates of area $A$. Its outward form is the same as the capacitor of Fig. 1(b), but $D$ and $E$ are not proportional. So below this is simply called the sample, and it is distinguished from the capacitor labelled C. The capacitance of the capacitor C is $C$.

A circuit in which this sample and the capacitor C are connected in series is connected to an AC power supply. Then the voltage $V_{\mathrm{s}}(t)$ (s = sample) between the metal plates of the sample and the voltage $V_{\mathrm{c}}(t)$ (c = capacitor or condenser) across the capacitor C oscillate with the same frequency as the AC electromotive force, and at the same time charge moves in the circuit with the same frequency.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-4-fig8.png

Fig. 8.

[Labels in the figure: 水平端子 = horizontal input terminals; 垂直端子 = vertical input terminals; 誘電体 = dielectric; 交流電源 = AC power supply.]

Q11. Explain that there is a proportional relation between $V_{\mathrm{c}}$ and the electric flux density $D$ in the dielectric, and write the relation between $V_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $D$.
[Hint] Consider the relation between the charge on the metal plates of the sample and the charge on the electrodes of the capacitor C.

Q12. Which of $D$ and $E$ in the dielectric of the sample do the horizontal axis and the vertical axis of the oscilloscope respectively represent?

[Reference]
All insulators have the properties of a dielectric. For the macroscopic polarization $P$ of a dielectric, the treatment as in Fig. 5 and Fig. 7 is only one model, and there are various ways of thinking about dielectrics, such as models that introduce hypothetical polarization charges.

Dielectrics have permittivities specific to the material, with various values, and the way and degree of their response to an external electric field are also diverse. Materials such as the one discussed here, a collection of non-polar molecules polarized by an external electric field, have a small permittivity, while materials whose molecules are themselves polarized, like water molecules, but which are not polarized as a whole in the absence of an external field and become polarized when an external electric field is applied, have a large permittivity. There are also cases, like the ferroelectrics mentioned in [VI], in which a body is polarized from the start even without an external electric field. Furthermore, there are materials called piezoelectrics, whose polarization changes greatly not only with the electric field but also with pressure, and materials whose polarization changes greatly with temperature. These diverse properties of dielectrics are applied in many places.

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (70 points)

[I] Lifetime

Some atomic nuclei are unstable and decay emitting radiation, and through the decay the probability that the original nucleus exists decreases. The time until the existence probability becomes half is called the half-life and is denoted by $t_{1/2}$. Instead of this, the lifetime $\tau$ (tau) is sometimes used; between these there is the relation $t_{1/2}=\tau\log 2$ ($\log 2=0.6931$). For a nucleus that existed as one nucleus at time $t=0$, after a time $t$ has passed, its existence probability decreases exponentially as

$$2^{-t/t_{1/2}}=e^{-t/\tau} \qquad (1)$$

Natural uranium contains the isotope ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ ($t_{1/2}=44.68\times 10^8$ years) at $99.28\%$ and the isotope ${}^{235}\mathrm{U}$ ($t_{1/2}=7.038\times 10^8$ years), which is the nuclear fuel of nuclear reactors, at $0.72\%$. In nuclear reactors using ordinary water (light-water reactors), the content of ${}^{235}\mathrm{U}$ must be enriched to $3\%$ to sustain the nuclear fission reaction. However, in the past there was a period when the content was $3\%$ or more even without enrichment. Therefore, if the environment of the uranium ore and the surrounding water and so on was favourable, a natural nuclear reactor could exist. Indeed, traces of a natural nuclear reactor were discovered in 1972 in the Oklo mine in the Gabonese Republic in Africa.

Q1. About how many years or more before the present is it thought that the natural nuclear reactor occurred?

In quantum mechanics there is the uncertainty principle, and time and energy cannot both be determined exactly at the same time. The uncertainty in the time at which an unstable nucleus decays is the lifetime $\tau$ of the nucleus. On the other hand, the rest energy of an unstable nucleus is not determined exactly; if its uncertainty is expressed by the width of the rest energy $\mathit{\Gamma}$ (the capital Greek letter gamma), then between it and the lifetime $\tau$, with Planck's constant $h$, there is the relation

$$\tau\mathit{\Gamma}=\frac{h}{2\pi}\quad,\qquad h=6.626\times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s} \qquad (2)$$

A europium nucleus ${}^{152}_{63}\mathrm{Eu}$ absorbs an electron in the atom, decays emitting a neutrino of energy $9.50\times 10^5\mathrm{eV}$ ($1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.602\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$), and becomes an excited state ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*$ of the samarium nucleus. (The neutrino is an electrically neutral elementary particle with a small rest mass, and it is denoted by $\nu$, using the lower-case Greek letter nu. From here on, the mass of $\nu$ is approximated as zero.) That ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*$ immediately, with half-life $t_{1/2}=2.05\times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{s}$, emits a gamma ray ($\gamma$ ray) of $9.61\times 10^5\,\mathrm{eV}$ and becomes a stable samarium nucleus ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}$. In summary,

$${}^{152}_{63}\mathrm{Eu}+\mathrm{e}\to{}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*+\nu \qquad (E_\nu=9.50\times 10^5\,\mathrm{eV})\,,\qquad (\text{the half-life of } {}^{152}_{63}\mathrm{Eu} \text{ is sufficiently long}) \qquad (3)$$

$${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*\to{}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}+\gamma \qquad (E_1\fallingdotseq\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2=9.61\times 10^5\,\mathrm{eV})\,,\quad t_{1/2}=2.05\times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{s} \qquad (4)$$

Here $\mathit{\Delta}M$ is the difference between the rest mass $M_2$ of the nucleus ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*$ and the rest mass $M_1$ of ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}$ ($\mathit{\Delta}M=M_2-M_1$), and $c$ is the speed of light ($c=2.9979\times 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$). The energy $E_1$ of the $\gamma$ ray is almost equal to the difference $\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2$ of the rest energies of ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*$ and ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}$, but when the nucleus can move it takes a value slightly different from $\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2$, as described below.

Q2. Find, in units of eV, the width $\mathit{\Gamma}$ of the uncertainty of the energy of ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*$ at rest.

[II] Recoil

When a nucleus decays and emits a particle such as $\nu$ or a $\gamma$ ray, by the law of conservation of momentum the nucleus after the decay acquires momentum by reaction. This phenomenon is called recoil, and the energy of the recoiling nucleus is called the recoil energy. In each of the processes (3) and (4) above, recoil of the nucleus occurs. By the law of conservation of energy, the energy of the emitted particle is smaller, by the amount of the recoil energy, than when recoil is not taken into account.

In the theory of relativity, the energy $E$ of a particle of mass $m$ and momentum $p$ is related, using the speed of light $c$, by

$$E=c\sqrt{(mc)^2+p^2}$$

From this, for particles whose mass may be taken as $m=0$ ($\gamma$ rays and $\nu$), $E=pc$, and for particles with a large mass $m$ and a speed sufficiently smaller than the speed of light (such as the nuclei treated here), one can approximate $E=mc^2+\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$ $\Bigl($when $|a|$ is sufficiently smaller than 1 ($|a|\ll 1$), $\sqrt{1+a}\fallingdotseq 1+\dfrac{a}{2}\Bigr)$. $mc^2$ is called the rest energy. The rest energy of a nucleus of mass number $A$ (for ${}^{235}\mathrm{U}$, $A=235$) is given approximately by the following expression:

$$mc^2=A\times 9.31\times 10^8\,\mathrm{eV} \qquad (5)$$

Q3. Assume that the momentum of the system ${}^{152}_{63}\mathrm{Eu}+\mathrm{e}$ in process (3) is zero. For each of the cases in which the direction of the $\gamma$ ray (momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$) emitted in process (4) is the same as, and opposite to, the direction of the neutrino (momentum $\overrightarrow{q}$) emitted in process (3), express the difference $E_\gamma-\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2$ between the energy $E_\gamma$ of the $\gamma$ ray and $\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2$ using $M_1$, $p$, $q$. Next, calculate their values (see Fig. 1). Note that $M_1\fallingdotseq M_2\gg\mathit{\Delta}M$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-5-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Schematic diagram of the decay of a system of an Eu nucleus and an electron at rest: the case in which finally the $\gamma$ ray and $\nu$ go out in the same direction (top) and the case in which they go out in opposite directions (bottom). (The arrow $\Longrightarrow$ means the change in time from the state to the left of the arrow to the state to the right.)

[Label in the figure: または = or.]

[III] Resonance

The $\gamma$ ray emitted in process (4) is directed at a target of ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}$ at rest. If the energy of the $\gamma$ ray is just suitable for causing the reaction

$$\gamma+{}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}\to{}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^* \qquad (6)$$

the probability of scattering as in Fig. 2 becomes very large. This is called resonance, and scattering with such a large probability is called resonant scattering.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-5-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Schematic diagram of resonant scattering in which a $\gamma$ ray is scattered via the intermediate stage of equation (6) and becomes a $\gamma$ ray ($\gamma'$) with changed momentum

The excited nucleus ${}^{152}_{62}\mathrm{Sm}^*$ has, as found in Q2, a width in its mass due to the uncertainty caused by the decay lifetime. Therefore, the condition for equation (6) above to occur has a width, and even when the mass difference differs from $\mathit{\Delta}M$ by several times $\dfrac{\mathit{\Gamma}}{c^2}$, resonance occurs and scattering takes place with a large probability. In the rest of this problem, the resonance condition is regarded as satisfied when it lies within 10 times $\dfrac{\mathit{\Gamma}}{c^2}$ of $\mathit{\Delta}M$.

Q4. Is it when the direction of the emitted $\gamma$ ray is the same as the direction of the neutrino, or when it is opposite, that the $\gamma$ ray emitted in process (4) undergoes the reaction of process (6) and satisfies the resonance condition? Answer, giving the grounds.

Taking the above into account, when resonant scattering is observed (when the direction is changed with a large probability), one can select whether the emission direction of the $\gamma$ ray of (4) is the same as or opposite to the emission direction of the neutrino of (3), without observing the neutrino directly. Since neutrinos hardly react with matter, they are very difficult to observe, but in this way, indirectly from conservation laws such as those of momentum and energy, physical quantities of the neutrino such as its momentum and energy can be observed.

It is known that $\gamma$ rays and $\nu$ are "spinning" right-handedly (in the direction of rotation of a right-handed screw with respect to the direction of travel) or left-handedly (they have spin; in the case of light, it has circular polarization). In 1958, the American M. Goldhaber and his colleagues determined the emission direction of the neutrino by selection using the resonant scattering described above, and, since the $\gamma$ rays then were only left-handed with respect to their direction of travel, they were able to discover the interesting property that $\nu$ is always left-handed.

[IV] The Mössbauer effect

The nucleus of the cobalt isotope ${}^{57}_{27}\mathrm{Co}$ absorbs an electron in the atom and decays with half-life $t_{1/2}=272$ days into iron, becoming the excited nucleus ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$, which with half-life $t_{1/2}=9.8\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}$ emits a $\gamma$ ray and becomes stable ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$. Expressed as a formula,

$${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*\to{}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}+\gamma\;,\qquad t_{1/2}=9.8\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s} \qquad (7)$$

The energy $E_\gamma$ of the $\gamma$ ray emitted by this excited state ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ is in general almost equal to the following energy, determined using the mass difference $\mathit{\Delta}M$ of the nuclei of the excited state ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ and the ground state ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ and the speed of light $c$:

$$E_\gamma\fallingdotseq\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2=1.44\times 10^4\,\mathrm{eV} \qquad (8)$$

Q5. Assuming that in process (7) the ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ was initially at rest in vacuum, find the kinetic energy (recoil energy) $\mathit{\Delta}E_1$ of the ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ that recoils because of the $\gamma$-ray emission.

If ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ was initially at rest in vacuum, the energy $E_1$ of the $\gamma$ ray emitted in process (7) is smaller than the value of equation (8) by the value $\mathit{\Delta}E_1$ of the recoil energy of ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$:

$$E_1=\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2-\mathit{\Delta}E_1 \qquad (9)$$

Conversely, when a $\gamma$ ray of energy $E_2$ reacts with a target of ground-state ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ at rest in vacuum to produce the excited state ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$, because the produced ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ recoils, $E_2$ must be larger than $\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2$ by a tiny amount ($\mathit{\Delta}E_2=E_2-\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2>0$). This $\mathit{\Delta}E_2$ is almost equal to the $\mathit{\Delta}E_1$ found above. Therefore, between the energy $E_1$ of the $\gamma$ ray emitted from a nucleus ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ at rest in vacuum and the energy $E_2$ of the $\gamma$ ray that should be absorbed by a target nucleus ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ at rest in vacuum, there is the difference $E_2-E_1=2\mathit{\Delta}E_1$.

From the above considerations, a $\gamma$ ray emitted from ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ at rest in vacuum lacks the energy $2\mathit{\Delta}E_1$ needed to produce ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ with ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ at rest in vacuum as the target, so it cannot produce ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$, and resonant scattering does not occur. Therefore the probability of scattering is small.

However, in 1958 the young German Mössbauer (R. L. Mössbauer), still in his twenties, discovered something unexpected. He discovered that resonant scattering occurs when the nucleus emitting the $\gamma$ ray and the nucleus that is the target of that $\gamma$ ray are both inside a solid crystal. How can something happen in nuclei inside a solid as if the recoil energy $2\mathit{\Delta}E_1$ were ignored?

Atoms in a solid form a crystal in a lattice with the surrounding atoms and cannot move around freely. Therefore the motion of the centre of mass of a nucleus is restricted, and even if it emits a $\gamma$ ray, when the momentum of the recoiling nucleus is small, it cannot excite vibrations of the atoms, and the effect of recoil does not appear. The whole crystal, so to speak, recoils, and since the mass of the whole crystal is large, the recoil energy produced by the emission of the $\gamma$ ray can become small enough to be ignored. It is thought that a phenomenon in which recoil can be ignored therefore occurred. This phenomenon is called the Mössbauer effect after its discoverer.

In 1959, the American R. Pound and his graduate student G. A. Rebka, Jr. performed, using the Mössbauer effect, an ingenious experiment confirming Einstein's prediction that the frequency of light changes under the influence of gravity.

They placed the radiation source (${}^{57}_{27}\mathrm{Co}$) producing ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ at a height $h_1$ in the laboratory, and placed stable ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$, as the target receiving the $\gamma$ rays emitted by the ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^*$ produced there, at a height $h_2$. If the heights are equal ($h_1=h_2$), then by the Mössbauer effect the emitted $\gamma$ ray and the scattered $\gamma$ ray both have energy equal to $\mathit{\Delta}Mc^2$, so resonant scattering occurs. Then, if there is a difference in height, does a difference arise in the frequency of the resonating $\gamma$ ray because of the influence of gravity? To investigate this, they embedded the target ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ in an acoustic loudspeaker, placed it directly below or directly above the radiation source, and observed the Doppler effect that arises because the target oscillates owing to the vibration of the loudspeaker (Fig. 3). As a result, with $g$ the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface, they confirmed that the condition for resonance to occur is that the speed $v$ with which the loudspeaker vibrates is $v=\dfrac{g}{c}|h_1-h_2|$, and that, in the case $h_1>h_2$, it is when the incoming $\gamma$ ray and ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ move in the same direction, and in the case $h_1<h_2$, when the $\gamma$ ray and ${}^{57}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ move in opposite directions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2016-5-fig3.png

Fig. 3. The experiment of Pound and Rebka

[Labels in the figure: $\gamma$ 線 = $\gamma$ ray; スピーカー = loudspeaker.]

Below, the direction from which the $\gamma$ rays come and the direction in which the detector (target) moves are both vertical and on the same straight line.

Q6. When a $\gamma$ ray of frequency $f$ hits a detector moving with speed $v$ and its frequency is measured with that detector, the measured value will deviate from $f$. Assuming that, when the speed $v$ is sufficiently small compared with the speed of light $c$, the shift of the frequency of the $\gamma$ ray may be obtained by reasoning in the same way as for the Doppler effect of sound, how large is the frequency shift $\mathit{\Delta}f$ that arises when the velocity of the loudspeaker is the speed $v=\dfrac{g}{c}(h_1-h_2)$ in the direction from which the $\gamma$ ray comes? Find it for the case $h_1>h_2$.

Einstein thought that, when there is a constant gravitational acceleration $g$, an observer falling freely with that acceleration $g$ would feel that he is in an inertial frame without gravity (a frame at rest, or a frame in uniform linear motion relative to a frame at rest) (even though the surrounding scenery appears to move). This way of thinking is fundamental in the general theory of relativity and is called the equivalence principle.

Q7. Explain the experimental result of Pound and Rebka for the case $h_1>h_2$ by the equivalence principle.

problems.title: Problem 1A
problems.problem:
Problem 1A (50 points)

In the analysis of the various motions of mechanics, the law of conservation of momentum and the law of conservation of energy are extremely useful. The following is one example.

A triangular prism as in Fig. 1 is placed on a horizontal, smooth floor. A small ball flying horizontally from the left collided with the slope of the prism, which is inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The slope of the prism is smooth, and the collision is elastic. Also, the small ball and the centre of mass of the prism are always in the same vertical plane.

After the collision, as shown in Fig. 2, the small ball was bounced off in a direction making an angle $\theta$ $(\theta>30^\circ)$ with the horizontal, and the prism began to slide to the right on the floor. The small ball moved along a parabola and collided with the slope of the prism again. It is said that, when the ratio of the mass of the small ball to the mass of the prism has a certain value, the small ball hits the position where it first collided with the slope (see Fig. 2). Let us find the ratio of the mass $m_1$ of the small ball to the mass $m_2$ of the prism in this case. Let $v_0$ be the speed of the small ball just before the collision, $v_1$ its speed just after the collision, and $\theta$ the angle that the direction of the velocity of the small ball just after the collision makes with the horizontal. Also let $v_2$ be the speed with which the prism starts to slide after the collision.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2

Q1. Consider the system consisting of the small ball and the prism. Since there is no friction on the floor, no horizontal external force acts on the system. Therefore the horizontal momentum of the system is conserved before and after the collision. Express this conservation law as an equation.

Q2. The collision is elastic, and the kinetic energy of the system is conserved before and after the collision. Express this conservation law as an equation.

Q3. Since the slope is smooth, the force acting on the small ball at the instant of the collision is perpendicular to the slope. If the collision time is sufficiently short, the impulse of the gravitational force acting on the small ball during this time can be neglected, so the component of the momentum of the small ball parallel to the slope is conserved. Express this conservation law as an equation.

Q4. For the position where the small ball hits the slope of the prism again to be the position where the small ball first collided, the horizontal distances moved by the two in the meantime must be equal. Find the relation derived from this.

Q5. Eliminate $v_1$, $v_2$, $\theta$ from the above equations and find the mass ratio $r=\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$.

Q6. When the mass ratio of the small ball and the prism is equal to the value found in the previous question, find the direction in which the small ball is bounced off in the second collision.

problems.title: Problem 1B
problems.problem:
Problem 1B (50 points)

Let us consider the deceleration of the Space Shuttle (Fig. 1), which was retired after its last launch on 8 July 2011, when it re-enters the atmosphere on returning to the Earth.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-2-fig1.jpg

Fig. 1

An example of the atmospheric re-entry process is as follows.

(i) The engines are fired (in reverse) towards the direction of motion for only 2 to 3 minutes, and the shuttle moves from the orbit around the Earth to an elliptical orbit for atmospheric entry.

(ii) It enters the atmosphere at an altitude of about $120\,\mathrm{km}$ with a speed of $7.6\,\mathrm{km}$ per second (about Mach 24). At this time the pitch angle of the orbiter (the angle the orbiter makes with the horizontal) is $40^\circ$.

(iii) At an altitude of about $70\,\mathrm{km}$, with a speed of about $6.7\,\mathrm{km}$ per second, the outside of the Space Shuttle orbiter receives the most intense heating.

(iv) At an altitude of about $55\,\mathrm{km}$ the speed is $3.7\,\mathrm{km}$ per second, and from about this time the pitch angle starts to be reduced from $40^\circ$.

(v) The landing gear is lowered at about $430\,\mathrm{km}$ per hour ($120\,\mathrm{m}$ per second), and it touches down at about $346\,\mathrm{km}$ per hour ($96\,\mathrm{m}$ per second).

(From the page "How does the Space Shuttle leave its orbit?" on the website of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), http://iss.jaxa.jp/iss_faq/shuttle/.)

Answer the following questions.

Q1. Suppose that at time $t$ the Space Shuttle of mass $m$ and velocity $v$ ejects gas in the direction of motion with a constant relative speed $u$ during a short time $\mathrm{d}t$, and its mass and velocity become $m+\mathrm{d}m$ and $v+\mathrm{d}v$, respectively. Answer the following questions taking $m\gg|\mathrm{d}m|$, $v\gg|\mathrm{d}v|$ (note that in the present case $\mathrm{d}m<0$, $\mathrm{d}v<0$).

(a) Find the relation between the acceleration of the Space Shuttle at time $t$ and the mass of the ejected gas per unit time.

(b) Taking the velocity of the Space Shuttle to be $v_{\mathrm{i}}$ when its mass is $m_{\mathrm{i}}$, find the velocity $v_{\mathrm{f}}$ when its mass has become $m_{\mathrm{f}}$.

Q2. As the Space Shuttle approaches the Earth's surface, the landing gear is lowered at a speed of $430\,\mathrm{km/h}$, and it touches down at about $346\,\mathrm{km/h}$. When the wheels touch the ground, a drag parachute of diameter $12\,\mathrm{m}$ opens (see Fig. 2). When the speed of the orbiter falls to $110\,\mathrm{km/h}$ or less, the parachute is released.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-2-fig2.jpg

Fig. 2

Suppose that the speed of the Space Shuttle from the touchdown of its tyres, through the opening of the drag parachute, until the parachute is released, varied with time as

$$v(t)=\frac{a}{b\,t+1}.$$

Here $t$ is the time elapsed since the tyres touched down, and $a$, $b$ are constants. Let $v_{\mathrm{i}}$ be the speed just after the tyres touch down, $v_{\mathrm{f}}$ the speed when the parachute is released, $\tau$ the time during which the parachute is open, and $m$ the mass of the Space Shuttle, and answer the following questions.

(a) Express the constants $a$, $b$ in terms of $v_{\mathrm{i}}$, $v_{\mathrm{f}}$, $\tau$.

(b) Express the magnitude of the force acting on the Space Shuttle at time $t$ in terms of $m$, $v_{\mathrm{i}}$, $v_{\mathrm{f}}$, $\tau$, $v(t)$.

(c) Suppose that, when $v(t)=1\,\mathrm{m/s}$, the magnitude of the force acting on the Space Shuttle is given by

$$\frac{1}{2}\times\text{drag coefficient}\times\text{air density}\times\text{cross-sectional area of the drag parachute}\times(1\,\mathrm{m/s})^2 .$$

Taking drag coefficient $=1.42$, air density $=1.225\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $m=78{,}000\,\mathrm{kg}$, how many seconds is the drag parachute open? Also, how many metres did the shuttle travel during that time?

(d) How many J of energy did the Space Shuttle lose between touchdown and the release of the parachute?

Q3. Now, when the Space Shuttle enters the atmosphere, the outside of the orbiter becomes hot (see Fig. 3). Let us assume that the cause of this is that the air molecules in front of the Space Shuttle come at the Space Shuttle at high speed. At the time (iv) above, roughly what is the temperature $T$ of the gas near the front of the Space Shuttle? Estimate a rough numerical value. If necessary, use the following values, etc. You may also assume numerical values of physical quantities that are not given. (This question does not necessarily require a correct answer. Your ideas for the estimate and the way you proceed with the reasoning will be evaluated.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-2-fig3.jpg

Fig. 3. The white parts are hotter.

• Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}\fallingdotseq1.4\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$

• Internal energy of a diatomic gas at high temperature, per molecule: $\dfrac{7}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ (this is the expression when the vibrational degrees of freedom are also taken into account)

• Mean molar mass of air: $29\,\mathrm{g/mol}$

• Avogadro constant $N_{\mathrm{A}}\fallingdotseq6.0\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$

(Figs. 1 and 2 are from the website of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/images; Fig. 3 is from Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org, article "Space Shuttle", file Stsheat.jpg.)

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (70 points)

On the Earth on which we live there are the circulation of the atmosphere surrounding the Earth (wind) and ocean currents in the seas, and these can be expected to be so-called renewable energy sources. Typical examples of such flows are

1) the flow of air (wind) $\Rightarrow$ wind power generation

2) the flow of sea water (ocean currents) $\Rightarrow$ ocean-current power generation

and so on. As is well known, the practical use of the former is already quite advanced. On the other hand, in the seas surrounding our country there are ocean currents such as the Kuroshio, and research on how to use them has just begun. In this problem we carry out a theoretical consideration of the upper limit of the energy that can be extracted from an ocean current.

For a liquid (e.g. water) or a gas (e.g. air) at rest, as long as the volume is kept constant, it deforms under any force however small, and no force acts to restore it to its original shape. A body that deforms freely under any small external force as long as its volume is kept constant is called a fluid. Water is one example of the most familiar fluids around us. The mechanics of water treated from now on may be unfamiliar, but if you proceed with the consideration recognising that the basic ideas of mechanics can be applied, you should surely arrive at the answers.

In general, a fluid whose density is constant independent of pressure and which has no viscosity is called an incompressible perfect fluid; water can in many cases be treated in this way to a good approximation. In what follows, friction and viscosity can be neglected. Also, for simplicity, the effect of gravity acting on the water is not considered.

[I]

First, consider water flowing in a pipe made of a solid material as in Fig. 1. When there is a flow, a curve whose tangent at each place is the direction of the velocity of the water at that place at a given instant is called a streamline. The many thin lines with arrows in Fig. 1 represent the streamlines in the pipe. In general streamlines change with time, but there are also cases in which they do not change with time; such a flow is called a steady flow. The flow in Fig. 1 is assumed to be a steady flow.

For real water the velocity of the water varies with the distance from the wall because of viscosity, but in this problem we consider the case in which the viscosity of the water may be neglected, and, except in the region $x_1<x<x_2$ where the streamlines are not parallel to the $x$ axis, the velocity of the water on a cross-section perpendicular to the axis of the pipe has a constant magnitude and is horizontal.

Also, let the velocity in $x<x_1$ be $v_1$ and the velocity in $x_2<x$ be $v_2$. Such velocities and other vector quantities are taken to have a positive sign when they point to the right.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[In the figure: 面積 = area; 断面 = cross-section.]

The cross-sections of the pipe are everywhere similar circles, and their area is a constant $S_1$ in the region $x<x_1$ and a constant $S_2$ in the region $x_2<x$.

Suppose that the water that was in the section AB (the region between cross-sections A and B) at a certain moment moved to the section A′B′ in a time $\Delta t$. Since A′B is common to these two sections, the volume of section AA′ is equal to the volume of section BB′. Let us denote the density of water by $\rho$. As can be seen from Fig. 1, the volume of section AA′ is $v_1\Delta tS_1$, and the mass of water in it is $\rho v_1S_1\Delta t$. This can also be rephrased as the mass of water that passed through cross-section A during $\Delta t$. The same can be said of the mass of water $\rho v_2S_2\Delta t$ in section BB′.

Now, according to the law of conservation of mass, the net mass of the water should not change during the motion of the water. Therefore the masses of water in sections AA′ and BB′ should be equal, and denoting their common mass by $J\Delta t$,

$$J\Delta t=\rho v_1S_1\Delta t=\rho v_2S_2\Delta t \qquad (1)$$

holds. Dividing the three sides of this equation by $\Delta t$, we obtain the relation between the masses of water passing through each surface per unit time,

$$J=\rho v_1S_1=\rho v_2S_2 . \qquad (2)$$

This equation is called the equation of continuity.

Cross-sections A and B are arbitrary cross-sections in the regions $x<x_1$ and $x_2<x$, respectively, and since the conservation of mass also holds exactly for the steady flow in the section $x_1<x<x_2$, the argument so far can be generalised, and it follows that the mass $J$ of water passing through any cross-section of the pipe per unit time is constant independent of position. Also, the right-hand equality of Eq. (2) means that when pipes of different thickness are joined, the speed of the water passing through them is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area of the pipe it passes through (note that in $x_1<x<x_2$ of Fig. 1 the velocity has a vertical component, so the expression for $J$ becomes a little more complicated).

In the above argument the masses of water in sections AA′ and BB′ are equal, but their momenta and kinetic energies are not equal. By considering this difference, we can calculate the changes in the momentum and in the kinetic energy of the water when the water moves from section AB to A′B′.

Q1. Let an external force $F$ act horizontally to the right, and let $\Delta p$ be the change in the momentum of the water while it moves from section AB to A′B′ in time $\Delta t$. Express $\Delta p$ in terms of $J$, $v_1$, $v_2$, $\Delta t$. Express the external force $F$ acting on this water at this time in terms of $\Delta p$, $\Delta t$.

Q2. Express the kinetic energy $\Delta K$ gained by the water during the motion of the previous question in terms of $J$, $v_1$, $v_2$, $\Delta t$.

The changes in momentum and kinetic energy calculated here were brought about by the force $F$ acting on the water from outside. The relation between the change in momentum and the force can be calculated from the equation of motion of the water. Also, since the change in kinetic energy is the result of the external force $F$ doing work on the water, the relation between them is also determined by the mechanical relation between energy and work.

Here we consider the case in which pistons are attached at both ends of the pipe and push the water inside from both sides, producing the pressure of the water. Suppose that the piston at the right end applies the atmospheric pressure $P_0$ to the water, and the piston at the left end pushes with a pressure $P_{\mathrm{A}}$ adjusted so that the velocity in $x<x_1$ is $v_1$.

The water is also subject to pressure from the wall of the pipe, but except in the region $x_1<x<x_2$ the force from the wall is perpendicular to the horizontal, so it has no effect of accelerating the water.

The water in the region $x_1<x<x_2$ is inside a truncated cone with slanted side surface as in Fig. 2, whose upper and lower bases have areas $S_1$ and $S_2$, respectively. This water is pushed to the right from the left by a force of magnitude $F_1=P_{\mathrm{A}}S_1$, and to the left from the right by a force of magnitude $F_2=P_0S_2$. Furthermore, it is also pushed from the side surface. In Fig. 2 one example of a force applied to the side surface is shown as $\overrightarrow{F_3}$. Since the side surface is slanted, the pressure force acting on the side surface can be resolved into a horizontal component and a component pointing towards the central axis of the truncated cone. The latter, summed over the whole circumference of the side surface, cancels out.

Therefore the total force acting on the side surface is horizontal, and we denote it by $F_{\mathrm{s}}$ (s = side). The resultant of these three forces changes the momentum of the water.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2

[In the figure: 中心線 = central line (axis).]

Q3. Express $F_{\mathrm{s}}$ in terms of $P_0$, $P_{\mathrm{A}}$, $S_1$, $S_2$ and the $\Delta p$, $\Delta t$ considered in Q1. Pay attention to the signs in your answer.

[II]

Next, consider the flow of water in the sea, that is, an ocean current. An ocean current does not pass through a pipe, but it is a steady water flow several hundred km wide and several thousand km long, and within it we can consider streamlines that continue nearly parallel to each other. When there is such a flow, consider a tube such that no streamline leaks out from inside it and no streamline enters it from outside; we call it a stream tube. The pipe in Fig. 1 can also be regarded as an artificially made stream tube.

Fig. 3 is an idealised image of the flow produced near a turbine when a turbine for power generation is installed in an ocean current flowing from left to right. The tube bounded by the two dashed lines will be called the "turbine stream tube", since the water flowing in it passes through the water wheel labelled "turbine". Outside the turbine stream tube, sea water with flow speed $v_1$ is flowing everywhere.

Inside the turbine stream tube too, the flow speed in the region $x<x_1$ is $v_1$, but its streamlines are deformed and disturbed when they pass between the blades of the turbine. As a result, the flow comes to contain irregularly eddies etc. that fluctuate in time, so streamlines cannot be drawn in the region $x_1<x<x_2$ inside the turbine stream tube. We call this region the turbine region.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[In the figure: 断面 = cross-section; タービン = turbine; タービン流管 = turbine stream tube.]

The disturbance of the streamlines gradually subsides further downstream, and in the region $x_2<x$ the water again flows with straight streamlines. However, since the mechanical energy of the water is used to turn the turbine, the water is decelerated. That is, the flow speed of the water becomes $v_2\ (<v_1)$.

The position and shape of the turbine stream tube are determined by the condition that the pressures of the water inside and outside it are equal and balance each other. Since the sea surface is in contact with the atmosphere, when considering an ocean current near the sea surface, the pressure of the sea water both inside and outside the turbine stream tube is taken to be the atmospheric pressure $P_0$. Therefore, also in the region $x_2<x$ the water inside and outside the turbine stream tube is in mechanical equilibrium, and as long as the effect of viscosity does not appear, the turbine stream tube continues far to the right.

In what follows, the position and shape of the turbine region do not change, and the density of the water in it is a uniform $\rho$, the same as elsewhere.

Even though the flow is disturbed in the turbine region, the conservation of mass holds, so the mass in AA′ and the mass in BB′ are equal.

From these considerations we see that the mass of water passing during $\Delta t$ through a cross-section of the turbine stream tube in $x<x_1$ or in $x_2<x$ has the same value wherever the cross-section is. Let us denote it by $J_{\mathrm{t}}\Delta t$ (t = turbine).

On the other hand, since the direction of the flow is irregular in $x_1<x<x_2$, the velocity of the water passing through the turbine varies irregularly with position and with time. So, letting $S_{\mathrm{t}}$ be the cross-sectional area of the turbine perpendicular to the $x$ axis, we define the mean velocity $v_{\mathrm{t}}$ of the water crossing the turbine by

$$J_{\mathrm{t}}=\rho v_{\mathrm{t}}S_{\mathrm{t}} . \qquad (3)$$

In the following questions too, the area of the upstream cross-section A of the turbine stream tube is denoted by $S_1$, and the area of the downstream cross-section B by $S_2$.

Q4. Suppose that the momentum of the water changed by $\Delta p$ while the water moved from section AB to A′B′ in the turbine stream tube in time $\Delta t$. Express $\Delta p$ in terms of $J_{\mathrm{t}}$, $v_1$, $v_2$, $\Delta t$.

Q5. Express the kinetic energy $\Delta K$ gained by the water during the motion of the previous question in terms of $J_{\mathrm{t}}$, $v_1$, $S_1$, $S_2$, $\Delta t$. Using the result, explain why in Fig. 3 the cross-sectional area of the turbine stream tube downstream of the turbine is drawn larger than upstream.

Since the pressure of the surrounding sea water is uniformly $P_0$, the sum of the forces acting on the water of the turbine stream tube is equal to the sum of the forces acting on the water of a subspace of the same shape in sea water at rest. Since the external pressures acting on water in still water all balance, the sum of the forces acting from outside on that subspace is 0. Therefore the sum of the forces acting on the turbine stream tube is also 0. Also, the momentum change of Q4 produced in the water flowing through the turbine stream tube is due to the external forces acting on that water. According to the above consideration, the sum of the external forces due to the pressure from the surrounding sea water is 0, so the only thing that gives the water a momentum change is the turbine.

Q6. Derive that the force applied by the turbine to the water passing through it is

$$F_{\mathrm{t}}=J_{\mathrm{t}}(v_2-v_1) . \qquad (4)$$

When an external force $F$ acts on a body and gives the body a small displacement, denoting the displacement vector by $\Delta x$, the work $\Delta W$ done by the external force on the body (fluid) is expressed as

$$\Delta W=F\Delta x .$$

If the two one-dimensional vectors $F$ and $\Delta x$ have the same direction, $\Delta W>0$, and if they have opposite directions, $\Delta W<0$. When this work is done in a short time $\Delta t$, the work per unit time is expressed as

$$\mathcal{P}=\frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}=F\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}=Fv , \qquad (5)$$

and this is called the power of the external force. This power can be calculated in two ways.

The first way uses Eq. (5). The force $F_{\mathrm{t}}$ that the turbine applies to the water was found in Q6. As the velocity of that water, the mean velocity $v_{\mathrm{t}}$ defined by Eq. (3) is used.

The second way uses the change per unit time in the kinetic energy of the water passing through the turbine region. When the turbine does work $\Delta W$ on the water, the kinetic energy of the water changes. The change during time $\Delta t$ is the $\Delta K$ found in Q5.

Q7. The power of the turbine found by the above two ways is expressed by different formulae. Setting them equal, we obtain an expression giving the mean velocity $v_{\mathrm{t}}$ of the water passing through the turbine in terms of $v_1$, $v_2$. Find this expression.

Let $\mathcal{P}_0$ be the kinetic energy (power) of sea water passing per unit time through a cross-section of area $S_{\mathrm{t}}$ when no turbine is installed and the steady flow of sea water of velocity $v_1$ passes through this cross-section without being disturbed. On the other hand, the power $\mathcal{P}$ found so far was the power that the turbine exerts on the steady flow of sea water. The power we want is the power $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}$ that the steady flow of sea water exerts on the turbine. According to the law of action and reaction, these are related by $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}=-\mathcal{P}$. In the case of ocean-current power generation, the ratio $\dfrac{\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}}{\mathcal{P}_0}$ of the $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}$ and $\mathcal{P}_0$ defined here gives the efficiency with which the turbine extracts the energy possessed by the steady flow of sea water. Let us call this the efficiency of the ocean-current turbine and denote it by $\eta$.

Q8. Using the result of the previous question (Q7), derive that $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}$ is given by

$$\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}=\frac{1}{4}\,\rho S_{\mathrm{t}}\,(v_1+v_2)\,({v_1}^2-{v_2}^2) . \qquad (6)$$

Q9. (a) Express $\mathcal{P}_0$ in terms of $\rho$, $v_1$, $S_{\mathrm{t}}$.

(b) Express the turbine efficiency $\eta$ as a function of the variable $r=\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$. Draw a rough graph of the function $\eta(r)$ on the interval $[0,1]$ of $r$.
