(c) Find the value of $r$ for which $\eta$ is maximum, and the value of the maximum $\eta_{\mathrm{max}}$ at that time.

In this model, the upper limit of the power $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{t}}$ that can be extracted by a turbine from a steady flow is given by $\eta_{\mathrm{max}}\mathcal{P}_0$. This is known as Betz's law, and $\eta_{\mathrm{max}}$ as the Betz limit.

[III]

In our country, the main stream of the Kuroshio flows east-north-eastwards from the sea area south of Shikoku through the sea area south of the Kii Peninsula. According to surveys by the Japan Coast Guard and others, the Kuroshio is $100\sim200\,\mathrm{km}$ wide and several hundred m thick, and its flow speed throughout the year is $2\sim4$ knots (knot: $1\ \text{knot}=1.852\,\mathrm{km/h}$). Based on the consideration carried out in [II], let us estimate the upper limit of the amount of power generation that can be extracted from the Kuroshio as a renewable energy source. The current has temporal variations such as seasonal changes and meandering, but for simplicity the Kuroshio is regarded as a steady flow.

Q10. (a) Assuming that the Kuroshio is $100\,\mathrm{km}$ wide and $400\,\mathrm{m}$ thick and that its flow speed is 3 knots on average, estimate how many W the kinetic energy $\mathcal{P}_0$ passing per unit time through the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the direction of motion of the Kuroshio is.

(b) Assume that about $\dfrac{1}{100}$ of the total cross-sectional area of the steady flow of the Kuroshio can be used for power generation by installing turbines, etc. Taking into account the above data on the Kuroshio, the Betz limit, etc., estimate the upper limit of the available power generation capacity (W) by ocean-current power generation through this cross-section.

Above, starting from the basics of mechanics and applying them to the mechanics of water, we carried out a theoretical consideration of the upper limit of the power in the case of extracting energy from a steady flow. For the case of the Kuroshio, we estimated the values of these upper limits on the basis of some assumptions. To put the extraction of energy from ocean currents into practical use, detailed studies from many viewpoints are needed, such as the engineering aspects of the structure, design and installation of turbines, methods of coping with the temporal and seasonal variations of the ocean currents, and environmental aspects.

[Reference]

Air too can be treated as an incompressible fluid if its motion is below the speed of sound. Moreover, its viscosity is also sufficiently small. Therefore the results of the theoretical consideration here of water as an incompressible perfect fluid can also be applied to the case of wind power generation by a steady flow of air.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (70 points)

In this problem we consider waves of the electromagnetic field, that is, electromagnetic waves. An electromagnetic wave is a wave in which oscillations of an electric field and a magnetic field perpendicular to each other propagate. The behaviour of oscillating electric and magnetic fields differs from that of static electric and static magnetic fields: the electric and magnetic fields influence each other. Here, using hypothetical circuits considered in vacuum, we express the fundamental laws of electromagnetism, examine the mutual relation between the electric and magnetic fields, and derive the existence of electromagnetic waves propagating in vacuum at the speed of light. Furthermore, we consider how the presence of charged particles (particles having charge, such as electrons) changes the propagation of electromagnetic waves.

In what follows we treat an electromagnetic wave in which the electric field has only a $z$ component and the magnetic field (magnetic flux density) only an $x$ component, propagating in the $y$ direction. The $z$ component $E$ of the electric field and the $x$ component $B$ of the magnetic flux density are expressed as follows.

$$E(y,\ t)=E_0\sin\phi(y,t) \qquad (1)$$

$$B(y,\ t)=B_0\sin\phi(y,t) \qquad (2)$$

Here $E_0$, $B_0$ are constants, and $\phi(y,t)$ is a function of the coordinate $y$ and the time $t$ called the phase,

$$\phi(y,t)=ky-\omega t , \qquad (3)$$

where the positive constants $k$, $\omega$ are defined in terms of the wavelength $\lambda$ and the period $T$ as follows.

$$k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}, \qquad \omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}$$

Also, in what follows a hypothetical circuit is simply called a closed path.

Furthermore, the electric constant (permittivity of vacuum) is denoted by $\varepsilon_0$ and the magnetic constant (permeability of vacuum) by $\mu_0$. They have the following values.

$$\varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}, \qquad \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{H/m}=1.257\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{H/m}$$

Also, the charge of the electron is denoted by $-e$ and its mass by $m$. $e$, $m$ have the following values.

$$e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}, \qquad m=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$$

[I]

In general, when the magnetic flux $\Phi$ through a closed path changes with time $t$, an emf $V$ is produced in that circuit as follows (Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction).

$$V=-\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\Phi(t+\Delta t)-\Phi(t)}{\Delta t} \qquad (4)$$

In this equation, the positive direction of the emf is the direction in which a right-handed screw is turned so that it advances in the direction of the magnetic flux.

Consider, as in Fig. 1, a closed path $\mathrm{C_1}$ ($\mathrm{P}\to\mathrm{Q}\to\mathrm{Q'}\to\mathrm{P'}\to\mathrm{P}$) in the $y$-$z$ plane, with a small width $\Delta y$ in the $y$ direction and a length $L$ in the $z$ direction. Since the magnetic flux through $\mathrm{C_1}$ is approximately expressed as $(L\Delta y)\cdot B_0\sin\phi(y,t)$, by Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction (4) the emf $V$ produced in $\mathrm{C_1}$ is given by

$$V=-\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{(L\Delta y)B_0\{\sin\phi(y,\ t+\Delta t)-\sin\phi(y,\ t)\}}{\Delta t} .$$

Setting $\Delta\phi=\phi(y,\ t+\Delta t)-\phi(y,\ t)$ and noting that

$$\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\sin\phi(y,\ t+\Delta t)-\sin\phi(y,\ t)}{\Delta t}=\lim_{\Delta\phi\to0}\frac{\sin(\phi+\Delta\phi)-\sin\phi}{\Delta\phi}\cdot\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t} ,$$

$V$ is expressed as follows.

$$V=(L\Delta y)\,\omega B_0\cos\phi \qquad (5)$$

Since $B_0\sin\phi$ is the $x$ component of the magnetic flux density, the positive direction of the emf is the direction of the arrows in Fig. 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

On the other hand, the emf produced in $\mathrm{C_1}$ is expressed by the components of the electric field along $\mathrm{C_1}$ as follows.

$$V=L\cdot E(y+\Delta y,\ t)-L\cdot E(y,\ t) \qquad (6)$$

Q1. Taking $\Delta y$ to be sufficiently small, show that the following equation holds.

$$\omega B_0=kE_0 \qquad (7)$$

[II]

When a constant straight current $I$ flows, a magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B_I}$ is produced around the current as in Fig. 2a. The magnetic flux density is in the circumferential direction of a circle centred on the straight current as in Fig. 2a, and at a distance $r$ from the current it has the magnitude

$$B_I=\mu_0\frac{I}{2\pi r} .$$

Now consider a circle $\mathrm{C_2}$ of radius $r$ with the orientation shown in Fig. 2b, divide $\mathrm{C_2}$ finely, and let the length of the $k$-th part be $\Delta s_k$ and the component of the magnetic flux density along $\mathrm{C_2}$ there be $B_k$. Adding up all the products $B_k\cdot\Delta s_k$ over the parts of $\mathrm{C_2}$ and making the division sufficiently fine, we obtain the following equation.

$$\lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k B_k\Delta s_k=2\pi rB_I=2\pi r\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}=\mu_0I$$

Here we used the fact that $\overrightarrow{B_I}$ is in the circumferential direction and has a constant magnitude on the circle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2

If the electromagnetic field does not change with time, it can be shown that the following equation, which holds for a circle around a straight current,

$$\lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k B_k\ \Delta s_k=\mu_0I \qquad (8)$$

holds even if the circle becomes an arbitrary closed curve, provided that $I$ is the current passing through a surface whose rim (edge) is that closed curve. The surface having the closed curve as its rim may be any curved surface. This is Ampère's law, which expresses the relation between a current and the magnetic field produced by the current.

Maxwell (J. C. Maxwell) found in 1864 that it is theoretically consistent to consider that a magnetic field is also produced in a space with a time-varying electric field, derived the Ampère–Maxwell law generalising Ampère's law, and predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves.

If the surface enclosed by the closed curve is a plane of area $S$ and the normal component $E_{\mathrm{n}}$ of the electric field is constant over the surface, the Ampère–Maxwell law is expressed as follows.

$$\lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k B_k\Delta s_k=\mu_0I+\mu_0\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(S\cdot\varepsilon_0E_{\mathrm{n}}) \qquad (9)$$

Here $S\cdot\varepsilon_0E_{\mathrm{n}}$ is called the electric flux, and the time derivative of the electric flux is called the displacement current. The direction of the normal of the surface through which the current and the displacement current pass is, as in the case of Ampère's law shown in Fig. 2b, the direction in which a right-handed screw advances when it is turned in the direction of the closed curve.

When there is a constant straight current $I$ as in Fig. 3a, Eq. (8) holds however we choose the surface whose rim is the circle $\mathrm{C_3}$ around the current. For example, as in Fig. 3b, even for a surface like an upside-down cup with $\mathrm{C_3}$ as its rim and the disk $\mathrm{S_1}$ or the disk $\mathrm{S_2}$ as its bottom, the current passing through the bottom is $I$, so Eq. (8) holds.

On the other hand, if we consider the case in which a parallel-plate capacitor is inserted in this current $I$ as in Fig. 3c, then when the bottom $\mathrm{S_1}$ is between the plates of the capacitor as in Fig. 3d, the current passing through the surface is 0. Therefore the value of the right-hand side of Eq. (8) changes depending on how the surface is chosen. In contrast, the value of the right-hand side of Eq. (9), which takes the displacement current into account, is the same whichever of $\mathrm{S_0}$, $\mathrm{S_1}$, $\mathrm{S_2}$ is the bottom.

Q2. Noting that the charge on the plates of the capacitor changes with time, show that in the case of Fig. 3d the value of the right-hand side of Eq. (9) is the same whichever of $\mathrm{S_0}$, $\mathrm{S_1}$, $\mathrm{S_2}$ is the bottom.

That the sum of the current and the displacement current does not depend on how the surface having the closed curve as its rim is chosen is only a necessary condition for the Ampère–Maxwell law to hold, and is not a proof. However, owing to the fact, among others, that electromagnetic waves exist as Maxwell predicted, the Ampère–Maxwell law is now established.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[III]

Let us consider electromagnetic waves in vacuum using the law of electromagnetic induction and the Ampère–Maxwell law.

Consider, as in Fig. 4, a long thin closed curve $\mathrm{C_4}$ ($\mathrm{P}\to\mathrm{P''}\to\mathrm{Q''}\to\mathrm{Q}\to\mathrm{P}$) in the $x$-$y$ plane, of small width $\Delta y$ and length $L$, and apply Eq. (9) to $\mathrm{C_4}$.

First, the left-hand side can be expressed as follows.

$$L\cdot B(y,\ t)-L\cdot B(y+\Delta y,\ t)$$

In vacuum the current in the first term on the right-hand side is 0. Also, since $\Delta y$ is small, the electric flux through the surface enclosed by $\mathrm{C_4}$ is approximately expressed, using the electric field at $y$, as $(L\Delta y)\cdot\varepsilon_0E(y,\ t)$, and the displacement current of the second term on the right-hand side is given by

$$\mu_0\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{(L\Delta y)\varepsilon_0[E(y,\ t+\Delta t)-E(y,\ t)]}{\Delta t}=-\varepsilon_0\mu_0\,(L\Delta y)\omega E_0\cos\phi .$$

Using these, Eq. (9) becomes as follows.

$$L\cdot B(y,\ t)-L\cdot B(y+\Delta y,\ t)=-\varepsilon_0\mu_0\,(L\Delta y)\omega E_0\cos\phi \qquad (10)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4

Q3. Taking $\Delta y$ to be sufficiently small, derive the following from Eq. (10).

$$kB_0=\varepsilon_0\mu_0\omega E_0 \qquad (11)$$

Q4. (a) From Eqs. (7) and (11), find the relation between $\omega$ and $k$, and express the speed of the wave $\dfrac{\lambda}{T}$ in terms of $\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0$.

(b) Find the numerical value of the speed of the wave.

Since the speed of the wave obtained in this way was close to the speed of light known at the time, Maxwell considered that "light is an electromagnetic wave". Today this is established.

From Eqs. (7) and (11), $E_0$ and $B_0$ have the same sign. Therefore the direction of propagation of the electromagnetic wave is the direction in which a right-handed screw advances when it is rotated by $90^\circ$ from the direction of the electric field to the direction of the magnetic field.

[IV]

So far we have considered electromagnetic waves in vacuum; in [IV] we consider the case in which charged particles are present. Also, the amplitude of the oscillation of the electromagnetic field is taken to be sufficiently small.

Suppose that electrons with negative charge $-e\ (<0)$ and ions with positive charge $e\ (>0)$ are both uniformly distributed with number density $n$. These charged particles are moved by the electromagnetic field and a current flows, so in this case, unlike [III], the current term, the first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (9), is not 0. So let us find the current through the surface of small width enclosed by $\mathrm{C_4}$ in Fig. 4. However, since the mass of the ions is very large compared with that of the electrons, the ions may be regarded as not moving. Also, the thermal motion of the electrons may be neglected.

Q5. Show that, when electrons of number density $n$ and charge $-e$ move in the $z$ direction with velocity $v_z$, the amount of charge passing per unit time through a surface of unit cross-sectional area perpendicular to the $z$ axis is $(-e)nv_z$.

An electron receives from the electric field the force $(-e)E_0\sin\phi$ in the $z$ direction. Noting that the acceleration in the $z$ direction is the time derivative of the velocity $v_z$, the equation of motion of the electron in the $z$ direction is given as follows (when the amplitude of the electromagnetic field is small, the oscillation of the electrons may be taken to be in the $z$ direction only).

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}v_z}{\mathrm{d}t}=(-e)E_0\sin\phi$$

Assuming that the velocity $v_z$ of the electron in the $z$ direction is expressed in the form

$$v_z=v_0\cos\phi ,$$

and finding the constant $v_0$, then using the expression of Q5, we find that the current through the surface enclosed by $\mathrm{C_4}$ is expressed as follows.

$$(L\Delta y)\frac{ne^2}{m\omega}E_0\cos\phi \qquad (12)$$

Q6. (a) Find the constant $v_0$.

(b) Show that the current through the surface enclosed by $\mathrm{C_4}$ is expressed by Eq. (12).

Substituting Eq. (12) into Eq. (9), we obtain the following equation instead of Eq. (10) for the case of vacuum ([III]).

$$L\cdot B(y,\ t)-L\cdot B(y+\Delta y,\ t)=-\varepsilon_0\mu_0\,(L\Delta y)\left(1-\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)\omega E_0\cos\phi \qquad (13)$$

If $\Delta y$ is sufficiently small, the following equation is derived from this.

$$kB_0=\varepsilon_0\mu_0\omega\left(1-\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)E_0 \qquad (14)$$

Q7. Derive Eq. (14) from Eq. (13).

Q8. From the form of Eq. (14), $\left(\dfrac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}\right)^{1/2}$ should have the dimension of a frequency. Show this using the dimensions of $n$, $e$, $\varepsilon_0$, $m$.

The frequency $\left(\dfrac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}\right)^{1/2}$ appearing in Eq. (14) is called the plasma (angular) frequency and is denoted by $\omega_{\mathrm{p}}$.

$$\omega_{\mathrm{p}}=\left(\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}\right)^{1/2} \qquad (15)$$

Using Eqs. (7) and (14), $\omega^2$ can be expressed as a function of $k$ as follows.

$$\omega^2=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}\,k^2+{\omega_{\mathrm{p}}}^2 \qquad (16)$$

Therefore, for the oscillation of the electromagnetic field to propagate as a wave, we must have $\omega>\omega_{\mathrm{p}}$.

Q9. Show that Eq. (16) can be derived from Eqs. (7) and (14).

When an electromagnetic wave (light) propagates in matter, as considered here, its speed $\dfrac{\lambda}{T}$ differs from that in vacuum. The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum $c$ to the speed $\dfrac{\lambda}{T}$ of the electromagnetic wave in matter,

$$\frac{c}{\lambda/T}=\frac{c}{\omega/k} , \qquad (17)$$

is called the refractive index of the matter (the speed $\dfrac{\lambda}{T}$ is the speed at which the phase of the electromagnetic wave advances; it is a concept different from the speed at which a signal of the electromagnetic wave or photons travel, but the refractive index for electromagnetic waves is defined by this speed).

Q10. Using Eq. (16), express the refractive index of the space in which the charged particles now considered are distributed in terms of $\omega$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{p}}$.

The process in which atoms or molecules emit electrons and become ions is called ionisation, and the part of the upper atmosphere at altitudes of $100\sim300\,\mathrm{km}$ above the Earth's surface in which the electrons and ions produced by ionisation exist is called the ionosphere. In the ionosphere ions and electrons exist with almost the same number density, and Eq. (16) holds for the oscillations of the electromagnetic field.

When radio waves are transmitted from the Earth's surface, they first propagate as electromagnetic waves (light) in vacuum, but eventually reach the ionosphere.

Q11. (a) Taking the number density $n$ of electrons in the ionosphere to be of the order of $10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, find the numerical value of the plasma (angular) frequency $\omega_{\mathrm{p}}$ in the ionosphere.

(b) Thinking in the same way as for light incident from a material of larger refractive index on a material of smaller refractive index, what behaviour can be expected of the radio waves when they reach the ionosphere?

[Supplement]

A physical quantity like the left-hand side of Eq. (9) for the magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B}$ can be defined in the same way for the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$. Using it, the emf produced in a closed path is expressed as

$$V=\lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k E_k\ \Delta s_k .$$

The orientation of the closed path is the positive direction of the emf. Using this, Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction (4) can be written in the following form.

$$\lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k E_k\ \Delta s_k=-\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (18)$$

Eq. (6) is this equation applied to $\mathrm{C_1}$.

The left-hand side of Eq. (18) is the work done by the electric field when a unit charge is taken once around the closed path. For example, when there is only the electric field produced by point charges at rest, this work is 0, but when there is a time variation of the magnetic flux, it becomes equal to the emf of the closed path.

If, corresponding to the magnetic flux $\Phi$, the electric flux is denoted by $\Phi_E$, Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction (18) and the Ampère–Maxwell law (9) are expressed in the following paired forms.

$$\lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k E_k\ \Delta s_k=-\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t}, \qquad \lim_{\Delta s\to0}\sum_k B_k\ \Delta s_k=\mu_0I+\mu_0\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

This is one example of the correspondence between the electric field and the magnetic field in electromagnetism.

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (60 points)

[What cosmic rays are]

There are high-energy electrons, protons and atomic nuclei that pour down on the Earth incessantly from space; they are called cosmic rays. About a hundred years ago, when the Austrian Hess (V. Hess) went up in a balloon and measured the radiation dose at an altitude of $5000\,\mathrm{m}$, it was as much as 9 times that on the ground. From this it was discovered that some natural radiation has its origin in space, and it was named cosmic rays. Inside aeroplanes flying high in the sky there are many cosmic rays, so the radioactivity is also stronger than on the ground, but even on the ground about 20% of the radiation dose that Japanese people receive from nature is due to cosmic rays, several tens of which pass through the body every second. Also, cosmic rays ionise the atmosphere, and it is thought that, indirectly through this, they probably play an important role in clouds and lightning, or in the weather. Thus, although we are not usually aware of the existence of cosmic rays, they are in fact deeply related to us.

Then where in the universe are cosmic rays accelerated to high energies? In recent years it has become clear that supernova explosions play an important role in the acceleration, so below let us consider the reason, using energy as a clue.

[The energy of cosmic rays and the energy of supernova explosions]

Since cosmic rays of protons, electrons and atomic nuclei have charge, they fly around in the galactic disk while being bent by the magnetic field of the Galaxy, and with a mean lifetime $\tau=$ about 10 million years they either leak out of the galactic disk or collide with the interstellar matter in the galactic disk and disappear. The radius $R_{\mathrm{G}}$ of the galactic disk of our Galaxy is about $5\times10^4$ light years, the thickness $D_{\mathrm{G}}$ of the disk is about $10^3$ light years, and the energy density $w$ of cosmic rays in it is about $w=10^6\,\mathrm{eV/m^3}$ ($1\,\mathrm{eV}\fallingdotseq1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$).

Q1. Assuming that the total energy of the cosmic rays is kept constant in the galactic disk, how many J/year do you think is the energy of the cosmic rays newly produced in the Galaxy to make up for the cosmic rays lost? (You may take $c=$ speed of light $\fallingdotseq3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$, 1 light year $=c\times1$ year $\fallingdotseq1\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}$.)

It is thought that what makes up for the cosmic-ray energy lost at this enormous rate is mainly supernova explosions. Heavy stars undergo a supernova explosion at the end of their evolution. At the end of the evolution the energy of nuclear fusion runs out, a high pressure can no longer be maintained, the central part of the star collapses under gravity and its radius shrinks, electrons and protons combine into neutrons, and a neutron star is formed. A neutron star is a star made mainly of neutrons; although its mass is as much as about $M=1.3\,M_{\mathrm{S}}$ ($M_{\mathrm{S}}=$ solar mass $=2.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$), its radius is only $R\fallingdotseq10\,\mathrm{km}$, and it is a star with a high density of the same order as an atomic nucleus. The potential energy produced by the shrinking is negative and, assuming for simplicity that the density is uniform, it is given by the following equation.

$$U=-\frac{3GM^2}{5R} \qquad (1)$$

($G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{J\,m\,kg^{-2}}$ is the universal gravitational constant.)

Q2. Derive Eq. (1).

[Hint] Let the mass density of the star be $\rho$. The small work (small increase of potential energy) needed to bring a small mass $\Delta m$ from far away and spread it uniformly over the surface of a sphere of radius $r$ and mass $m$ is (see Fig. 1)

$$\Delta U=-\frac{Gm\Delta m}{r} . \qquad (2)$$

Regard this as the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}m}=-\dfrac{Gm}{r}$, and express its right-hand side, using the density $\rho$, as a function of the variable $m$ only; then this equation can be integrated and $U$ will be obtained as a function of $\rho$ and the mass $M$. By eliminating $\rho$ from it, $U$ is obtained as a function of the radius $R$ and the mass $M$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-5-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Small masses $\Delta m$ are brought from infinity and placed uniformly on the surface of a sphere of radius $r$ and mass $m$, and this is continued until the mass becomes $M$ and the radius $R$.

The positive energy $|U|$ that offsets this negative energy becomes the energy produced by the explosion. Most of that energy is used for the emission of invisible elementary particles, neutrinos, and the remaining about 1% is used for the great explosion of visible matter, which is observed as a supernova explosion. Let us suppose that a further about 1% of this visible explosion energy (in the end, $\varepsilon=0.01\%=0.0001$ of the total energy produced by the explosion) is used for the acceleration of cosmic rays.

Q3. Assuming that $0.01\%$ of $|U|$ is used for the acceleration of cosmic rays, find the energy $W_1$ of the cosmic rays obtained in one explosion. Also, taking the frequency with which supernova explosions such as the above occur in the Galaxy to be once per hundred years, $f=\dfrac{1}{100\ \text{years}}$, find the supply rate $W_1f$ of cosmic-ray energy to the Galaxy by supernovae in units of J/year.

From the results of Q1 and Q3 we see that the rate at which cosmic-ray energy is lost from the Galaxy and the rate at which supernova explosions supply cosmic-ray energy are within a factor of several of each other. Considering that the values of the mean lifetime $\tau$ of cosmic rays, the frequency $f$ of supernova explosions and the fraction $\varepsilon$ of the energy used for cosmic rays are rough and have large errors, it is possible that the two rates are equal. Since there is no other energy source this large, supernova explosions are the most likely origin of cosmic rays.

[Acceleration of cosmic rays]

In the interstellar space of the Galaxy there is, depending on the location, an extremely dilute gas of, for example, about one atom per $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, which, though dilute, plays an important role when considered over a large space. Suppose that in the Galaxy there are dilute plasma clouds (assemblies of gas of charged particles), and that in the coordinate system moving with such a plasma cloud (the rest frame of the plasma cloud) there is no electric field and there is only a static magnetic field (a magnetic field that does not vary with time). In a static magnetic field the direction of motion of a charged particle is bent, but it is not accelerated. Then how are cosmic rays accelerated? As an answer to this question, the mechanism called "Fermi acceleration" proposed by Fermi (E. Fermi) is promising.
 It is the idea that moving plasma clouds accelerate cosmic rays by repeatedly bouncing them back. Below, let us consider Fermi acceleration.

However, since we consider the motion of charged particles flying at speeds close to the speed of light, we need to use the theory of relativity. So let us explain the necessary relativity. It is (i) the expression of energy and momentum in terms of velocity, and (ii) the relation between their values seen in different coordinate systems (Lorentz transformation).

(i) Energy and momentum

According to the theory of relativity, when a particle of mass $M$ is at rest, its energy $E$ is given by Einstein's formula $E=Mc^2$ and is called the rest energy. The energy $E$ and momentum $p$ when the particle is moving with speed $V$ are derived to be, with $\beta=\dfrac{V}{c}$, $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}$,

$$E=Mc^2\gamma, \qquad p=Mc\gamma\beta . \qquad (3)$$

Q4. (a) Show that when the speed $V$ is very close to the speed of light $c$ $(\beta\to1)$ the following relation holds.

$$E\fallingdotseq pc \qquad (4)$$

(b) Show that when the speed $V$ is sufficiently smaller than the speed of light $c$ $(\beta\ll1)$ the following relations hold.

$$E\fallingdotseq Mc^2+\frac{1}{2}MV^2, \qquad p\fallingdotseq MV \qquad (5)$$

Apart from the rest-energy term (a constant) of $E$, both the energy and the momentum are probably familiar expressions.

(ii) Lorentz transformation

Suppose that, seen in the coordinate system O, the energy of a particle is $E$ and its momentum is $p$. Suppose that when a person riding on a coordinate system S (Fig. 2) moving with velocity $v$ in the $z$ direction relative to this coordinate system looks at this particle, its energy is $E^*$ and its momentum is $p^*$. Then, with $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^2}}$, these quantities are related by

$$\begin{aligned} &p_x=p_x^*,\ \ p_y=p_y^*,\ \ p_z=\gamma\left(p_z^*+\frac{vE^*}{c^2}\right) \\ &E=\gamma\,(E^*+vp_z^*) \end{aligned} \qquad (6)$$

Eqs. (6) are called the Lorentz transformation for momentum and energy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-5-fig2.png

Fig. 2. The relation between the coordinate system O and the coordinate system S moving with velocity $v$ relative to it.

[In the figure: $x$ または $y$ = $x$ or $y$; 系O = frame O; 系S = frame S.]

[Fermi acceleration]

When a supernova explodes, its hot gas expands at high speed together with the surrounding dilute gas, which it takes in. When the expansion speed is faster than the speed of sound of the surrounding gas, a boundary surface forms between the expanding gas and the surrounding gas; it is called the shock front. Even if the mass of hot gas spreads out nearly spherically, if its radius is sufficiently large, the shock front can probably be approximated as a plane in a narrow region. Let us take the $z$ axis parallel to the normal of that plane, in the direction in which the front advances (Fig. 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-5-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Expansion of the hot plasma produced by a supernova explosion and the shock front, and cosmic rays that bounce off the plasma and gain energy.

[In the figure: 膨張 = expansion; プラズマの雲 = plasma cloud; 速度 = velocity; 超新星の爆発 = supernova explosion; プラズマの雲に入る宇宙線 = cosmic ray entering the plasma cloud; 跳ね返った宇宙線 = bounced cosmic ray; 衝撃波面 = shock front.]

Let us call the coordinate system in which the centre of mass of the supernova is at rest frame O. Consider a charged particle flying at a speed close to the speed of light in front of, outside, the shock front. This particle is constantly deflected in the surrounding random magnetic field, so it does not go very far, and suppose that eventually it is swallowed by a plasma cloud flying in the $z$ direction with speed $v$ inside the shock front of the supernova. In the coordinate system moving with this plasma cloud (the rest frame of the plasma cloud, hereafter called frame S) there is assumed to be no electric field, and the magnetic field is assumed to be static. The charged particle changes its direction in the random magnetic field in the plasma cloud and eventually escapes from the plasma cloud (Fig. 3). Let the momentum and energy of the incident particle seen in frame S be $\overrightarrow{p^*}$, $E^*$, the angle of incidence $\theta_1$, and the angle of emission $\theta_2$ (Fig. 4). Seen in frame S, since there is no electric field and the magnetic field is static, the energy $E^*$ of the charged particle does not change and is equal at incidence and at emission. However, seen in frame O, the energy $E$ at incidence and the energy $E'$ at emission are, from Eq. (6),

$$\begin{aligned} E&=\gamma\,(E^*-vp^*\cos\theta_1) \\ E'&=\gamma\,(E^*+vp^*\cos\theta_2) \end{aligned} \qquad (7)$$

Here the energy of the particle is very high, and taking the energy $E\gg Mc^2$ we use Eq. (4) and approximate

$$E^*=p^*c .$$

Also, taking the speed $v$ of the plasma cloud to be sufficiently small compared with the speed of light $\left(\beta=\dfrac{v}{c}\ll1\right)$ and neglecting $\beta^2$ and higher, from Eq. (7) the rate of energy change seen in frame O is

$$\frac{\Delta E}{E}=\frac{E'-E}{E}=\beta\,(\cos\theta_1+\cos\theta_2) . \qquad (8)$$

Since the directions of motion of the charged particles vary, let us average Eq. (8) over the angles. However, we consider only the case in which the charged particle is incident from the front of the plasma moving with velocity $v$ and is reflected and emitted to the front.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-5-fig4.png

Fig. 4. A charged particle enters a plasma cloud, changes its direction and comes out. Seen in the frame moving with the plasma cloud (the rest frame S of the plasma cloud), the energy is the same at incidence and at emission. On the other hand, seen in frame O, the energies differ and the particle has been accelerated.

[In the figure: プラズマの雲 = plasma cloud; 荷電粒子 = charged particle.]

Let $\cos\theta_1\geqq0$, $\cos\theta_2\geqq0$. Then the mean value $\langle g(\theta_i)\rangle$ of an arbitrary function $g(\theta_i)$ of $\theta_i$ ($i=1$ or 2) can be calculated using the following formula.

$$\langle g(\theta)\rangle=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{0\leqq\theta\leqq\pi/2}g(\theta)\,\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\Omega}{\displaystyle\int_{0\leqq\theta\leqq\pi/2}\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\Omega}=\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}g(\theta)\,\cos\theta\cdot2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta}{\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\cdot2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta}$$

Here $\mathrm{d}\Omega=2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$ is the factor because the probability that the cosmic ray points at an angle $\theta\sim\theta+\mathrm{d}\theta$ is proportional to it, and $\cos\theta$ is the factor because the flux (probability) of cosmic rays incident per unit time on an $x$-$y$ plane perpendicular to the $z$ axis is proportional to the $z$ component of the velocity of the cosmic rays.

Q5. Show that the mean value $\left\langle\dfrac{\Delta E}{E}\right\rangle$ of $\dfrac{\Delta E}{E}$ is given by the following equation. Below, this mean value is denoted by $\alpha$.

$$\left\langle\frac{\Delta E}{E}\right\rangle=\frac{4\beta}{3} \qquad (9)$$

[Hint] It is useful to put $\cos\theta=t$ and convert to an integral with respect to $t$. Pay attention to the values of the upper and lower limits of the definite integral.

Even after a charged particle (cosmic ray) has been bounced back (and accelerated) by a plasma cloud inside the shock front of a supernova, while it is bent many times by the magnetic field of the plasma outside the shock front and does not go far away, it is swallowed again by the advancing shock front and is again bounced back and accelerated (see Fig. 5). In this way it is bounced back by the shock front and accelerated again and again, and each time its energy becomes $(1+\alpha)$ times larger. Using the approximation $(1+x)\fallingdotseq\mathrm{e}^x$, when it has been accelerated $N$ times, the energy $E$, compared with the initial energy $E_0$, becomes

$$E\fallingdotseq E_0\mathrm{e}^{N\alpha} .$$

Even if a particle once passes through to the rear without being bounced back to the front of the shock front, as long as it is afterwards bounced back by some plasma cloud and eventually comes out in front of the shock front, the path of the cosmic ray has only become longer in the above analysis and the result for the acceleration rate does not change. A particle that has slipped deep through to the far side no longer comes back,
but most cosmic rays eventually cross the shock front and come back. Letting $\delta$ ($\delta\ll1$) be the probability that a cosmic ray that has once entered the shock front from outside slips deep through, the probability $P_N$ that it comes out in front of the shock front $N$ times or more and is accelerated is given by the following equation.

$$P_N=(1-\delta)^N\fallingdotseq\mathrm{e}^{-N\delta}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2017-5-fig5.png

Fig. 5. The $N$-th bounce of a cosmic ray that has been bounced back $N-1$ times by the shock wave.

[In the figure: プラズマの雲 = plasma cloud; 衝撃波面 = shock front; 確率 = probability.]

Q6. Show that the probability $P_E$ that the energy becomes $E$ or more is

$$P_E=\left(\frac{E}{E_0}\right)^{-\delta/\alpha} . \qquad (10)$$

In the environment of the shock wave accompanying a supernova explosion, it is known theoretically, though we omit the details, that $\delta=\alpha$. Therefore, with $\dfrac{\delta}{\alpha}=1$, the probability that the energy of a cosmic ray just after its production is $E$ or more is

$$P_E=\left(\frac{E}{E_0}\right)^{-1} .$$

Averaging over $E_0$, the probability that the energy of a produced cosmic ray is $E$ or more is given by

$$f_1(E)=CE^{-1} \qquad (C\ \text{is a constant}) . \qquad (11)$$

Q7. Show that, if the probability that the energy is between $E$ and $E+\Delta E$ is expressed as $f_2(E)\Delta E$,

$$f_2(E)=CE^{-2} \qquad (12)$$

($f_2(E)$ is called the probability density).

[Leakage of cosmic rays from the Galaxy]

After leaving the acceleration region, charged cosmic-ray particles are confined in the Galaxy for a long time while their tracks are bent and they gyrate in the magnetic field of the Galaxy, but eventually they leak out of the Galaxy and are lost. The higher the energy, the less they are bent by the magnetic field and the larger their gyration radius, so the more easily they leak out of the Galaxy; observationally, it is known that the residence time in the Galaxy becomes shorter in proportion to $E^{-0.7}$. Therefore the energy distribution of the cosmic rays remaining in the Galaxy is modified from Eq. (12) and becomes on average

$$f_3(E)=C'E^{-2}\times E^{-0.7}=C'E^{-2.7} . \qquad (13)$$

The observed energy distributions of protons, oxygen nuclei, etc. agree well with Eq. (13).

Now, when the abundance ratios of the elements in the Galaxy are examined using spectral lines of light, meteorites, etc., the abundance of boron is as much as 5 orders of magnitude smaller than that of oxygen, and it is one of the very rare elements. However, in cosmic rays boron nuclei exist at about $1/10$ of oxygen nuclei, and are not so rare. This is thought to be because, when cosmic rays such as oxygen nuclei collide with the interstellar gas, they emit some protons and neutrons and with a high probability become boron nuclei.

Q8. For simplicity, assume that when an oxygen nucleus collides with the interstellar gas it becomes a boron nucleus having half its energy. Consider how, in the Galaxy, the energy distribution of cosmic-ray boron nuclei compares with the energy distribution (13) of oxygen nuclei etc., in terms of the way it depends on the energy. However, the probability of collision is taken not to depend on the energy of the oxygen.

problems.title: Problem 1: Two metal rods sliding on rails in a magnetic field
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (60 points)

Let us consider the motion of two metal rods sliding on two rails in a magnetic field.

As shown in Fig. 1, two metal rods can slide without friction on two parallel rails fixed horizontally, keeping at right angles to the rails and in electrical contact with them. The distance between the two rails is $a$, and the mass of each metal rod is $m$. The electrical resistance of each metal rod is $R$ $(R>0)$, and the electrical resistance of the rails can be neglected. The two metal rods are initially at rest, and the distance between them is $l$. The inductance of the circuit formed by the metal rods and the rails may be neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. The case in which the magnetic field points "from bottom to top".

Q1. Initially there was no magnetic field in space, but a uniform magnetic field was applied in the direction perpendicular to the plane containing the rails; the magnitude $B$ of the magnetic flux density increased rapidly in proportion to time and became $B_0$ after a short time $\Delta t$. During this time the displacement of the metal rods is almost negligible, and the distance $l$ may be taken as unchanged. Find the magnitude $I$ of the current flowing through the metal rods during this short time.

Q2. A metal rod carrying a current experiences a force in the magnetic field. Whether the magnetic field is applied from bottom to top as in Fig. 1 or, contrary to Fig. 1, from top to bottom, the force acting on the metal rods acts either in the direction that widens the distance between the metal rods or in the direction that narrows it. State the reason why the direction of the force does not depend on the direction of the magnetic field, and answer whether it is the widening direction or the narrowing direction.

Q3. Find the magnitude of the impulse acting on each metal rod during this short time $\Delta t$.

Q4. Receiving the impulse of the previous question, the two metal rods start moving symmetrically. Find the speed $v_0$ with which each metal rod starts moving.

Q5. After that, the direction of the magnetic field in space and the magnitude $B_0$ of the magnetic flux density were kept constant. When the speed of the metal rods, which started moving with initial speed $v_0$, has become $v$, find the magnitude $I$ of the current flowing through the metal rods. Also find the magnitude $F$ of the force acting on the metal rods at this moment.

Q6. Since the metal rods have electrical resistance, heat energy is generated when a current flows. Because of this, the kinetic energy of the metal rods is lost, and after a sufficiently long time the metal rods come to rest. Write the equation of motion of the metal rods for the period from when the metal rods start moving until they come to rest. Denote the speed of the metal rods by $v$ and their acceleration by $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$.

Q7. Find the distance between the two metal rods when, after a sufficiently long time, the metal rods have come to rest.

Q8. Express the total heat energy generated in the metal rods until the two metal rods come to rest, using $a$, $l$, $m$, $R$, $B_0$.

Q9. So far, as stated in Q1, the magnitude $B(t)$ of the magnetic flux density was assumed to increase from $0$ to $B_0$ in proportion to time during $\Delta t$. In fact, however, as long as the magnitude of the magnetic flux density increases from $0$ to $B_0$, the speed $v_0$ with which the metal rods start moving is the same as the result of Q4 even if $B(t)$ is not proportional to time. Explain the reason for this.

problems.title: Problem 2: Removal of space debris
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (100 points)

Space debris (space junk), such as the remains of rockets that launched artificial satellites, is spread over altitudes from $500\ \mathrm{km}$ to $40{,}000\ \mathrm{km}$ above the ground. The number of observed pieces of space debris with a diameter of $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ or more is about 20,000, and the number with a diameter from $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ to $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ reaches about 500,000.

The distribution of space debris is shown in Fig. 1. Space debris flies in orbits around the Earth at speeds of $3$–$8\ \mathrm{km}$ per second, and some of it has a speed relative to artificial satellites of $10\ \mathrm{km/s}$ or more, far faster than a bullet. It is predicted that if a large piece of space debris of the $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ class collided with an artificial satellite, the satellite would be completely destroyed. For this reason, the orbits of space debris are constantly observed, and collisions are avoided. At the same time, research is being carried out on methods of making space debris fall toward the ground or of ejecting it out of the Earth's gravitational sphere.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-2-fig1.jpg

Fig. 1. Quoted from http://fanfun.jaxa.jp/faq/detail/338.html

In this problem, let us analyse the motion of space debris and consider methods of removing space debris (below, space debris is also simply called debris). Assume that the Earth is a perfect sphere and that the gravity (universal gravitation) acting on an external object is the same as if the whole mass were concentrated at the centre. The radius of the Earth is $R_{\mathrm{E}}=6.4\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{km}$, and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Orbit of space debris

Due to the Earth's gravity, space debris moves on an elliptical orbit with the centre of the Earth as one focus (Kepler's first law). As shown in Fig. 2, take the centre E of the Earth as the origin, the $x$ axis in the direction of the major axis of the elliptical orbit ($\mathrm{Q'Q}$ in Fig. 2), and the $y$ axis perpendicular to the major axis. If the other focus of the ellipse is $\mathrm{E'}$ and the length of the major axis is $2R\ (=\overline{\mathrm{QQ'}})$, then the distances $r=\overline{\mathrm{EP}}$, $r'=\overline{\mathrm{E'P}}$ from the foci $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{E'}$ to a point $\mathrm{P}$ on the ellipse satisfy the relation

$$r+r'=2R \qquad (1)$$

If the angle that EP makes with the $x$ axis is $\theta$, the coordinates $(x,y)$ of the point $\mathrm{P}$ can be expressed as

$$x=r\cos\theta\,,\qquad y=r\sin\theta \qquad (2)$$

With respect to the Cartesian coordinates $(x,\,y)$, the coordinates $(r,\,\theta)$, whose variables are the distance $r$ from the centre and the angle $\theta$ measured counterclockwise from the $x$ axis, are called polar coordinates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q1. Letting the distance between the foci $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{E'}$ be $2a\ (=\overline{\mathrm{EE'}})$, show that the ellipse of Eq. (1) is expressed in polar coordinates as

$$r=\frac{R^2-a^2}{R-a\cos\theta} \qquad (3)$$

Setting $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\pi$ in Eq. (3), we find that the lengths of EQ and EQ′ are expressed as follows:

$$\overline{\mathrm{EQ}}=R+a\,,\qquad \overline{\mathrm{EQ'}}=R-a$$

The force exerted by the Earth on space debris points toward the centre E of the Earth, and its magnitude is inversely proportional to the square of the distance $r$ $(>R_{\mathrm{E}})$ from E. If the mass of the space debris is $m$, the magnitude of the force acting on space debris at a point P at distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth can be written, using the magnitude $g$ of the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface and the radius $R_{\mathrm{E}}$ of the Earth, as

$$F=mg\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{E}}}{r}\right)^2$$

The $x$, $y$ components of the acceleration of the space debris are $\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2x(t)}{\mathrm{d}t^2},\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y(t)}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\right)$, and the $x$, $y$ components of the force are $(-F\cos\theta\,,-F\sin\theta)$; therefore the $x$ component and the $y$ component of the equation of motion of the space debris are as follows:

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=-mg\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{E}}}{r}\right)^2\frac{x}{r} \qquad (4\mathrm{a})$$

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=-mg\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{E}}}{r}\right)^2\frac{y}{r} \qquad (4\mathrm{b})$$

Q2. (a) The kinetic energy $K$ of the space debris is given by the following expression:

$$K=\frac{m}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2\right]$$

Derive from the equations of motion that the time variation of the kinetic energy satisfies

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}t}=-mg\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{E}}}{r}\right)^2\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

(b) The potential energy due to the Earth's gravity (universal gravitation), with infinity as the reference, can be expressed as follows:

$$U=-\frac{mg{R_{\mathrm{E}}}^2}{r}$$

Using this, show that the total energy $W=K+U$ is conserved (is constant).

Next, regarding the orbit of space debris, we derive the law of conservation of areal velocity (the areal velocity is constant; Kepler's second law) from the equations of motion (4a), (4b). The areal velocity is the rate of increase with time of the area $S$ of the grey part bounded by EP, EQ and the orbit $\overset{\frown}{\mathrm{QP}}$ in Fig. 3. When the debris moves from P to P′ during a short time $\Delta t$ and the angle $\theta$ increases to $\theta+\Delta\theta$, the increase $\Delta S$ of $S$ is approximately $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\Delta\theta$; therefore, writing the areal velocity as $\dot{S}$, it is expressed as

$$\dot{S}=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{2}\,r^2\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (5)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Q3. (a) Paying attention to the relation between $(x,\,y)$ and $(r,\,\theta)$ [Eq. (2)], show the following equation:

$$2\dot{S}\,=\,x\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}-y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

(b) Using the equations of motion (4a), (4b), derive the law of conservation of areal velocity

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\dot{S}}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$$

(c) Show that the kinetic energy $K$ is expressed as follows:

$$K=\frac{m}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(r\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2\right]=\frac{m}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{2\dot{S}}{r}\right)^2\right]$$

Q4. Show that the total energy $W=K+U$, the areal velocity $\dot{S}$, the major axis $2R$ of the elliptical orbit and the distance $2a$ between the foci satisfy the following relations:

$$2R=-\frac{mg{R_{\mathrm{E}}}^2}{W} \qquad (6)$$

$$2a=\left[\left(\frac{mg{R_{\mathrm{E}}}^2}{W}\right)^2+\frac{8m(\dot{S})^2}{W}\right]^{1/2} \qquad (7)$$

[Hint] When the space debris is at Q or Q′, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$.

Q5. The perigee of the debris is Q′ in Fig. 2. Express the distance $d$ from the Earth's surface to the perigee in terms of $m$, $g$, $R_{\mathrm{E}}$, $W$, $\dot{S}$.

Removal of space debris by changing its orbit

Since the speed of space debris is smallest at the apogee, it is conceivable to remove space debris by applying a suitable impulse at the apogee and changing its orbit. There are two ways of doing this: making it enter the Earth's atmosphere, and taking it out of the Earth's gravitational sphere. Below, we investigate and compare them.

For simplicity, assume that the orbit of the space debris is a circular orbit of radius $R_0$ and that its speed is $v_0$. Let the total energy at this time be $W_0$ and the areal velocity be $\dot{S}_0$.

Q6. Express the total energy $W_0$ in terms of $m$, $g$, $R_0$, $R_{\mathrm{E}}$, and the areal velocity $\dot{S}_0$ in terms of $v_0$, $R_0$.

Deceleration of space debris and entry into the atmosphere

As shown in Fig. 4, at the point Q the space debris has a velocity in the $y$ direction. Let us give the space debris an impulse in the $-y$ direction at the point Q, turning its orbit into an elliptical orbit like the dashed line, and make it enter the atmosphere when it reaches the perigee P.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

Let the magnitude of the impulse in the $-y$ direction given to the space debris at the point Q be $\Delta p$ (the momentum in the $y$ direction changes by $-\Delta p$). If, for the elliptical orbit after receiving the impulse, the length of the major axis PQ is $2R$, the distance between the two foci E, E′ is $2a$, the total energy is $W$ and the areal velocity is $\dot{S}$, then (6), (7) of Q4 hold among $R$, $a$, $W$, $\dot{S}$.

Q7. Let us find the magnitude $\Delta p$ of the impulse needed to make the debris enter the atmosphere.

(a) Express $(\dot{S})^2$ in terms of $R$, $a$, $g$, $R_{\mathrm{E}}$.

(b) We regard the debris as having entered the atmosphere if the perigee P becomes lower than the upper limit of the Earth's atmosphere. When the distance between the upper limit of the atmosphere and the centre E of the Earth is $h$, express $\dfrac{\Delta p}{mv_0}$ in terms of the radius $R_0$ of the circular orbit and $h$.

[Hint] $R_0$ and $h$ can be written in terms of $R$ and $a$ as $R_0=R+a$, $h=R-a$. Also, the ratio $\dfrac{\dot{S}}{\dot{S}_0}$ of the areal velocities after and before receiving the impulse can be expressed, using $\dfrac{\Delta p}{mv_0}$, as $\dfrac{\dot{S}}{\dot{S}_0}=1-\dfrac{\Delta p}{mv_0}$.

Q8. Suppose that the mass $m$ of the debris is $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the radius $R_0$ of the circular orbit is $7.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{km}$.

(a) Let the distance (altitude) from the Earth's surface to the upper limit of the atmosphere be $1.0\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{km}$. Find the magnitude of the impulse needed for the perigee of the debris to be at this altitude.

(b) Find the difference between the speeds of the debris before and after receiving the impulse, and the speed of the debris immediately after receiving the impulse.

Acceleration of space debris and launch out of the gravitational sphere

Next, let us consider the method of accelerating the space debris and taking it out of the Earth's gravitational sphere.

Q9. As shown in Fig. 5, we want to accelerate debris of speed $v_0$ on a circular orbit of radius $R_0$ by giving it an impulse in the direction of revolution ($y$ direction) at the point Q, making the total energy $W$ equal to $0$, and send it out of the gravitational sphere. When the speed immediately after applying the impulse that makes $W=0$ is $v_1$, find $\dfrac{v_1}{v_0}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

[Label in the figure: 力積 = impulse.]

Among circular orbits due to the Earth's gravity, the orbit that goes round once in 24 hours in the same direction as the Earth's rotation (the orbit of a geostationary satellite) is called the geostationary orbit.

Q10. (a) Find the numerical value of the radius $R_0$ of the geostationary orbit.

(b) When debris of mass $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ is in the geostationary orbit, find the numerical value of the magnitude of the impulse needed to make its total energy $0$ and take it out of the gravitational sphere.

Comparison of the two methods

From Q7 and Q9, the magnitudes of the impulses needed for space debris on a circular orbit for the method of making it enter the atmosphere and for the method of taking it out of the gravitational sphere are known.

Q11. When the radius $R_0$ of the circular orbit is given, state which is more suitable: the method of making the debris enter the atmosphere or the method of taking it out of the gravitational sphere. For entry into the atmosphere, it suffices to take the altitude above the Earth's surface as $1.0\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{km}$. The phenomena to be considered may be limited to the scope considered in this problem.

problems.title: Problem 3: Heat pumps and entropy
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (70 points)

Of the total energy consumption of our country, about half is used for manufacturing and the other half for daily life. Of the part used in daily life, the share used for heating and hot-water supply, cooling and refrigeration, and lighting in homes and offices reaches about 60 %. It is important to do these things efficiently. Among these, the heat pump is a device that performs heating and hot-water supply as well as cooling and refrigeration. It is a device that, when work is supplied, moves heat from a low-temperature heat reservoir to a high-temperature heat reservoir, and it is already present in our daily life in almost every home and office as an air conditioner or a water heater. This is an energy conversion between heat (random motion) and work (ordered motion), and it is a problem of thermodynamics. In the following discussion we also deepen our understanding of the physical meaning of the physical quantity entropy, which plays an important role.

[I]

In general, a device that converts heat energy into work is called a heat engine (Fig. 1(a)). On the other hand, a device that, when work is supplied, moves heat, i.e. performs heating or cooling, is called a heat pump (Fig. 1(b)). These repeat a cyclic process (Cycle: C) between a high-temperature heat reservoir and a low-temperature heat reservoir, using a working substance as described below. A heat pump may also be said to be a device that efficiently creates a temperature difference. In this problem, let us take up the physics of the heat pump in order to understand in a unified way the physics of heating and hot-water supply and of cooling and refrigeration, which are important in our daily lives.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Heat engine and heat pump.

[Labels in the figure: 高温熱源 = high-temperature heat reservoir; 低温熱源 = low-temperature heat reservoir; (a) 熱機関 = heat engine; (b) ヒートポンプ = heat pump.]

From now on, for a while, we consider an idealized heat pump. As an example, consider a cylinder such as that in Fig. 2, in which a gas is confined by a smoothly moving piston. The left wall conducts heat, and by bringing it into contact with a heat reservoir at a fixed temperature, the temperature of the gas in the cylinder can be controlled. The side walls of the cylinder and the piston are made of a heat-insulating material that does not conduct heat. A substance, such as this gas, that is used in a heat engine or a heat pump is called a working substance.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

[Labels in the figure: 断熱材 = heat-insulating material; 熱源 = heat reservoir; 気体 = gas.]

The state of the gas in the cylinder is specified by the pressure $P$, the volume $V$ and the absolute temperature $T$ (below simply called the temperature; note that $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\fallingdotseq 273\,\mathrm{K}$). The energy that this gas has is called the internal energy $U$. The internal energy $U$ of a gas is a physical quantity that is determined once the state of the gas is specified, and like $P$, $V$, $T$ it is a state quantity. Whatever path the state of a gas follows in changing, if it returns to the initial state, the values of the state quantities return to their initial values. When a system undergoes a change of state, "the change $\Delta U$ of the internal energy, which is a state quantity of this system, is equal to the sum of the heat $Q$ absorbed by this system during the change of state and the work $W$ done on it from outside $(\Delta U=Q+W)$". This is called the first law of thermodynamics. Heat is one form of energy, and this law is nothing but the law of conservation of energy.

A heat pump is a cycle in which, in the $PV$ diagram of Fig. 3, work $W\ (>0)$ is done from outside on the gas serving as the working substance in the cylinder, heat $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$ is pumped up from the low-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{L}}$), and heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$ is released to the high-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$). In a heat engine the cyclic process of the change of state of the gas in Fig. 3 proceeds clockwise, but in a heat pump it proceeds counterclockwise. Specifically, the gas starts from the initial state A and, passing through B, C, D, returns to the initial state A via the following four quasi-static processes (processes of change in which the state changes so "slowly" that it deviates only extremely little from equilibrium states).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Heat pump.

[Labels in the figure: A→B 等温膨張 = isothermal expansion; B→C 断熱圧縮 = adiabatic compression; C→D 等温圧縮 = isothermal compression; D→A 断熱膨張 = adiabatic expansion; 図形ABCDの面積 = 外からされる仕事 $W$: area of the figure ABCD = work $W$ done from outside.]

• $\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{B}$: The left wall of the cylinder is brought into contact with the low-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{L}}$), and the gas is expanded isothermally while its temperature is kept at $T_{\mathrm{L}}$. At this time the gas absorbs a positive amount of heat $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$.
• $\mathrm{B}\to\mathrm{C}$: The cylinder is separated from the heat reservoir, and the gas is compressed adiabatically, raising its temperature to $T_{\mathrm{H}}$.
• $\mathrm{C}\to\mathrm{D}$: The left wall of the cylinder is brought into contact with the high-temperature heat reservoir (temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$), and the gas is compressed isothermally while its temperature is kept at $T_{\mathrm{H}}$. At this time the gas releases a positive amount of heat $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$.
• $\mathrm{D}\to\mathrm{A}$: The cylinder is separated from the heat reservoir, and the gas is expanded adiabatically, lowering its temperature to $T_{\mathrm{L}}$.

In the case of a heat pump, the gas in the cylinder does work on the outside in the expansion processes $\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{B}$, $\mathrm{D}\to\mathrm{A}$, and has work done on it from outside in the compression processes $\mathrm{B}\to\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{C}\to\mathrm{D}$. The difference is the net work $W$ done on the gas from outside, and it is represented by the area of the figure ABCD in Fig. 3.
If the change in each process of the cycle is a quasi-static process, the cycle is called a reversible cycle. Expressing the change $\Delta U$ of the internal energy of the gas during one cycle of the heat pump in terms of $Q_{\mathrm{H}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{L}}$, $W$, we have

$$\Delta U=Q_{\mathrm{L}}+W-Q_{\mathrm{H}}$$

Taking into account that the internal energy $U$ is a state quantity, the gas has returned to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$, and therefore

$$Q_{\mathrm{L}}+W=Q_{\mathrm{H}} \qquad (1)$$

holds.

When a hot body and a cold body are brought into contact, the two bodies eventually reach the same temperature, but heat never flows in the reverse direction so that the temperatures of the bodies return to their original values. That is, the flow of heat between two bodies with a temperature difference is an irreversible process. We experience many things similar to this. The quasi-static changes described above are reversible processes, but this is a kind of idealization. The irreversibility of thermal phenomena was studied by Clausius and Thomson (later Lord Kelvin), and as the second law of thermodynamics it is stated as the following two mutually equivalent principles.

Clausius's principle: "A process whose only result is to transfer heat from a body at low temperature (low-temperature heat reservoir) to a body at high temperature (high-temperature heat reservoir), leaving no other change in the surroundings, is impossible."

Thomson's principle: "A process whose only result is to take heat from a single heat reservoir and do a positive amount of work on the surroundings, without causing any other change, is impossible."

In order to describe this irreversibility quantitatively, Clausius introduced the entropy $S$ defined as follows, and showed that $S$ is a state quantity (it has a value determined by the state and does not depend on the history of that state). When a system at temperature $T$ absorbs an amount of heat $\Delta Q$, the change $\Delta S$ of the entropy of this system is given by

$$\Delta S=\frac{\Delta Q}{T} \qquad (2)$$

Also, the entropy of a system consisting of several parts at different temperatures is the sum of the entropies of the parts.

"In a closed system (a system with neither inflow nor outflow of heat nor of matter), the entropy increases or stays unchanged; it never decreases." This is called the law of increase of entropy. Therefore, if an adiabatic expansion process or an adiabatic compression process is carried out quasi-statically, it is reversible and the entropy does not change, but if it is irreversible the entropy increases. According to a detailed discussion, the law of increase of entropy is another expression of the second law of thermodynamics.

Now, let us return to the cyclic process of the heat pump. When each process during one cycle of the heat pump is carried out quasi-statically, that is, reversibly, considering the increase and decrease of the entropy of the gas during one cycle, the entropy change $\Delta S$ is

$$\Delta S=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{L}}}{T_{\mathrm{L}}}-\frac{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}}} \qquad (3)$$

Entropy is a state quantity and the system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta S=0$. That is, the relation

$$\frac{Q_{\mathrm{L}}}{T_{\mathrm{L}}}=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}}} \qquad (4)$$

is obtained.

Q1. Using the indoors as the low-temperature heat reservoir and the outdoors as the high-temperature heat reservoir, the heat pump is used as a cooling device. In general, the cooling efficiency of a cooling device is defined as $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{Q_{\mathrm{L}}}{W}$ (r: refrigeration), and in particular the cooling efficiency of a reversible heat pump is denoted by $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$. Using the above relations, express $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$ in terms of the temperatures $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ only ($\varepsilon$ and $\eta$ are the Greek letters epsilon and eta, respectively).

So far we have assumed that all processes of the cyclic process are reversible. In reality, because of irreversibilities such as friction, entropy is always generated in the processes of change of state. Taking this into account, it can be shown that the cooling efficiency of a general heat pump is always smaller than that of a reversible heat pump, and that the reversible heat pump is the ideal cooling device. That is, the inequality

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}<\eta_{\mathrm{r}} \qquad (5)$$

holds in general. The reversible cycle discussed here is also called the reverse Carnot cycle, and it is known that $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$ is the theoretical upper limit of the cooling efficiency of a heat pump.

Q2. (a) When the outdoors is a high-temperature heat reservoir at temperature $35.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the indoors is a low-temperature heat reservoir at temperature $25.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, calculate the theoretical upper limit $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$ of the cooling efficiency. How does the theoretical upper limit $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$ of the cooling efficiency change when the indoor temperature is set higher, changing it to $28.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$?

(b) Also, what is the minimum electric power, in W, needed in each case to extract $1000\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat per second from the room?

The discussion so far holds basically in the same way for heating and hot-water supply. Taking heating as an example, it suffices to regard the indoors as the high-temperature heat reservoir and the outdoors as the low-temperature heat reservoir. In general, if the heating efficiency in heating is $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{h}}=\dfrac{Q_{\mathrm{H}}}{W}$ and the heating efficiency of a reversible heat pump in heating is $\eta_{\mathrm{h}}$ (h: heating), then, as in the case of cooling and refrigeration, the inequality

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{h}}<\eta_{\mathrm{h}} \qquad (6)$$

holds.

Q3. (a) Show that the relations $\eta_{\mathrm{h}}=\eta_{\mathrm{r}}+1$, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{h}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}+1$ hold.

(b) Express $\eta_{\mathrm{h}}$ of a reversible heat pump in terms of $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$.

Q4. With the room temperature at $25.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the outdoor air temperature at $5.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $1000\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy per second is pumped from outdoors and used for heating the room. What is the minimum electric power, in W, needed for this? As a result, how many J of heat energy per second are brought into the room?

Q5. It is generally said that heating in winter consumes more energy (that is, more electric power) than cooling in summer. With reference to the discussion so far, consider the reason for this.

The temperatures at which we live our daily lives are in the vicinity of $T\fallingdotseq 300\,\mathrm{K}$, and in the problems considered so far the temperatures of the high-temperature and low-temperature heat reservoirs are also in a temperature range close to it. On the other hand, a heat pump has a cooling capability. Let us consider the case of producing a state of extremely low temperature from a state at $T\fallingdotseq 300\,\mathrm{K}$ using a reversible heat pump.

Q6. (a) When $1000\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat per second is pumped out of a low-temperature heat reservoir at $T=10\,\mathrm{K}$ and moved to a high-temperature heat reservoir at $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$, calculate $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$.

(b) What is the minimum electric power, in W, needed to carry this out? Also, how many J of heat energy per second are brought into the high-temperature heat reservoir?

(c) When the temperature difference between the high-temperature and low-temperature heat reservoirs is increased, aiming at extremely low temperatures, what tendency arises regarding the amount of work needed to move the heat? Consider this, paying attention to the change in the value of $\eta_{\mathrm{r}}$ in the cases treated here.

Note: In practice, the efficiency of a heat pump is called the energy consumption efficiency (Coefficient of Performance: abbreviated COP, also called the coefficient of performance), and it is an important index showing the performance of the air conditioners we use daily at home. The energy consumption efficiency of air conditioners currently on the market is about 6, considerably lower than the efficiency of a reversible heat pump [see Eqs. (5), (6)]. For the effective use of energy, efforts from the technical side are needed to bring the efficiency of heat pumps closer to their theoretical upper limits (that is, to reduce the losses due to irreversibility).

[II]

So far, we have treated the problem of energy consumption directly connected with our daily life as an applied problem of thermodynamics, and have considered this problem by means of the basic laws of thermodynamics, namely the first law of thermodynamics based on energy conservation and the second law of thermodynamics based on the existence of irreversible processes, and in particular by introducing the state quantity called entropy $S$ [see Eq. (2)]. Now, in order to deepen further our understanding of the physical content of the entropy $S$, let us consider the change of entropy for two examples of irreversible processes that we experience close at hand:

1) transfer of heat from a hot body to a cold body,
2) mixing of gases.

When there are two systems, the total entropy is the sum of the entropies of each.

Q7. When two bodies at temperature $T_{\mathrm{H}}$ and temperature $T_{\mathrm{L}}$ $(T_{\mathrm{H}}>T_{\mathrm{L}})$ were brought into contact for a short time, a small amount of heat $Q$ moved from the hot body to the cold body.

(a) Express the total entropy change $\Delta S$ of the two bodies at this time in terms of $T_{\mathrm{H}}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}$, $Q$. Here the heat capacities of these bodies are sufficiently large, and the temperatures of both bodies do not change. Also, explain that always $\Delta S>0$.

(b) Calculate $\Delta S$ in the case $T_{\mathrm{H}}=300\,\mathrm{K}$, $T_{\mathrm{L}}=273\,\mathrm{K}$, $Q=100\,\mathrm{J}$.

Q8. There are $n$ moles of an ideal gas. Its heat capacity at constant volume is $C_{\mathrm{v}}$.

(a) When the temperature is changed by a small amount from $T$ to $T+\Delta T$ with the volume $V$ kept constant, how much heat is added to the ideal gas?

(b) Keeping the volume at the constant value $V_0$, the temperature was changed slowly, that is quasi-statically, from $T_0$ to $T$. Denoting the entropy at temperature $T$ and volume $V$ by $S(T,V)$, explain that the entropy change in this case is given by the following expression:

$$S(T,V_0)-S(T_0,V_0)=C_{\mathrm{v}}\log\frac{T}{T_0}$$

(c) Next, from temperature $T$ and volume $V_0$, the volume was changed quasi-statically to $V$, keeping the temperature constant. Explain that the entropy change in this case is given by the following expression:

$$S(T,V)-S(T,V_0)=nR\log\frac{V}{V_0}$$

Here $R$ is the gas constant $(R=8.314\,\mathrm{JK^{-1}mol^{-1}})$.

From the results of the previous question, we see that the entropy change $\Delta S$ when the state is changed quasi-statically from the state of temperature $T_0$, volume $V_0$ to the state of temperature $T$, volume $V$ is given by the following expression:

$$\Delta S=S(T,V)-S(T_0,V_0)=C_{\mathrm{v}}\log\frac{T}{T_0}+nR\log\frac{V}{V_0} \qquad (7)$$

As on the left side of Fig. 4, suppose that a box is divided by a partition and that two kinds of ideal gases A, B are in containers of capacity $V_{\mathrm{A}}$, $V_{\mathrm{B}}$, respectively. Their numbers of moles are $n_{\mathrm{A}}$, $n_{\mathrm{B}}$, their temperatures are equal to $T$, and the volumes are proportional to the numbers of moles $\left(\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{A}}}{V_{\mathrm{A}}}=\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{B}}}{V_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)$. Therefore the pressures of gases A and B are equal.

As on the right side of Fig. 4, when the wall separating A and B is removed, the molecules of A and B mix, and the molecules of both are distributed uniformly within the volume $V_{\mathrm{A}}+V_{\mathrm{B}}$. How does the entropy of this system change at this time?

Q9. In an ideal gas there is no interaction between gas molecules. Even for a mixture of several kinds of gases, if it is treated as an ideal gas, each gas behaves independently of the presence of the other kinds of gas. Taking these into account, let us find the change of entropy upon mixing. Here, denote the entropies of the ideal gases A, B by $S_{\mathrm{A}}$, $S_{\mathrm{B}}$.

(a) Focusing on the ideal gas A, the temperature is constant and the volume changed quasi-statically from $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ to $V_{\mathrm{A}}+V_{\mathrm{B}}$. Find the change $\Delta S_{\mathrm{A}}$ of $S_{\mathrm{A}}$ at this time.

(b) Focusing on the ideal gas B, the temperature is constant and the volume changed quasi-statically from $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ to $V_{\mathrm{A}}+V_{\mathrm{B}}$. Find the change $\Delta S_{\mathrm{B}}$ of $S_{\mathrm{B}}$ at this time.

(c) The entropy change $\Delta S$ due to the mixing of these gases is given by the sum of the above entropy changes $\Delta S_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\Delta S_{\mathrm{B}}$. Express the entropy change $\Delta S$ due to the mixing in terms of the numbers of moles $n_{\mathrm{A}}$, $n_{\mathrm{B}}$. Show that it is positive if $n_{\mathrm{A}},n_{\mathrm{B}}>0$.

(d) Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S$ upon mixing of the ideal gases for the case $n_{\mathrm{A}}=n_{\mathrm{B}}=1.0\,\mathrm{mol}$. The increase $\Delta S$ of entropy upon mixing is called the entropy of mixing.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Mixing of ideal gases.

We see that in the two irreversible processes taken up here the entropy increases. Furthermore, we can understand that, if the whole system consisting of the two systems considered here is regarded as an isolated system, the law of increase of entropy holds.

problems.title: Problem 4: Water waves, Green's law and tidal bores
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (70 points)

A phenomenon in which a change of state at one point in space is transmitted one after another to its surroundings is called a wave or wave motion. The medium through which a wave propagates is called the medium. In the natural world around us, various waves exist depending on the medium. For example, water waves and sound waves are examples of these. A wave in which the direction of the oscillation transmitted as the wave coincides with the direction of propagation of the wave is called a longitudinal wave, and the sound wave is a representative example of a longitudinal wave. On the other hand, a wave in which the direction of oscillation and the direction of propagation of the wave are at right angles is called a transverse wave, and light and radio waves are examples of transverse waves. There are also waves, such as waves travelling on the surface of water, that are characterized by a two-dimensional motion in which vertical and horizontal motions are superposed. At the seashore we often see scenes in which waves steepen and their crests break into white water. Below, we first consider the behaviour of waves such as tsunamis near the coastline, then waves that arise when the amplitude becomes large (such waves are called finite-amplitude waves) and the steepening of waves, and further the tidal bore (潮津波, shiotsunami), a special wave phenomenon.

1. Behaviour of waves near the coastline and of waves going up rivers

Here, let us consider how a tsunami behaves as it rushes in from a deep-sea region toward a coastline where the water becomes shallower. Specifically, depending on the topography of the sea bottom, the structure of the coastline, etc., amplification of the wave height, refraction, etc. occur, and as a result a concentration of energy may also occur. We consider such complicated behaviour with a simple model. The amplitude of the wave is assumed to be sufficiently small.

As shown in Fig. 1, when waves come from the deep part of the sea toward the shallows, it is observed that the wave fronts gradually become parallel to the coastline. There are several kinds of water waves, but here we consider waves for which the wavelength is sufficiently long compared with the depth and whose propagation speed $v$ is given by $v=\sqrt{gh}$, where $h$ is the depth from the water surface to the sea bottom and $g$ is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration (such waves are called shallow-water waves).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. (a) Near the coast, the wave fronts of the incident wave become parallel to the coastline. (b) Cross-section of the change of water depth of the sea bottom near the coast.

[Labels in the figure: 海岸線 = coastline; 入射波 = incident wave.]

Q1. As shown in Fig. 2, consider a sinusoidal wave incident on a place where the water depth changes stepwise. Let the water depths on the deep side and on the shallow side be $h_0$, $h_1$, respectively.

(a) Express the relation (Snell's law) between the angle of incidence $\theta_0$, the angle of refraction $\theta_1$ and the water depths.

(b) When, as in Fig. 1, the water depth becomes gradually shallower near the coast, briefly explain why the wave fronts become parallel to the coastline as they approach the coast.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2. (a) Wave fronts of the incident wave and the refracted wave at the place where refraction occurs (view from above). (b) Cross-section of the sea bottom where the water depth changes stepwise.

[Labels in the figure: 屈折波の進行方向 = direction of propagation of the refracted wave; 屈折波の波面 = wave fronts of the refracted wave; 入射波の波面 = wave fronts of the incident wave; 入射波の進行方向 = direction of propagation of the incident wave.]

For the waves considered here, when viewed from vertically above, the mean energy of the wave per unit area of the horizontal plane is given, with $\rho$ the density of water and $a$ the amplitude of the oscillation of the water surface, by

$$T=\frac{1}{2}\rho g a^2 \qquad (1)$$

Also, the energy carried by the wave per unit time through a unit length (on the horizontal plane) perpendicular to the direction of propagation (the energy flux) is $E=vT$.

As in Fig. 3, how does a wave travelling upstream behave when the river width gradually narrows toward upstream and the water depth also gradually becomes shallower?
