Assuming that the changes of river width and water depth are sufficiently gradual compared with the wavelength of the wave and that reflection of the wave can be neglected, it is known that when the river width, the water depth and the amplitude of the wave change from $B_0$ to $B$, from $h_0$ to $h$, and from $a_0$ to $a$, respectively, the following Green's law holds among them:

$$\frac{a}{a_0}=\left(\frac{h_0}{h}\right)^{1/4}\left(\frac{B_0}{B}\right)^{1/2} \qquad (2)$$

Q2. Derive Green's law by considering the conservation of the energy flux. The density $\rho$ is constant.

Q3. Ocean tides cause oscillations in estuaries, and at times such as spring tides a phenomenon is observed in which these oscillations travel up rivers. In the Amazon River and the Yangtze River such waves are observed even more than $800\,\mathrm{km}$ upstream. Assuming that a wave of amplitude $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ goes up the river at a point at the river mouth where the river width is $2.0\,\mathrm{km}$ and the water depth is $10\,\mathrm{m}$, and that Green's law holds, find the amplitude, in m, of the wave at a point where the river width is $1.0\,\mathrm{km}$ and the water depth is $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3. (a) River width at two particular points of the river (view from above). (b) Water depth and wave height (view from the side).

[Labels in the figure: 下流 = downstream; 上流 = upstream.]

Within the scope of the discussion so far, when the characteristic length of the wave (the wavelength) is sufficiently long compared with the depth $h$ and the speed of the wave is given by $\sqrt{gh}$, the wave travels keeping the same waveform, even if it is not sinusoidal, provided the depth and width are constant.

On the other hand, in actual tsunamis, even if the depth and width are constant, the wave may deform into a step-like wave as it travels. The cause of this difference is that in the above discussion the higher-order amplitude dependence of the wave (nonlinear effects), friction and similar effects are neglected. Next, let us consider an example of the relation between the amplitude-dependent effect and the deformation of the wave.

2. Deformation of waves due to finite-amplitude effects

When there is water of constant depth $h$, for a wave whose wavelength is long compared with the depth (a shallow-water wave), the velocity $u$ of the oscillation of the medium in the $x$ direction and the change $\Delta h$ of the height of the water surface due to a sinusoidal wave travelling in the $x$ direction are expressed as follows:

$$u=v\,\frac{a}{h}\,\sin(kx-\omega t) \qquad (3)$$

$$\Delta h=a\sin(kx-\omega t) \qquad (4)$$

Here, $a\ (>0)$ is the amplitude of $\Delta h$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, and if the wavelength is $\lambda$, then $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$. The amplitude is assumed to be sufficiently small. The density of water is the constant value $\rho$, and when there is no wave the water is at rest.

The wave fronts of this wave travel in the $x$ direction with speed $v=\dfrac{\omega}{k}$. Let the coordinate system in which this wave is expressed by Eqs. (3), (4) be the S system, and let the coordinate system moving with speed $v$ in the $x$ direction relative to the S system be the S′ system. Writing the coordinate (in the $x$ direction) in the S′ system as $X$, we have $X=x-vt$, so in the S′ system this wave is expressed as follows:

$$(\text{velocity of water})=v\,\frac{a}{h}\,\sin kX-v \qquad (5)$$

$$(\text{height of water surface})=h+a\,\sin kX \qquad (6)$$

Drawing these gives Fig. 4.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Water wave seen in the coordinate system S′.

[Labels in the figure: (水面の高さ) = (height of water surface); (水の速度) = (velocity of water); $X$ 軸 = $X$ axis.]

First, in the S system, let us confirm that Eq. (1), used in the derivation of Green's law, is derived from Eqs. (3) and (4).

Q4. Noting that the energy associated with the wave consists of kinetic energy and potential energy, show that Eq. (1) for the mean energy of the wave holds. Use the fact that the mean of $\sin^2(kx-\omega t)$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Next, let us consider the S′ system.

Q5. Focus on the plane, shown by the dashed line in Fig. 4, that is perpendicular to the $X$ axis at $X$. Also, let the length in the direction perpendicular to the page be $L$.

(a) Let the mass flowing per unit time through this plane in the positive direction of $X$ be $F(X)$. Find $F(X)$ using Eqs. (5), (6).

(b) Show that, within the range in which $F(X)$ is considered up to first order in the amplitude $a$, the height of the water surface does not change with time.

(c) When terms up to second order in the amplitude $a$ are taken into account, $F(X)$ depends on $X$. State what effect the term proportional to the second order of $a$ has on the height of the water surface.

[Hint] If $\Delta X\ (>0)$ is a small quantity, $-\Delta X\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}F(X)}{\mathrm{d}X}$ is the mass flowing per unit time into the part sandwiched between the two planes perpendicular to the $X$ axis at $X+\Delta X$ and at $X$.

Thus, a waveform that was a sinusoidal wave for infinitesimal amplitude is no longer a simple sinusoidal wave when terms of higher order in the amplitude $a$ are taken into account. That waves cause steepening and similar phenomena as they travel is an example of the effect of such higher-order terms (the amplitude-dependent effect).

3. The tidal bore (潮津波, shiotsunami; Tidal bore, ボア) phenomenon

Tsunamis rushing onto the coast and tidal bores (bores) running backward up rivers are both wave behaviours that make one feel the force of water waves. A tidal bore is a step-like wave produced by the change of the sea water level due to tidal action; large ones can be more than $3\,\mathrm{m}$ high, and it is a wave phenomenon famous as the pororoca of the Amazon, the great bore (大海嘯) of the Qiantang River (銭塘江) in China (Fig. 5(a)), etc. Below, as shown in Fig. 5(b), assume that the bore advances toward the upstream side of the river with a constant speed $c$, and let us consider the propagation of the bore, with the water depth and flow velocity behind the bore being $h_1$, $u_1$ and those in front of it being $h_2$, $u_2$. Assume $c>u_2$ and that the shape of the bore does not change with time. That is, seen from a coordinate system moving with speed $c$, the shape of the wave is constant in time.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-4-fig5.jpg

Fig. 5. (a) A bore on the Qiantang River, Zhejiang Province, China. The side with the higher water surface (at the back) is the downstream side, and the lower side (in front) is the upstream side. Quoted from http://www.hztour.jp/lgyakuryu.html. (b) Model water level of the bore. The arrows indicate the positive directions.

Q6. Let the coordinate in the coordinate system moving with speed $c$ be $X$, and suppose that the step-like change of height occurs between $X_1$ and $X_2$ (see Fig. 6). Noting that in this coordinate system the velocities of the water at $X_1$, $X_2$ are $u_1-c$, $u_2-c$, show that the following equations hold. The density of water is constant.

(a) $h_1\,(u_1-c)=h_2(u_2-c)$

(b) $h_1\,(u_1-c)^2+\dfrac{1}{2}\,g{h_1}^2=h_2\,(u_2-c)^2+\dfrac{1}{2}\,g{h_2}^2$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2018-4-fig6.png

Fig. 6. The arrows indicate the positive directions.

[Hint] Focusing on the part sandwiched between $X=X_1$ and $X=X_2$, use the law of conservation of mass and the relation between momentum and impulse. Also take into account the difference in water pressure at $X=X_1$ and $X=X_2$.

Q7. Using the fact that the equations (a), (b) of the previous question hold, show that the speed $c$ of the bore is expressed, using the heights $h_1$, $h_2$ behind and in front of the bore, the velocity $u_2$ in front, and $g$, as follows:

$$c=u_2+\sqrt{gh_1\frac{h_1+h_2}{2h_2}}$$

Q8. Consider the case in which the bore advances against the river flow. Let $u_2=-U$ $(U>0)$, and define the height of the bore as $H=h_1-h_2\ (>0)$. Write the height $H$ in terms of $c$, $U$, $g$, $h_2$, and further find the value $c_2$ of $c$ for which $H=0$. Then, by comparing a general value of $c$ with $c_2$, show that, if $h_2$ is kept constant, the height $H$ of the bore increases monotonically with the value of $c-c_2$.

problems.title: Problem 1: Hitting a tennis ball against a wall
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (70 points)

Hitting a tennis ball against a wall

Consider the motion of a ball when practising tennis or table tennis against a wall. To simplify the situation, we model it as follows. In Fig. 1, the intersection of the wall and the floor is the origin O; the positive direction of the $x$ axis is horizontally to the right along the floor, and the positive direction of the $y$ axis is vertically upward along the wall. The velocities of the ball in the $x$ and $y$ directions are $v_x$, $v_y$, and its accelerations are $a_x$, $a_y$. Further, the mass of the ball is $m$ and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$; air resistance is neglected. The size of the ball and its rotation are also neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. [Labels in the figure: 壁 = wall; 床 = floor; ラケット = racket.]

Assumption ①: We start from the moment when the ball has bounced off the smooth wall at the point P at height $h$, horizontally to the right with speed $v$.

Assumption ②: After that, the ball bounces once at the point A of the smooth floor with coefficient of restitution $e$ $(0<e<1)$, and before the ball reaches the floor again it is hit with the racket (the point where it is hit with the racket is called R). The racket face is smooth, and the collision with the ball is an elastic collision.

Assumption ③: However, when the ball and the racket collide, the racket face is kept tilted by an angle $\theta$ $\left(0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ to the vertical, and the racket is swung with speed $V$ in the direction perpendicular to its face. The mass of the person holding the racket and of the racket is sufficiently large compared with that of the ball, and the speed of the racket does not change between before and after hitting the ball.

Below, let us consider how to determine the position R where the ball is hit, the tilt $\theta$ of the racket and the speed $V$ with which the racket is swung, in order to repeat the wall practice along the same trajectory ($\mathrm{P}\to\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{R}\to\mathrm{P}$).

Q1. Write the equations of motion in the $x$ and $y$ directions of the ball launched from the point P.
Next, for the initial values $x=0$, $y=h$, $v_x=v$, $v_y=0$, find $x$ and $y$ as functions of the time $t$. It is sufficient to do so until the ball reaches the point A.

Q2. Taking the coefficient of restitution when the ball bounces off the wall to be the same $e$ as when it bounces off the floor, show, using the result of Q1, that the trajectories $\mathrm{J_1}$, $\mathrm{K}$ until reaching the floor of the balls launched horizontally from the point P at height $h$ with velocities $v$ and $\dfrac{v}{e}$ are

$$\mathrm{J_1}\quad\cdots\quad y=h-\frac{gx^2}{2v^2} \qquad (1)$$

$$\mathrm{K}\quad\cdots\quad y=h-\frac{g\,e^2x^2}{2v^2} \qquad (2)$$

and that the distance $\overline{\mathrm{OA}}=x_{\mathrm{A}}$ is

$$x_{\mathrm{A}}=v\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} \qquad (3)$$

Q3. Show that the trajectory $\mathrm{J_2}$ of the ball that has bounced at the point A on the floor is, using the position $x_{\mathrm{A}}$ of the point A,

$$\mathrm{J_2}\quad\cdots\quad y=e\sqrt{2gh}\,\frac{x-x_{\mathrm{A}}}{v}-\frac{g\,(x-x_{\mathrm{A}})^2}{2v^2}\qquad (x>x_{\mathrm{A}}) \qquad (4)$$

[Hint] The initial values of the ball that has bounced at the point A are $x=x_{\mathrm{A}}$, $y=0$, $v_x=v$, $v_y=e\sqrt{2gh}$.

Let B be the position on the floor directly below the point R where the trajectories $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{J_2}$ intersect, and let the ratio of the distance $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}\,(=x_{\mathrm{R}}-x_{\mathrm{A}})$ between the point B and the point A, where the ball bounces off the floor, to the distance $\overline{\mathrm{OA}}\,(=x_{\mathrm{A}})$ be

$$f=\frac{x_{\mathrm{R}}-x_{\mathrm{A}}}{x_{\mathrm{A}}} \qquad (5)$$

Q4. (a) Express $f$ in terms of the coefficient of restitution $e$. Consider the case $f<1$.
(b) Show that when $e=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (in which case $f=1$) the trajectories $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{J_2}$ touch each other, and that for $e<\dfrac{1}{2}$ there is no intersection point of the trajectories $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{J_2}$.

Q5. Let the velocity vectors of the ball at the point R on the trajectories $\mathrm{J_2}$ and $\mathrm{K}$ be $\overrightarrow{v_1}=(v_{1x},\,v_{1y})$ and $\overrightarrow{v_2}=(v_{2x},\,v_{2y})$, respectively. Express the components of each velocity in terms of $g,\,h,\,v,\,e$. You may also use $f$.

Q6. As shown in Fig. 2, if the ball arriving along the trajectory $\mathrm{J_2}$ is hit at the point R with a racket of appropriate speed and angle so that its velocity after being hit is $-\overrightarrow{v_2}=(-v_{2x},\,-v_{2y})$, then the ball hits the point P of the wall with horizontal velocity $-\dfrac{v}{e}$ and bounces back horizontally with velocity $v$. Explain why.

Q7. To return the ball as in Q6, what impulse (equal to the change in momentum) should be given to the ball with the racket? Referring to Fig. 2, express the $x$ component and the $y$ component of the impulse in terms of $v_{1x},\ v_{1y},\ v_{2x},\ v_{2y}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2. The vectors $\overrightarrow{n_{\perp}}$, $\overrightarrow{n_{\parallel}}$ are the unit vectors perpendicular and parallel to the racket face, and they are $(-\cos\theta,\,\sin\theta)$ and $(\sin\theta,\,\cos\theta)$, respectively.

Q8. Assuming that only a force perpendicular to the racket face (normal force) acts on the ball, express, in order to give the ball the impulse of Q7, $\tan\theta$ of the tilt of the racket in Fig. 2 and the speed $V$ with which the racket is swung in terms of $g,\ v,\ h,\ e$, using the results of Q5. You may also use $f$.

[Hint] As in Fig. 2, the direction of the vector $\overrightarrow{\varDelta v}=(\varDelta v_x,\,\varDelta v_y)$ is parallel to the direction $\overrightarrow{n_{\perp}}=(-\cos\theta,\,\sin\theta)$ perpendicular to the racket face and perpendicular to the direction $\overrightarrow{n_{\parallel}}=(\sin\theta,\,\cos\theta)$ parallel to the racket face. The ball hits the racket face perpendicularly with the relative velocity $V-\overrightarrow{n_{\perp}}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_1}=V+v_{1x}\cos\theta-v_{1y}\sin\theta$ and bounces back with a relative velocity of the same magnitude. You may therefore use the fact that the impulse given to the ball in the direction of $\overrightarrow{n_{\perp}}$ is $2m\,(V-\overrightarrow{n_{\perp}}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_1})$.

problems.title: Problem 2: Flow of fluids and flow of sand
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (80 points)

Flow of fluids and flow of sand

Fluids such as water and air, and objects such as fine sand (these are called granular materials), flow under external forces. Let us investigate their behaviour when the flow is slow.

1. Flow of a fluid

In general, a body is made of atoms and molecules, and the parts of the body exert forces on each other. When a body is treated on a length (scale) sufficiently larger than the atoms and molecules that make it up, the behaviour of the atoms and molecules is averaged and the body can be regarded as continuous. This is called a continuum. If we imagine an arbitrary surface inside this body, the two sides of that surface exert forces on each other, and the force per unit area depends on the position and the orientation of the surface. This force per unit area is called stress. A fluid is a continuum. The pressure in a fluid is a typical example of such a stress; it arises because gravity acts, and it is perpendicular to the surface considered.

As in Fig. 1, let us consider a system in which a fluid fills the space between horizontal, sufficiently large parallel plates. We take the origin on the bottom surface, the $x$ axis horizontally and the $y$ axis vertically upward. Everything is uniform in the $z$ direction. The thickness (depth) of the fluid is $h$, and the area of the plates is $S$. When the upper plate is pulled slowly in the positive $x$ direction with a force of constant magnitude $F$, the plate eventually reaches a constant speed $U$, and this steady state is maintained. The upper and lower plates stick to the fluid, and the fluid in contact with each plate has the same velocity as the plate. That is, directly below the upper plate the speed of the fluid is $U$, and the fluid at the bottom is at rest. How do the stress in the fluid and the motion of the fluid behave in this case?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Diagram of the flow of the fluid

The upper plate exerts on the fluid in contact with it a force per unit area in the $x$ direction

$$f_h=\frac{F}{S} \qquad (1)$$

Here, imagine in the fluid a horizontal plane at height $y$ $(0<y<h)$ above the bottom, and let us consider the fluid divided into the part $\mathrm{L_1}$ above this horizontal plane and the part $\mathrm{L_2}$ below it. $\mathrm{L_1}$ receives the force of equation (1) from the upper plate, and also receives a force from $\mathrm{L_2}$ at this horizontal plane. On the other hand, $\mathrm{L_2}$ receives a force from $\mathrm{L_1}$ at this horizontal plane, and also receives a force from the lower plate.

Q1. (a) Find the direction and the magnitude $f(y)$ of the force per unit area that $\mathrm{L_2}$ receives from $\mathrm{L_1}$, and show that it does not depend on the height $y$ of the horizontal plane.
(b) Find the direction and the magnitude of the force per unit area that $\mathrm{L_2}$ receives from the lower plate.
[Hint] Neither $\mathrm{L_1}$ nor $\mathrm{L_2}$ is in accelerated motion.

Such a stress acting in a fluid is called shear stress (ずれ応力), since it causes a "shear" (ずれ) in the fluid, or shearing stress (剪断応力; the latter comes from the force acting when cutting something with scissors). In the case of a slow flow like the present one, if the velocity of the flow at height $y$ $(0<y<h)$ is $u(y)$ in the $x$ direction, we may take the magnitude $f(y)$ of the shear stress to be proportional to $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u(y)}{\mathrm{d}y}$:

$$f(y)=\mu\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u(y)}{\mathrm{d}y} \qquad (2)$$

The proportionality coefficient $\mu$ (the Greek letter mu) is called the viscosity (coefficient of viscosity) of the fluid. The property that fluids moving with different speeds exert forces on each other when in contact is called the viscosity of the fluid.

Q2. Express the unit of the viscosity $\mu$ in SI units.

Incidentally, $0.1$ SI unit is called $1\,\mathrm{P}$ (poise). The viscosity of water at room temperature is about $1\,\mathrm{cP}$ $(=10^{-2}\,\mathrm{P}$: centipoise$)$, and that of air at room temperature is about $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{P}$.

Now, the speed of the flow of the fluid is $0$ at the bottom $y=0$. Writing the speed $u(h)$ at the top $y=h$ as $U=u(h)$, if the flow is slow, the flow speed $u(y)$ in between may be written as follows:

$$u(y)=\frac{U}{h}\,y \qquad 0<y<h \qquad (3)$$

Q3. Using equations (1), (2), (3), express the force $F$ pulling the upper plate in terms of $\mu,\,U,\,h,\,S$.

Now, assuming that the fluid consists of $n$ molecules of mass $m$ per unit volume, let us consider from the motion of the molecules how this viscosity arises. Even when the fluid is at rest, the molecules in the fluid are in fast thermal motion. The flow velocity of the fluid is the average velocity of the molecules in random motion, and the speed $v$ of the thermal motion of the molecules is sufficiently larger than the flow speed. Also, the molecules collide with each other frequently, and the average distance $l$ they move between collisions is sufficiently short compared with the characteristic distance over which the flow speed changes. $l$ is called the mean free path.

So, consider a region $\varDelta y=2l$ in a fluid in which the flow velocity in the $x$ direction varies in the $y$ direction (there is a velocity gradient), and let us focus on the motion of the molecules in this region (see Fig. 2).

Now let us focus on the molecules crossing the horizontal plane at height $y$ (called plane $y$). The molecules passing downward through plane $y$ are those in the group of molecules above plane $y$ having velocity in the $-y$ direction. When $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}y}>0$, the average velocity $u$ in the $x$ direction of the molecules passing downward is larger than the average velocity of the molecules below plane $y$. On the other hand, the molecules passing upward through plane $y$ are those in the group of molecules below plane $y$ having velocity in the $+y$ direction, and their average velocity in the $x$ direction is smaller than that of the molecules above plane $y$.

In the group of randomly moving molecules, we consider that the molecules taking part in the motion in the $\pm y$ directions, out of the three directions, number $\dfrac{n}{3}$ per unit volume; further, dividing them into the $+y$ direction and the $-y$ direction, we may consider that the molecules taking part in each of the $\pm y$ motions number $\dfrac{n}{6}$ per unit volume. Also, since the mean free path is $l$, the molecules crossing downward are between plane $y$ and plane $y+l$, and their average velocity in the $x$ direction can be taken to be $u\Big(y+\dfrac{l}{2}\Big)$. Similarly, the average velocity in the $x$ direction of the molecules crossing upward can be taken to be $u\Big(y-\dfrac{l}{2}\Big)$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Diagram of the motion of the molecules and the flow: the motion of the molecules is much faster than the flow speed (thick arrows).

Q4. (a) As the total of the contributions of the molecules crossing in the upward and downward directions, find the (net) momentum in the $x$ direction transferred per unit time and per unit area from above plane $y$ to below it. You may take the speed $v$ of the thermal motion to be constant.
(b) Since the change of momentum per unit time is a force, the momentum found in (a) is equal to the force per unit area acting from above plane $y$ to below it. Express the viscosity $\mu$ in terms of $m,\,n,\,v,\,l$.

Above, we have represented the motion of the molecules by a rough model and considered the origin of viscosity.

Next, as in Fig. 3, let us consider the case in which a viscous fluid flows slowly and steadily on a gentle slope. This flow is brought about by gravity. Let the angle between the slope and the horizontal be $\alpha$; we take the $x$ axis pointing downstream, and the $y$ axis perpendicular to the slope. The flow is laminar, parallel to the slope, with thickness from $y=0$ to $y=h$, and we may assume that the flow speed $u(x,y)$ does not depend on $x$ and is $u(y)$. The fluid is at rest just above the slope $y=0$ $(u(0)=0)$. Also, at $y=h$ the fluid flows with speed $u(h)$ under the atmospheric pressure $p_0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3. A fluid flows steadily with thickness $h$ on a slope of angle $\alpha$. The pressures acting on the upper, lower and side faces of the rectangular region are shown. [Label in the figure: 水平線 = horizontal line.]

Here, let us focus on the rectangular region of unit width in depth, bounded by the small intervals $x\sim x+\varDelta x$ and $y\sim y+\varDelta y$ in the flow. In the $x$ direction, a stress $f(y+\varDelta y)$ acts on plane $y+\varDelta y$ in the $x$ direction, and a stress $f(y)$ acts on plane $y$ in the direction opposite to $x$. This balances the downstream component of gravity in the $x$ direction, $\rho g\varDelta x\varDelta y\sin\alpha$. Here $\rho$ is the density of the fluid and $g$ is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Also, in the $y$ direction, the face at $y+\varDelta y$ is pushed from above, downward, with pressure $p(y+\varDelta y)$, including the pressure due to the atmospheric pressure, and the face at $y$ is pushed back upward with pressure $p(y)$. This difference balances the $y$ component of gravity. Here too, we take the viscosity of the fluid to be $\mu$. Note that the pressures acting on the faces $x$ and $x+\varDelta x$ are equal and cancel each other (the pressure is constant in the $x$ direction).

Q5. (a) Considering the balance of forces in the $y$ direction, find the equation describing the variation of the pressure $p(y)$.
[Hint] You may use the approximation $p(y+\varDelta y)-p(y)\fallingdotseq\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}y}\varDelta y$.
(b) Considering the balance of forces in the $x$ direction, find the equation describing the variation of the shear stress $f(y)$.

Q6. (a) Solve the equation found in Q5 (a) to find $p(y)$.
(b) Show from the equation found in Q5 (b) and equation (2) that the flow speed $u(y)$ in the $x$ direction is

$$u(y)=Cy\,(2h-y) \qquad (4)$$

and find the coefficient $C$. Note that the atmospheric pressure acts perpendicular to the surface of the flowing fluid. Therefore $f(h)=0$.

Q7. Find the flow rate $Q$ per unit width in depth. Here the flow rate is the mass flowing per unit time.

2. Flow of sand

A layer of sand on a plate does not move when the plate is tilted only slightly. However, as the inclination of the plate is increased, the sand eventually begins to flow. Let us consider this flow by focusing on the motion of the sand grains. Here too, as in the case of the fluid, the sand in contact with the plate is assumed to stick to the plate.

An aggregate of fine solid particles such as sand grains is called a granular material; its flow resembles the flow of a fluid such as water in some respects, but the flow is not as simple as that of a fluid, and shows complex and varied behaviour depending on the properties and the state of the particles. Here, however, let us consider the flow of sand with a model simplified as much as possible, following the behaviour of fluids described in 1. That is, actual sand grains have various shapes, and their motion is correspondingly complicated, but the sand here consists of simple, identical particles whose shape need not be considered apart from their mass and size. The particles keep colliding with each other, the motion of each particle keeps changing randomly, and only the average motion is the object of observation.

Let $\theta$ be the inclination angle of the plate when the sand is in a state of steady flow. Let us assume that the sand grains then form layers as in Fig. 4 and flow while colliding with the grains of the adjacent layers. The sand grains have mass $m$ and size $d$ (corresponding to the diameter if the sand grains are assumed spherical). These are far larger than water molecules.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Schematic diagram of the flow of sand

If there were neither collisions nor friction between the sand grains, they would all flow uniformly in uniformly accelerated motion; but since the sand grains are in contact with each other and move while colliding with each other, the surface layer will flow fastest, and the closer to the plate, the slower the flow. So, as in the figure, let us find the behaviour of the speed of each of the imaginary layers. That is, here we assume that the flow in each layer is uniform and steady.

As for the layers, starting from the immobile layer 0 stuck to the plate, the layers are $0,\,1,\,2,\,\cdots,\,i\,,\,i+1,\,\cdots$, and their spacing, parallel to the plate, is approximately equal to the size of the particles, $d$. Further, the figure shows a cross-section of the slope, but taking it to be uniform in depth, we consider the behaviour of layers with unit length in depth. The average spacing of the particles is about $d$. That is, the number density $n$ of this sand is uniform and equal to $\dfrac{1}{d^3}$. Then we take the coordinate axes with the $x$ axis in the direction in which the flow goes down, and the $y$ axis perpendicular to the slope, upward. We assume that a sand grain collides with another sand grain after moving on average a distance $d$, and moves in a straight line until then. Apart from the size of the particles, both the distance between sand grains and the spacing of the layers are taken to be $d$, but even in this case there are suitable gaps between the sand grains, and here we assume that random motion is always possible. $d$ is the mean distance of straight-line motion under such random motion.

For this flow, let us consider, in the same way as in 1., the relation between layer $i$ and layer $i+1$, the one above it. The higher the layer, the faster it is; let the average speeds in the $x$ direction of the grains of layer $i$ and layer $i+1$ be $u_i,\ u_{i+1}$ $(u_{i+1}>u_i)$, respectively. That is, the magnitude of the relative velocity of layer $i+1$ and layer $i$ is $u_{i+1}-u_i$. The sand grains will then keep colliding not only within each layer but also between layers.

When a sand grain in layer $i$ is struck by a sand grain of the slightly faster layer $i+1$, the impact, through subsequent collisions within the layers, affects the flow of each layer so as to suppress the speed of the upper layer and increase the speed of the lower layer.

So, let us first find the change of momentum, i.e. the impulse, in a collision between sand grains of layer $i$ and layer $i+1$. The collision is an inelastic collision with coefficient of restitution $e<1$, and takes place along a straight line.

Q8. (a) When a sand grain of speed $u_{i+1}$ collides along a straight line with a sand grain of speed $u_i$, find the change of momentum (impulse) $J_i$ of the sand grain of speed $u_i$. The sand grains may be treated as point masses of mass $m$.
(b) What is the decrease $\varDelta E$ of the total kinetic energy of the two sand grains in this collision?

However, the collisions of sand grains are in reality not as simple as the straight-line collisions found here; they are extremely complicated, being affected by the velocities and angles at the time of collision, the direction of the momentum change received, and so on, and we do not go into their details.

For these reasons, although the motion of individual sand grains is complicated, we may assume that the difference $u_{i+1}-u_i$ (relative velocity) between the average speeds $u_i$ and $u_{i+1}$ in layers $i$ and $i+1$ is on average the same not only for the $x$ direction but also for the random motion in the $y$ direction. Therefore, let us find the momentum in the $x$ direction transferred per unit time from layer $i+1$ to layer $i$ by the collisions between particles in relative motion caused by this random motion in the $y$ direction.

Q9. The force per unit area in the $x$ direction (flow direction) that layer $i$ receives through collisions between layer $i$ and layer $i+1$, i.e. the stress $f_i$, is obtained as the change of momentum per unit time and per unit area. Taking the number of sand grains per unit volume to be $n$, show that $f_i$ is

$$f_i=B(u_{i+1}-u_i)^2 \qquad (5)$$

and express the factor $B$ in terms of $n$, $d$, $m$, $e$.
[Hint] You may take the number of collisions per unit time and per unit area between particles of layer $i+1$ and layer $i$ to be equal to the product of the number of collisions per unit time of one sand grain, $\dfrac{u_{i+1}-u_i}{d}$, and the number of particles per unit area, $nd$: $nd\times\dfrac{u_{i+1}-u_i}{d}=n\,(u_{i+1}-u_i)$.

Here, we replace the discrete $u_i$ by the continuous flow speed $u(y)$. That is, $u_{i+1}-u_i$ is replaced by $\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}y}\right)\times d$. Therefore $f_i$ of Q9 becomes

$$f(y)=Bd^2\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}y}\right)^2 \qquad (6)$$

This result differs from that for the flow of a fluid.

At the surface layer $y=h$, the sand flows steadily with $f(y)=0$. The gravitational force acting on all the particles between the surface $(y=h)$ and plane $y$ inside a vertical column-shaped region with unit area on the slope is $\rho g\,(h-y)$, where the mass density is $\rho\ (=nm)$; so from the balance with the force along the slope we obtain

$$f(y)=\rho g(h-y)\sin\theta \qquad (7)$$

That is,

$$\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}u(y)}{\mathrm{d}y}\right)^2=C(h-y) \qquad (8)$$

where the coefficient $C$ is a constant. By integrating this, $u(y)$ can be found.

Q10. Express the coefficient $C$ in terms of $g,\,d,\,\sin\theta$, $\rho$, $B$, and find $u(y)$.

Q11. It has been shown experimentally that between the flow speed $u(h)=u_h$ of the surface layer and the thickness $h$ of the layer

$$\frac{u_h}{\sqrt{gh}}=\frac{h}{h_{\theta}} \qquad (9)$$

holds. Derive this relation, and express the constant $h_{\theta}$ in terms of $d$, $\rho$, $B$, $\sin\theta$ (or $d$, $e$, $\sin\theta$).

Above, the flow of sand was discussed with an extremely simplified model. However, actual sand flows behave in a much more complicated way, and they continue to be studied from various angles as a subject of research in "the physics of granular materials".

problems.title: Problem 3: Electric circuits
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (70 points)

Electric circuits

Let us consider direct-current electric circuits made of constant electrical resistances (below simply called resistors) and power sources. There are two kinds of power source: voltage sources and current sources. A voltage source is a source that has a constant electromotive force and whose internal resistance (for a voltage source, connected in series) has the value zero; a current source is a source that supplies a constant current and whose internal resistance (for a current source, connected in parallel) is infinite. Also, the current $I$ flowing through a resistor and the potential difference $E$ across its ends are proportional. When this relation is written as

$$E=R\,I \qquad (1)$$

the proportionality constant $R$ is the value of the resistance, and equation (1) is called Ohm's law.

Q1. (a) Making the value of the resistor $R$ connected between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ of a voltage source as in Fig. 1(a) zero, i.e. shorting (short-circuiting) the terminals, is not permitted as a physical state. Consider what would happen and state the reason.
(b) Making the value of the resistor $R$ connected to the terminals $\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{D}$ of a current source as in Fig. 1(b) infinite, i.e. opening the terminals (open circuit), is not permitted as a physical state. Consider what would happen and state the reason.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. [Labels in the figure: 電圧源 = voltage source; 電流源 = current source.]

Suppose there are different circuits $\mathrm{C_1}$, $\mathrm{C_2}$, each having two terminals. When, on connecting an arbitrary identical circuit $\mathrm{C}$ to their terminals, the relations between the current flowing through the terminals and the voltage between the terminals of the circuits $\mathrm{C_1}$, $\mathrm{C_2}$ are the same, the two circuits $\mathrm{C_1}$, $\mathrm{C_2}$ are said to be equivalent. Equivalence of circuits is defined in the same way when there are three or more terminals.

Q2. Let $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$, $\mathrm{C}$ be the terminals of the circuit in which the resistors $R_1$, $R_2$, $R_3$ are connected in a Y shape as in Fig. 2(a). Also, let $\mathrm{D}$, $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{F}$ be the terminals at the vertices of the circuit in which the resistors $R_{12}$, $R_{23}$, $R_{31}$ are connected in a $\Delta$ (delta) shape as in Fig. 2(b). If the resistances between the terminals A, B, between B, C and between C, A are equal to the resistances between the terminals D, E, between E, F and between F, D of the $\Delta$ circuit, respectively, what relations hold between the resistance values? Express $R_1$, $R_2$, $R_3$ in terms of $R_{12}$, $R_{23}$, $R_{31}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

When relations like those found above hold between the resistance values, the two circuits are equivalent; the conversion from the Y shape of Fig. 2(a) to the $\Delta$ shape of (b) is called the Y-$\Delta$ transformation, and the conversion from the $\Delta$ shape of Fig. 2(b) to the Y shape of (a) is called the $\Delta$-Y transformation.

When a circuit consisting of several resistors is connected between terminals, that resistor circuit can be replaced by a single resistor between the terminals. This single resistor equivalent to the resistor circuit is called the combined resistance.

Q3. Five resistors $R_1$, $R_2$, $R_3$, $R_4$ and $R_5$ are connected between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ as in Fig. 3 (such a circuit is called a bridge circuit). Find this combined resistance for the case $R_1=R_3=R_5=R$, $R_2=R_4=2R$.
[Hint] It is useful to apply the $\Delta$-Y transformation to one $\Delta$-shaped part of the circuit and use the result of the previous question.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

In general, let us consider a direct-current electric circuit combining a finite number of resistors, voltage sources and current sources. Solving an electric circuit means finding the voltages of the nodes of the circuit (connection points or branch points) and the currents flowing in the wires (branches) connecting the nodes. The necessary and sufficient basic laws for solving an electric circuit are known as Kirchhoff's laws. These laws consist of the following two laws.

(1) Kirchhoff's first law (current law)
At any node of a circuit, the sum of the currents flowing in from the connected wires is $0$. Here incoming currents and outgoing currents are taken with opposite signs.

(2) Kirchhoff's second law (voltage law)
Around any loop in a circuit (closed circuit or closed path; see Fig. 4), the sum of the potential differences arising across the elements (resistors, voltage sources, etc.) on the wires making up the loop is $0$. Here the sign of the potential differences is taken with reference to one and the same direction along the loop.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4. [Labels in the figure: 節点 = node; 結線 (枝路) = wire (branch); ループ (閉回路) = loop (closed circuit).]

Q4. The potential difference between two points of a circuit is called the voltage. Taking the node 3 of the circuit of Fig. 5 as the reference, verify, by applying Kirchhoff's laws to different loops, that the voltage of the node 1 is uniquely determined.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

Using voltages, Kirchhoff's second law can also be stated as follows.

(2$'$) Alternative statement of Kirchhoff's second law (voltage law)
Each node in a circuit has a potential. If the potential of each node, taken with the potential of one node as the reference, is called its voltage, then the voltage of each node is uniquely determined.

Let us consider an electric circuit consisting of several resistors, voltage sources and current sources. By Kirchhoff's laws, the current flowing through each resistor is obtained as the solution of a system of linear equations. This system of linear equations contains the electromotive forces $E_i$ $(i=1,2,\cdots N)$ of the voltage sources and the currents $I_j$ $(j=1,2\cdots M)$ of the current sources linearly. Therefore the current flowing through each resistor, or the current flowing in any wire (branch) of the circuit, is in general expressed as

$$I=\sum_{i=1}^{N}f_iE_i+\sum_{j=1}^{M}g_jI_j \qquad (2)$$

where $f_i$, $g_j$ are constants determined only by the resistors contained in the circuit (of course, the current $I$ differs from wire to wire).

According to equation (2), in an electric circuit with several power sources (voltage sources, current sources), the current flowing in any wire of the circuit is equal to the sum of the currents flowing in that wire when each power source is present alone (the other power sources being removed). This is called the principle of superposition, and it is a theorem that holds generally in direct-current electric circuits. Here "removing" a voltage source means short-circuiting the terminals of the voltage source ($E_i=0$ when the $i$-th voltage source is removed), and "removing" a current source means opening the terminals of the current source ($I_j=0$ when the $j$-th current source is removed).

Q5. For the circuit shown in Fig. 6 below, find the current $I$ flowing into the $2\,\mathrm{V}$ power source, using the principle of superposition.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

From two points that are not short-circuited in a direct-current electric circuit consisting of several resistors, voltage sources and current sources, wires are led out and taken as the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ (see Fig. 7). The inside of the dashed rectangle of Fig. 7 is a circuit in which a finite number of resistors are connected, and the voltage sources and current sources have all been taken out to the left side. The figure shows two voltage sources and two current sources, but it is understood that as many are drawn as there are voltage sources and current sources in the circuit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig7.png

Fig. 7.

In this case, the following "equivalent source theorem", or "Thévenin's theorem" (in Japan also called the "Ho–Thévenin (鳳・テブナン) theorem"), is known.

Equivalent source theorem
Any electric circuit with terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ is equivalent to the circuit of Fig. 8(a), which has a single voltage source $E_0$ and a resistor $R_0$ connected in series with it.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig8.png

Fig. 8. [Labels in the figure (c): 電圧源を取り除き短絡 = voltage sources removed and short-circuited; 電流源を取り除き開放 = current sources removed and opened.]

Here $E_0$ is, as in Fig. 8(b), the voltage appearing between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ when the terminals are open. Also, $R_0$ is, as in Fig. 8(c), the combined resistance of the circuit seen from the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ when all the voltage sources are removed and their terminals short-circuited (shorted, i.e. the electromotive force is made $0$), and all the current sources are removed and their terminals opened (open, i.e. the current is made $0$).

Let us prove this equivalent source theorem in a simple case using the principle of superposition. Let us connect a resistor $R$ between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ of the circuit of Fig. 7 as in Fig. 9, and consider the current $I$ flowing through this resistor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig9.png

Fig. 9.

The state of the circuit of Fig. 9 does not change if, as in Fig. 10(a), two voltage sources $V_1$, $V_2=-V_1$ are inserted in series into the resistor $R$ between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig10.png

Fig. 10. [Labels in the figure: 回路 1 = circuit 1; 回路 2 = circuit 2.]

According to the principle of superposition, the circuit of Fig. 10(a) can be regarded as the superposition of circuit 1 of Fig. 10(b) and circuit 2 of Fig. 10(c). That is, the current $I$ flowing through the resistor $R$ between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ of Fig. 10(a) is the sum of the current $I_1$ flowing through the resistor $R$ of circuit 1 of Fig. 10(b) and the current $I_2$ flowing through the resistor $R$ of circuit 2 of Fig. 10(c):

$$I=I_1+I_2 \qquad (3)$$

Q6. (a) In circuit 1 of Fig. 10(b), take $V_1$ equal to the voltage $E_0$ appearing between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ of Fig. 10(a) when they are open. Find the current $I_1$ flowing through the resistor $R$ in this case.
(b) In circuit 2 of Fig. 10(c), take $V_2=-V_1=-E_0$. Letting $R_0$ be the combined resistance of the circuit on the left side seen from the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$, find the current $I_2$ flowing through the resistor $R$.
(c) From the above, explain that the equivalent circuit of Fig. 7 is Fig. 8(a).

Using the equivalent source theorem, the calculation of a circuit can sometimes become easy. Let us find, by different methods in Q7 and Q8 below, the current $I$ flowing through the resistor $R_5$ of the circuit of Fig. 11, in which a voltage source $E$ is connected between the two terminals of the bridge circuit shown in Fig. 3.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig11.png

Fig. 11.

Q7. (a) Let the current flowing through the terminal $\mathrm{C}$ of Fig. 11 be $I_0$, the current flowing through the resistor $R_1$ be $I_1$, and the current flowing through the resistor $R_5$ be $I$. The circuit of Fig. 11 has three independent loops (closed circuits). Specifying these loops suitably, and considering that the potential difference around a loop is zero (Kirchhoff's second law), derive a system of equations with $I_0$, $I_1$, $I$ as unknowns.
(b) Next, solve the system of equations for the case $R_1=R_3=R_5=R$, $R_2=R_4=2R$ and find $I$.

Q8. (a) Considering the ends $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ of the resistor $R_5$ as terminals, find the voltage $E_0$ of the voltage source of the equivalent source circuit (the potential of A relative to B) and the combined resistance $R_0$ when the bridge circuit is viewed from these terminals (see Fig. 12).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-3-fig12.png

Fig. 12.

(b) Next, for the case $R_1=R_3=R$, $R_2=R_4=2R$, find, using the "equivalent source theorem", the current $I$ flowing through this resistor when a resistor $R_5=R$ is connected between the terminals $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ of Fig. 12.

You will see that, using the equivalent source theorem, the same result as in the previous question is obtained more easily.

problems.title: Problem 4: Electromagnetic waves and gravitational waves
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (80 points)

Electromagnetic waves and gravitational waves

What are gravitational waves and electromagnetic waves? A hint for understanding them is that, when we observe the universal gravitation (gravity) of a star or the electric field of a charge, if that star or charge moves, the direction and magnitude of the gravitational field or the electromagnetic field at a distant observation point change, but it takes time for the information about that change to reach the observer. Even if the position of a body changes, in the theory of relativity the effect of the change does not reach the observer instantaneously; the information propagates at the speed of light. Therefore the time at which the change is observed lags behind the time at which the position of the body changed, and the change of the gravitational field or the electromagnetic field travels to the observer as a wave. These waves are gravitational waves and electromagnetic waves.

Below, use the following numerical values if necessary.
Speed of light $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$
Gravitational constant $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}$
Planck constant $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\ s}$
Solar mass $M_{\odot}=1.99\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$
$\dfrac{GM_{\odot}}{c^2}=1.47\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m}$

1. Electromagnetic waves

Emission of electromagnetic waves from a charge

Electromagnetic waves are emitted from a charge in accelerated motion, but when a charge moves in uniform linear motion in vacuum, no electromagnetic waves are emitted.

Q1. Why does an electron not emit electromagnetic waves when it moves in uniform linear motion in vacuum?
[Hint] How does the electron look to an observer moving with the same velocity as this electron?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Accelerated motion of a charge and emission of electromagnetic waves. [Labels in the figure: 電磁波 = electromagnetic wave; 荷電粒子 = charged particle.]

Dimensional analysis (analysis of units)

In physics there are four basic physical quantities in all. Any four independent ones may be chosen, but usually length $\mathrm{L}$, mass $\mathrm{M}$, time $\mathrm{T}$ and electric current $\mathrm{I}$ are adopted. A general physical quantity $W$ is expressed by a combination of these, $\mathrm{L}^a\mathrm{M}^b\mathrm{T}^c\mathrm{I}^d$ ($a,\,b,\,c,\,d$ are integers), and this is called "the dimension of $W$". The dimension of $W$ is written $[W]$. For example, from the definitions, $[\text{velocity}]=\mathrm{LT^{-1}}$, $[\text{acceleration}]=\mathrm{LT^{-2}}$; from Newton's second law, $[\text{force}]=\mathrm{MLT^{-2}}$; and in addition $[\text{charge}]=\mathrm{IT}$, $[\text{energy}]=\mathrm{ML^2T^{-2}}$, and so on. The dimension of a physical quantity is determined from the definition of the physical quantity or from a law containing the physical quantity.

The SI system of units expresses the units of the basic physical quantities $\mathrm{L,\ M,\ T,\ I}$ as the metre $(\mathrm{m})$, the kilogram $(\mathrm{kg})$, the second $(\mathrm{s})$ and the ampere $(\mathrm{A})$, respectively, and the unit of a physical quantity of dimension $\mathrm{L}^a\mathrm{M}^b\mathrm{T}^c\mathrm{I}^d$ is $\mathrm{m}^a\mathrm{kg}^b\mathrm{s}^c\mathrm{A}^d$. Because of this correspondence, dimensional analysis is also an analysis of units.

Q2. Verify from definitions or laws that the dimension of the electric constant (permittivity of vacuum) $\varepsilon_0$ is given by the following equation.

$$[\varepsilon_0]=\mathrm{L^{-3}M^{-1}T^{4}I^{2}} \qquad (1)$$

[Hint] The relation between the proportionality constant $k$ of Coulomb's law and the electric constant (permittivity of vacuum) $\varepsilon_0$ is expressed as $k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$.

Let us understand the emission of electromagnetic waves by dimensional analysis. In the previous consideration, acceleration was needed for emission; when the velocity is small, let us consider the electric field proportional to the acceleration, sufficiently far from the charge. Suppose that a charge $q$ is near the origin, and that when the magnitude of its acceleration is $a$, the magnitude $E$ of the electric field at a distance $r$ from the origin is proportional to the product of the charge $q$ and the acceleration $a$. Then, also taking the distance $r$ into account, $E$ may be taken to have the following form ($E$ depends on the angle, but here we ignore the angle).

$$E=K_1\frac{qa}{r^n} \qquad (2)$$

$K_1$ is unknown; since it is related to electromagnetism, let us suppose that it depends on the electric constant $\varepsilon_0$ and the speed of light $c$. So we assume

$$K_1=A_1{\varepsilon_0}^{l}c^{m} \qquad (3)$$

where $A_1$ is a dimensionless (unitless) constant of magnitude about $1$.

Q3. Using equations (2), (3) above, show by dimensional analysis that $n=1$, and determine $l$, $m$.

Thus the distant electric field produced by acceleration is proportional to $r^{-1}$; it decays more slowly than the $r^{-2}$ of the electric field of a charge at rest, and so it reaches far away. The decay of the magnetic flux density $B$ is likewise proportional to $r^{-1}$.

Q4. Writing the distant magnetic flux density as

$$B=K_2\frac{qa}{r^{n'}} \qquad (4)$$

and assuming the constant to be $K_2=A_2{\varepsilon_0}^{l'}c^{m'}$ ($A_2$ is a dimensionless constant with $|A_2|\fallingdotseq1$), show that $n'=1$ and find $l',\ m'$. (The constant $K_2$ may also depend on the magnetic constant (permeability of vacuum) $\mu_0$, but since $\varepsilon_0\mu_0c^2=1$, the above assumption is sufficient.)
[Hint] The dimension $[B]$ of the magnetic flux density $B$ can also be found from the fact that the magnitude of the Lorentz force on a charge $q$ moving with velocity $v$ perpendicular to the magnetic flux density is $F=qvB$.

Dipole radiation

From the above considerations, both the distant electric field and magnetic flux density decay as $r^{-1}$. It is known that the flow of the energy of the electromagnetic field per unit time and per unit area is proportional to "the product of the electric field and the magnetic flux density". It therefore decays as $r^{-2}$. As a result, the total energy $P$ passing per unit time through the surface area $4\pi r^2$ of a sphere of sufficiently large radius $r$ is constant, independent of $r$. That is, the flow of the energy of the electromagnetic field reaches out to infinity, $r\to\infty$. This is interpreted as electromagnetic waves being emitted.

As expected from this consideration as well, when the velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ of the charge is sufficiently slower than the speed of light ($|\overrightarrow{v}|\ll c$, where in general $|\overrightarrow{A}|$ denotes the magnitude of the vector $\overrightarrow{A}$), the energy $P$ emitted per unit time by a charge in accelerated motion is proportional to the product of equations (2) and (4) multiplied by $4\pi r^2$; independently of $r$,

$$P\propto K_1K_2\,(qa)^2 \qquad (\text{the symbol }\propto\text{ means "is proportional to"}) \qquad (5)$$

According to a detailed calculation, when $P$ is expressed in terms of the acceleration vector $\overrightarrow{a}$,

$$P=\frac{1}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}\,|\,q\overrightarrow{a}\,|^2 \qquad (6)$$

this is known, and is called dipole radiation.

Q5. Verify that the right-hand side of equation (6) has the dimension of energy emitted per unit time.

If the acceleration is expressed as the time derivative of the velocity, equation (6) becomes the following.

$$P=\frac{1}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}\left|\,q\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|^2 \qquad (7)$$

(Note: the time derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}$ of a vector $\overrightarrow{A}=(A_x,\,A_y,\,A_z)$ is a new vector whose components are $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_x}{\mathrm{d}t},\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_y}{\mathrm{d}t},\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_z}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)$. For example, the time derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{x}}{\mathrm{d}t}$ of the position vector $\overrightarrow{x}=(x,\,y,\,z)$ is the velocity vector $\overrightarrow{v}$, $\overrightarrow{v}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{x}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t},\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t},\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)$, and its derivative is the acceleration vector $\overrightarrow{a}$, $\overrightarrow{a}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v_x}{\mathrm{d}t},\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v_y}{\mathrm{d}t},\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v_z}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)$.)

When several charges $q_i$ $(i=1,\,2,\,3,\,\cdots N)$ move with accelerations $\overrightarrow{a}_i$, then, based on the principle of superposition, $q\overrightarrow{a}$ in equation (7) should be replaced by $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_i\overrightarrow{a_i}$. The energy emitted per unit time is then given by the following equation.

$$P=\frac{1}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_i\overrightarrow{a_i}\right|^2 \qquad (8)$$

2. Gravitational waves

When a particle with charge moves in a circle, it emits electromagnetic waves, since circular motion involves acceleration. Similarly, when a star with mass moves in a circle, it emits gravitational waves. The fact that the star gradually loses energy by emitting gravitational waves and its orbital radius shrinks is also similar to the emission of electromagnetic waves by a charged particle.

Electromagnetic waves and gravitational waves are alike in other respects as well. Both propagate at the speed of light $c$, and both oscillations are transverse waves. As for the centripetal force of circular motion, the electric force is proportional to the product of the charges and gravity is proportional to the product of the masses. Also, the magnitudes of both forces are inversely proportional to the square of the distance. On the other hand, they differ in that charge can be positive or negative, but mass cannot be negative. Although electromagnetic waves and gravitational waves differ in some respects, let us focus on the respects in which they are alike and try to understand the emission of gravitational waves by analogy with the emission of electromagnetic waves.

In the formula (8) for the emission of electromagnetic waves, the product of charge and acceleration

$$\overrightarrow{d}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_i\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v_i}}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (9)$$

appeared. Let us apply this to gravitational waves. In the case of gravity, mass will correspond to charge. So, by analogy with equation (9), let us consider as a candidate contributing to the amplitude of the gravitational waves of a system of $N$ stars

$$\overrightarrow{f}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_i\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v_i}}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (10)$$

However, for a system of stars this sum is $0$! This is the difference between the emission of electromagnetic waves by charges and the emission of gravitational waves by stars.

Q6. Prove that in the absence of external forces, equation (10) gives

$$\overrightarrow{f}(t)=0 \qquad (11)$$

(the case of two bodies $(N=2)$ is sufficient).

However, gravitational waves have actually been observed. So let us consider by what mechanism gravitational waves are generated. For simplicity, suppose that two stars A, B of equal mass, separated by a distance $2L$ in the $x$-$y$ plane, move in circles about the centre of mass as in Fig. 2. Let the angular velocity of rotation be $\omega$, and, for simplicity, suppose that a distant observer is on the $y$ axis $(y>0)$ in the $x$-$y$ plane. Let the circular motion of body A be

$$\overrightarrow{x}_{\mathrm{A}}(t)=(x_{\mathrm{A}}(t),\,y_{\mathrm{A}}(t),\,z_{\mathrm{A}}(t))=L\,(\cos\omega t,\,\sin\omega t,\,0) \qquad (12)$$

Below, to simplify the notation, let us write the first time derivative of an arbitrary function $g(t)$ as $\dot{g}$ (with one dot above $g$), and similarly the second time derivative as $\ddot{g}$. Then the contribution of A to equation (10) is

$$\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}=m\,\ddot{\overrightarrow{x}}_{\mathrm{A}}(t)=-\omega^2mL\,(\cos\omega t,\,\sin\omega t,\,0) \qquad (13)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Cancellation of $\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t)$ and $\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{B}}(t)$. [Label in the figure: 重心 = centre of mass.]

Since the motion of body B is $\overrightarrow{x}_{\mathrm{B}}(t)=-\overrightarrow{x}_{\mathrm{A}}(t)$,

$$\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{B}}(t)=-\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t) \qquad (14)$$

Hence the contributions of A and B cancel, and no radiation occurs (Fig. 2). This is an example of equation (11).

Retardation

However, even if the accelerations at the same instant cancel each other, the waves emitted by the stars A, B are not completely cancelled. This is because the waves arriving at the observation point at the same time were emitted by A, B at different times. This is retardation. In the theory of relativity, information is not transmitted instantaneously to a distant place. The electromagnetic force and gravity propagate at the speed of light $c$. Therefore, if a wave from a source at (time, position) $=(t',\,\overrightarrow{r}\,')$ reaches an observer at (time, position) $=(t,\,\overrightarrow{r})$, the following relation holds.

$$t'=t-\frac{|\overrightarrow{r}-\overrightarrow{r}\,'|}{c} \qquad (15)$$

The effect that the time $t$ at which the information is observed lags behind the time $t'$ at which the information was sent by $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{r}-\overrightarrow{r}\,'|}{c}$ is called "retardation". In the case of electromagnetic waves, if the acceleration of the charge at time $t'$ is $\overrightarrow{a}(t')$, the magnitude of the electric field at time $t$ of the distant observer may have the form found in Q2, but when the times are written in detail, because of retardation, the time on the right-hand side of equation (2) becomes, using $t'$ of equation (15),

$$E(t,\,r)=K_1\frac{qa(t')}{r} \qquad (16)$$

Here, the observation point being sufficiently far away $(r\gg r')$, we have approximated $|\overrightarrow{r}-\overrightarrow{r}\,'|\fallingdotseq r$. The important points of equation (16) are that the observation time $t$ on the left-hand side is retarded with respect to the time $t'$ at which the information on the right-hand side was sent, being in the relation (15), and that the electric field produced by a particle in accelerated motion decays slowly at large distances, as $r^{-1}$. These two points are the same for gravitational waves.

Retardation in the case of gravity

The amplitudes of the gravitational waves from the sources A and B reach the observer at a common time $t$ and are superposed. However, the times $t'_{\mathrm{A}}$, $t'_{\mathrm{B}}$ at which the gravitational waves are sent from the respective sources A, B differ in retardation, because the distances from the sources to the observer differ slightly; the difference is

$$\varDelta t'=t'_{\mathrm{A}}-t'_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{|\overrightarrow{r}-\overrightarrow{r}\,'_{\mathrm{B}}|}{c}-\frac{|\overrightarrow{r}-\overrightarrow{r}\,'_{\mathrm{A}}|}{c}\fallingdotseq\frac{(\overrightarrow{r}\,'_{\mathrm{A}}-\overrightarrow{r}\,'_{\mathrm{B}})\cdot\overrightarrow{n}}{c}\qquad\left(\overrightarrow{n}=\frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{r}\right)$$

From Fig. 3,

$$\varDelta t'=\frac{2L\sin\theta}{c} \qquad (17)$$

Since $t'_{\mathrm{A}}\neq t'_{\mathrm{B}}$, B at the time when the information reaches the observer simultaneously (when $t$ is common) is at a position $\mathrm{B'}$ slightly shifted from the position opposite to A (Fig. 3), and the contributions of A and B do not cancel completely:

$$\overrightarrow{f}(t')\equiv\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t')+\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{B}}(t'-\varDelta t')=\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t')-\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t'-\varDelta t')\fallingdotseq\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t')}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\varDelta t' \qquad (18)$$

$$\therefore\quad\overrightarrow{f}(t')\fallingdotseq\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{f}_{\mathrm{A}}(t')}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\frac{2L\sin\theta}{c}=\frac{2mL\sin\theta}{c}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^3\overrightarrow{x}_{\mathrm{A}}(t')}{\mathrm{d}t^3} \qquad (19)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Generation of gravitational waves by retardation. [Labels in the figure: 観測者 = observer; 重心 = centre of mass.]

Using equation (12) for $\overrightarrow{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$, from equation (19) and $\theta=\omega t'$, the contribution to the gravitational wave is proportional to

$$\overrightarrow{f}(t')=\frac{2\omega^3mL^2}{c}\,\left(\sin^2\omega t',\,-\sin\omega t'\cos\omega t',\,0\right)$$

Since the gravitational wave is transverse and the observer is in the $y$ direction, considering now only the $x$ component,

$$f_x(t')=\frac{2\omega^3mL^2}{c}\,\sin^2\omega t'=\frac{\omega^3mL^2}{c}\,(1-\cos2\omega t')$$

Since only the oscillating part matters for the gravitational wave, the contribution to the gravitational wave is proportional to the following expression.

$$f_x(t')\to-\frac{mL^2\omega^3}{c}\,\cos2\omega t' \qquad (20)$$

Thus, because of the time difference of retardation, the contributions to the radiation from A, B do not cancel completely and are proportional to equation (20). Above we obtained the gravitational wave by a rather forced analogy with electromagnetic waves, and in detail there are parts for which the above analogy alone is insufficient. Here, let us be satisfied that the correct results have been derived: that the amplitude of the energy emission is proportional to $mL^2\omega^3$, as in equation (20), and that the angular frequency of the gravitational waves of a binary in circular motion is not $\omega$ but $2\omega$.

Energy emitted by gravitational waves

The energy $P_{\mathrm{G}}$ emitted per unit time by gravitational waves is proportional to the square of the amplitude of $f_x(t')$ of equation (20):

$$P_{\mathrm{G}}\propto m^2L^4\omega^6 \qquad (\propto\text{ means "is proportional to"}) \qquad (21)$$

As a result, with the distance between A and B being $D=2L$,

$$P_{\mathrm{G}}=K_3m^2D^4\omega^6 \qquad (22)$$

Here $K_3$ is a constant that depends neither on the size $D$ of the source, nor on the mass $m$, nor on the angular velocity of rotation $\omega$. Physically, the constant $K_3$ may be taken to depend on Newton's constant $G$ and the speed of light $c$. We therefore assume that it is expressed as

$$K_3=A_3G^ac^b \qquad (a,\ b\text{ are integers}, A_3\text{ is a dimensionless constant with about }|A_3|\fallingdotseq1) \qquad (23)$$

Since the constants $a$, $b$ are determined as follows, the formula is determined apart from the uncertainty of the constant $A_3$.

Q7. Find the constants $a$, $b$.

Q8. Two black holes of mass $m=30M_{\odot}$ ($M_{\odot}$ is the solar mass) are separated by a distance $D$ and orbit each other with radius $\dfrac{D}{2}$ and angular frequency $\omega$. The motion may always be approximated as circular motion. Gravitational waves from this system were observed, and the angular frequency of the oscillation of the observed gravitational waves was initially $\omega_{\mathrm{G}}=2\omega_0=300\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Find the initial distance $D_0$ between the members of this binary.

Q9. Find the time from the start of the observation until the black holes merge (until the distance between the two bodies becomes sufficiently small). Take $A_3=1$ in equation (23).
[Hint] The gravitational potential energy $U$ of the two stars, taking infinity as the reference $U=0$, is $U=-\dfrac{Gm^2}{D}$, and the kinetic energy $K$, considering that universal gravitation acts as the centripetal force, is $K=-\dfrac{U}{2}$. You may therefore use the fact that the mechanical energy $W$ is (negative and) $W=K+U=\dfrac{U}{2}$. Also, in reality $U=-\dfrac{Gm^2}{D}$ can no longer be used as $D\to0$, but such considerations are ignored here.

Observation of gravitational waves

A gravitational wave may be described as an oscillation of the distortion of space-time. Since it is transverse, consider that it distorts lengths in the directions perpendicular to the direction of propagation, and let the small amount of this distortion be $k$. That is, lengths in space become $(1+k)$ times those in the absence of the gravitational wave.

For example, in the case of the motion of a binary as in Q8, when the gravitational wave is observed at a place at a distance $r$ far from the stars, the oscillation of the distortion $k$ of space due to the gravitational wave is expressed as

$$k=\overline{k}\sin2\omega t \qquad (24)$$

Its amplitude $\overline{k}$ is the amplitude of the distortion of the gravitational wave, and the power of $\omega$ may differ from that of the amplitude of the energy emission. So let us estimate (ignoring the observation angle)

$$\overline{k}=K_4\frac{mD^2\omega^{d'}}{r} \qquad (25)$$

The constant coefficient $K_4$ is assumed to be $K_4=A_4G^{a'}c^{b'}$, using a dimensionless constant $A_4$ close to $1$.

Q10. Find the constants $a',\ b',\ d'$ by dimensional analysis.

Suppose a gravitational wave comes in Fig. 4 from the direction joining M4 to M3. Since the gravitational wave is transverse, suppose that the length in the transverse direction (the direction joining M1 and M2) changes by a factor $(1+k)$ compared with the length in the direction of propagation (the direction joining M3 and M4). Now, as in Fig. 4, laser light (wavelength $\lambda$) emitted from A is split into two at B; the laser light that has made $N$ round trips along the baseline of length $b$ in the transverse direction (M1, M2) and the laser light that has made $N$ round trips along the baseline of length $b$ in the longitudinal direction (M3, M4) are made to interfere at B and split into two, and the laser light in the direction in which they cancel each other by interference in the absence of a gravitational wave is observed.

When there is a gravitational wave, because of the distortion of space, an optical path difference $\varDelta s=2Nbk$ arises between the two laser beams, giving a phase difference $\varDelta\varphi=\dfrac{2\pi\varDelta s}{\lambda}$ between the two laser beams. Then the intensity of the interference light superposed at B changes. The gravitational wave is observed by observing this change of intensity. The number of photons (the intensity of the light) is relevant to this measurement. If the number of photons measured in one period of the oscillation of the gravitational wave is $n$, it is known that, according to the uncertainty relation of quantum theory, the observation limit $\varDelta\varphi_{\min}$ of the phase difference is about $\varDelta\varphi_{\min}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. Therefore the limit of the observational precision is $\varDelta\varphi\geqq\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, or

$$\frac{2\pi\varDelta s}{\lambda}\geqq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \qquad (26)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2019-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Laser interferometer. [Labels in the figure: A レーザー光源 = A: laser light source; B ビームスプリッター = B: beam splitter; M1 ~ M4 反射鏡 = M1 to M4: mirrors; 観測する干渉光 = interference light to be observed.]

From equation (26), a large photon number $n$ is needed to observe a shift $\varDelta s$ much smaller than the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light. To observe the small distortion $k$, efforts are made to increase the baseline length $b$, the number of round trips $N$ and the photon number $n$.

Q11. With an apparatus in which the wavelength of the laser light is $1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, the baseline length is $b=3000\,\mathrm{m}$ and the number of round trips is $N=100$, estimate roughly how many watts the minimum light intensity needed to observe a gravitational wave with space distortion $\overline{k}=10^{-21}$ and frequency $\nu_{\mathrm{G}}=100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ is. You need not take into account observational noise or efficiencies other than those in equation (26).

Concluding remarks

Gravitational waves were first observed with the LIGO detectors in the United States. One LIGO is in the desert of Washington State in the USA and the other in a forest in Louisiana, $3000\,\mathrm{km}$ away; both are interferometers with $4000\,\mathrm{m}$ baselines, and having two of them gives information on the direction of arrival of gravitational waves from the difference of the observation times. The first observation was in 2015: gravitational waves emitted by two huge black holes with masses of several tens of solar masses as they orbited each other. They were observed until the orbit shrank through loss of energy and the black holes merged. In 2017, gravitational waves up to the merger of neutron stars were also observed; in this event the light and $\gamma$ rays emitted at the same time were also observed, and detailed analyses were made. By 2018, gravitational waves from 11 events had been observed, and a new window of astronomy using gravitational waves has been opened. In Japan too, the observatory KAGRA will soon begin full operation.

Note: LIGO is an abbreviation of Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory.
KAGRA is the nickname of the Large-scale Cryogenic Gravitational-wave Telescope, combining "KA" from Kamioka, where it is built, and "GRA", evoking gravity and gravitational wave.

problems.title: Problem 1: Physics of bubbles
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (90 points)

Physics of bubbles

When a sparkling drink is poured into a glass, bubbles rise. Swimming in a pool without making bubbles is extremely difficult, and there are the bubbles that come out of the air pump of a tropical-fish aquarium: we come across bubbles in many situations of daily life. In recent years it has become possible, simply by pumping water through a nozzle, to generate ultra-fine bubbles of size $1\,\mathrm{\mu m}$–$100\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ at a concentration of more than 1500 per $1\,\mathrm{mL}$. On the other hand, bubbles are generated by pressure changes inside pipes through which a liquid flows and on the surface of ship screws (cavitation), and they not only produce noise and vibration in the pipes and screws but can also cause serious damage such as destruction.

A deep-sea submersible has observed bubbles welling up from the sea floor of the Izena Hole (伊是名海穴) in the Nansei Islands (water depth $1{,}333\,\mathrm{m}$). In the process by which bubbles generated on the deep sea floor reach the sea surface, the changes in water pressure and water temperature have a large effect.

Let us examine, with a simple physical model, how a bubble rising in water behaves. The bubble is regarded as sufficiently small and spherical, and the temperature of the gas inside the bubble is assumed to be the same as the water temperature. Assume that the bubble contains an ideal gas. Because of surface tension, the pressure of the gas inside the bubble is higher than the water pressure at the position (water depth) of the bubble, and the difference $\varDelta P$ is given, with $r$ the radius of the bubble, by

$$\varDelta P=\frac{2\gamma}{r}$$

Here $\gamma$ is the surface tension (coefficient) of water; in general it depends on temperature, but here it is taken to be constant, independent of temperature.

Let the atmospheric pressure at the water surface be $P_\mathrm{a}$, the density of water $\rho_\mathrm{w}$, the mass of a gas molecule $\mu$, the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration $g$, and the Boltzmann constant $k_\mathrm{B}$, and answer the following questions.

Q1. Find the pressure $P_0$ inside, and the density $\rho_0$ of the gas in, a bubble of radius $r_0$ at absolute temperature (below simply temperature) $T_0$ and water depth $d_0$.

Q2. A bubble of radius $r_0$ at water depth $d_0$ where the temperature is $T_0$ moves to water depth $d$ where the temperature is $T$, and its radius changes to $r$. During this process the number of gas molecules in the bubble is constant.

(a) Find the equation expressing the relation between the radii $r_0$ and $r$ of the bubble.

(b) In the case where the effect of surface tension can be neglected, find the radius $r$ of the bubble at water depth $d$.

Q3. At water depth $d_0$, two bubbles of radius $r_0$ merge into one bubble of radius $r$. We want to find the relation between $r$ and $r_0$, assuming that the number of gas molecules does not change and that the temperature of the gas inside the bubbles is always $T_0$. When the relation satisfied by $r$, $r_0$ is written in the form

$$\left(1+\frac{\beta}{r}\right)r^b=a\left(1+\frac{\beta}{r_0}\right)r_0^b$$

determine $a$, $b$, $\beta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Schematic diagram of the bubble. [Labels in the figure: 大気圧 $P_\mathrm{a}$ = atmospheric pressure $P_\mathrm{a}$; 水面 = water surface; 水 = water; 密度 $\rho_\mathrm{w}$ = density $\rho_\mathrm{w}$; 水温 $T$, 水温 $T_0$ = water temperature $T$, $T_0$.]

Q4. In the case where the effect of $\beta$ is small, we want to find approximately the $r$ that satisfies the relation of the previous question.

(a) First, let $r_1$ be $r$ when $\beta=0$. Express $r_1$ in terms of $r_0$, $a$, $b$.

(b) When $\beta\neq0$, $r$ deviates from $r_1$. In the case $\dfrac{|\beta|}{r_1}\ll1$ the deviation is small; suppose that, to first order in $\dfrac{\beta}{r_1}$, it is given by $r\fallingdotseq r_1\left(1+C\dfrac{\beta}{r_1}\right)$. Express the coefficient $C$ in terms of $a$, $b$ so that this expression satisfies the relation of the previous question to first order in $\dfrac{\beta}{r_1}$. Use the approximation $(1+x)^q\fallingdotseq1+qx$ for $|x|\ll1$, and neglect small quantities of second and higher order in $\dfrac{\beta}{r_1}$.

Bubbles arouse human curiosity in East and West alike. Gérard Liger-Belair of France, as a graduate student, became interested in the phenomenon on seeing bubbles rising in a glass, and, learning that hardly any research had been done on it, decided to make it the theme of his doctoral thesis. He wrote a letter to the company selling the French luxury champagne "Moët & Chandon", asking whether it was proper for a company selling champagne to leave the questions about its bubbles unanswered; his proposal was accepted, the company adopted it and he came to do the research. He moved to the University of Reims near the company and devoted himself to research on champagne bubbles. He not only measured the size and rising speed of the bubbles, but also clarified how bubbles are generated continuously in a glass and how they burst.

First, how are the bubbles generated? With the cork in place, high-pressure carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_2}$) is sealed in the champagne, and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ at a concentration in balance with it is dissolved in the liquid champagne. However, when the cork is removed, the pressure falls to atmospheric pressure, so the balance is broken and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ can vaporize from the liquid surface. It cannot vaporize directly in the bulk of the liquid, but vibration or stirring of the liquid, or scratches or dirt on the inner surface of the container, trigger vaporization and tiny bubbles are formed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-1-fig2.jpg

Fig. 2. Champagne bubbles. Gérard Liger-Belair, translated by Mineo Tachibana, シャンパン 泡の科学 (Hakusuisha), p. 57 Fig. 5 and p. 64 Fig. 8.

Up to now the amount of gas in a bubble has been taken to be constant, but in the case of champagne $\mathrm{CO_2}$ also vaporizes from the liquid surface on the inside of the bubble (the inner wall), so the amount of gas inside the bubble increases. Also, when a spherical bubble of radius $r$ moves with speed $v$ in a liquid of viscosity coefficient $\eta$ (the Greek letter eta), it experiences a resistive force of magnitude $4\pi\eta rv$.

Taking these circumstances into account, let us consider the generation and motion of the bubbles. Below, the temperature $T$ of the champagne is the same everywhere, the gas in the bubbles is also at the same temperature $T$, the pressure of the liquid is equal to atmospheric pressure independent of depth, and the gas in the bubbles is entirely $\mathrm{CO_2}$. In answering, use the symbols and values of the physical quantities in Table 1 as needed.
