$$\begin{array}{lcl} \text{Physical quantity} & \text{Symbol} & \text{Value} \\ \hline \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{CO_2} & M & 44.0\,\mathrm{g/mol} \\ \text{Density of champagne} & \rho_\mathrm{L} & 0.983\,\mathrm{g/cm^3} \\ \text{Atmospheric pressure} = 1\text{ atm} & P_\mathrm{a} & 1.013\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa} \\ \text{Magnitude of gravitational acceleration} & g & 9.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \\ \text{Avogadro constant} & N_\mathrm{A} & 6.02\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{/mol} \\ \text{Boltzmann constant} & k_\mathrm{B} & 1.38\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K} \end{array}$$

Table 1. Physical quantities and their values.

If the internal pressure of a bubble is larger than the pressure inside the bottle before opening, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ cannot vaporize from the inner wall of the bubble, so such bubbles are not formed even after opening. On the other hand, because of the effect of surface tension, the smaller the bubble, the larger its internal pressure, so the minimum radius of the bubbles formed just after opening is determined by the pressure inside the bottle before opening. Let us estimate the surface tension of champagne, assuming that the internal pressure of the smallest bubble is equal to the pressure in the bottle before opening.

Q5. Taking the pressure of the champagne before the cork is removed to be 5.0 atm and the radius of the smallest bubble formed just after opening to be $0.30\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, find the surface tension $\gamma$ of champagne. Also find the number $N$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ molecules in that bubble. Take the temperature of the champagne to be $280\,\mathrm{K}$ ($7\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

Q6. Let $\alpha$ be the rate of production of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ from the inner wall of a bubble per unit time and per unit surface area. Find the time rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t}$ of the number $N$ of gas molecules in a bubble of radius $r$.

Q7. Find the resultant $F$ of the gravitational force, the buoyant force and the resistive force acting on a bubble of radius $r$ rising with velocity $v$ in champagne. Take forces as positive upward.

In the following questions you may use $F$ unless otherwise specified.

Q8. The bubble takes in gas from its inner wall. Let the mass of the gas in the bubble at time $t$ be $m$ and the velocity of the bubble $v$, and let the mass of the gas in the bubble at time $t+\varDelta t$ be $m'$ and the velocity of the bubble $v'$. Taking the force $F$ acting on the bubble during the time $\varDelta t$ to be constant, write the relation that holds between the change in momentum during that time and the force. Assume that the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ gas in the champagne is at rest before it is taken into the bubble.

Q9. For the relation obtained in the previous question, with $\varDelta v=v'-v$ and $\varDelta m=m'-m$, take the limit $\varDelta t\to0$ and express the equation of motion of the bubble in terms of $m$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}$, $v$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$, $F$. The second-order small quantity $\varDelta m\varDelta v$ may be neglected.

When the water depth is less than about $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ and the radius of the bubble is more than about $100\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, then, to the accuracy we are considering, the effects of water pressure and surface tension on the pressure of the gas in the bubble can be neglected compared with atmospheric pressure. Below, we consider the motion of the bubble taking the gas pressure in the bubble to be equal to atmospheric pressure.

Q10. When the internal pressure of the bubble is constant, the production rate $\alpha$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ from the inner wall of the bubble is constant. Taking $\alpha$ in Q6 as a constant, find the time variation of the radius $r$ of a bubble whose radius is $r_0$ at $t=0$, as a function of the elapsed time $t$.

Q11. Since the mass of the gas in the bubble is small compared with the mass of the liquid displaced by the bubble, when the bubble rises one can regard the buoyant force and the resistive force as approximately balanced. From this condition, express the rising speed $v$ of the bubble by an expression containing $r$.

When champagne is poured into a very clean glass, it hardly foams at all. Continuous bubbles from a particular place are in many cases generated from the lumen of tubular cellulose fibres that have come off paper or cloth and stuck to the inside of the glass; in that case the initial diameter of the bubbles coincides with the inner diameter of the fibre. The bubbles are generated periodically, as precisely as a clock, and the frequency of bubble generation is constant for each generation site.

Q12. Fig. 3 is an image, at one instant, of bubbles being generated continuously every $70\,\mathrm{ms}$. Taking the temperature of the champagne to be $280\,\mathrm{K}$, focus on the second bubble from the top of the figure and, using the top three bubbles, roughly estimate the viscosity coefficient $\eta$ of the champagne and the production rate $\alpha$ of the number of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ molecules in the bubble per unit time and per unit surface area. Treat the bubbles as spherical and evaluate the positions of the bubbles at the centres of the spheres. Show not only the numerical calculation but also the reasoning of the calculation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-1-fig3.jpg

Fig. 3. Champagne bubbles generated at regular intervals. Gérard Liger-Belair, translated by Mineo Tachibana, シャンパン 泡の科学 (Hakusuisha), p. 64 Fig. 8, modified.

problems.title: Problem 2A: Refractive index of a dielectric
problems.problem:
Problem 2A (50 points)

Refractive index of a dielectric

Light travels in straight lines when it propagates in vacuum or in a uniform medium, but when it enters a medium from vacuum, or passes from one medium into another, it is reflected and refracted. For reflection, the law of reflection, "the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal", holds.

On the other hand, for refraction, a law of refraction based on the (absolute) refractive index characteristic of each medium holds between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction. This law of refraction is generally called Snell's law, and the refractive index is determined by the physical properties of the medium.

In this Problem A we consider how the refractive index of a transparent dielectric (with no absorption or scattering of light) is determined.

I. Refractive index

According to the laws of electromagnetism, the speed $c_0$ of light (an electromagnetic wave in which electric and magnetic fields oscillate and propagate) travelling in vacuum is given in terms of the permittivity of vacuum (also called the electric constant) $\varepsilon_0$ and the permeability of vacuum (also called the magnetic constant) $\mu_0$ by

$$c_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}} \qquad (1)$$

and the speed of light travelling in a medium of permittivity $\varepsilon$ and permeability $\mu$ is given by

$$c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}} \qquad (2)$$

The refractive index $n$ of the medium is defined by

$$n=\frac{c_0}{c} \qquad (3)$$

In this problem we consider the refractive index of dielectrics taking $\mu=\mu_0$. The relative permittivity $\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}$ of the medium is defined by

$$\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}=\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad (4)$$

Q1. Express the refractive index $n$ of a medium in terms of the relative permittivity $\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}$ of that medium.

II. Gauss's law

When a force $\overrightarrow{f}$ acts on a point charge $q$ placed at a point, the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ at that point is defined by the relation

$$\overrightarrow{f}=q\overrightarrow{E} \qquad (5)$$

From Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges at rest in vacuum and the definition (5) of the electric field, the force $\overrightarrow{f}$ acting on a point charge $q'$ at the point with position vector $\overrightarrow{r}$ at distance $r$ from a point charge $q\ (>0)$ at the origin, as in Fig. 1, and the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ at that point are expressed, using the proportionality constant $k_0$ of Coulomb's law in vacuum, as follows.

$$\overrightarrow{f}=k_0\frac{qq'}{r^2}\frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{r}$$

$$\overrightarrow{E}=\frac{\overrightarrow{f}}{q'}=k_0\frac{q}{r^2}\frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{r}$$

Here $\dfrac{\overrightarrow{r}}{r}$ represents the unit vector in the direction of $\overrightarrow{r}$. Since $q\ (>0)$, the strength of the electric field is

$$E=k_0\frac{q}{r^2}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

The curves obtained by connecting tiny arrows that represent the direction of the electric field at each point are called electric field lines. Therefore the electric field on a field line is along its tangent, and the density of the field lines (the number of field lines per unit area perpendicular to the field lines) gives the strength of the electric field. That is, $E$ field lines are drawn per unit area of a surface perpendicular to the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$.

Q2. Show that the total number of field lines coming out of a point charge $q\ (>0)$ is expressed, using the permittivity of vacuum $\varepsilon_0$, as

$$\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad (6)$$

Here the proportionality constant $k_0$ of Coulomb's law is given in terms of $\varepsilon_0$ by

$$k_0=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$$

In the same way as in Q2, it can be shown that when $q<0$ the point charge $q$ absorbs $\dfrac{|q|}{\varepsilon_0}$ field lines. It is known that these results can be further generalized as follows.

As in Fig. 2, the total number of field lines going out from an arbitrary closed surface S (a closed curved surface such as a spherical surface or the surface of a rectangular box), with $Q$ the total charge inside S, is

$$\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad (7)$$

Here $Q$ may be either positive or negative, and the number of field lines entering through the closed surface is counted with a negative sign. This is called Gauss's law.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

III. Electric field inside and outside a sphere with uniformly distributed charge

Using Gauss's law explained above, let us consider the electric field inside and outside a sphere of radius $R$ with charge uniformly distributed inside it.

Q3. As in Fig. 3, with O the centre of the sphere, the electric field produced at a point $\mathrm{P_1}$ outside the sphere at distance $r\ (>R)$ from the point O is equal to the electric field produced at the point $\mathrm{P_1}$ when the total charge $Q$ in the sphere is placed at the centre O of the sphere. Explain this using Gauss's law.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Furthermore, from Gauss's law it can be shown that, as in Fig. 4, the electric field produced at a point $\mathrm{P_2}$ inside the sphere at distance $r\ (<R)$ from the centre O of the sphere is equal to the electric field produced at the point $\mathrm{P_2}$ when the total charge distributed inside the sphere of radius $r\ (<R)$ centred at the point O is placed at the point O.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

IV. Model of the electric polarization of a dielectric

The displacement of the centres of the positive and negative charge distributions by an electric field is called electric polarization. An atom consists of a nucleus, a positive point charge, and electrons with negative charge of finite extent (this is called the electron cloud); when no electric field is applied the centres of the charge distributions coincide, but when an electric field is applied the charge distribution changes and electric polarization occurs. When there is no electric field, as in the left diagram of Fig. 5, the position O of the positively charged nucleus and the position O$'$ of the centre of the negative charge of the electron cloud coincide. When an electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ is applied to the atom, the heavy nucleus hardly moves, but the light electrons move in the direction opposite to the field, and, as in the right diagram of Fig. 5, the position O of the nucleus and the position of the centre O$'$ of the electron cloud are displaced. This is called the electric polarization of the atom.

Now take the $x$ axis in the direction of the electric field with the position O of the nucleus as origin. Let the displacement between the centre of the electron cloud and the position of the nucleus be $x$ (the coordinate of the centre O$'$ of the electron cloud is $-x$), the charge of the nucleus $q$, and the charge of the electron cloud $-q$. The positively charged nucleus is a point charge, while the negative charge $-q$ of the electron cloud is assumed to be distributed uniformly inside a sphere of radius $a$. When the centre of the electron cloud is displaced in this way, a restoring force acts between the nucleus at the centre and the electron cloud.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5. Model of the electric polarization of an atom.

Q4. When the nucleus and the centre of the electron cloud are displaced (right diagram of Fig. 5) and the coordinate of the centre O$'$ of the electron cloud is $-x$ ($-a<-x<0$), show that the electric field in the $x$ direction (positive in the positive $x$ direction) produced by the electron cloud at the point O of the nucleus can be written as $E_x=-K_1x$, and express the proportionality constant $K_1$ in terms of $a$, $k_0$, $q$.

Q5. In the case of Q4 (the coordinate $-x$ of the centre O$'$ of the electron cloud satisfies $-a<-x<0$), show that the force acting from the nucleus on the electron cloud of negative charge $-q$ can be written as

$$f=Kx$$

and express the proportionality constant $K$ in terms of $a$, $k_0$, $q$.

When the coordinate of the centre O$'$ of the electron cloud satisfies $0<-x<a$, the force acting from the nucleus on the electron cloud is also expressed by the same formula. Therefore, below, the force acting on the electron cloud with centre coordinate $-x$ is put, in the range $|x|<a$, as

$$f=Kx \qquad (8)$$

As in Fig. 6, when a uniform external electric field directed to the right is applied to a flat slab of dielectric, the atoms in the dielectric are polarized, and positive charge due to the polarization appears in region I at the right end face of the dielectric and negative charge due to the polarization appears in region II at the left end face. The end faces of the dielectric are sufficiently wide, and the polarization charges appear uniformly. Taking the rightward direction (the direction of the $x$ axis) as positive, let the electric field in the dielectric be $E(t)$, the external electric field $E_\mathrm{ex}(t)$, and the oppositely directed electric field due to the polarization of the dielectric $-E_\mathrm{p}(t)$; then

$$E(t)=E_\mathrm{ex}(t)-E_\mathrm{p}(t) \qquad (9)$$

holds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6. [Labels in the figure: 領域 I = region I; 領域 II = region II.]

In general, when two charges, one positive and one negative, exist as a pair, this is called an electric dipole. An electric dipole in which point charges $q\ (>0)$ and $-q$ are separated by a distance $x$ has the dipole moment $p=qx$.

Let the displacement of the electron cloud be $-x(t)$ and the atomic number density (the number of atoms per unit volume) be $N$, and suppose that charge of uniform surface density $\sigma$ appears on the end face (region I) of the dielectric. When the thickness of the dielectric slab of Fig. 6 (the distance between region I and region II) is $L$ and its cross-sectional area is $S$, the dipole moment $P$ of the whole slab is the sum of the dipole moments $p=qx$ of the atoms contained in the volume $LS$, so $P=LSNp$. Also, since $P$ can be expressed in terms of the surface charge density $\sigma$ as $P=LS\sigma$, we have $\sigma=Nqx(t)$.

Q6. Show that the electric field $-E_\mathrm{p}(t)$ due to the polarization charges at time $t$ is proportional to $x(t)$, and, writing $E_\mathrm{p}=K_2x(t)$, express the proportionality constant $K_2$ in terms of $\varepsilon_0$, $N$, $q$.

Using equation (9), the relative permittivity $\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}$ of the dielectric is expressed in terms of the electric field $E(t)$ in the dielectric, the external electric field $E_\mathrm{ex}(t)$ and the polarization field $E_\mathrm{p}$ as

$$\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}=\frac{E_\mathrm{ex}(t)}{E(t)}=1+\frac{E_\mathrm{p}(t)}{E(t)} \qquad (10)$$

Therefore we see that $\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}$ is determined by the dipole moment $p=qx$ of the atoms.

V. Oscillation of the electron cloud and the refractive index

As found in Q5, when the centre coordinate of the electron cloud of an atom in the dielectric is $-x$, the force $f=Kx$ acts on it from the nucleus. In addition, the force $-qE(t)$ acts on the electron cloud from the electric field $E(t)$ in the dielectric given by equation (9). As a result, the equation of motion of the electron cloud (mass $m$, charge $-q$) is

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}(-x)=Kx-qE(t)$$

and therefore

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=-m{\omega_0}^2x+qE(t) \qquad (11)$$

Here we have put $K=m{\omega_0}^2$.

Q7. When an electric field $E_\mathrm{ex}(t)$ of angular frequency $\omega$ is applied from outside, in the steady state the electric field and the charges in the dielectric are considered to oscillate at $\omega$ as well. Therefore, with $E(t)=E_0\cos\omega t$ ($E_0>0$), put the position coordinate of the charge as

$$x(t)=A\cos\omega t \qquad (12)$$

From the equation of motion (11), express the amplitude $A$ in terms of $m$, $q$, $\omega$, $\omega_0$ and $E_0$.

Q8. Let the magnitude of the charge of the electron (the elementary charge) be $e$ and the mass of the electron $m_\mathrm{e}$, and put $q=\beta e$, $m=\beta m_\mathrm{e}$. Write the angular frequency ${\omega_0}^2$ in terms of $\beta$, $a$, $e$, $k_0$, $m_\mathrm{e}$. Also, with $a=1.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$, $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $k_0=9.0\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m^2/C^2}$, $m_\mathrm{e}=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\beta=7$, find $\omega_0$ numerically to two significant figures.

Q9. (a) The relative permittivity $\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}$ of the dielectric is expressed by equation (10) in terms of the electric field $E(t)$ in the dielectric and the external electric field $E_\mathrm{ex}(t)$. Then, with $n$ the refractive index of the dielectric, show from Q6 and Q7 that

$$n^2-1=N\alpha(\omega) \qquad (13)$$

holds, and find $\alpha(\omega)$ as a function of $\omega$ in terms of $\varepsilon_0$, $\omega_0$, $m$, $q$.

(b) From (a), we see that the refractive index $n$ of a dielectric depends on the atomic number density $N$. Furthermore, from the result of Q8, we see that as long as we consider the refraction of visible light with angular frequency $2.4\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{rad/s}<\omega<5.0\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, ${\omega_0}^2\gg\omega^2$ and $\omega^2$ can be neglected. Show that, dropping the $\omega^2$ term and putting $k_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$, $\alpha$ is determined only by the radius $a$ of the electron cloud and is expressed as

$$\alpha=4\pi a^3 \qquad (14)$$

Q10. The measured refractive indices of water (liquid) and of air at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm are $n_\mathrm{H_2O}=1.3$ and $n_\mathrm{Air}=1.00028$, respectively. By choosing suitably the radii $a_\mathrm{H_2O}$, $a_\mathrm{Air}$ of the electron clouds of the water and air molecules in equation (14), the refractive indices of water (liquid) and air obtained from the model of the electric polarization of atoms of Q9 can be made to agree with the measured values. Find the radii of the electron clouds of the water and air molecules in that case numerically to two significant figures. Take the molecular number densities of water molecules and air molecules to be $N_\mathrm{H_2O}=3.3\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ and $N_\mathrm{Air}=2.7\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, respectively.

Here we have considered the electric polarization of atoms and molecules that are not polarized when there is no electric field, but in general there are also molecules that, while electrically neutral as a whole, are polarized, like water (molecules with polarity). What is relevant to the refractive index is the electric polarization induced by electromagnetic waves in the visible region, and here we have treated one model of it.

problems.title: Problem 2B: Light-ray trajectories in the atmosphere
problems.problem:
Problem 2B (80 points)

Light-ray trajectories in the atmosphere

Here the atmosphere is taken to be an ideal gas consisting of one kind of gas molecule of mass $m$; it can be regarded as a dielectric, and the model of the electric polarization of atoms can be applied to the gas molecules of the atmosphere as considered in Problem 2A. Therefore the refractive index $n$ of the atmosphere for visible light is given, in terms of its molecular number density (number of molecules per unit volume) $N$ and a coefficient $\alpha$, by

$$n^2-1=\alpha N \qquad (1)$$

I. Mirage (蜃気楼)

It is known that a "mirage" occurs when there is a large temperature difference between the atmosphere at the ground and the atmosphere above. The "floating island", which occurs when air is cooled by a cold sea surface, is one example, and it is known to appear often in Toyama Bay in early spring.

The ground surface is taken to be horizontal. Consider the case in which the absolute temperature (below simply temperature) $T$ of the atmosphere rises as the height $h$ above the sea surface increases, so that the refractive index of the atmosphere changes. The effect of gravity is not considered, so the air pressure is 1 atm independent of altitude.

The refractive index of the standard atmosphere ($T_0=273\,\mathrm{K}$, $p_0=1$ atm) for visible light is taken to be $n_0=1.00028$.

The temperature of the atmosphere, and hence its refractive index, is determined only by the altitude above the ground surface and is constant in the horizontal direction. Taking the refractive index of the atmosphere at altitude $h$ to be given by $n(h)$, consider the law of refraction (Snell's law) for a light ray emitted in the direction making an angle $\theta_\mathrm{S}$ with the ground surface.

Q1. As in Fig. 1, divide the atmosphere into layers of thickness $\varDelta h$. Let the refractive index of the atmosphere at altitudes $0\sim\varDelta h$ be $n_\mathrm{S}$. For $l=1,\ 2,\ 3,\ \cdots$, let the angle that the light ray makes with the horizontal plane at altitudes $h_{l-1}\ (=h_l-\varDelta h)\sim h_l$ be $\theta_l$, and the refractive index of the atmosphere there be $n_l$. Here $h_0=0$, $n_1=n_\mathrm{S}$, $\theta_1=\theta_\mathrm{S}$. Letting the angle that the light ray makes with the horizontal plane at altitudes $h_l\sim h_{l+1}\ (=h_l+\varDelta h)$ be $\theta_{l+1}$ and the refractive index of the atmosphere there be $n_{l+1}$, write the law of refraction at the point of refraction P.

Next, after writing out the equations obtained by substituting $l=1,\ 2,\ 3,\ \cdots$, take $\varDelta h\to0$, $h_l\to h$, $\theta_l\to\theta(h)$, $n_l\to n(h)$ and derive the relation

$$n(h)\cos\theta(h)=n_\mathrm{S}\cos\theta_\mathrm{S} \qquad (2)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. [Label in the figure: 地表 = ground surface.]

Consider the case in which, for altitude $h$ in the range $0\leqq h\leqq H$, the temperature $T(h)$ rises in proportion to $h$, and for $H<h$ it is constant:

$$\frac{T(h)}{T_\mathrm{S}}=\begin{cases}1+\dfrac{T_\mathrm{H}-T_\mathrm{S}}{T_\mathrm{S}}\dfrac{h}{H} & 0\leqq h\leqq H\\[2ex] \dfrac{T_\mathrm{H}}{T_\mathrm{S}} & H<h\end{cases}$$

Here $T_\mathrm{S}=T(0)<T_\mathrm{H}=T(H)$.

Q2. (a) With $p(h)$ the pressure and $N(h)$ the molecular number density at altitude $h$, write down the equation of state of an ideal gas in terms of $T(h)$, $p(h)$, $N(h)$ and the Boltzmann constant $k_\mathrm{B}$.

(b) Derive that the molecular number density $N(h)$ of the atmosphere at altitude $h$ ($0\leqq h\leqq H$) is given by

$$\frac{N(h)}{N_\mathrm{S}}=1-\frac{N_\mathrm{S}-N_\mathrm{H}}{N_\mathrm{S}}\frac{h}{H}$$

Here $N_\mathrm{S}=N(0)$, $N_\mathrm{H}=N(H)$. For $T_\mathrm{H}-T_\mathrm{S}<20\,\mathrm{K}$, $\dfrac{T_\mathrm{H}-T_\mathrm{S}}{T_\mathrm{S}}$ can be regarded as a small quantity $\left(\dfrac{T_\mathrm{H}-T_\mathrm{S}}{T_\mathrm{S}}\ll1\right)$, and you may use the fact that this allows the approximation

$$\frac{T_\mathrm{H}}{T_\mathrm{S}}+\frac{T_\mathrm{S}}{T_\mathrm{H}}\fallingdotseq2$$

and the approximation formula

$$\frac{1}{1+x}\fallingdotseq1-x\quad\text{for }|x|\ll1$$

(c) Derive that the refractive index $n(h)$ of the atmosphere at altitude $h$ is given by

$$n(h)=\begin{cases}\sqrt{{n_\mathrm{S}}^2-\left({n_\mathrm{S}}^2-{n_\mathrm{H}}^2\right)\dfrac{h}{H}} & 0\leqq h\leqq H\\[2ex] n_\mathrm{H} & H<h\end{cases} \qquad (3)$$

Here $n_\mathrm{S}=n(0)$, $n_\mathrm{H}=n(H)$.

Take the $x$ axis horizontally to the right along the ground surface ($h=0$), and consider the trajectory of a light ray emitted in the direction making an angle $\theta_\mathrm{S}$ upward from the ground surface. Suppose that the light ray, after reaching its highest point at height $h_\mathrm{m}\ (\leqq H)$, then descends; with the equation of the trajectory $h=f(x)$ and the angle that the light ray makes with the ground surface $\theta$ (positive upward and negative downward relative to the ground surface), we can write

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan\theta=\pm\sqrt{\frac{1}{\cos^2\theta}-1} \qquad (4)$$

Here, on the rightmost side of equation (4), the $+$ sign gives the equation while the light ray is rising, and the $-$ sign the equation while it is descending.

Q3. (a) Express the refractive index $n(h_\mathrm{m})=n_\mathrm{m}$ at the height $h_\mathrm{m}$ of the highest point of the light-ray trajectory in terms of $n_\mathrm{S}$ and $\theta_\mathrm{S}$. Note that at the highest point $h=h_\mathrm{m}$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}x}=0$.

(b) Also, show that when the height of the highest point is $h_\mathrm{m}$, using equations (2) and (3), equation (4) for the rising case can be written, for $0\leqq h\leqq h_\mathrm{m}$, as

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}x}=\sqrt{a\left(1-\frac{h}{b}\right)},\qquad a=a_\mathrm{m}\frac{h_\mathrm{m}}{H} \qquad (5)$$

and express the constants $a_\mathrm{m}$ and $b$ using those of $h_\mathrm{m}$, $n_\mathrm{H}$, $n_\mathrm{S}$, $n_\mathrm{m}$ that are needed.

Q4. The light-ray trajectory that passes through the origin $(x,h)=(0,0)$ and satisfies equation (5) is a parabola and is expressed as

$$h=cx+dx^2 \qquad (6)$$

Determine the constants $c$, $d$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.

Q5. Let $n_0=1.00028$, $T_\mathrm{S}=275\,\mathrm{K}$ ($2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), $T_\mathrm{H}=290\,\mathrm{K}$ ($17\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), $H=20\,\mathrm{m}$, and let the observer be on the ground surface ($h=0$). Also, assume that the mountain of the island rises vertically upward from the coastline, and answer the following questions.

(a) Suppose that the observer could see the middle of the mountain of the raised-up island (height $h_\mathrm{g}$ above the coastline). Express the height $h_\mathrm{g}$, as a function of the horizontal distance $L$ from the observer to the island (its coastline), using the constants $b$, $c$. Answer with the number ① or ② whether the farthest island that can be seen is seen at ① the summit of the island's mountain, or ② the island's coastline.

(b) Determine, in terms of $b$ and $c$, the upper limit $L_\mathrm{max}$ of the horizontal distance to an island of which the observer can see a part.

Below we consider the case $h_\mathrm{m}=H$.

(c) Noting from equation (1) that $n^2-1=\alpha N\ll1$, express the constant $c$ in terms of ${n_0}^2$, $T_0$, $T_\mathrm{S}$, $T_\mathrm{H}$. Also, find $c$ numerically to two significant figures ($T_0=273\,\mathrm{K}$).

Hint: when $h_\mathrm{m}=H$, one can approximate $a\fallingdotseq{n_\mathrm{S}}^2-{n_\mathrm{H}}^2$.

(d) Find $L_\mathrm{max}$ and the elevation angle (the angle between the light-ray trajectory and the ground surface) $\theta_\mathrm{S}$ in that case, each numerically to two significant figures.

II. Distribution of the atmosphere

In I, we considered the refractive index of the atmosphere neglecting the effect of gravity and taking into account the temperature variation of the atmosphere only near the ground surface. As the altitude above the ground surface increases, the temperature of the atmosphere decreases, but the molecular number density of the atmosphere is strongly affected by gravity. Therefore, from here on, for simplicity, the temperature $T$ of the atmosphere is taken to be the same everywhere, and we consider the change of the refractive index of the atmosphere due to the effect of gravity.

As the altitude above the ground surface increases, the air pressure decreases and the molecular number density of the atmosphere decreases. Here we consider how the molecular number density of the atmosphere changes with altitude $h$. The magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is taken to be a constant $g$.

Q6. As in Fig. 2, consider the balance of the forces acting on the atmosphere between altitudes $h$ and $h+\mathrm{d}h$. The molecular number density of the atmosphere in this interval may be taken to be equal to the number density $N(h)$ at altitude $h$. From this, derive that the number density $N(h)$ is

$$N(h)=N_0\exp\left(-\frac{mgh}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right) \qquad (7)$$

Here, with $\mathrm{e}$ the base of natural logarithms, $\exp(x)$ denotes $\mathrm{e}^x$. Also, $N_0$ is the molecular number density of the atmosphere at $h=0$.

Hint: when a function $y$ of $x$ satisfies the equation

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=ay\quad(a:\ \text{constant})$$

this function $y$ is expressed, with $C$ an arbitrary constant, as

$$y=C\,\mathrm{e}^{ax}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

III. Curvature of the light-ray trajectory

As considered in I, let the refractive index of the atmosphere at altitude $h$ be $n(h)$, and let the angle that a light ray (visible light) emitted from the ground surface $h=0$ makes with the ground surface at the point at altitude $h$ be $\theta(h)$, and consider the trajectory of the light ray. The curvature of the Earth's surface is neglected.

Q7. Let $R$ be the radius of curvature of the light-ray trajectory at the point at altitude $h$ (the radius of the circle that coincides with the trajectory at that point). With $\mathrm{d}\theta=\theta(h+\mathrm{d}h)-\theta(h)$, and referring to Fig. 3, express $\dfrac{1}{R}$ in terms of $\theta(h)$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}h}$. Here $\mathrm{d}\theta$ and $\mathrm{d}h$ are small quantities, and terms of second and higher order in small quantities may be neglected. Since Fig. 3 shows a light-ray trajectory that is convex upward, the angle $\theta$ between the trajectory and the horizontal plane decreases as $h$ increases. Note therefore that, since $\mathrm{d}\theta<0$, the magnitude of the small central angle of the sector that coincides with the trajectory at the point P at altitude $h$ is written as $-d\theta\ (>0)$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3. The magnitude of the small central angle of the sector is written as $-\mathrm{d}\theta\ (>0)$. [Label in the figure: 光線軌道 = light-ray trajectory.]

Q8. Using equation (2) of Q1 together with the result of Q7, derive the relation

$$\frac{1}{R}=-\frac{1}{n}\frac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}h}\cos\theta(h) \qquad (8)$$

Q9. For a light ray emitted at the ground surface slightly upward from the horizontal direction, find the radius of curvature $R$ of the trajectory at a point at altitude $h\fallingdotseq0$ near the ground surface, in terms of $m$, $g$, $n_\mathrm{E}$, $T$ and $k_\mathrm{B}$. Here, with the refractive index of the atmosphere for the emitted light ray $n=n_\mathrm{E}$, its molecular number density $N=N_\mathrm{E}$ and the coefficient $\alpha=\alpha_\mathrm{E}$, equation (1) holds. Also, you may take $\dfrac{mgh}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\ll1$, $(n_\mathrm{E}-1)\ll1$, and $\theta(h)\fallingdotseq0$ at $h\fallingdotseq0$ near the ground surface.

Q10. On the Earth, find the radius of curvature of the trajectory that a light ray emitted horizontally from the ground surface describes near the ground surface, and determine numerically whether this light ray goes out of the Earth or not. The Earth is taken to be a sphere of radius $R_\mathrm{E}=6.4\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{km}$. Also, $n_\mathrm{E}=1.00027$, $m=29\times1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $T=300\,\mathrm{K}$, $k_\mathrm{B}=1.38\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

The atmosphere of Venus consists of carbon dioxide as an ideal gas, and the electric polarization model can be applied to carbon dioxide. The atmospheric pressure at the surface of Venus is $p_\mathrm{V}=93$ atm ($1\text{ atm}=1.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$), and the temperature of the atmosphere is $T_\mathrm{V}=740\,\mathrm{K}$.

Q11. Find the radius of curvature of a ray of visible light emitted horizontally from the surface of Venus, and determine numerically whether this light ray goes out of Venus or not. Venus is taken to be a sphere of radius $R_\mathrm{V}=6.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{km}$, the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration at the surface of Venus $g_\mathrm{V}=8.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and the mass of one carbon dioxide molecule $m_\mathrm{C}=44\times1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$. Also, with the refractive index of the atmosphere of Venus $n=n_\mathrm{V}$, its molecular number density $N=N_\mathrm{V}$ and the coefficient $\alpha=\alpha_\mathrm{V}$, equation (1) holds. The coefficient $\alpha_\mathrm{V}$ is expressed, with the radius of the electron cloud $a_\mathrm{C}=1.4\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$, as $\alpha_\mathrm{V}=4\pi{a_\mathrm{C}}^3$.

problems.title: Problem 3: Special relativity
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (80 points)

Special relativity

A coordinate system in which a body on which no force acts moves with constant velocity is called an inertial coordinate system (inertial frame). A coordinate system that moves in translation in an arbitrary direction with an arbitrary speed relative to an inertial frame is also an inertial frame, so there are infinitely many inertial frames. However, in whichever inertial frame one observes, the laws of physics are the same. This is called the principle of relativity.

Einstein proposed the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, according to which the speed of light in vacuum (here denoted $c$) is the same in every inertial frame. The theory based on this principle is the special theory of relativity. If the principle of the constancy of the speed of light is accepted, time depends on the coordinate system.

Consider another inertial frame O$'$-$x'y'z'$ (frame S$'$) moving with constant speed $V\ (<c)$ in the $+x$ direction relative to an inertial frame O-$xyz$ (frame S) (see Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Frame S and frame S$'$. [Labels in the figure: S 系 = frame S; S$'$ 系 = frame S$'$.]

Suppose that at the instant when the origin O$'$ of frame S$'$ coincides with the origin O of frame S, light emitted from the origin O$'$ of frame S$'$ travels in the positive direction along the $y'$ axis, is reflected by a mirror at the point P$'$ on the $y'$ axis, and returns to the origin O$'$. Let the position of P$'$ at the instant the light reaches the point P$'$ of frame S$'$ be the point P of frame S, and the position of O$'$ at the instant the light returns to the origin O$'$ be the point Q of frame S. The phenomenon in which, in frame S$'$, light leaves O$'$, is reflected at P$'$ and returns to O$'$ is observed in frame S as light leaving O, being reflected at P and reaching Q. Let the time in frame S$'$ from when the light leaves O$'$ until it is reflected by the mirror and returns to O$'$ be $t'$, and the time in frame S from when it leaves O until it is reflected at P and reaches Q be $t$. According to the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, the speed of light is the same in both inertial frames, so $2\,\overline{\mathrm{O'P'}}=ct'$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OP}}+\overline{\mathrm{PQ}}=ct$. Since $\overline{\mathrm{OP}}=\overline{\mathrm{PQ}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}=Vt$, $\left(\dfrac{ct}{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{Vt}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{ct'}{2}\right)^2$; that is, the times $t$ and $t'$ are related by

$$t'=t\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{V}{c}\right)^2} \qquad (1)$$

In Newtonian mechanics time is an absolute quantity that does not depend on the coordinate system, but we see that if the principle of the constancy of the speed of light is accepted, time depends on the coordinate system.

Let us consider the time experienced by a person riding in a vehicle moving relative to an inertial frame. This time is the time observed in the coordinate system moving with the vehicle, and is called the proper time. Even when the velocity $v\ (<c)$ of the vehicle changes with time, if we consider a small time interval $\mathrm{d}t$ of the inertial frame and the small interval $\mathrm{d}\tau$ ($\tau$ is the Greek letter tau) of proper time observed in the coordinate system moving with the vehicle, the two are related by the same relation as equation (1).

$$\mathrm{d}\tau=\mathrm{d}t\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^2}=\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\gamma} \qquad (2)$$

Here

$$\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac{v}{c}\right)^2}} \qquad (3)$$

is a quantity that depends on $v$.

In Newtonian mechanics, when in an inertial frame the position vector $\overrightarrow{r}$ of a particle of mass $m$ undergoes a small displacement $\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}$ during a small time interval $\mathrm{d}t$ (see Fig. 2), the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$ of the particle is defined, using the velocity of the particle $\overrightarrow{v}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}}{\mathrm{d}t}$, by the following equation.

$$\overrightarrow{p}=m\overrightarrow{v} \qquad (4)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

In relativity, time depends on the coordinate system, so equation (4) is not appropriate; but the time measured by a clock moving with the particle (the proper time) is a time intrinsic to the particle, so let us express the momentum using the small interval of proper time $\mathrm{d}\tau$ as

$$\overrightarrow{p}=m\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}}{\mathrm{d}\tau} \qquad (5)$$

Using equation (2), equation (5) is expressed as

$$\overrightarrow{p}=\frac{m}{\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac{v}{c}\right)^2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\gamma m\overrightarrow{v} \qquad (6)$$

The expression $\overrightarrow{p}=\gamma m\overrightarrow{v}$ of equation (6) is the definition of momentum in relativity.

In relativity too, as in Newtonian mechanics, force is defined as the time rate of change of momentum. That is, the relation between the force $\overrightarrow{F}$ and the momentum $\overrightarrow{p}$ is given by the following equation.

$$\overrightarrow{F}=\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{p}}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (7)$$

Also, when a particle acted on by the force $\overrightarrow{F}$ undergoes a small displacement $\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}$, the small work $\mathrm{d}W$ done by the force is given by the following equation.

$$\mathrm{d}W=\overrightarrow{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r} \qquad (8)$$

Here $\overrightarrow{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}$ is the scalar product of $\overrightarrow{F}$ and $\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}$.

In general, when there are two vectors $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$, the product $AB\cos\theta$ of the magnitudes $A$, $B$ of the vectors and the cosine of the angle $\theta$ between the two vectors is called the scalar product (inner product) of the two vectors and is denoted $\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}$ (see Fig. 3). That is,

$$\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}=AB\cos\theta$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Let us find the work needed to accelerate a particle of mass $m$ at rest until its speed becomes $v$. With the velocity of the particle $\overrightarrow{v}$, $\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{r}=\overrightarrow{v}\,\mathrm{d}t$, so, noting that $\gamma$ depends on $v$,

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{d}W&=\overrightarrow{F}\cdot\overrightarrow{v}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{\mathrm{d}(\gamma m\overrightarrow{v})}{\mathrm{d}t}\cdot\overrightarrow{v}\,\mathrm{d}t=m\left(\gamma\frac{\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}}{\mathrm{d}t}+\frac{\mathrm{d}\gamma}{\mathrm{d}t}\overrightarrow{v}\right)\cdot\overrightarrow{v}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=m\left(\gamma\overrightarrow{v}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}+\overrightarrow{v}\cdot\overrightarrow{v}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\right)\end{aligned}$$

Therefore

$$\mathrm{d}W=m\left(\gamma v\,\mathrm{d}v+v^2\mathrm{d}\gamma\right) \qquad (9)$$

Note that here $\mathrm{d}v$ is the small change in the speed, not the magnitude of the small vector $\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}$. $\mathrm{d}v$ is the magnitude of the component of the vector $\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}$ in the direction of the vector $\overrightarrow{v}$, that is, $\mathrm{d}v=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{v}}{v}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{v}$.

Q1. Using equation (3), derive the following equation from equation (9).

$$\mathrm{d}W=mc^2\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\gamma}{\mathrm{d}v}\,\mathrm{d}v=mc^2\,\mathrm{d}\gamma \qquad (10)$$

The work needed to accelerate a particle from rest to speed $v$ is called the kinetic energy. With $K$ the kinetic energy, since $\gamma=1$ when $v=0$, from equation (10)

$$K=mc^2\int_0^v\frac{\mathrm{d}\gamma}{\mathrm{d}v}\,\mathrm{d}v=mc^2\int_1^\gamma\mathrm{d}\gamma=mc^2(\gamma-1) \qquad (11)$$

If this equation is expressed as

$$K=E-E_0 \qquad (12)$$

$$E=\gamma mc^2=\frac{mc^2}{\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac{v}{c}\right)^2}} \qquad (13)$$

$$E_0=mc^2 \qquad (14)$$

then $E$ can be interpreted as the total energy that a particle of mass $m$ has when moving with speed $v$, $E_0$ as the energy that a particle at rest has (the rest energy), and their difference $E-E_0$ as the kinetic energy. From equations (6) and (13), the following relation holds among $m$, $p$, $E$.

$$(cp)^2+(mc^2)^2=E^2 \qquad (15)$$

Q2. (a) Suppose that a rocket of mass $m$ is accelerated from rest in an inertial frame in gravity-free space by a constant force $F$. Find the speed $v$ after time $t$. Assume that the motion is one-dimensional and treat it relativistically.

Confirm that when $t\ll\dfrac{mc}{F}$, $v(t)$ agrees with the result of Newtonian mechanics.

(b) Find the distance $x$ travelled during the time $t$.

Hint: it is useful to change variables, for example to $u=(Ft)^2$.

(c) The relation between the time (proper time) $\tau$ experienced by the occupants of the rocket and the time $t$ in the inertial frame in which the motion of the rocket is observed is

$$\tau=\int_0^t\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t$$

Find the relation between the proper time $\tau$ and $t$ in the case of (a) (express $\tau$ in terms of $t$).

Hint: you may use the indefinite integral $\displaystyle\int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=\log\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right|+\text{constant}$.

Q3. (a) When the rocket is accelerated with an acceleration $\dfrac{F}{m}=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, close to the gravitational acceleration on the Earth, find, in units of days ($1\text{ day}=24\text{ hours}=8.64\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s}$), the time until the speed of the rocket becomes 0.9 times the speed of light ($c=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$). Give two significant figures (likewise below).

(b) Find, in units of light years ($1\text{ light year}=3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}\times8.64\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s/day}\times365\,\mathrm{day}=9.46\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{m}$), the distance travelled until the speed of the rocket becomes 0.9 times the speed of light.

(c) Find, in units of days, the time experienced by the occupants until the speed of the rocket becomes 0.9 times the speed of light.

The force $\overrightarrow{F}$ experienced by a charged particle of charge $q$ moving with velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ in a space where there is a magnetic field of magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B}$ is expressed by the following equation.

$$\overrightarrow{F}=q\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{B} \qquad (16)$$

Here $\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{B}$ is the vector product of $\overrightarrow{v}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$.

In general, the vector that is perpendicular to the plane (parallelogram) formed by two vectors $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$, whose magnitude is the area $AB\sin\theta$ of the parallelogram ($\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors), and whose direction is the direction in which a right-handed screw advances when it is turned from $\overrightarrow{A}$ to $\overrightarrow{B}$ (through the angle smaller than $180^\circ$), is called the vector product (outer product) of $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$ and is denoted $\overrightarrow{A}\times\overrightarrow{B}$ (see Fig. 4). When $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$ are parallel ($\theta=0$) or antiparallel ($\theta=180^\circ$), $\overrightarrow{A}\times\overrightarrow{B}=0$. Note that the vector product reverses sign when the order of the product is reversed ($\overrightarrow{B}\times\overrightarrow{A}=-\overrightarrow{A}\times\overrightarrow{B}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2020-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Vector product.

In a magnetic field, the force experienced by a charged particle always acts perpendicular to the velocity of the particle, so no work is done on the particle and the kinetic energy of the particle does not change. In a uniform magnetic field a charged particle can move in a circle with constant speed.

Q4. A charged particle of mass $m$ and charge $q\ (>0)$ is moving in a circle of radius $R$ in a uniform magnetic field of magnetic flux density of magnitude $B$. Treating it relativistically, find the speed $v$ of the charged particle (express $v$ in terms of $m$, $q$, $B$, $R$).

Q5. Show that the angular velocity of the particle (the angular frequency of the rotation) $\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}$ is expressed as

$$\omega=\frac{qB}{m}\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^2}$$

When the speed of the particle is small compared with the speed of light ($v\ll c$), $\omega$ has a constant value $\Bigl(\dfrac{qB}{m}$, the cyclotron angular frequency$\Bigr)$, but relativistically it depends on the speed.

Microscopic particles such as light and electrons have both particle-like and wave-like properties. This is called wave–particle duality. This duality was elucidated by quantum mechanics, established in the first half of the 20th century. The duality of classical particles and waves is a characteristic of quantum-theoretical "quanta". Roughly speaking, we may consider that light behaves as particles (photons) when it is emitted and when it is annihilated, and behaves as a wave (light wave) when it propagates through space. A light wave is characterized by its frequency $\nu$ and wavelength $\lambda$, and a photon by its energy $E$ and momentum $p$. Between $\nu$ and $\lambda$, and between $E$ and $p$, there are respectively the following relations.

$$\lambda=\frac{c}{\nu},\qquad p=\frac{E}{c} \qquad (17)$$

Since the mass of the photon is 0, putting $m=0$ in equation (15) gives the relation between $p$ and $E$ in equation (17). The magnitude $p$ of the momentum and the energy $E$ of a photon are related to the wavelength $\lambda$ and the frequency $\nu$ as a light wave, respectively, as follows. $h$ is the Planck constant.

$$p=\frac{h}{\lambda},\qquad E=h\nu \qquad (18)$$

Although the mass of the photon is 0, it has momentum, so one can consider a rocket propelled using the reaction when photons are emitted. The reaction of photons is one of the candidates for an effective propulsive force in gravity-free outer space. Such a rocket is called a photon rocket.

In Q2 we did not consider the origin of the force that propels the rocket, but energy is needed to accelerate a rocket. Suppose that an ideal photon rocket that can convert rest energy (mass) into photon energy without loss has been realized. Suppose that this photon rocket is accelerated from rest in gravity-free space. Let the initial mass of the rocket be $m_0$, and the speed of the rocket when its mass has become $m$ be $v$. The motion of the rocket is assumed to be one-dimensional.

According to the law of conservation of energy, the sum of the energy $\gamma mc^2$ of the rocket of speed $v$ and the total energy $E_\mathrm{p}$ of the photons emitted in the meantime is equal to the energy $m_0c^2$ of the rocket at rest.

$$\gamma mc^2+E_\mathrm{p}=m_0c^2 \qquad (19)$$

Also, according to the law of conservation of momentum, the magnitude $\gamma mv$ of the momentum of the rocket when its speed has become $v$ is equal to the magnitude $\dfrac{E_\mathrm{p}}{c}$ of the total momentum of the emitted photons.

$$\gamma mv=\frac{E_\mathrm{p}}{c} \qquad (20)$$

Q6. Eliminating $E_\mathrm{p}$ from equations (19) and (20), express the mass ratio $\dfrac{m}{m_0}$ in terms of $\dfrac{v}{c}$.

Q7. (a) Show that the following relation holds between the time rate of change of the momentum $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t}$ of the ideal photon rocket and its acceleration $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$.

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{m_0}{\left(1+\dfrac{v}{c}\right)^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

(b) Find the time variation of the momentum $p$ of an ideal photon rocket accelerated from rest with a constant acceleration $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=a$.

Q8. (a) When the speed of the ideal photon rocket has become 0.9 times the speed of light, what percentage of the initial mass $m_0$ is the mass $m$ of the rocket? Give two significant figures (likewise below).

(b) When the speed of the ideal photon rocket has become 0.9 times the speed of light, what percentage of $m_0c$ is the momentum $p$ of the rocket?

Q9. (a) If the ideal photon rocket is accelerated from rest with a constant acceleration $10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ as seen from a rest frame on the Earth (which may be regarded as an inertial frame), how long does it take until its velocity becomes 0.9 times the speed of light? How far does it travel during this time? Answer the time as a time in the rest frame on the Earth in units of days, and the distance in units of light years.

(b) If the ideal photon rocket is accelerated thereafter by a constant propulsive force $F$ (the same as $F$ in Q2 and Q3) that gives an acceleration of $10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ at departure, how long does it take until its velocity becomes 0.9 times the speed of light? How far does it travel during this time? Answer the time in units of days and the distance in units of light years.

problems.title: Problem 1: Stable configurations of an iceberg floating in the sea
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (80 points)

Stable configurations of an iceberg floating in the sea

There is the expression "the tip of the iceberg": of an iceberg floating in the sea, only about one tenth is above the water surface, and the remaining nine tenths are hidden under the water. What does the hidden part look like? Does it stand vertically, deep into the sea? Or does it lie horizontally near the sea surface?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. An iceberg standing vertically deep in the water (left) and an iceberg lying horizontally (right).

To simplify the problem, we ignore the depth direction and take space to be two-dimensional, considering only motion in a plane parallel to the page. Suppose that a rectangular block of ice of width $W$ and height $H$, elongated vertically $(H>W)$, floats upright as in Fig. 2 or lying on its side as in Fig. 3, and let us examine whether these states are stable, that is, whether the block returns to its original orientation when it is tilted slightly.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Rectangular block of ice floating upright.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Rectangular block of ice floating on its side.

Below, the densities (per unit area) of ice and of water are denoted by $\rho_{\mathrm{ic}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{wa}}$ respectively, the acceleration of gravity by $g$, the specific gravity of ice by $\rho=\dfrac{\rho_{\mathrm{ic}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{wa}}}$, and the mass of the rectangular block of ice by $M=HW\rho_{\mathrm{ic}}$ (Table 1).

Give your answers, as appropriate to the intent of each question, using the symbols of Table 1 and the symbols defined up to that question.

$$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Symbol} & \text{Physical quantity} \\ \hline g & \text{acceleration of gravity} \\ \rho_{\mathrm{wa}} & \text{density of water (per unit area)} \\ \rho_{\mathrm{ic}} & \text{density of ice (per unit area)} \\ \rho & \text{specific gravity of ice } \left(\dfrac{\rho_{\mathrm{ic}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{wa}}}\right) \\ H & \text{height of the iceberg} \\ W & \text{width of the iceberg} \\ M & \text{mass of the iceberg } (HW\rho_{\mathrm{ic}}) \\ (X_0,Y_0) & \text{coordinates of the centre of gravity of the iceberg in the reference state} \\ \theta & \text{tilt angle of the iceberg} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Table 1. Table of the symbols of the physical quantities

First, let us think about buoyancy. The force that a body receives from the surrounding water (or fluid) is called the buoyant force. The magnitude of the buoyant force is equal to the gravitational force that was acting on the displaced water, and its direction is opposite to gravity. This is called Archimedes' principle. The centre of gravity of the displaced water is called the centre of buoyancy, and it can be regarded as the point of application of the buoyant force.

Q1. Explain why "the magnitude of the buoyant force is equal to the gravitational force that was acting on the displaced water". You may ignore the effect of atmospheric pressure.
[Hint] Imagine a thin, light membrane with the same shape as the surface of the body, and consider the balance of the forces acting on the membrane from inside and from outside.

Q2. Suppose that, as in Fig. 2, the rectangular block of ice of width $W$ and height $H$ floats straight upright. In the left diagram of the answer box, show the position of the centre of gravity G of the ice by a black dot (●), and in the right diagram show the position of the centre of buoyancy G$'$ by a white dot (○), and in each diagram represent by arrows the gravitational force and the buoyant force acting on the ice, paying attention to their magnitudes, directions and points of application. Further, find the length $H_1$ of the part submerged below the water surface.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-1-fig4.png

[Editorial note: the two diagrams of the answer box for Q2, reproduced from the official answer sheet (left: for G and the gravitational force; right: for G$'$ and the buoyant force).]

Q3. Similarly, find the length $W_1$ of the part submerged below the water surface when the rectangular block of ice floats lying on its side as in Fig. 3.

The stability of the configuration of a floating iceberg can be determined by examining the potential energy of the system.

First, let us compare the potential energies of the case in which the ice column floats upright and the case in which it floats on its side.

To consider the gravitational potential energy, take the coordinate axes as in Fig. 4, with the origin O on the sea surface. Since the sea is very large, the change in the height of the sea surface caused by the ice displacing water can be ignored.

As the potential energy of the system, we must take into account not only the potential energy of the ice but also the potential energy of the surrounding water. However, the potential energy of the whole of the sea water is enormous, and it also depends on the shape of the sea. We therefore choose a reference state, denote its potential energy by $U_0$, and consider differences from it.

As the reference state, consider the hypothetical state, shown in Fig. 4, in which the ice is in the air and not immersed in the water. Let the coordinates of the centre of gravity G of the ice in the reference state be $(X_0,Y_0)$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-1-fig5.png

Fig. 4. Configuration of the iceberg in the reference state, and the coordinate axes.

First, consider the state in which the rectangular ice column floats upright (Fig. 2). The water displaced when the ice is immersed in the water spreads thinly over the wide sea surface, and the height of the sea surface does not change.

Q4. Express the $y$ coordinate $y_H$ of the centre of gravity of the ice and the $y$ coordinate $y'_H$ of the centre of buoyancy using $H$ and $H_1$.

Q5. Denoting the potential energy of the ice by $U_{\mathrm{ic}}$, express the difference $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ic}}=U_{\mathrm{ic}}-U_{0,\,\mathrm{ic}}$ from the potential energy $U_{0,\,\mathrm{ic}}$ of the ice in the reference state, using the coordinates $y_H$ and $Y_0$ of the centre of gravity of the ice.

Q6. Denoting the potential energy of the water by $U_{\mathrm{wa}}$, express the difference $\Delta U_{\mathrm{wa}}=U_{\mathrm{wa}}-U_{0,\,\mathrm{wa}}$ from the potential energy $U_{0,\,\mathrm{wa}}$ of the water in the reference state, using the coordinate $y'_H$ of the centre of buoyancy.

Q7. From the above results, show that the change $\Delta U_H=U_H-U_0$ of the potential energy $U_H$ of the state floating upright from the potential energy $U_0$ of the reference state is given by

$$\Delta U_H=Mg\left(\frac{1}{2}(1-\rho)H-Y_0\right).$$

Next, consider the state in which the rectangular ice column floats on its side (Fig. 3). Since the considerations so far do not depend on which of $H$ and $W$ is larger, the change $\Delta U_W$ of the potential energy in this case can be obtained immediately using the results so far.

Q8. Find the change $\Delta U_W=U_W-U_0$ of the potential energy of the state floating on its side from the reference state.

Q9. Using these results, find which of the state floating upright and the state floating on its side has the smaller potential energy. The ice is assumed to be elongated vertically, $H>W$.

Now let us discuss the stability of the configuration of the iceberg using the potential energy.

An iceberg spontaneously changes its orientation towards a configuration of smaller potential energy, but conversely it never changes by itself from a configuration of smaller potential energy to one of larger potential energy unless an external force is applied. In particular, an iceberg in a configuration in which the potential energy is a minimum or a local minimum is mechanically stable, because its potential energy always increases for a small change of its orientation.

As on the right of Fig. 5, consider the state tilted by an angle $\theta$ from the state floating upright. Let the potential energy in that state be $U_H(\theta)$. $U_H(0)$ is the potential energy $U_H$ when floating upright, and $U_H(\pi/2)$ is the potential energy $U_W$ when floating on its side. Below, the tilt angle $\theta$ is small and the waterline does not reach the corners of the rectangle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-1-fig6.png

Fig. 5. Ice floating upright (left), and ice hypothetically floating tilted by an angle $\theta$ (right).

[Japanese labels in the figure: 三角形1 = triangle 1; 三角形2 = triangle 2.]

Suppose that the iceberg is tilted slowly. Since the magnitude of the buoyant force must be the same in the tilted state as well, the area of the part of the ice below the sea surface does not depend on the tilt angle $\theta$. Therefore, the areas of the two triangles 1 and 2 marked with ∘ in the right figure are equal. From this we see that the waterline when floating upright and the waterline when floating tilted intersect exactly at each other's midpoints. Take the coordinate axes with this midpoint as the origin O, and let the coordinates of the centre of gravity G of the iceberg when the tilt angle is $\theta$ be $(x_\theta,y_\theta)$, and the coordinates of the centre of buoyancy G$'$ be $(x'_\theta,y'_\theta)$.

Q10. Express the difference $\Delta U_H(\theta)=U_H(\theta)-U_0$ of the potential energy of the system at tilt angle $\theta$ from the reference state, using the $y$ coordinates $y_\theta$, $y'_\theta$, $Y_0$ of the centre of gravity, the centre of buoyancy and the centre of gravity in the reference state.

Q11. Find the coordinates $(x_\theta,y_\theta)$ of the centre of gravity G of the ice when it is tilted by $\theta$.

Next, we want to find the coordinates $(x'_\theta,y'_\theta)$ of the centre of buoyancy G$'$ in this state. They can be expressed using
• the area $S_1$ of triangle 1 and the coordinates $(x_1,y_1)$ of its centre of gravity
• the area $S_2$ of triangle 2 and the coordinates $(x_2,y_2)$ of its centre of gravity
• the area $S$ of the part of the ice below the water surface
and these quantities can easily be found from simple geometrical considerations.

Q12. Find $S_1$, $(x_1,y_1)$, $S_2$, $(x_2,y_2)$ and $S$ defined above.

Q13. Express the coordinates $(x'_\theta,y'_\theta)$ of the centre of buoyancy G$'$ using the quantities defined above and $y'_H$.

Using the above results, $\Delta U_H(\theta)$ found in Q10, expressed with the symbols of Table 1, becomes

$$\Delta U_H(\theta)=MgH\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\rho\right)\cos\theta+\frac{1}{24\rho}\left(\frac{W}{H}\right)^{2}\tan\theta\sin\theta\right)-MgY_0 \qquad (1)$$

Q14. Derive the expression (1) for $\Delta U_H(\theta)$.

Taking the tilt angle $\theta$ to be small ($|\theta|\ll1$) and expanding $\Delta U_H(\theta)$ of Eq. (1) up to second order in $\theta$ ($\theta^2$), one obtains

$$\frac{1}{MgH}\Big(\Delta U_H(\theta)+MgY_0\Big)\fallingdotseq\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\rho\right)+\frac{1}{4}\rho\left(1-\frac{1}{\rho}+\frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{W}{\rho H}\right)^{2}\right)\theta^{2} \qquad (2)$$

Q15. Using the expansions of the trigonometric functions for $|\theta|\ll1$,

$$\sin\theta\fallingdotseq\theta-\frac{1}{6}\theta^3+\cdots,\qquad \cos\theta\fallingdotseq1-\frac{1}{2}\theta^2+\cdots,\qquad \tan\theta\fallingdotseq\theta+\frac{1}{3}\theta^3+\cdots$$

derive the expansion (2) from Eq. (1).

Q16. Using the expansion (2), find the condition for the ice to return to its original position when it is tilted by a small angle from the state floating upright.

Q17. Similarly, find the condition for the ice to return to its original position when it is tilted by a small angle from the state floating on its side.

Q18. What do the two conditions above become when $\rho=0.90$? For vertically elongated ice ($H>W$), discuss the conditions for the stability of ice floating upright and of ice floating on its side, using concrete numerical values to 2 significant figures.

In this problem we examined the stability of a rectangular iceberg standing straight up in a two-dimensional world. In general there are also conditions under which an oblique state is stable, and even if the shape is restricted to a rectangle, finding the stable posture of a floating body with arbitrary specific gravity and aspect ratio is not simple. In the real three-dimensional problem there is also the possibility of rotation in the depth direction, and it is even more complicated.

problems.title: Problem 2: A pendulum of variable length
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (60 points)

A pendulum of variable length

[A] As in Fig. 1, a simple pendulum, consisting of a small bob of mass $m$ hanging from a string of length $\ell_0$, oscillates in a single vertical plane. The angle that the string makes with the vertical is denoted by $\theta$, and the displacement of the bob along the circle from the lowest point by $x$ (both positive to the right). $|\theta|$ is sufficiently small compared with 1, and the approximations $\sin\theta\fallingdotseq\theta$, $\cos\theta\fallingdotseq1-\dfrac{1}{2}\theta^2$ can be made. The mass and the stretching of the string are ignored, and the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity is $g$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1. Denoting time by $t$, when the equation of motion of the bob along the circle is written in the following form, express the force $F$ using $x$.

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=F \qquad (1)$$

Q2. Expressing $x$ in terms of $\theta$, and taking the amplitude of $\theta$ to be $A$ and $\theta=0$ at time $t=0$, find $\theta$ as a function of $t$ from the equation of motion (1).

Q3. Find the kinetic energy $K$ of the bob as a function of $t$.

Q4. Taking the lowest point as the reference, find the potential energy $U$ of the bob as a function of $t$.

Q5. Find the total energy $E=K+U$, and show that $E$ is constant.

Q6. The tension $S$ of the string is the sum of the component of the gravitational force acting on the bob along the direction of the string and the centrifugal force. Show that $S$ can be expressed as the sum of a term that depends on time $t$ and a term that does not depend on $t$, in the form of the following Eq. (2).

$$S(t)=C_0+C_1\cos(2\omega t) \qquad (2)$$

Here, $C_0$, $C_1$, $\omega$ are positive constants. Also express $C_0$, $C_1$, $\omega$ using $m,g,\ell_0,A$.

[B] Suppose that the point of suspension of the simple pendulum of [A] is a small hole, and that the length of the string can be changed through the hole. Let us consider how the oscillation of the simple pendulum changes when the length of the string is changed.

Q7. When the length of the string changes, work is done on the pendulum through the string. When the length of the string is expressed as a function $\ell(t)$ that depends on time $t$, express the work done on the pendulum per unit time (the power) in terms of the length $\ell(t)$ of the string and the tension $S(t)$ of the string.

In general, when the length of the string changes, the tension $S(t)$ of the string differs from Eq. (2). In the following questions, however, we consider the case in which the change in the length of the string is sufficiently small, and you may use Eq. (2) as $S(t)$.

Q8. First, consider the case in which the rate of change of $\ell(t)$ with time is sufficiently small compared with $\omega$. To find the work done on the pendulum in this case, it suffices to ignore the contribution of the second term on the right-hand side of Eq. (2), which oscillates with $\omega$, and to consider only the first term.

(a) Thinking as above, find the work $\Delta W$ done on the pendulum when the length of the string is changed by a small amount $\Delta\ell$. Note that when $\Delta\ell>0$ the string becomes longer.

When the length of the string changes by $\Delta\ell$, the lowest point of the oscillation changes downward by $\Delta\ell$. Therefore, the energy $E$ of the pendulum defined in Q4, with the lowest point as the reference of the potential energy, changes by the following $\Delta E$, obtained by subtracting from $\Delta W$ of Q8(a) the part due to the change of the reference.

$$\Delta E=\Delta W-(-mg\Delta\ell)=\Delta W+mg\Delta\ell$$

(b) When the length of the string changes, the period $T$ of the pendulum also changes to $T+\Delta T$. Show that, to first order in the small quantity $\Delta\ell$, the following relation (3) holds.

$$\frac{\Delta E}{E}+\frac{\Delta T}{T}=0 \qquad (3)$$

Note that, in general, when $|\delta|$ is sufficiently small compared with 1, the approximation $(1+\delta)^\alpha\fallingdotseq1+\alpha\delta$ can be made.

Since the change $(E+\Delta E)(T+\Delta T)-ET$ of the product of the energy $E$ and the period $T$ is, to first order in $\Delta\ell$, approximately expressed as

$$ET\left(1+\frac{\Delta E}{E}+\frac{\Delta T}{T}\right)-ET=ET\left(\frac{\Delta E}{E}+\frac{\Delta T}{T}\right)$$

Eq. (3) means that the product $ET$ is kept constant in this range.

(c) When the length $\ell$ of the string is changed slowly, how does the amplitude $A\ell$ of the pendulum depend on $\ell$?

Q9. Next, suppose that the length of the string changes as follows.

$$\ell(t)=\ell_0-a\sin(\Omega t)$$

Here, $0<a\ll\ell_0$, and $\Omega\,(>0)$ is assumed to be of the same order of magnitude as $\omega$.

(a) Using Eq. (2), find the work done on the pendulum from time 0 to $t$. Note that, unlike the case of Q8, in this case the contribution of the second term on the right-hand side of Eq. (2) cannot be ignored.

(b) Show that when $\Omega=2\omega$, after a sufficiently long time, the energy of the pendulum increases in proportion to $t$.

Shifting the position of one's centre of gravity when "pumping" a swing can be regarded as having the same effect as changing the length of the string in Q9.

problems.title: Problem 3: Homopolar generator and homopolar motor
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (80 points)

Homopolar generator and homopolar motor

In a uniform magnetic field, consider a conducting disc of radius $a$ that rotates with constant angular velocity $\omega$, in the sense shown in Fig. 1, about a rotation axis parallel to the magnetic field. The magnitude of the magnetic flux density is $B$.

A charged particle of charge $q$ located at a distance $r$ from the rotation axis moves with speed $v=\omega r$ in the direction tangent to the circle of radius $r$, and therefore receives a force from the magnetic field. That the charged particle receives a force means that an electromotive force is generated.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1. For a charge $q>0$, find the magnitude and direction of the force that the charged particle receives.

Q2. Explain, on the basis of the fundamental laws, that regardless of the sign of $q$, the potential difference (induced electromotive force) generated in the small interval between the distances $r$ and $r+\mathrm{d}r$ from the rotation axis is expressed as $\omega rB\,\mathrm{d}r$.

Q3. Using the potential difference found in the previous question, derive that the induced electromotive force $\mathcal{E}$ between the centre ($r=0$) and the rim ($r=a$) of the disc is expressed as

$$\mathcal{E}=\frac{1}{2}\omega Ba^2 \qquad (1)$$

Therefore, as in Fig. 2, when a load resistor is connected between the rim of the disc and the conducting central axis, a current flows. In general, the phenomenon in which an induced current is generated by the motion of a conductor in a magnetic field is called homopolar induction, and a generator that makes use of it is called a homopolar generator.

When a steady current $I$ flows through the resistor $R$, electric power is consumed, so in order to keep the angular velocity of the disc at the constant value $\omega$, a moment of force in the sense that rotates it about the central axis must be applied to the disc. Here the magnitude of the moment of force is called the torque. Let us find the torque needed to keep the rotation of the disc constant. Below, the resistances of the disc, the wires and the central axis can be ignored, and the current on the disc is assumed to flow radially and uniformly in all directions from the centre towards the rim. Then the current flowing from the centre towards the rim through a small arc of length $\mathrm{d}s$ on the concentric circle at distance $r$ from the centre is $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}s}{2\pi r}I$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q4. A magnetic field parallel to the rotation axis and pointing upward is applied to the disc, and a magnetic force acts on the current. Explain, on the basis of the fundamental laws, that the magnetic force acting on the current in the small area $\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}r$ on the disc is parallel to the tangent of the concentric circle and opposite to the sense of rotation, and that its magnitude is expressed as

$$\frac{IB}{2\pi r}\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}r \qquad (2)$$

Q5. The torque of the magnetic force acting on the small area is expressed as

$$\frac{IB}{2\pi r}\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}r\times r=\frac{IB}{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}r \qquad (3)$$

Show that the torque acting on the whole disc is expressed by the following equation.

$$N=\frac{1}{2}IBa^2 \qquad (4)$$

Hint: integrate Eq. (3) with respect to $s$ over one full turn of the concentric circle of radius $r$, and then integrate with respect to $r$.

Since this torque tends to stop the rotation of the disc, in order to keep the angular velocity of the disc constant, the torque given by Eq. (4) must be applied in the sense of rotation.

Suppose that at a point at distance $r$ from the centre of the disc a force $F$ is applied in the direction tangent to the concentric circle of radius $r$, giving the torque $N=rF$. In this case, since the direction of the force is the same as the direction of the velocity of the point of application, the work done by the force per unit time (the power) $P$ is the product $Fv$ of the force and the speed of the point of application. Since $v=\omega r$, the following relation holds.

$$P=Fv=Fr\omega=N\omega$$

Even when the torque is due to many forces, the power of the torque is in general expressed as $N\omega$.

Q6. When the electromotive force $\mathcal{E}$ given by Eq. (1) is generated, the current flowing in the circuit with the load resistance $R$ is $I=\dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R}$. Find the power $N\omega$ of the torque needed in this case to keep the angular velocity of the disc constant. On the other hand, calculate the electric power consumed in the resistor, and confirm that it is equal to $N\omega$ (that the law of conservation of energy holds).

Next, as in Fig. 3, a switch S and a battery of electromotive force $V$ are inserted between the centre and the rim of the conducting disc placed in the uniform magnetic field. As before, the resistances of the disc, the wires and the central axis can be ignored, and the current on the disc is assumed to flow uniformly from the rim towards the centre.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Initially the switch S is "off" and the disc is at rest. When the switch S is turned "on", a current $I=\dfrac{V}{R}$ flows in the circuit and a torque arises that tends to rotate the disc in the sense shown in Fig. 3, but because the disc has inertia, its angular velocity is still 0 at the instant the switch is closed. The magnitude $N_0$ of the initial torque at this time is given, using Eq. (4), by

$$N_0=\frac{1}{2}IBa^2=\frac{VBa^2}{2R} \qquad (5)$$

Receiving this torque, the disc starts to rotate. When the angular velocity of the disc has become $\omega$, the induced electromotive force $\mathcal{E}$ given by Eq. (1) is generated. Since this electromotive force is a back electromotive force that tends to drive a current in the direction opposite to the current due to the electromotive force of the battery, the current flowing in the circuit becomes

$$I=\frac{V-\mathcal{E}}{R} \qquad (6)$$

and the torque rotating the disc becomes

$$N=\frac{1}{2}IBa^2=\frac{V-\mathcal{E}}{2R}\,Ba^2=N_0\left(1-\frac{\omega}{\omega_{\mathrm{m}}}\right) \qquad (7)$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ is

$$\omega_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{2V}{Ba^2} \qquad (8)$$

Here let us give a brief explanation of the equation of motion describing the rotational motion of a rigid body.

First, suppose that a point mass of mass $m$ moves in a plane with speed $v$ on a circular orbit of radius $r$ centred on a fixed point O, receiving a force $F$ in the direction tangent to the orbit (see Fig. 4). A centripetal force $m\dfrac{v^2}{r}$ acts on the point mass, but since $r$ is taken to be constant, the motion in the radial direction is not of concern here. The equation of motion of the point mass in the tangential direction is

$$m\,\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=F \qquad (9)$$

Multiplying both sides of this equation by $r$ and using the relation $v=r\omega$ between the velocity $v$ of the point mass and the angular velocity $\omega$ of the rotation, Eq. (9) becomes

$$mr^2\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=rF \qquad (10)$$

Introducing here $I_{\mathrm{m}}=mr^2$ and $N=rF$, the above equation is expressed as

$$I_{\mathrm{m}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=N \qquad (11)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2021-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

A rigid body can be regarded as a collection of many point masses $m_i$ ($i=1,\,2,\,3,\cdots,\,n$; $n$ is the total number). When a rigid body rotates about a fixed axis, the angular velocities of all the point masses making up the rigid body are equal, so taking the distance from the fixed axis to each point mass to be $r_i$ and setting $I_{\mathrm{m}}=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i{r_i}^2$, Eq. (11) can be applied. However, when a tangential force $F_i$ acts on each point mass, the torque is $N=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_iF_i$.

$I_{\mathrm{m}}$ is called the moment of inertia (do not confuse it with the current $I$). Eq. (11) is the equation of motion describing the rotational motion of a rigid body.

For a uniform disc of radius $a$ and mass $M$ rotating about an axis through its centre perpendicular to the plane of the disc, it can be calculated that its moment of inertia is given by the following equation.

$$I_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{1}{2}Ma^2 \qquad (12)$$

Let us also consider the kinetic energy of a rotating rigid body. When a rigid body rotates with angular velocity $\omega$, its kinetic energy is expressed, using the moment of inertia $I_{\mathrm{m}}$, as

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i{v_i}^2&=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i(\omega r_i)^2=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i{r_i}^2\right)\omega^2\\&=\frac{1}{2}I_{\mathrm{m}}\omega^2\end{aligned} \qquad (13)$$

Now, letting the moment of inertia of the conducting disc of Fig. 3 be $I_{\mathrm{m}}$, since the torque acting on the disc is given by Eq. (7), the rotational motion of the disc is described by the following equation.

$$I_{\mathrm{m}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t}=N_0\left(1-\frac{\omega}{\omega_{\mathrm{m}}}\right) \qquad (14)$$

Here there is no mechanical resistance to the rotational motion, such as friction at the rotation axis of the disc or friction at the contact between the rim of the disc and the electrode.

Q7. Taking $t=0$ at the instant the disc starts to rotate, the solution of the equation of motion (14) is expressed, using a constant $\tau$ (the Greek letter tau), as

$$\omega(t)=\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\right) \qquad (15)$$

Express the constant $\tau$ using $I_{\mathrm{m}}$, $N_0$, $\omega_{\mathrm{m}}$.
