The torque of the rotor is maximum at rest and decreases as the elevator starts to rise and its speed increases. After some time, the rise of the elevator could be regarded as uniform motion.

Q13 Express the speed of the elevator when it rises at constant velocity using whichever of $\mathit{\Omega}, T_0, k, a, M, g$ are needed.

Q14 How should the reduction ratio $k$ be set to maximize the power of the elevator when it rises at constant velocity? Express it using whichever of $T_0, a, M, g$ are needed.

4 Generation of the rotating magnetic field and control of the induction motor

We examine the power-supply part of the induction motor that generates the rotating magnetic field. As in Fig. 6, to an AC power supply of angular frequency $\mathit{\Omega}$ are connected two identical coils of self-inductance $L$ whose resistance can be ignored (coil 1 and coil 2), a resistor of resistance $R$, a capacitor of capacitance $C$, and a switch SW (conducting on the terminal 1 side). The two coils are placed on the $x$ axis (coil 1) and on the $y$ axis (coil 2) respectively, and in the region near the origin the magnetic fields produced by the two coils are superposed.

Let the voltage of the AC power supply at time $t$ be $V(t) = V_0\cos\mathit{\Omega}t$, and let the currents flowing in coil 1 and coil 2 be $I_1(t), I_2(t)$ respectively (the positive directions are the directions of the arrows in Fig. 6). The apparatus is adjusted so that the $x, y$ components of the magnetic flux density in the region near the origin are, with a positive constant $D$,

$$B_x(t) = DI_1(t), \quad B_y(t) = DI_2(t) \qquad (8)$$

The purpose of this apparatus is to create the magnetic field (2) rotating near the origin, so let us set $L, C, R$ so that the currents $I_1(t), I_2(t)$ satisfy

$$I_1(t) = \frac{B}{D}\cos\mathit{\Omega}t, \quad I_2(t) = \frac{B}{D}\sin\mathit{\Omega}t \qquad (9)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

[Labels in Fig. 6: コイル1 = coil 1; コイル2 = coil 2.]

Q15 The current $I_2(t)$ is equal to the current flowing in a circuit in which only coil 2 is connected to the AC power supply. Because of the coil, the phase of the current lags the phase of the voltage by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and the amplitude ratio of current and voltage is determined by the reactance $\mathit{\Omega}L$ of the coil. Express the current $I_2(t)$ using whichever of $V_0, \mathit{\Omega}, L, t$ are needed. Express the $L$ needed to satisfy the second equation of condition (9) using whichever of $B, V_0, D, \mathit{\Omega}$ are needed.

Q16 The current $I_1(t)$ is equal to the current flowing in a circuit in which a capacitor, a resistor and a coil are connected in series to the AC power supply. From condition (9), it suffices to make the phase of the current $I_1(t)$ equal to the phase of the voltage and its amplitude the same as the amplitude of $I_2(t)$. To bring the phase of the current $I_1(t)$ into line with the voltage, the effects of the reactance $\dfrac{1}{\mathit{\Omega}C}$ of the capacitor and the reactance $\mathit{\Omega}L$ of the coil should cancel each other, so that the phase lead due to the capacitor and the phase lag due to the coil cancel. Express $C$ and $R$ each using whichever of $L, \mathit{\Omega}$ are needed.

When the torque needed for the work suddenly increases, the induction motor responds by lowering its angular velocity of rotation so as to increase its torque, but this can be a problem in some cases. For the control of the induction motor, consider a method of varying the voltage of the AC power supply in Fig. 6.

Q17 When the required torque suddenly becomes $\alpha$ times as large, by what factor should the AC supply voltage be changed immediately so that the angular velocity of the rotor does not change?

Q18 If, while the motor is rotating, the switch SW in Fig. 6 is switched to the opposite terminal 2 side, the structure of the circuit changes. Stating explicitly how the currents flowing in the two coils change compared with the terminal 1 case, and how the rotating magnetic field produced by the coils changes, describe qualitatively the subsequent operation of the motor.

Owing to recent technological innovation in power electronics, it has become easy to change the frequency of alternating current. The applications of the induction motor, whose reference for the rotation rate is the supply frequency, have expanded dramatically, and with its features of stable long-duration operation owing to its simple structure, the range of situations in which it is used keeps increasing.

problems.title: Problem 3: Aberration of light — observational proof of the Earth's orbital motion
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (75 points)

Aberration of light — observational proof of the Earth's orbital motion

1 Prologue: aberration of light, discovered in the search for parallax

As a way of directly proving the correctness of Copernicus's heliocentric theory (1543), the detection of the parallax produced by the Earth's orbital motion was considered. Parallax is the difference between the directions of an object point seen from two different positions. Now let the position vector of the Sun with a certain star as starting point be $\overrightarrow{d}$, the position vector of the Earth be $\overrightarrow{d'}$, and the position vector of the Earth with the Sun as starting point be $\overrightarrow{a}$; let $\theta$ be the angle between $\overrightarrow{a}$ and $-\overrightarrow{d}$, and $\theta'$ the angle between $\overrightarrow{a}$ and $-\overrightarrow{d'}$ (see the left diagram of Fig. 1). Then the angular difference $\theta'-\theta$ is the parallax.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Conceptual diagrams of (left) parallax and (right) aberration. In both diagrams, $\theta$ represents the true direction of the star seen from the rest frame, and $\theta'$ the apparent direction seen from the moving Earth.

Q1 Consider the triangle in the left diagram of Fig. 1.

(a) Using, for example, the law of sines, express the ratio of $\sin(\theta'-\theta)$ to $\sin\theta'$ in terms of $d = |\overrightarrow{d}|$ and $a = |\overrightarrow{a}|$.

(b) Making use of, for example, the addition theorem for sin, express $\tan\theta'$ in terms of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, $a$ and $d$.

(c) Making use of, for example, the approximation $\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta'} \fallingdotseq \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} - \dfrac{(\theta'-\theta)}{\sin^2\theta}$ for $|\theta'-\theta| \ll 1$, express $\theta'-\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$, $a$ and $d$.

Tycho Brahe in the 16th century carried out the most precise and extensive observations of his time, but even he could not detect parallax however precise his observations, and so he was sceptical of the heliocentric theory. From the analysis of the observational records left by Tycho Brahe, Kepler found the three laws of planetary motion (1609–19), and even after Newton gave a theoretical explanation of these laws (1687), many attempts to detect parallax were made, but none succeeded.

Meanwhile, James Bradley and Samuel Molyneux detected a tiny variation from measurements of the position of Gamma Draconis ($\gamma$ Dra), carried out in 1725–27 with the aim of detecting parallax. However, the way it moved was different from that expected from parallax. Bradley gave the theoretical interpretation that the variation was a phenomenon, now called aberration of light, in which the apparent position of a star on the celestial sphere varies, again, owing to the Earth's orbital motion; this gave the heliocentric theory its first direct proof by observation.

Incidentally, the detection of parallax was first achieved by Friedrich Bessel in 1838, more than 100 years after the detection of aberration. The reason it took so long is that the distances to the stars were greater than assumed and the parallax was very small.

Now, Bradley's interpretation was as follows. Just as one's face gets wet when walking quickly even if the rain falls vertically, if the Earth is moving, light must come in from the front. So consider light from a distant star received on the Earth, which orbits the Sun at rest. Denote the velocity of the Earth relative to the rest frame by $\overrightarrow{v}$, and the velocity of light in the rest frame by $\overrightarrow{c}$. According to Bradley's way of thinking, the velocity of light observed on the Earth is

$$\overrightarrow{c'} = \overrightarrow{c} - \overrightarrow{v}$$

Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\overrightarrow{v}$ and $-\overrightarrow{c}$, and $\theta'$ the angle between $\overrightarrow{v}$ and $-\overrightarrow{c'}$ (see the right diagram of Fig. 1 on the previous page). $\theta$ corresponds to the true angular position of the star (that is, the position seen by an observer in the rest frame), and $\theta'$ corresponds to the apparent position of the star seen from the moving Earth.

Q2 Consider the triangle in the right diagram of Fig. 1 on the previous page.

(a) Express the ratio of $\sin(\theta'-\theta)$ to $\sin\theta'$ in terms of $v = |\overrightarrow{v}|$ and $c = |\overrightarrow{c}|$.

(b) Express $\tan\theta'$ in terms of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, $v$ and $c$.

(c) Making use of, for example, the approximation $\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta'} \fallingdotseq \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} - \dfrac{(\theta'-\theta)}{\sin^2\theta}$ for $|\theta'-\theta| \ll 1$, express $\theta'-\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$, $v$ and $c$.

In this way Bradley derived that $\theta'$ and $\theta$ differ because of the Earth's orbital velocity.

2 How can annual parallax and annual aberration be distinguished?

As can be seen from the results of Q1 and Q2, the apparent direction of a star depends on the Earth's position vector in the case of parallax, and on the Earth's velocity vector in the case of aberration. When both vectors point in the same direction, as in Fig. 1, it cannot be determined whether the variation in the apparent direction of the star is parallax or aberration. However, if the Earth orbits the Sun, the direction of the Earth's position vector $\overrightarrow{a}$ with the Sun as starting point can be recognized as an azimuth angle, and moreover it differs in direction from the velocity vector $\overrightarrow{v}$ of the Earth's orbital motion, so it is possible to distinguish whether the change in apparent direction is a variation due to parallax or a variation due to aberration. To show this, in what follows we assume the orbit is circular and find the change in the apparent direction of the star concretely as a function of time, for parallax and for aberration.

Consider a Cartesian coordinate system with the position of the Sun as the origin, the Earth's orbital plane as the $x$-$y$ plane, and the $z$ axis perpendicular to it. Let $\overrightarrow{n} = -\dfrac{\overrightarrow{d}}{d} = -\dfrac{\overrightarrow{c}}{c}$ be the unit vector pointing from the origin towards the observed star; take the direction of the vector obtained by projecting it onto the Earth's orbital plane as the $y$ axis direction, and take the $x$ axis in the orbital plane perpendicular to the $y$ axis (see Fig. 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2. The Sun is the origin and the Earth's orbital plane is the $x$-$y$ plane.

[Labels in Fig. 2: 天球面の接平面 = tangent plane of the celestial sphere; 地球の公転面 = Earth's orbital plane.]

Expressed in Cartesian components, $\overrightarrow{n}$ is

$$(n_x, n_y, n_z) = (0,\, \cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)$$

where here $\theta$ is the angle between $\overrightarrow{n}$ and the $y$ axis (see Fig. 2).

Treating the Earth's orbit as a circle, and taking $t = 0$ as the time when the Earth is on the positive side of the $x$ axis, the position vector $\overrightarrow{a}$ of the Earth at time $t$ is

$$(a_x, a_y, a_z) = a(\cos\mathit{\Omega}t,\, \sin\mathit{\Omega}t,\, 0)$$

Here $\mathit{\Omega}$ is the angular velocity of the orbital motion, and $\mathit{\Omega}t$ is the azimuth angle measured from the positive side of the $x$ axis. The orbital velocity vector $\overrightarrow{v}$ is the time derivative of $\overrightarrow{a}$, and its direction is tangential to the orbit.

2.1 Annual parallax

To consider the apparent motion of the star on the celestial sphere due to parallax, let $\dfrac{v}{c} \ll \dfrac{a}{d} \ll 1$. Then the unit vector $\overrightarrow{n'} = -\dfrac{\overrightarrow{d'}}{d'}$ pointing in the apparent direction of the star seen from the Earth at position vector $\overrightarrow{a}$ is

$$\overrightarrow{n'} = \frac{\overrightarrow{n} - \left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{a}}{d}\right)}{\left|\overrightarrow{n} - \left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{a}}{d}\right)\right|} \fallingdotseq \overrightarrow{n} - \left\{\frac{\overrightarrow{a}}{d} - \left(\overrightarrow{n}\cdot\frac{\overrightarrow{a}}{d}\right)\overrightarrow{n}\right\}$$

Consider the $X$-$Y$ plane perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{n}$, tangent to the celestial sphere; the $X$ axis is taken parallel to the $x$ axis and the $Y$ axis perpendicular to it (see Fig. 2). If $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_x}$, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_y}$, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_z}$ are the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes respectively, and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_X}$, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_Y}$ the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $X$, $Y$ axes respectively, they are related as follows:

$$\begin{cases} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_X} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_x} \\[1ex] \overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_Y} = -\sin\theta\,\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_y} + \cos\theta\,\overrightarrow{\mathrm{e}_z} \end{cases}$$

Q3 Express the $X$ component and the $Y$ component of the difference between the apparent direction $\overrightarrow{n'}$ of the star due to the position vector $\overrightarrow{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{n}$,

$$\overrightarrow{n'} - \overrightarrow{n} = -\left\{\frac{\overrightarrow{a}}{d} - \left(\overrightarrow{n}\cdot\frac{\overrightarrow{a}}{d}\right)\overrightarrow{n}\right\}$$

each as a function of time $t$.

2.2 Annual aberration

To consider the apparent motion of a star on the celestial sphere due to aberration alone, the star in question is assumed to be so distant that its parallax cannot be detected. Also, the aberration due to the Earth's rotation is assumed to be negligible. Denoting the Earth's orbital velocity vector (whose direction is tangential to the orbit) by $\overrightarrow{v}$ and assuming $\dfrac{v}{c} \ll 1$, the unit vector $\overrightarrow{n'} = -\dfrac{\overrightarrow{c'}}{c'}$ pointing in the apparent direction of the star seen from the orbiting Earth is

$$\overrightarrow{n'} = \frac{\overrightarrow{n} + \left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{v}}{c}\right)}{\left|\overrightarrow{n} + \left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{v}}{c}\right)\right|} \fallingdotseq \overrightarrow{n} + \left\{\frac{\overrightarrow{v}}{c} - \left(\overrightarrow{n}\cdot\frac{\overrightarrow{v}}{c}\right)\overrightarrow{n}\right\}$$

Q4 Express the $X$ component and the $Y$ component of the difference between the apparent direction $\overrightarrow{n'}$ of the star due to the orbital velocity vector $\overrightarrow{v}$ and $\overrightarrow{n}$,

$$\overrightarrow{n'} - \overrightarrow{n} = \frac{\overrightarrow{v}}{c} - \left(\overrightarrow{n}\cdot\frac{\overrightarrow{v}}{c}\right)\overrightarrow{n}$$

each as a function of time $t$.

From the results of Q3 and Q4, it can be seen that the time variation of the apparent position of a star due to aberration accompanying the Earth's annual orbital motion and the time variation of the apparent position of the star due to parallax differ in phase. From the phase of the time variation, Bradley concluded that the time variation of the apparent position of Gamma Draconis was due not to parallax but to aberration. Furthermore, the agreement of the $Y$ component of the annual aberration of several stars with different $\theta$ with the result of Q4 served as verification of Bradley's interpretation.

Q5 The amplitude (half the difference between the maximum and minimum values) of the $X$ component of the observed annual aberration is 20.5 seconds of arc (1 degree is 3600 seconds of arc). From this observational fact, find the distance between the Earth and the Sun, as the time (in seconds) light takes to propagate over that distance, to 3 significant figures. Note that the orbital speed $v$ is determined by the radius $a$ of the circular orbit and the orbital period.

In this way Bradley succeeded in measuring the Earth–Sun distance with high precision, as the propagation time of light.

3 Considering aberration on the basis of the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light"

Aberration is often explained by analogy with the everyday experience that the direction of falling rain seen by a person at rest differs from that seen by a moving person, and that the way it differs depends on the speed of the moving person. In fact, the interpretation and explanation by Bradley described in the preceding sections was of this kind. In this explanation by analogy, just as the speed of the rain falling on a person at rest differs from that of the rain falling on a moving person, the speed of light would differ depending on how the observer moves. However, this contradicts the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light", one of the important fundamentals of modern physics.

The essential difference between light waves and sound waves is that, whereas for sound waves there always exists some medium, such as air, in which they propagate, for light waves there is no medium in which they propagate. However, before the 20th century, most physicists found it hard to accept the concept of a wave propagating without a medium, and they assumed that some medium existed for the propagation of light waves too. In fact, various experiments were performed to prove the existence of a medium for the propagation of light waves, but none of them achieved such a proof.

In 1905, Einstein, without assuming the existence of a medium for the propagation of light (electromagnetic waves), constructed the "special theory of relativity" on the basis of the principle that "the fundamental laws of physics take the same form in all inertial frames". As a direct consequence of this principle, the so-called "principle of the constancy of the speed of light", that "the speed of light in vacuum is the same in all inertial frames", is derived.

In the following questions, let us derive some results of the special theory of relativity from this "principle of the constancy of the speed of light", and see how the aberration of a star is obtained using them.

3.1 Relativity of time

Consider an experiment in which a light ray propagating in vacuum is reflected by a mirror at distance $l$ from the light source. As in the left diagram of Fig. 3, in the laboratory frame in which the light source is at rest (hereafter called the $S$ frame), the time $t$ needed for the light ray to go from the source to the mirror and back is $t = \dfrac{2l}{c}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Path of light propagating in vacuum. Left: the experiment in the $S$ frame. Right: the same experiment observed in the $S'$ frame.

[Labels in Fig. 3: S系 = $S$ frame; S′系 = $S'$ frame; 反射鏡 = mirror; 光源 = light source.]

Next, as in the right diagram of Fig. 3, let us observe the same light source and mirror from a frame in uniform motion (hereafter called the $S'$ frame) moving with constant velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ relative to the $S$ frame. Here the direction of $\overrightarrow{v}$ is perpendicular to the light ray in the $S$ frame. Let $t'$ be the time needed in the $S'$ frame for the light to travel from the source to the mirror and come back. In the $S'$ frame, during this time interval the light source moves a distance $vt'$ in parallel (with $-\overrightarrow{v}$). The vertical distance $l$ from the light source to the mirror is the same in both frames.

Q6 Express the length $L$ of the round-trip path of the light in the $S'$ frame in terms of $l$, $v$ and $t'$.

Q7 According to the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, $t' = \dfrac{L}{c}$. By substituting the $L$ found in the previous question, express $\gamma$, when written as $t' = \gamma t$, in terms of $v$ and $c$.

3.2 Relativity of distance

As in Fig. 4, consider the case where the above experimental apparatus is rotated by 90 degrees and the same experiment is performed with the direction of propagation of the light parallel to $\overrightarrow{v}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Light propagating in vacuum. Left: the experiment in the $S$ frame. Right: the same experiment observed in the $S'$ frame.

[Labels in Fig. 4: S系 = $S$ frame; S′系 = $S'$ frame; 光源 = light source; 反射鏡 = mirror.]

As before, let $l$ be the distance between the light source and the mirror in the $S$ frame. Also, let $l'$ be the distance between the light source and the mirror in the $S'$ frame. In the $S'$ frame, both the mirror and the light source appear to move with constant velocity $-\overrightarrow{v}$ (because both are at rest in the $S$ frame, and $-\overrightarrow{v}$ is the velocity of the $S$ frame relative to the $S'$ frame). In the $S'$ frame, let $t'_a$ be the time needed for light to reach the mirror from the light source. The propagation distance of the light is $l' - vt'_a$.

Considering that, by the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light", light travels with speed $c$ in the $S'$ frame as well, $t'_a$ is

$$t'_a = \frac{l'-vt'_a}{c}$$

which means that the following holds:

$$t'_a = \frac{l'}{c+v}$$

Q8 In the $S'$ frame, let $t'_b$ be the time needed for light to return from the mirror to the light source. Express $t'_b$ in terms of $l'$, $c$ and $v$.

Q9 Express the time $t' = t'_a + t'_b$ for light to go from the light source to the mirror and return to the light source again, in terms of $\dfrac{l'}{c}$ and $\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$.

Q10 As derived in Q7, the progress of time $t'$ in the $S'$ frame is related to the progress of time $t$ in the $S$ frame by $t' = \gamma t$. Taking this into account, express $l'$ in terms of $l$ and $\gamma$.

3.3 Relativity of simultaneity

As in Fig. 5, two screens A and B are placed a distance $l$ apart, and a light source is at the midpoint between them. These devices are at rest in the $S$ frame. The $S'$ frame moves relative to the $S$ frame with constant velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ parallel to the apparatus. The times at which a light pulse emitted from the light source at time zero reaches A and B are measured in each of the two frames $S$ and $S'$. Observed in the $S$ frame, all the devices are at rest and the light source is at the midpoint, so the light reaches A and B at the same time. On the other hand, what happens when the same experiment is observed in the $S'$ frame moving with velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig5.png

Fig. 5. Light propagating in vacuum. Left: the experiment in the $S$ frame. Right: the same experiment observed in the $S'$ frame.

[Labels in Fig. 5: S系 = $S$ frame; S′系 = $S'$ frame; 光源 = light source.]

The distance $l'$ between the two screens in the $S'$ frame differs from the distance $l$ in the $S$ frame, but the light source is still located midway between the two screens. Furthermore, the two screens appear to move with the same velocity $-\overrightarrow{v}$. In the $S'$ frame, let $t'_{\mathrm{A}}$ be the time needed for the light pulse to reach A from the light source. Since the light pulse travels a distance $\dfrac{l'}{2} - vt'_{\mathrm{A}}$ at the speed of light $c$,

$$t'_{\mathrm{A}} = \frac{l'}{2(c+v)}$$

Q11 In the $S'$ frame, let $t'_{\mathrm{B}}$ be the time needed for the pulse to reach B from the light source. Express $t'_{\mathrm{B}}$ in terms of $l'$, $c$ and $v$.

In the $S$ frame the pulse reaches A and B at the same time. However, in the $S'$ frame, as is clear from the result of the question above, $t'_{\mathrm{A}} < t'_{\mathrm{B}}$, so the pulse reaches A before arriving at B. In other words, even if events occur simultaneously at two separated points in one inertial frame, in another inertial frame moving in the direction of the mutual displacement of those events, the times at which the two events occur are not the same.

Q12 Derive that the time difference between the two events in the $S'$ frame, $\mathit{\Delta}t' = t'_{\mathrm{B}} - t'_{\mathrm{A}}$, is $\dfrac{\gamma vl}{c^2}$.

3.4 Velocity addition law

Let us continue to consider the setting of Fig. 5 on the previous page. At time $t$ in the $S$ frame, the origin of the $x'$ axis of the $S'$ frame is at distance $vt$ from the origin of the $x$ axis of the $S$ frame. Consider a point located on the $x'$ axis of the $S'$ frame. Seen from the $S'$ frame, the $S$ frame moves with constant speed $v$ in the $-x'$ direction, so the distance between the origin of the $S'$ frame and that point in the $S$ frame differs from the distance in the $S'$ frame. That is, noting the relation obtained in Q10, the coordinate $x$ in the $S$ frame is related to the coordinate $x'$ in the $S'$ frame by $x = vt + \dfrac{x'}{\gamma}$. Rewriting,

$$x' = \gamma(x-vt) \qquad (1)$$

Between the two inertial frames there is no motion in the $y$ and $z$ directions, and there is no contraction of lengths perpendicular to the $x$ axis, so the following hold:

$$y' = y \qquad (2)$$

$$z' = z \qquad (3)$$

By the relation between the rates of time in the $S$ and $S'$ frames obtained in Q7, if the elapsed time in the $S$ frame is $t$, the elapsed time in the $S'$ frame is $\gamma t$. Even for simultaneous events at two separated points in the $S$ frame, there is a time difference in the $S'$ frame, as shown in Q12. That is, the elapsed time $t$ at a point at distance $x$ from the origin on the $x$ axis in the $S$ frame becomes the elapsed time $\gamma t - \dfrac{\gamma vx}{c^2}$ in the $S'$ frame:

$$t' = \gamma\left(t - \frac{vx}{c^2}\right) \qquad (4)$$

Consider a particle moving in the $S$ frame with constant velocity (less than the speed of light) $\overrightarrow{u} = (u_x, u_y, u_z)$. If the particle is at the origin at time $t = 0$, its position at time $t$ is

$$(x,\, y,\, z) = (u_x t,\, u_y t,\, u_z t) \qquad (5)$$

The motion of the same particle is observed in the $S'$ frame. As can be confirmed from equation (4), the particle is at the origin of the $S'$ frame at $t' = 0$. Hence the position of the particle in the $S'$ frame at time $t'$ is

$$(x',\, y',\, z') = (u'_x t',\, u'_y t',\, u'_z t') \qquad (6)$$

Q13 From the relations (1)–(6), express the components $(u'_x, u'_y, u'_z)$ of the velocity $\overrightarrow{u'}$ in the $S'$ frame in terms of the components $(u_x, u_y, u_z)$ of the velocity $\overrightarrow{u}$ in the $S$ frame, $\gamma$, $v$ and $c$ (velocity transformation law).

3.5 Derivation of aberration based on the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light"

Consider light travelling from a star to an observer located at the origin of the inertial frame $S$. Let the velocity of the light be $\overrightarrow{c}$. $|\overrightarrow{c}|$ is the speed of light in vacuum $c$. As shown in the left diagram of Fig. 6 on the next page, $\overrightarrow{c}$ lies in the $x$-$z$ plane, and its direction makes an angle $\theta$ with the $-x$ direction. $c_x = -c\cos\theta$ and $c_z = -c\sin\theta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6. Left: direction from the star to the observer in the $S$ frame. Right: direction from the same star to the observer in the $S'$ frame.

[Labels in Fig. 6: S系 = $S$ frame; S′系 = $S'$ frame.]

Suppose a second observer, moving with velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ in the $x$ direction relative to the first observer, observes the same star. Let $\overrightarrow{c'}$ be the velocity of the light in the inertial frame $S'$ of the second observer. By the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light", $|\overrightarrow{c'}| = c$. As shown in the right diagram of Fig. 6, $\overrightarrow{c'}$ lies in the $x'$-$z'$ plane, and its direction makes an angle $\theta'$ with the $-x'$ direction. $c'_x = -c\cos\theta'$ and $c'_z = -c\sin\theta'$.

Q14 Using the velocity transformation law derived in Q13, express $\tan\theta'$ in terms of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, $\dfrac{v}{c}$ and $\gamma$.

The result derived in Q14 is the aberration formulated on the basis of the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light". However, since the magnitude of the Earth's orbital velocity is $v = 3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the corresponding value of $\gamma$ differs by only $5\times10^{-9}$ from the value $1.0$ for $v = 0$, and numerically it is practically indistinguishable from the value derived by Bradley. The significance of the treatment here lies in having formulated aberration consistently with the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, a fundamental principle of modern physics.

4 Epilogue: if the motion were fast

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig7.png

Fig. 7. Comparison of the result of Q2 (left) and the result of Q14 (right) against the angle of incidence $\theta$ in the rest frame.

The left diagram of Fig. 7 shows $\theta'$ found in Q2 (b), and the right diagram shows $\theta'$ found in Q14, against the angle of incidence $\theta$ in the rest frame, with $\dfrac{v}{c}$ as a parameter. According to the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, when $\dfrac{v}{c}$ becomes as large as $0.9$, light in the range $\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ falls within the range $\theta' < \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and even light from behind ($\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{2}$) appears to the observer as light coming from near straight ahead in the direction of motion. For an observer moving at a speed close to the speed of light through an isotropic radiation field, the radiation appears strongly concentrated in the direction of motion; conversely, even if light (electromagnetic waves) is emitted isotropically from a source moving at a speed close to the speed of light, seen from the rest frame it appears as emission strongly concentrated in the direction of motion.

problems.title: Problem 4: Astronomical X-ray observation with the XRISM satellite
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (75 points)

Astronomical X-ray observation with the XRISM satellite

Astronomy has developed dramatically along with the development of observational techniques. In addition to observations with visible light and radio waves, X-ray observation began in earnest in the 1960s, and celestial objects emitting strong X-rays, such as neutron stars and black holes, as well as the hot ionized gas (plasma) filling clusters of galaxies, were discovered. Since X-rays are strongly absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere, observations must be made using rockets or artificial satellites. Japan has launched X-ray astronomy satellites such as "Hakucho", "Ginga", "Tenma", "Asuka" and "Suzaku", and has contributed greatly to the development of X-ray astronomy.

The Japanese X-ray astronomy satellite XRISM (X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission), launched in 2023, observes X-rays emitted from celestial objects using two X-ray telescopes named Xtend and Resolve. Xtend is an imaging device with an element called a CCD (Charge-Coupled Device) placed at its focal plane. Resolve is a spectroscopic device with a detector capable of precisely measuring the energy of X-ray photons placed at its focal plane. With these it is possible to determine elemental compositions and to determine the velocity of a radiation source from the Doppler shift.

Below we treat the principles of these devices and astronomical X-ray observation using line spectra.

1 X-ray mirror

As in Fig. 1, suppose X-rays are incident at an angle $\alpha$ to the surface on a material with a flat surface placed in vacuum. Let the refractive index of this material be $n$. The refractive index for visible light is larger than 1, but it is known that for X-rays the refractive index is slightly smaller than 1. Since the refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum $c$ to the speed at which a surface of constant phase of the light wave propagates in the material (phase velocity), when the refractive index is smaller than 1 the phase velocity is larger than $c$. However, the speed at which energy and information are actually transmitted is smaller than $c$, and there is no contradiction with relativity. Bragg reflection is not considered.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[Label in Fig. 1: X線 = X-rays.]

Q1 Find the condition for X-rays incident at an angle $\alpha$ to the surface to be totally reflected at the surface of this material.

Q2 Let $n = 1-\beta$, with $\beta \ll 1$ and $\alpha > 0$. Using the following approximation, express the maximum value $\alpha_{\max}$ of $\alpha$ for which X-rays are totally reflected, in terms of $\beta$.

For $|x| \ll 1$, $\cos x \fallingdotseq 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$

A visible-light telescope collects light by combining lenses and mirrors, but for X-rays the reflectivity for light incident on a mirror from the front (normal incidence) is small, and it is hard to focus X-rays by making them incident from the front. Therefore X-ray telescopes adopt a method in which X-rays are made incident obliquely and are collected using total reflection.

The XRISM satellite uses a multilayer mirror in which many thin aluminium mirrors are nested axisymmetrically (concentrically). In each layer, as in Fig. 2, X-rays incident parallel to the central axis are totally reflected twice, by the conical mirror 1 and mirror 2, and are thereby focused at the focal point on the central axis.

As shown in Fig. 3, the angles that the incident X-rays make with the surfaces of mirror 1 and mirror 2 are equal, both being $\alpha$. The central axis is taken as the $x$ axis and the focal point as the origin. Let the $x$ coordinate of the first reflection point be $x_1$ and its distance from the axis $r_1$, and the $x$ coordinate of the second reflection point be $x_1 - d$ and its distance from the axis $r_2$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[Labels in Figs. 2 and 3: ミラー1 = mirror 1; ミラー2 = mirror 2; X線 = X-rays; 内側の層のミラー = mirror of the inner layer; 焦点 = focal point; 焦点O = focal point O.]

Q3 Express $r_2$ in terms of $r_1$, $d$ and $\alpha$.

Q4 Express $x_1$ in terms of $r_1$, $d$ and $\alpha$. For $0 < \alpha \ll 1$, use the approximations $\sin\alpha \fallingdotseq \alpha$, $\cos\alpha \fallingdotseq 1$, $\tan\alpha \fallingdotseq \alpha$.

Q5 In the XRISM satellite, $d = 0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ and $x_1 = 5.6\,\mathrm{m}$, and the distance from the central axis of the reflection point of the outer mirror 1 is $r_1 = 0.22\,\mathrm{m}$. Find $\alpha$ of the outer mirror in degrees ($^\circ$).

Here we found $\alpha$ for the outer mirror, but for the inner mirrors too the value of $\alpha$ can be determined so that X-rays totally reflected twice are collected at the focal point.

2 X-ray imaging device Xtend

A device that images, with a CCD, the X-rays collected by the X-ray mirror. When an X-ray is absorbed in the CCD, an electron is ejected, and a hole is created at the place where this electron was. This set of an electron and a hole is called an electron–hole pair. For each photon of energy $E$ [eV] absorbed in the CCD, $N = \dfrac{E}{3.65\,\mathrm{eV}}$ electron–hole pairs are produced, and this number $N$ is counted.

Q6 The energy of the incident photon can be estimated from the count of electron–hole pairs, but the number of electron–hole pairs produced has an uncertainty of about $\sqrt{N}$. For $E = 10\,\mathrm{keV}$, find the uncertainty in energy due to this uncertainty, in units of eV.

3 High-resolution X-ray spectrometer Resolve

As the X-ray spectrometer, a microcalorimeter of 36 pixels $(6\times6)$ is used. A microcalorimeter is a device that measures the energy of an incident photon by detecting the slight temperature rise caused by absorbing an X-ray. Each pixel consists of a mercury telluride (HgTe) absorber with a square base of side $820\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ and thickness $10\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, as in Fig. 4, and a thermometer using a silicon semiconductor element (thermistor) whose electrical resistance changes greatly when the temperature changes, and it is connected by thin silicon wires to a low-temperature heat reservoir kept at $50\,\mathrm{mK}$. When an X-ray photon is absorbed, the temperature of the absorber rises, but after a sufficiently long time the absorber is cooled down to the temperature of the low-temperature heat reservoir.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4

[Labels in Fig. 4: X線 = X-rays; 吸収体 (HgTe) = absorber (HgTe); シリコン 半導体温度計 = silicon semiconductor thermometer; 50mKに保たれた熱源 = heat reservoir kept at 50 mK.]

Q7 Let the density of HgTe be $\rho$, the volume per pixel $V$, and the specific heat $C$. Find the temperature rise $\mathit{\Delta}T$ when one photon of energy $E$ is absorbed in the absorber. Heat conduction through the wires connecting the pixel to the heat reservoir kept at $50\,\mathrm{mK}$ and heat transport to the thermometer can be neglected.

Q8 For $C = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$ and $\rho = 8.1\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, find the temperature rise of the HgTe due to the absorption of a photon of $E = 10\ \mathrm{keV}$, in units of mK, to 2 significant figures. $1\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Q9 Ion-implanted silicon is used as the thermometer. Since its resistance changes greatly with temperature at low temperatures, this material is sensitive to temperature changes, and temperature differences down to $5.0\ \mathrm{\mu K}$ can be measured. This measurable temperature difference is called the precision of the temperature measurement. If the ability to separate and measure energies (energy resolution) is determined by this precision of the temperature measurement, find the energy resolution at $E = 10\ \mathrm{keV}$ in units of eV, to 2 significant figures.

4 Energy of iron emission lines

By observing the line spectra emitted by ionized elements such as iron and nickel, the XRISM satellite can measure the temperature and velocity of astrophysical plasmas emitting X-rays. A state in which ionization has advanced and only one electron orbits the nucleus can be treated, using the Bohr model, in the same way as the hydrogen atom.

Q10 Suppose an electron of mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}$ and charge $-e$ $(e > 0)$ moves in uniform circular motion with orbital radius $r$ and speed $v$ around a nucleus of positive charge $Q$. In the Bohr model it is assumed that the electron takes only circular orbits satisfying the following condition:

$$m_{\mathrm{e}}vr = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$$

Q13 Express $E_{21}$ in units of keV. If necessary, use the following values: $h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $m_{\mathrm{e}} = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $\epsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$.

The line spectra observed by the XRISM satellite include, besides the above emission lines emitted from hot regions of high ionization, fluorescent iron lines emitted when a non-ionized iron atom absorbs an X-ray and emits an electron, and another electron makes a transition into the energy level that this electron occupied. By precisely measuring the energies of these spectral lines, it has become possible to measure the velocity of the emitting matter more accurately from the wavelength shift due to the Doppler effect.

5 Formation of disk winds

From observations of iron emission lines and absorption lines by the XRISM satellite, the velocity of hot outflows ejected from the central region (nucleus) of a galaxy, which is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its centre, has been measured when the luminosity (energy radiated per unit time) of this region increased.

In the vicinity of the nuclei of active galaxies, absorbers are ionized by strong X-rays and no longer emit visible line spectra, so understanding had not progressed with conventional visible-light observations. X-ray observations by the XRISM satellite have made it possible to observe in detail the distribution and velocities of absorbers in such regions, and research on the activity of galactic nuclei is progressing rapidly.
